- Optional nuance: if the solution claims the thin-ring expression as exact for a finite-thickness torus (uses strict equality and asserts exactness) without the permitted neglect, prefer a stronger flag; if the solution marks it as an approximation (≈) or qualifies with small a/R, do not flag.

rules.title: Do not set V_D = V0 for an ideal threshold diode when I_D = 0 (steady-state/open-circuit)
rules.description: This rule checks for misuse of the ideal threshold-diode model defined by: I_D = 0 for V_D < V0 and V_D = V0 for I_D > 0. In steady-state DC conditions where the series current is zero (e.g., because a capacitor blocks DC or an open-circuit is present), the diode must be OFF; therefore its voltage must be strictly less than V0. The solution must not set the diode drop to the threshold value V0 when simultaneously asserting zero current. The rule flags any instance where: (a) the solution asserts or implies I_D = 0 (e.g., mentions t → ∞, steady state, capacitor is an open circuit, no current flows, or uses V_L = 0 and I_C = 0), and (b) the solution also sets V_D = V0 or treats the diode as a fixed V0 drop in KVL at that same condition (e.g., computes voltages by subtracting V0 from the source). Correct usage: if V_D = V0 is used, the solution must also assert I_D > 0; if I_D = 0 is asserted, then V_D must be < V0 and no fixed V0 drop should be included in KVL. This rule is intended to catch modeling errors where a threshold diode is treated as a constant-voltage drop even when no current flows, such as concluding a final capacitor voltage equals the source minus V0 in a DC steady state with zero series current.

rules.title: Wiley–McLaren time-focusing stationarity and full time-of-flight accounting
rules.description: This rule checks solutions to dual-field TOF mass spectrometer focusing problems for correct use of the Wiley–McLaren first-order time-focusing condition and complete time-of-flight modeling. The solver must: (1) explicitly construct the total arrival time T as a function of the initial creation position x0 (within the source) and system parameters, with T written as a sum/integral of the transit times through each region: first acceleration field, second acceleration field, and the drift region (no implicit assumption of instantaneous acceleration); (2) impose the first-order focusing (stationarity) condition by taking the derivative of the total arrival time with respect to the initial position and setting it to zero at the detector, i.e., dT/dx0 = 0 (equivalently ∂T/∂x0 = 0), and solve for the drift length L; (3) consistently treat small source spread ΔS (x0-variation) via a first-order expansion of T(x0) about a nominal position (e.g., x0 = 0), not by heuristic “balancing” of times. The rule flags solutions that: • determine L by equalizing or ‘balancing’ time differences between regions without deriving T(x0) and enforcing dT/dx0 = 0; • omit or declare negligible the time spent in the first acceleration region while still using post-acceleration velocities (e.g., starting from v0^2 = 2 e E0 S / m and ignoring the finite acceleration time); • include only the drift time’s dependence on ΔS while neglecting the dependence of times in the acceleration regions; • fail to mention or use any stationarity criterion (keywords/notation accepted include dT/dx0 = 0, ∂T/∂x0 = 0, first-order focusing, time focus, Wiley–McLaren). If any of these deficiencies are detected, the solution is flagged as a conceptual error in time focusing.

rules.title: Time-varying magnetic field requires induced E-field; forbid unjustified conservation of mechanical L or kinetic energy
rules.description: This rule flags solutions to problems involving a time-dependent magnetic field (e.g., B increases/decreases over time, 'adiabatically', 'slowly varying', dB/dt ≠ 0) that ignore the induced electric field mandated by Faraday’s law and consequently make unsupported conservation claims. Trigger conditions: the problem or solution mentions B changing with time (keywords such as 'time-dependent B', 'B increases', 'adiabatic', 'slowly', 'dB/dt') and the derivation either (a) uses only the magnetic part of the Lorentz force F = q v × B without the electric term qE, or (b) asserts that speed v or kinetic energy is constant because 'magnetic force does no work', or (c) invokes conservation of mechanical angular momentum L = m r v in a uniform B without addressing torques from the induced E-field, or (d) derives radius scaling (e.g., r ∝ 1/B) by holding v or L constant during B(t) changes. Pass conditions: the solution explicitly accounts for the induced electric field via Faraday’s law (∇×E = −∂B/∂t), discusses its work/torque on the particle, or correctly employs appropriate adiabatic invariants (e.g., magnetic moment μ = m v⊥²/(2B)) to relate v and r during slow B changes; alternatively it provides a quantitative justification for neglecting the induced E (beyond merely 'slowly varying'). Detection heuristics: if 'dB/dt', 'adiabatic', or 'slowly varying B' appear and terms like 'Faraday', 'induced electric field', 'E-field', '∇×E', 'μ (magnetic moment)', or 'adiabatic invariant' are absent while phrases such as 'v is constant', 'no work done by magnetic field', 'conserve angular momentum', 'L = m r v constant', or reliance solely on F = q v × B appear, flag the solution as a modeling error. Rationale: when B(t) changes, an azimuthal E-field is induced that does work and exerts torque; mechanical angular momentum and kinetic energy are generally not conserved.

rules.title: Check one-way vs two-way time-of-flight (factor-of-two) consistency
rules.description: This rule verifies that the relationship between propagation time τ, speed of light c, and path length/range is modeled with the correct one-way or two-way convention, and that the choice is justified by the problem context. Detection logic: 1) Parse the solution for equations linking τ and distance/range d (or path length L). Flag if any of the following patterns appear without explicit justification: τ = 2 d / c, d = c τ / 2, L = 2 d, √(R^2 + H^2) = c τ / 2, H^2 = (c τ / 2)^2 − R^2. 2) Scan the text for contextual justification. Acceptable justification keywords for two-way include: "round-trip", "radar echo", "monostatic", "transmit and receive at the same station", "returned signal", or an explicit statement that τ is a round-trip time. For one-way, keywords include: "broadcast", "downlink", "passive reception", "from satellite to ground", "one-way delay", GPS-like time-of-flight. If the student assumes two-way (factor 2 or 1/2) without these justifications and the problem statement does not explicitly describe a return path, flag a modeling error. 3) Context cross-check: If the problem describes passive ground observations (e.g., receiving a satellite signal) with no transmit-return cycle, require one-way modeling (d = c τ). If it describes a radar/echo measurement or explicit round-trip, allow two-way. 4) Numerical sanity check for error propagation: Given an uncertainty Δτ, compare the solution’s implied distance sensitivity. If the solution’s Δdistance (or propagated ΔH before geometric projection) is approximately c Δτ / 2 (±30%) while the context indicates one-way, flag; if it is approximately c Δτ (±30%) while the context indicates two-way, flag. When ΔH is computed, allow for stated geometric factors (e.g., projection via angle θ), but the baseline factor-of-two should match the context. 5) Special-case geometry forms: If the solution uses two-way path length in spherical geometry (e.g., total path = 2 √(R^2 + H^2)) yet the problem defines τ as a received signal delay or one-way time, flag. Rationale: Misinterpreting τ as round-trip vs one-way introduces a factor-of-two error in range and in derived quantities (e.g., ΔH), commonly halving or doubling the result. The rule enforces that the assumed convention matches the problem statement and that any factor-of-two is explicitly justified.

rules.title: Toroidal axion-induced flux scaling: log(R_out/R_in) and independence from N
rules.description: This rule verifies the geometric/dimensional scaling of the magnetic flux Phi_B induced by an axion-effective current in toroidal geometries. It applies when the solution computes Phi_B through a pickup loop for a toroid (or toroidal solenoid) under an axion field a(t) = a0 sin(ω t) with effective current density J = g * dot(a) * B, where dot(a) = a0 ω cos(ω t). Checks: (1) Time dependence: Phi_B must contain cos(ω t) (from dot(a)); absence is flagged. (2) Radial/geometric dependence: For a toroidal field that scales as 1/r, the radial integration must produce a logarithmic dependence ln(R_out/R_in); results that depend on R_loop^2, (R_out^2 − R_in^2), or any purely area-like quadratic radius terms without a logarithm are flagged. (3) Expected scaling: Up to order-unity geometric factors, Phi_B should scale as ~ μ0 g a0 B_max ω R_in^3 ln(R_out/R_in) cos(ω t); results missing the ln(R_out/R_in) term or the cubic inner-radius scaling are flagged. (4) Independence from winding number: If the result is re-expressed in terms of the maximum toroidal field B_max, the final Phi_B must not depend explicitly on the winding number N; any residual N-dependence is flagged. Rationale: In toroidal geometries, the effective field generated by J ∝ B produces a 1/r dependence, and the correct flux integration over r yields a logarithmic term, not a quadratic area scaling. This rule catches solutions with incorrect dimensional/geometric dependencies, such as Phi_B ∝ R_loop^2 and missing ln(R_out/R_in), or spurious dependence on N once B_max is used.

rules.title: Missing v×B coupling terms in cylindrical EOM with B_phi and B_z
rules.description: Checks equations of motion for a charged particle written in cylindrical/toroidal coordinates (r, phi, z) in the presence of a magnetic field that has both B_phi and B_z components. In such cases, the Lorentz force q(v×B) yields characteristic cross-coupling terms between velocities and field components that must appear in the component equations. For B_r ≈ 0 and nonzero B_phi and B_z, the minimal required magnetic terms are: (1) radial: a term proportional to q r phi_dot B_z (i.e., m(ddot r − r phi_dot^2) includes + q r phi_dot B_z, up to sign convention, and optionally − q z_dot B_phi), (2) azimuthal: a term proportional to − q r_dot B_z in m(r ddot phi + 2 r_dot phi_dot), and (3) axial: a term proportional to + q r_dot B_phi in m ddot z (optionally also − q r phi_dot B_r if B_r is retained). The rule flags a solution as incorrect if the student claims or implies both B_phi ≠ 0 and B_z ≠ 0 but omits any of these characteristic coupling terms, or replaces them with same-component products (e.g., q r_dot B_r, q phi_dot B_phi, q z_dot B_z) inconsistent with v×B. Allowable exceptions: the omission is acceptable only if the student explicitly sets the corresponding field or velocity component to zero (e.g., B_phi = 0, B_z = 0, r_dot = 0, or z_dot = 0) or clearly states an approximation that removes the term. This rule is typically applicable to toroidal/axisymmetric setups and should also verify the presence of the standard cylindrical inertial terms (− r phi_dot^2 in the radial equation and + 2 r_dot phi_dot in the azimuthal equation), although the primary error detected is the missing v×B couplings tied to B_phi and B_z.

rules.title: Require ln(R_out/R_in) from 1/r field integration in toroidal/annular geometries
rules.description: Checks solutions that compute axial magnetic field or magnetic flux produced by azimuthal currents (including effective currents like J = g·ȧ·B) in a toroidal or annular geometry. In such cases the static toroidal field inside the magnet obeys B(r) ∝ 1/r (e.g., B(r) = μ0 N I / (2π r)), and any radial integration over the annulus Rin < r < Rout must yield a logarithmic geometry factor ln(R_out/R_in). The rule flags a modeling error if: (a) the solution assumes a uniform B inside the toroid or uses a single radius (R_avg) without radial integration; (b) the final expression for the axial field or flux depends linearly on (R_out − R_in) or only on an average radius and lacks ln(R_out/R_in), ln(R2/R1), log(Ro/Ri), or an explicit ∫(dr/r) integral; (c) Ampère’s law or B(r) ∝ 1/r is invoked but the necessary radial integral over the annulus is omitted. Acceptable indicators include an explicit integral ∫_{R_in}^{R_out} (dr/r) or a final result containing the logarithmic factor. Trigger heuristics: presence of toroidal/annular geometry terms (toroid, toroidal solenoid, annulus, ring, inner radius, outer radius) and 1/r field statements (B = μ0 N I /(2π r), B ∝ 1/r). If these appear without the logarithmic factor or equivalent radial integral, flag the solution.

rules.title: Toroidal cavity EOM: missing axial Bz or introducing unspecified current
rules.description:
This rule verifies modeling consistency for charged-particle equations of motion in a toroidal cavity (major radius R0, minor radius r0 << R0) when no current/coil parameters are specified in the problem. It flags solutions that (a) assume a purely azimuthal magnetic field or omit the axial component, and/or (b) invent a magnetic field by introducing an unspecified current I via Biot–Savart/Ampère. It also checks that the resulting equations of motion contain the expected cross-coupling terms from Bz and Bφ.

Trigger context:
- Problem statements referencing a toroidal cavity/geometry with given R0 and r0 << R0, asking for equations of motion (r, φ, z) for a charged particle, without providing a current I, number of turns N, or coil details.

Checks (any failure triggers this rule):
1) Missing axial component:
- The solution declares B to be purely azimuthal (e.g., B = Bφ(r) φ-hat, or Bz = 0) without explicit justification in the problem. Expected modeling for this context includes both Bz ≈ B0 ≠ 0 and Bφ ≈ α0 B0 R0 / r (Br ≈ 0 acceptable), or an equivalent statement. Heuristics: absence of any mention of Bz/B_z, or explicit statements like "purely azimuthal" or B = Bφ φ-hat.

2) Unspecified source parameters:
- The solution constructs B using Biot–Savart/Ampère with an unprovided current/turns (e.g., symbols like I, NI, μ0 I/(2π...), coil parameters) when the problem does not supply them. Any magnetic-field expression parameterized by I or NI without being given in the prompt is flagged.

3) EOM cross-term consistency:
- In cylindrical coordinates, with B = Bz z-hat + Bφ φ-hat (Br ≈ 0), the Lorentz force imposes specific couplings:
  • Radial: m (r¨ − r φ̇²) contains + q r φ̇ Bz and − q ż Bφ terms.
  • Azimuthal: m (r φ¨ + 2 ṙ φ̇) contains − q ṙ Bz.
  • Axial: m z¨ contains + q ṙ Bφ.
  The rule checks that at least the Bz-driven couplings (q r φ̇ Bz in the r-equation and/or − q ṙ Bz in the φ-equation) appear when Bz is modeled nonzero, and that Bφ-driven couplings (q ṙ Bφ in z-equation and/or − q ż Bφ in r-equation) are not universally absent. Equivalent sign conventions and symbol names (e.g., B0 for Bz, α0 B0 R0/r for Bφ) are accepted.

Exceptions:
- If the problem explicitly specifies Bz = 0 or provides a current/coil configuration defining B in terms of I, the corresponding checks are skipped.

Purpose:
- To prevent under-specified or physically inconsistent field models in toroidal cavities (e.g., B = Bφ only, or ad hoc μ0 I ... terms), and to ensure the equations of motion reflect the essential r–φ–z couplings arising from simultaneous axial and toroidal magnetic-field components.

rules.title: Incorrect use of V/R in RLC transient analysis
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that compute currents or voltages in circuits containing inductors or capacitors during a transient by directly applying DC Ohm's law (e.g., I = V / (R1 + R2) or using a simple resistor divider) without accounting for dynamic behavior. Trigger conditions: (1) The problem includes energy storage elements (L and/or C). (2) The source or excitation is time-dependent (e.g., induced emf from dB/dt, a step, ramp, or pulse), or the question asks for values at a finite time t after a change. (3) The student’s computation uses only summed resistances or resistor ratios to obtain current/voltage at that finite time and contains no transient terms (no exponentials, no time constants, no initial conditions), nor a differential-equation/Laplace treatment of the RLC dynamics. Exceptions: If the solution explicitly justifies steady-state conditions (t >> relevant time constants such as L/R or RC) and correctly models L as a short and C as an open (or vice versa for AC steady state), V/R may be acceptable. Example of a flagged pattern: "I = E/(R1+R2)" at t within the transient window (e.g., 10 ms) in a circuit with L or C, especially when τ = L/R or RC is not negligible relative to t.

rules.title: Time-of-flight height uncertainty must scale with c and correct geometry
rules.description:
Purpose: Catch order-of-magnitude and modeling errors when propagating timing uncertainty (Δτ) to height uncertainty (ΔH) in satellite ranging problems using signal time-of-flight.

What it checks:
- Scaling check: In EM time-of-flight ranging, range uncertainty is ~ c·Δτ for one-way and ~ (c·Δτ)/2 for round-trip. Conversion from slant range to height introduces only an O(1) geometric factor. Therefore, |ΔH| should be on the order of c·|Δτ| (within a factor ~0.1–10 unless geometry is extremely grazing). Flags results where |ΔH|/(c·|Δτ|) < 1e-3 or > 1e3 (strong fail), and warns if outside [0.1, 10]. This catches unphysical results like nanometer-level ΔH for microsecond-level Δτ.

- Geometry check with elevation/central angle: If an elevation/central angle θ relative to Earth of radius R is provided, the correct one-way model is: s = c·τ (or s = c·τ/2 if τ is explicitly a round-trip time); r = R cosθ + sqrt(max(s^2 − R^2 sin^2θ, 0)); H = r − R; sensitivity dH/dτ = (c·s)/(r − R cosθ) for one-way (halve s if round-trip). The verifier recomputes |ΔH_expected| = |dH/dτ|·|Δτ| and compares to the student’s |ΔH|. Flags if the ratio |ΔH|/|ΔH_expected| is outside [0.1, 10] (configurable), and hard-fails if outside [0.01, 100].

- Factor-of-two misuse: Flags if the student uses τ = 2·(distance)/c while the problem context indicates τ is one-way, or uses τ = (distance)/c while clearly modeling a two-way echo. Heuristic indicators include path length written as 2√(R^2 + H^2) or τ = 2√(R^2 + H^2)/c without explicit round-trip context.

- Angle omission: If θ is given but the student models the path as purely radial (e.g., distance = √(R^2 + H^2)) or uses 2√(R^2 + H^2), ignoring the θ-dependent slant range geometry, flag as incorrect model likely leading to wrong sensitivity.

Reference numeric cross-check (when inputs match): For θ = 45°, τ = 0.10 s, R = 6.38×10^6 m, c ≈ 2.998×10^8 m/s: s = cτ, r = R cosθ + sqrt(s^2 − R^2 sin^2θ), dH/dτ ≈ 3.0×10^8 m/s. Thus ΔH ≈ 3.0 m for Δτ = 0.010 μs. Any result differing by orders of magnitude (e.g., ΔH ~ 10^−8 m) is flagged.

rules.title: Incorrect uniform-field coefficient for induced B inside a finite capacitor
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that compute the induced magnetic field inside a capacitor by assuming a spatially uniform electric field E(t) = Q(t)/(ε0 A) across a finite plate (A = π a^2) and use Ampère–Maxwell with displacement flux Φ_E = E · π r^2 to obtain B(r,t) ∝ r with coefficient μ0 ε0 r/2 · dE/dt. Indicators include: (1) explicit use of E(t) = Q(t)/(ε0 A) with A = π a^2 in a geometry with finite plate radius a, ring electrodes, or specified r < a and z < d; (2) using Φ_E = E π r^2 or writing ∮ B · dl = μ0 ε0 π r^2 dE/dt; (3) deriving B = μ0 ε0 r/2 · dE/dt and, for RC discharge, concluding B(r,t) = −(μ0 Q0 r)/(2 π a^2 R C) e^(−t/RC) φ̂; (4) a final B(r,t) that lacks any z dependence or geometry/fringing corrections (no functions of z, a, d, or edge factors). The rule specifically catches the wrong coefficient that arises from neglecting fringing and actual displacement-current distribution in finite geometries or near ring electrodes. Exception: do not flag if the solution explicitly justifies the infinite parallel-plate limit (a → ∞) or a central-region approximation (d ≪ a and r ≪ a, away from edges) and the problem permits that approximation, while clearly stating the approximation domain. Otherwise, flag the result as a modeling error with incorrect coefficient.

rules.title: Small oscillations near center of uniformly charged cube: linear field and quadratic potential
rules.description:
Scope: Solutions for a charged particle performing small oscillations near the center of a uniformly charged cube (charge density ρ), with motion constrained along a straight channel through the center. The cube has cubic symmetry; gravitational effects are neglected. The rule targets misuse of the electric field/potential near the center and incorrect dependence on the cube size a or channel geometry L.
Checks:
1) Local field linearity: Near the center (x ≪ a), the electric field along the channel must be linear and finite: E(x) = (ρ/(3ε0)) x + O(x^3). Flag any expression for E(x) that is non-analytic at x = 0 (e.g., terms ∝ 1/x or 1/x^2), has E(0) ≠ 0, or has a linear coefficient different from ρ/(3ε0) (beyond tolerance).
2) Potential curvature: The electrostatic potential energy must be harmonic to leading order with no linear term: U(x) = U0 + (1/2) k x^2 + O(x^4), where k = −U''(0) = |q ρ|/(3ε0) for opposite-signed q and ρ. Equivalently, U''(0) = − q ρ/(3ε0). Flag any quadratic coefficient differing by a factor from 1/3 (e.g., k = |q ρ|/(ε0) or |q ρ|/(2ε0)), or incorrect sign that would make the center unstable for opposite-signed charges.
3) Independence from geometry in the quadratic term: The quadratic coefficient (k or U''(0)) must not depend on the cube side a or the channel offset/length L. An additive constant in U may depend on a, but any a- or L-dependence in the x^2 coefficient is an error. Flag forms like U(x) = (q ρ/(6ε0))(a^2 − 3x^2) where the x^2 coefficient is incorrect and/or a appears in the x^2 term.
4) Period consistency: From k = |q ρ|/(3ε0), the small-oscillation period must be T = 2π √(3ε0 m / |q ρ|). Flag results where T carries factors of a or L, or has an incorrect numerical factor (e.g., missing √3 or extra √3), given the stated model.
5) Gauss/Poisson consistency: The derivation should be consistent with ∇·E = ρ/ε0 and cubic symmetry at the center (isotropic second derivatives of the potential). Flag uses of field formulas that contradict this (e.g., importing sphere results without justification, or asserting E ∝ a^2/x near x = 0).
Notes: Allow arbitrary additive constants in potential energy. Tolerate minor algebraic rearrangements that preserve the required curvature and period. This rule is intended to catch incorrect potential/field expansions near the center and spurious dependence on geometric parameters in the harmonic term.

rules.title: Small-oscillation period in uniform volume charge: require 1/3 factor and |qρ|
rules.description: This rule verifies solutions that compute the period (T) or angular frequency (ω) of small oscillations of a point charge q of mass m about the symmetric center of a body with uniform volume charge density ρ in vacuum (ε0). Near the symmetry center, the electric field must be linear and isotropic with E = (ρ/(3ε0)) r, independent of the body's specific shape (provided it has inversion/cubic symmetry about the center). Consequently, the effective spring constant is k_eff = |q|ρ/(3ε0), the angular frequency is ω^2 = |q|ρ/(3ε0 m), and the period is T = 2π √(3ε0 m/|q|ρ). The rule flags results that (a) omit the factor 1/3 (equivalently, miss a factor √3 in T), or (b) fail to take the absolute value of qρ in ω^2 or under the square root in T, which would lead to an unphysical imaginary period for oppositely charged particle and medium. Implementation notes: Identify contexts mentioning uniform charge density ρ and small oscillations near a symmetry center. Parse final expressions for ω^2 or T and normalize constants. Accept equivalent correct forms (e.g., ω^2 = (−qρ)/(3ε0 m) with an explicit statement qρ < 0; or T^2 = 12π^2 ε0 m/|qρ|). Flag if the numerical coefficient corresponds to ω^2 = |q|ρ/(ε0 m) (missing 1/3) or T = 2π √(ε0 m/|qρ|) (missing √3), and flag if qρ appears without absolute value or explicit sign handling in any radicand or ω^2 expression.

rules.title: Sector-plate variable capacitor: capacitance must increase with overlap and use correct sector area
rules.description:
This rule verifies the modeling of capacitance for interleaved variable capacitors built from opposed double-sector plates. It targets solutions that incorrectly make capacitance decrease with the rotor angle or use the wrong overlap area. The rule applies when a solution involves N+1 fixed double-sector plates and N rotatable double-sector plates arranged alternately, with uniform separation s, radius R, sector central angle θ0 (π/2 ≤ θ0 < π), and an electrostatic constant k (Coulomb constant).

Checks performed:
- Monotonicity with overlap: If the derived C(θ) decreases with increasing overlap angle (e.g., contains 1/θ or θ in the denominator for positive θ), flag an error. Capacitance must increase with increased overlapping area.
- Correct overlap area: For sector geometry, the maximum overlap area per adjacent pair of double-sector plates is A_pair_max = R^2 · θ0. Flag use of π R^2 (full disk area) or omission of θ0 when computing area at maximum alignment. Also flag use of only (1/2) R^2 · θ0 without accounting for the “double-sector” (which doubles a single-sector area).
- Effective parallel count: In an alternately stacked set of (N+1)+N = 2N+1 plates, the number of adjacent gaps between opposite terminals is 2N. Flag models that use the wrong count of gaps (e.g., N instead of 2N) unless the per-gap area has been doubled consistently for double-sector geometry (the product 2N × A_single-sector should equal N × A_pair_max).
- Dependence on k: With k as the Coulomb constant, capacitance scales as C ∝ 1/k. Flag expressions that place k in the numerator (C ∝ k) for vacuum/air unless k is explicitly defined as a dielectric constant.
- Maximum capacitance consistency: At maximum overlap, require the scaling C_max ∝ (2N · A_pair_max) / (4π k s) = N · R^2 · θ0 / (2π k s). Flag expressions that contradict this scaling (e.g., missing θ0, using π R^2, or introducing 1/θ).

This rule is designed to catch modeling errors where C(θ) is made inversely proportional to θ and where the overlap area is incorrectly taken as the full disk area rather than the correct sector-based area for double-sector plates.

rules.title: Missing vector time-averaging for rotating-induced magnetic field
rules.description: Applies to problems where a sensor/needle aligns with the average magnetic field over time (e.g., due to mechanical inertia) while a conductor loop rotates in a static external field. The rule flags solutions that (a) use the instantaneous induced field to compute deflection without performing a time average over one full rotation, or (b) perform a scalar average (e.g., averaging sin or magnitudes) instead of a vector average of the rotating field. Required checks: (1) The solution must explicitly compute the time-average of the loop’s magnetic field vector at the center over one period T: <B_loop> = (1/T) ∫_0^T B_loop(t) dt, or equivalently over 0→2π in angle. (2) If B_loop(t) has form k B_h sin(φ) n(φ) with n(φ) rotating with the loop, the vector average must use <sin φ n(φ)> = (1/2) n_perp (nonzero and perpendicular to B_h). Flag if the average is taken as <sin φ> = 0 (leading to <B_loop> = 0) or if |B_loop| is averaged instead of the vector. (3) For a circular ring with resistance R_el = ρ(2πR)/s, flux Φ = A B_h cos φ, E = −dΦ/dt, I = E/R_el, and B_center = μ0 I/(2R), the expected mean magnitude is |<B_loop>| = μ0 s ω B_h /(8 ρ) (independent of R). Consequently tan α = |<B_loop>|/B_h = μ0 s ω /(8 ρ). Flag if the final deflection lacks the 1/2 reduction from vector averaging (e.g., uses μ0 s ω /(4 ρ)), incorrectly depends on R, yields zero by averaging sin alone, or otherwise ignores the required vector time-averaging step. (4) Heuristics for detection: references to ∮ v×B·dl or instantaneous emf without subsequent time averaging; absence of any integral over a full period; language suggesting a steady/instantaneous induced field despite rotation. Accept equivalent algebraic forms that include the correct vector-averaging factor and independence from R.

rules.title: First-order perturbation of sqrt-acceleration velocity (Δv0 for v0 = sqrt(2 q E S / m))
rules.description: This rule verifies the correctness of a first-order (Taylor/linear) approximation for the change in ion velocity due to a small change in acceleration length within a uniform electric field. In contexts where the post-acceleration velocity is v0 = sqrt(2 q E S / m), and a small variation in the effective acceleration length is considered (S_eff = S ± ΔS with |ΔS| << S), the correct first-order change must satisfy Δv0 ≈ (dv0/dS) ΔS = (ΔS / (2 S)) v0, with the sign determined by whether the effective length increases or decreases (e.g., Δv0 ≈ −(ΔS / (2 S)) v0 if the effective length is S − ΔS). The verifier checks that: (1) Δv0 is proportional to v0 and to the dimensionless ratio ΔS/S; (2) the coefficient is 1/2 in magnitude; (3) Δv0/v0 is dimensionless and does not introduce q, E, m explicitly outside of v0; (4) no higher-order terms (e.g., ΔS^2) are used in the first-order approximation; and (5) the sign is consistent with the defined perturbation of the effective acceleration length. The rule flags expressions for Δv0 that mix parameters (q, E, m) improperly, have incorrect coefficients, wrong dimensions, or omit the proportionality to v0 and ΔS/S.

rules.title: Voltmeter reading must be the drop across the voltmeter (include RV)
rules.description:
This rule checks solutions to circuit problems that explicitly include a voltmeter with finite internal resistance RV placed in series with a source (EMF E, internal resistance r) and a series resistor R (e.g., 'voltmeter connected through a variable resistor R'). The voltmeter reading must be the voltage across the voltmeter itself: VV = I*RV, with I computed from the total series resistance. The rule flags the following:
- The voltmeter reading is expressed as the voltage across a different element (e.g., VV = I*R, VV = I*r), or textually claims 'the voltmeter measures the drop across R' or 'across r'.
- The expression for VV omits RV entirely (e.g., VV = E*R/(R + r) or VV = E*r/(R + r)).
- The current I used to compute VV is obtained from a total resistance that excludes RV when the voltmeter is in the same series branch (e.g., I = E/(R + r)).
Accepted forms include VV = I*RV and VV = E*RV/(r + R + RV), or any algebraically equivalent expression showing the drop across RV. Exceptions: Do not apply this rule if the problem explicitly models an ideal voltmeter of infinite resistance connected in parallel to an element, where the reading equals that element's drop (i.e., not a series insertion scenario). Rationale: A voltmeter measures the potential difference across its own terminals; in series, it reads its own voltage drop.

rules.title: Mis-modeling a voltmeter as a series element and deriving non-physical parameters
rules.description:
This rule verifies that circuits involving a voltmeter, a source with internal resistance, and an external variable resistor are modeled consistently. It flags solutions that (a) place the voltmeter’s resistance in series or (b) add reciprocal resistance terms directly to series sums, leading to dimensional inconsistencies and non-physical conclusions (e.g., negative resistances).

The rule checks:

1) Topology and placement of the voltmeter
- If a voltmeter is present, it must be modeled as a high-resistance branch in parallel with the element whose potential difference is being measured. The equivalent seen by the source should include a parallel combination with R_V (e.g., r + (R || R_V) if the meter is across R). 
- Flag any statement or equation that treats the voltmeter resistance R_V as a series element with R and r (e.g., expressions of the form R_total = R + r + ... + R_V or R_total = R + r + 1/R_V).

2) Dimensional consistency in resistance combinations
- In series combinations, only resistances (units of ohms) may be summed. Flag expressions that add conductances (1/R terms) directly to resistances without inversion (e.g., R_total = R + r + 1/R_V). 
- Suggest the correct parallel form when appropriate: R_parallel = (R * R_V) / (R + R_V).

3) Voltmeter reading consistency
- The voltmeter reading must equal the potential difference across the element it is connected across. Flag use of V_meter = I_total * R when the voltmeter is across R but the presence of the voltmeter changes the branch current (i.e., current division is ignored). 
- If the solution invokes the approximation R_V >> R (or R_V >> network) to neglect loading, require that (a) it is explicitly stated and (b) subsequent conclusions (e.g., large fractional changes in meter reading) are not sensitive to R_V. Otherwise, flag as inconsistent use of approximations.

4) Plausibility of derived parameters
- In passive DC networks, resistances must be non-negative. If algebraic results yield negative component values (e.g., R = -5 r) or the solution concludes the problem is inconsistent based on such results, flag as a likely modeling/topology error rather than a contradiction in the problem.

5) Reference structural template check (optional heuristic)
- For a source with EMF E and internal resistance r, voltmeter of resistance R_V across external R, the meter reading should be expressible as V_meter = E * (R || R_V) / (r + (R || R_V)). If the presented relations for V_meter vs. R deviate strongly from this structure (e.g., lack of any parallel combination with R_V), flag as a mis-modeling error.

This rule is intended to catch errors that lead to contradictions like R = -k r (k > 0) and claims of inconsistency arising from placing the voltmeter incorrectly in series or from adding 1/R_V to series resistances.

rules.title: Voltmeter reading must equal the drop across the voltmeter element
rules.description:
This rule detects misidentification of what a voltmeter measures in circuit solutions. It flags cases where a student treats the voltmeter reading as the voltage across some other element (e.g., a series variable resistor) instead of the voltage across the voltmeter itself.

The rule checks:
- Reading assignment: If a variable described as the "voltmeter reading" (e.g., V, V_meter, V_read) is defined as I*R or I*(R + ...), where R is a circuit element different from the voltmeter’s resistance (R_V, Rv, Rmeter), flag an error. The correct assignment in a series current path is V_meter = I*R_V.
- Dependence on meter resistance: In solutions that include a voltmeter in the current path, the expression for the meter reading must depend on R_V. If R_V is absent from the reading or the total current calculation (without an explicit, justified idealization such as R_V → ∞ in a parallel measurement), flag an error.
- Dimensional consistency of total resistance: If the total series resistance is written with a term like 1/R_V (or any 1/R term) added to other resistances (e.g., R_total = R + r + 1/R_V), flag an error for mixing conductance with resistance, indicating a likely misplacement of the voltmeter in the model.

What is flagged:
- Statements or equations equating the voltmeter reading to the drop across a non-meter element (e.g., "V = I*R" where R is the variable resistor, not R_V).
- Omitting R_V entirely from the meter reading/current expressions in a configuration where the meter is part of the series load.
- Adding 1/R terms to series resistance sums.

Rationale:
- A voltmeter measures its own terminal voltage. In any modeled current path that includes the voltmeter, its reading must be the potential drop across the voltmeter element. Equating the reading to a different element’s drop leads to incorrect dependence on circuit parameters and can produce unphysical results (e.g., negative resistance when solving). The rule enforces correct measurement mapping and dimensional consistency.

rules.title: Voltmeter modeling must include internal resistance R_V and correct connection
rules.description:
This rule verifies that solutions involving a voltmeter correctly model the instrument and its effect on circuit behavior. The voltmeter must be represented as a high resistance R_V connected in parallel with the element or source terminals whose voltage is being measured. The voltmeter reading equals the voltage across that element/terminal, not the drop across an unrelated series resistor. The verifier should flag the following modeling errors: 
- Omitting R_V from the expressions that determine the voltmeter reading when the meter is non-ideal.
- Placing R_V in series with the circuit instead of in parallel with the measured node/component.
- Writing the total resistance as a series sum that includes 1/R_V (dimensionally incorrect) or otherwise treating R_V as a series term (e.g., R_total = R + r + 1/R_V).
- Using V_meter = I·R or V_meter = I·r when the voltmeter is connected across the battery terminals or another element, where the correct reading is the voltage across that element (e.g., V_terminal = E − I·r for battery terminals).
- Deriving relations that depend only on r (e.g., R = k·r) when the correct relation must include r + R_V (e.g., R = k·(r + R_V)) for changes in the voltmeter reading driven by the variable series resistor R.
- Dropping R_V under a "R_V ≫ others" assumption while simultaneously attributing changes in the voltmeter reading to the loading effect; unless the problem explicitly states an ideal voltmeter, R_V must appear in the governing expressions.
This rule targets consistency of circuit topology (parallel vs series), dimensional correctness in resistance sums, and proper dependence of the voltmeter reading on R_V in problems where meter loading affects the result.

rules.title: Voltmeter resistance must appear in current and reading when it is the load
rules.description:
Check solutions of circuit problems that include a voltmeter connected to a source (with internal resistance) through other elements (e.g., a variable resistor) to ensure the modeling includes the voltmeter's finite resistance R_V in both the circuit current and the measured voltage. Flag the solution if any of the following are detected: 
- The current is computed as I = E/(R + r) or with a total resistance that omits R_V, even though the voltmeter is part of the conducting path or is the element across which the reading is taken.
- The voltmeter reading is written independent of R_V (e.g., taken as the terminal voltage of the source or as the voltage across R or r) instead of V_meter being determined by a relation that includes R_V (e.g., V_meter = I * R_V if in series, or via a divider that contains R_V if in parallel).
- The solution explicitly assumes R_V >> R, r and then drops R_V from the model while still using a nonzero current through the meter, or uses inconsistent forms like R_total = R + r + 1/R_V and then approximates to R + r.
- In comparative/ratio questions about how the voltmeter reading changes when another resistance is varied, the final expression for the reading does not depend on R_V, despite the configuration implying that R_V determines both the current and the measured voltage.
Require that either (a) R_V appears correctly in the total resistance and in the expression for the meter reading, or (b) an ideal-meter assumption is justified and used consistently (e.g., R_V → ∞ implies zero current through the meter and appropriate open-circuit analysis). If neither is satisfied, report a modeling error: neglect of instrument resistance that determines the measurement.

rules.title: Voltmeter-in-series modeling: include R_V additively and read V = I·R_V
rules.description: This rule checks whether a solution correctly models a voltmeter with finite internal resistance R_V placed in the only conduction path (series) with a variable resistor R and a source with EMF E and internal resistance r. Required modeling: (1) The series current must be I = E / (r + R + R_V). (2) The voltmeter reading must be the drop across the voltmeter: V = I·R_V = E·R_V / (r + R + R_V). The rule flags the following errors: • Treating the voltmeter’s resistance incorrectly in a series path, e.g., writing the total resistance as r + R + 1/R_V (dimensionally wrong) or otherwise combining R_V as a conductance. • Neglecting R_V in the series denominator on the basis that the voltmeter’s resistance is “very large” (in a series path, a large R_V increases the total resistance and cannot be dropped). • Using I = E/(R + r) or R_total = R + r when R_V is explicitly present in series. • Taking the voltmeter reading as the drop across R or r (e.g., V = I·R or V = I·r) instead of across R_V. • For ratio-based conditions involving changing R (e.g., ‘reducing R by 2/3 doubles the reading’), the model must yield V(R) ∝ R_V/(r + R + R_V) and enforce V(R/3)/V(R) = 2, which simplifies to R = 3(r + R_V); solutions that produce a relation independent of R_V, or derived from an incorrect V(R), are flagged. This rule enforces additive inclusion of R_V in series, correct definition of the measured quantity, and dimensional consistency in resistance sums.

rules.title: Proper use of Ampère’s law with volume current density (no coil-formula substitution)
rules.description:
This rule flags solutions that misuse Ampère’s law by treating a continuous current density (e.g., axion-induced J = g · ȧ · B) as if it were a discrete line current or a multi-turn coil. The verifier checks: 
- If formulas for discrete line/coil currents (e.g., B = μ0 I/(2π r) or B = μ0 N I/(2π r)) are invoked when the source is a distributed volume current density with no physical windings, flag. 
- If I_enclosed is set equal to J (A/m^2) or to J times a path length, instead of computing I_enclosed = ∫ J · dA over a surface bounded by the chosen Ampère loop, flag. 
- If the solution asserts local proportionalities like B ∝ μ0 J without specifying and justifying the Ampère loop, symmetry, and boundary conditions needed to infer field direction and spatial dependence, flag. 
- If geometric/linking factors are imported from coil analogies (e.g., using N, toroid geometry factors) when no actual turns exist, or if flux through a pickup loop is computed without integrating B over the loop area, flag. 
- Unit consistency check: substituting J (A/m^2) into equations that require I (A) without an explicit area integral leads to a dimensional mismatch; flag. 
- For axion effective currents, the field must be obtained from Maxwell–Ampère (∇×B = μ0 J_total + μ0 ε0 ∂E/∂t) or Biot–Savart with the actual geometry; relying solely on coil/solenoid analogies without a proper derivation is insufficient.

rules.title: Incorrect distance modeling to a long straight wire
rules.description: This rule checks problems that use the magnetic field of an infinite straight wire (B ∝ I/ρ). It verifies that the distance ρ in B = k·I/ρ is modeled as the perpendicular (shortest) distance from the particle to the wire line, not as the Euclidean distance to a point on the wire. Flag solutions that: (1) define r(t) or r(θ) via a point-to-point law of cosines (e.g., r = sqrt(d^2 + R^2 − 2·d·R·cos θ)), (2) use B(r) = k·I/r where r is computed from a triangle between the circle center, particle, and a point on the wire, or (3) produce a ρ(t) that is a square root of a quadratic in cos/sin rather than a linear function of cos/sin. For setups with a particle of radius R circling a center and a wire at distance d > R from that center, the correct perpendicular distance varies as ρ(t) = d ± R·cos(ωt + φ) (orientation-dependent) and stays within [d − R, d + R]. If the modeled distance violates these characteristics or ignores the point-to-line geometry, mark a modeling error and reject any derived I(t) based on the incorrect r(t).

rules.title: Ensure calibration curve follows the correct mathematical model
rules.description: The calibration curve relates the instrument output (e.g., voltage, reading) to the true physical quantity being measured. Verify that the chosen mathematical model (linear, polynomial, logarithmic, etc.) fits the expected physical relationship and experimental data.
rules.check_logic: Use statistical methods, such as linear regression or non-linear curve fitting techniques, to compare experimental data points to the selected model and evaluate goodness-of-fit using measures like R² (coefficient of determination).
common_errors: Using an incorrect model for the calibration curve (e.g., linear instead of exponential).
Not verifying the goodness-of-fit of the model to the data.

rules.title: Verify consistency in sign conventions for physical quantities
rules.description: Ensure that the sign conventions for all physical quantities (e.g., positive/negative voltage, displacement, current) are consistent throughout the calibration process. This is especially important for measurements involving directional quantities.
rules.check_logic: Check that all measurements respect the defined sign convention for the experiment, and conduct a review for consistency across all phases of calibration (e.g., upward voltage is positive, leftward displacement is negative).
common_errors: Inverting the sign of measurements.
Using different conventions for the same quantity in different parts of the calculation.

rules.title: Ensure proper alignment and positioning of the instrument during calibration
rules.description: For accurate calibration, the instrument must be properly aligned with the reference standard or source. Misalignment introduces systematic errors.
rules.check_logic: Use geometric tools such as spirit levels, laser alignment devices, or computer-aided alignment systems to verify that the instrument is aligned (e.g., level, perpendicular, or at the correct angle) per the setup requirements.
common_errors: Instrument not leveled properly.
Angle of incidence not matching the setup requirements.

rules.title: Verify operating range of the instrument
rules.description: Ensure that the instrument is calibrated within its specified operating range (e.g., voltage, temperature, pressure). Operating outside this range can cause non-linear responses or damage.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the calibration data points lie within the manufacturer's specified range for the instrument, consulting technical specifications to determine appropriate parameters.
common_errors: Calibrating the instrument outside its operational range.
Assuming linearity beyond the specified range.

rules.title: Check dimensional consistency of calibration equation
rules.description: The calibration equation must respect dimensional consistency. For example, if the input is a length (m) and the output is a force (N), the calibration constant should have appropriate dimensions.
rules.check_logic: Use dimensional analysis to ensure that all terms in the calibration equation balance dimensionally, and inspect units for compatibility across all calculations.
common_errors: Ignoring the units of the calibration constant.
Mixing units inconsistently (e.g., mm with m).

rules.title: Evaluate uncertainty in calibration measurements
rules.description: Calibration should include an evaluation of the uncertainties associated with both the instrument being calibrated and the standard/reference. This includes random and systematic errors.
rules.check_logic: Calculate uncertainty using standard propagation of uncertainty formulas, identify all significant sources of uncertainty, and ensure it is within acceptable limits for the application.
common_errors: Neglecting to calculate uncertainty in calibration.
Ignoring systematic errors in the uncertainty calculation.

rules.title: Verify the accuracy of the reference standard
rules.description: The reference standard used for calibration must itself be calibrated and traceable to a recognized metrological standard (e.g., NIST).
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the reference standard has a valid calibration certificate and document its traceability to a national or international standard, reviewing certificates for expiration dates and recent upgrades.
common_errors: Using an uncalibrated or expired reference standard.
Not verifying traceability of the reference standard.

rules.title: Ensure environmental conditions are within acceptable limits
rules.description: Calibration must be conducted under controlled environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, humidity) as specified by the instrument manufacturer to avoid errors.
rules.check_logic: Use environmental monitoring equipment to check that the environmental parameters during calibration are within the specified range for the instrument and document any fluctuations.
common_errors: Calibrating in an environment with significant temperature or humidity fluctuations.
Ignoring the effects of environmental drift during calibration.

rules.title: Ensure consistency through repeated measurements
rules.description: Conduct multiple measurements across different trials to assess variability and ensure reliability and consistency in calibration results.
rules.check_logic: Perform repeated measurements and analyze resultant data for variance or deviation, standard deviation can be used as a consistency metric.
common_errors: Failure to perform repeat measurements leading to increased uncertainty.
Ignoring outliers or discrepancies across trials and datasets.

rules.title: Define and Maintain Control Variables
rules.description: Control variables are constants in experimental setups that should remain unaltered to prevent confounding effects. Proper definition and maintenance of these variables is essential for reproducibility.
rules.check_logic: Verify that control variables are explicitly identified and kept constant during all trials to ensure valid results.
common_errors: Failure to define control variables
Accidental variation of control parameters during experiment

rules.title: Check Reproducibility with Independent Replications
rules.description: Reproducibility requires that an experiment can be repeated with consistent results. Using independent replications ensures reliability by reducing errors and inherent biases.
rules.check_logic: Ensure at least three independent replications are conducted with identical methodologies and consistent result reporting.
common_errors: Insufficient number of replications
Discrepancies in methodological approaches across replications

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional and Unit Consistency
rules.description: All measurements should consistently adhere to specified units and dimensions across the experimental setup for clarity and comparability of data.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all physical quantities are reported in consistent units and dimensions, ensuring calculations respect dimensional consistency.
common_errors: Mixing units (e.g., cm with inches)
Omitting units in calculations or results

rules.title: Adhere to Geometric Constraints
rules.description: Geometric constraints influence the organization of elements in an experiment and must be adhered to for accurate interpretation.
rules.check_logic: Check that the experimental setup adheres to geometric constraints related to control variables and measurement instruments to prevent misalignment.
common_errors: Ignoring spatial alignment requirements
Misalignment of measurement tools

rules.title: Observe Kinematic Constraints for Repeatability
rules.description: Kinematic constraints on motion parameters must be consistently applied in repeated experiments to ensure reproducibility.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the movement parameters of any experimental machinery or subject remain consistent across all trials, documenting any necessary alterations.
common_errors: Variable speed in kinematic setups
Changing trajectory without documenting alterations

rules.title: Consistent Application of Sign Conventions
rules.description: Sign conventions should be consistently applied to avoid misinterpretation of results, especially when dealing with vector quantities or directional measurements.
rules.check_logic: Ensure all vector quantities have clearly defined sign conventions that are applied consistently across all trials.
common_errors: Inconsistent sign application for vector directions
Confusion between positive and negative axis identifiers

rules.title: Evaluate Validity Conditions for Experimental Laws
rules.description: Ensure the laws or models applied in the experiment are valid under the specific conditions (e.g., temperature, pressure, environment).
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the experimental conditions align with the assumptions of the theoretical framework or model being used.
common_errors: Applying laws outside their valid range
Ignoring environmental factors that affect law applicability

rules.title: Standardize Data Collection Protocols
rules.description: The procedures followed for data collection should be standardized to ensure repeatability and consistent data acquisition.
rules.check_logic: Verify that data collection methods are clearly defined, standardized, and consistently followed across all trials.
common_errors: Variable data collection techniques
Inconsistent parameters during data acquisition

rules.title: Conduct Thorough Error Analysis
rules.description: Error analysis identifies potential discrepancies or inaccuracies in experimental results, ensuring reliable interpretation.
rules.check_logic: Ensure all potential sources of error are accounted for, documented, and analyzed consistently across experimental trials.
common_errors: Failure to account for measurement error
Inadequate analysis of data variability

rules.title: Ensure entropy decreases with temperature in ideal systems
rules.description: For cryogenics, entropy in a system decreases as the temperature is reduced, following the Third Law of Thermodynamics. This holds unless external entropy sources (e.g., heat influx or system imperfections) are present.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the entropy S approaches zero as the temperature T approaches absolute zero, provided no residual entropy is present. Ensure that any deviations are justified by material-specific properties or external factors.
common_errors: Incorrectly assuming entropy is zero at non-zero temperatures.
Ignoring residual entropy due to material imperfections or quantum effects.

rules.title: Verify thermal conductivity decreases with lower temperatures
rules.description: In cryogenic systems, thermal conductivity of most materials decreases as temperature drops, except for superconductors or specific materials showing anomalous behavior.
rules.check_logic: Check if the thermal conductivity κ decreases with temperature for conventional materials. Ensure exceptions for superconductors and materials with known anomalous behavior are handled correctly.
common_errors: Failing to account for material-specific thermal conductivity behavior.
Applying high-temperature thermal conductivity models to cryogenic ranges.

rules.title: Check dimensionless group consistency in cryogenic equations
rules.description: Many cryogenic equations involve dimensionless quantities, such as Reynolds number, Knudsen number, or Biot number. Ensure consistency in their definitions and application.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the variables in dimensionless groups are correctly substituted and have no dimensional inconsistencies. Ensure that the physical meaning of the dimensionless group is preserved in the context of cryogenic systems.
common_errors: Using incorrect definitions for dimensionless groups.
Mixing incompatible unit systems when calculating dimensionless numbers.

rules.title: Ensure correct handling of liquid-gas transitions at low temperatures
rules.description: During liquid-gas transitions in cryogenic systems, the Clausius-Clapeyron equation governs the relationship between pressure and temperature.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the Clausius-Clapeyron equation is applied correctly for phase transitions, and the latent heat is treated as temperature-dependent. Ensure that vapor pressure changes are accurately modeled at cryogenic temperatures.
common_errors: Assuming latent heat is constant across the temperature range.
Ignoring changes in vapor pressure at cryogenic temperatures.

rules.title: Verify correct sign convention for heat flow
rules.description: In cryogenics, heat flow direction is critical. Heat flow into the system is positive, while heat flow out is negative.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that heat flow terms in equations are consistent with the sign convention. Verify that the direction of heat flow is correctly interpreted in thermal balance equations.
common_errors: Reversing the sign of heat flow when calculating cooling power.
Misinterpreting heat flow direction in thermal balance equations.

rules.title: Check criteria for superfluid transition in helium-4
rules.description: Helium-4 undergoes a superfluid transition at the lambda point (~2.17 K). Verify that equations and models account for the unique properties of superfluid helium below this temperature.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the temperature is below 2.17 K and superfluid-specific properties (e.g., zero viscosity, quantized vortices, second sound) are considered. Verify that normal fluid dynamics are not applied to superfluid helium.
common_errors: Applying normal fluid dynamics to superfluid helium.
Ignoring the unique heat transport properties of superfluid helium (e.g., second sound).

rules.title: Verify conditions for adiabatic demagnetization cooling
rules.description: Adiabatic demagnetization is used for cooling in cryogenics. The process relies on isolating the system thermally and applying/removing magnetic fields.
rules.check_logic: Check that the system is thermally insulated and the magnetic field variation is slow enough to maintain quasi-equilibrium. Verify that the entropy change corresponds to the expected cooling effect.
common_errors: Ignoring thermal insulation requirements.
Assuming instantaneous magnetic field changes, violating adiabatic conditions.

rules.title: Ensure unit consistency in cryogenic parameters
rules.description: Cryogenic systems often involve parameters like temperature (K), pressure (Pa), and energy (J). Ensure all units are consistent to avoid calculation errors.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all equations use consistent units (SI units are preferred unless specified otherwise). Ensure that unit conversions are correctly applied where necessary.
common_errors: Using temperature in Celsius instead of Kelvin.
Mixing units (e.g., bar for pressure and SI energy units).

rules.title: Verify material property data at cryogenic temperatures
rules.description: Material properties such as specific heat, thermal expansion, and electrical resistivity can vary significantly at cryogenic temperatures. Ensure accurate data is used.
rules.check_logic: Verify that material property data is sourced from reliable cryogenic-specific references. Ensure that temperature-dependent variations are accounted for in calculations.
common_errors: Using room-temperature material properties for cryogenic calculations.
Ignoring temperature-dependent variations in material properties.

rules.title: Ensure proper vacuum insulation in cryogenic systems
rules.description: Vacuum insulation is critical to minimize heat transfer in cryogenic systems. Verify that the vacuum level and insulation design meet the required specifications.
rules.check_logic: Check that the vacuum pressure is sufficiently low to minimize conduction and convection. Verify that insulation materials and designs are appropriate for cryogenic applications.
common_errors: Using inadequate vacuum levels, leading to excessive heat transfer.
Failing to account for material outgassing or thermal bridging in insulation design.

rules.title: Ensure the regression model matches the expected equation form
rules.description: Verify that the chosen regression model (linear, quadratic, exponential, etc.) aligns with the physical principles governing the underlying experimental data. For example, linear regression is suitable for a linear trend, while exponential regression is appropriate for decay processes.
rules.check_logic: Check if the functional form of the regression model matches the anticipated theoretical or experimental relationship, referencing existing literature or theoretical models.
common_errors: Using a linear model for non-linear data trends.
Choosing a higher-order polynomial unnecessarily, leading to overfitting.
Ignoring the underlying physics to select the regression model.

rules.title: Verify unit consistency in regression parameters
rules.description: Ensure that the coefficients and constants in the regression equation have physically consistent units when interpreting the model or equation. The units of the dependent variable must match the computed units from the regression equation.
rules.check_logic: Verify the dimensional consistency of terms in the regression equation by performing unit analysis.
common_errors: Assigning unitless coefficients to terms with units.
Mismatching units due to inconsistent data scaling or transformations.
Failing to check the units of derived regression constants.

rules.title: Analyze residuals to ensure model adequacy
rules.description: Residuals should be randomly distributed around zero. If they exhibit non-random patterns (e.g., systematic trends or clustering), it indicates the model is inadequate for the data.
rules.check_logic: Perform a residual plot analysis and check for randomness by examining whether residuals show systematic deviations or patterns.
common_errors: Interpreting systematic patterns as noise.
Ignoring large residuals that indicate poor model fitting.
Failing to examine residuals in nonlinear models.

rules.title: Evaluate goodness-of-fit metrics
rules.description: Verify the model's fit to the data using metrics such as R-squared, adjusted R-squared, or reduced chi-squared, ensuring they meet the acceptable thresholds without being artificially inflated by overfitting.
rules.check_logic: Compute and interpret goodness-of-fit metrics. Ensure they indicate a sufficient fit by evaluating them alongside residual analysis.
common_errors: Misinterpreting R-squared as a sole indicator of fit quality.
Relying on adjusted R-squared without considering residual analysis.
Overfitting the model to maximize R-squared.

rules.title: Ensure correct data transformations
rules.description: Verify that any transformations (e.g., logarithmic, reciprocal) applied to the data are appropriate and consistent with the underlying physics.
rules.check_logic: Validate that the transformation is justified by the theoretical model or experimental setup. Cross-examine transformations with the expected outcomes.
common_errors: Applying transformations without justification.
Failing to revert transformations when interpreting results.
Using inconsistent transformation methods for different variables.

rules.title: Account for measurement uncertainties in regression
rules.description: Ensure that measurement uncertainties in the dependent and independent variables are incorporated into the regression analysis, where applicable. Consider weighted regression if uncertainties are non-uniform.
rules.check_logic: Ensure uncertainties are included in the regression analysis and that weights are applied correctly based on uncertainty quantification.
common_errors: Ignoring measurement uncertainties in fitting.
Incorrectly weighting data points with smaller uncertainties.
Failing to propagate errors through transformed variables.

rules.title: Check boundary and limiting conditions
rules.description: Verify that the regression model satisfies known boundary or limiting cases of the physical system. For example, a linear model should pass through the origin if the system requires it.
rules.check_logic: Compare the regression model's behavior at boundaries with the expected behavior based on theory or previous experimental data.
common_errors: Forgetting to enforce boundary conditions in the model.
Using regression models that yield non-physical results at limits.
Ignoring known asymptotic behavior in the data.

rules.title: Ensure proper sign conventions and coordinate system usage
rules.description: Verify that the regression analysis respects the sign conventions and coordinate systems defined in the experimental setup. Misaligned conventions can lead to incorrect parameter interpretation.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that regression parameters align with the selected coordinate system and sign conventions, ensuring consistency across the analysis.
common_errors: Misinterpreting the sign of slope or intercept in a linear regression.
Ignoring coordinate system transformations before fitting the data.
Failing to standardize sign conventions across all variables.

rules.title: Check for multicollinearity in regression analysis
rules.description: Verify that the independent variables in the regression model are not excessively correlated, as multicollinearity can affect the reliability of the parameter estimates.
rules.check_logic: Identify and assess multicollinearity using variance inflation factors or correlation coefficients among independent variables.
common_errors: Overlooking multicollinearity among predictors that can inflate standard errors.
Interpreting correlation without accounting for combined predictive effects.
Failing to diagnose multicollinearity in complex models with multiple predictors.

rules.title: Ensure correctness of fundamental statistical equations
rules.description: Verify the proper use of fundamental statistical equations such as mean ([3mbc = a3x/N[0m), standard deviation ([3mc3 = sqrt(a3(x-bc)^2/N)[0m), and variance ([3mc3�b2 = a3(x-bc)^2/N[0m). These equations form the basis of statistical analysis in experimental physics.
rules.check_logic: Check if the student used the correct formula for mean, variance, or standard deviation. Ensure all terms (e.g., N, x, bc) are properly defined and consistently used. Verify whether the equations are applied to the correct dataset (e.g., population vs. sample).
common_errors: Dividing by N-1 instead of N for population statistics
Using a3x^2 instead of a3(x-bc)^2 when calculating variance
Forgetting to take the square root when calculating standard deviation from variance

rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency in statistical calculations
rules.description: Ensure that all the quantities in statistical computations maintain consistent units. For example, if the data points x are measured in meters, then the mean and standard deviation must also have units of meters.
rules.check_logic: Check if the units of output (mean, standard deviation) match the units of the input dataset. Verify that unit conversions, if any, are performed correctly.
common_errors: Failing to include units in final results
Mixing incompatible units (e.g., adding meters to seconds)
Incorrect unit conversions during intermediate steps

rules.title: Verify adherence to sign conventions in error analysis
rules.description: In experimental error analysis, absolute errors are always positive, while signed deviations can be either positive or negative depending on the direction of the deviation from the true value.
rules.check_logic: Check if absolute errors are always reported as positive values and if signed deviations respect the proper sign convention relative to the reference value. Ensure clarity in distinguishing between absolute and percentage errors.
common_errors: Reporting absolute errors as negative
Misinterpreting the direction of deviation (e.g., swapping the sign of signed errors)
Mixing absolute error and percentage error without proper clarity

rules.title: Check validity of curve fitting models
rules.description: Ensure that the chosen curve fitting model appropriately represents the data based on the underlying physical principles and the type of data distribution (e.g., linear for straight-line trends, exponential for decay processes).
rules.check_logic: Check if the student justifies the choice of the fitting model based on data characteristics. Verify if the residuals are randomly distributed, indicating a good fit. Ensure that overfitting or underfitting is avoided.
common_errors: Applying a linear fit to non-linear data without justification
Ignoring residual analysis to validate the fit
Using an over-complicated model (e.g., higher-order polynomial) for simple data trends

rules.title: Validate proper application of error propagation rules
rules.description: Error propagation must follow specific rules depending on the operations: addition/subtraction (94z = sqrt(94x^2 + 94y^2)) and multiplication/division (94z/z = sqrt((94x/x)^2 + (94y/y)^2)).
rules.check_logic: Check if the correct error propagation equations are applied for the given operations and ensure consistency with the data's uncertainty values. Verify that intermediate steps in calculations also account for propagated errors.
common_errors: Using incorrect formulas for error propagation in non-linear operations
Forgetting to propagate uncertainties for intermediate calculations
Mixing relative and absolute uncertainties without proper conversion

rules.title: Ensure correct calculation and interpretation of correlation coefficient
rules.description: The correlation coefficient (r) quantifies the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables. It ranges from -1 to +1. Ensure that students use the correct formula and interpret the result appropriately.
rules.check_logic: Check if the correlation coefficient is calculated correctly using r = a3((x-bcx)(y-bcy))/(Nc3xc3y) and if its value is within the range [-1, 1]. Verify that the interpretation of r aligns with the data's characteristics.
common_errors: Incorrectly computing the mean or standard deviation during calculation
Reporting a correlation coefficient outside the valid range [-1, 1]
Misinterpreting the value of r (e.g., confusing strong negative correlation with no correlation)

rules.title: Check methodology for outlier detection
rules.description: Outliers are data points that deviate significantly from the rest of the dataset. Ensure that the student uses appropriate statistical methods (e.g., Z-scores, IQR method) to identify and justify the treatment of outliers.
rules.check_logic: Check if the student calculates Z-scores (Z = (x-bc)/c3) or uses the IQR method (outliers are 1.5�d7IQR beyond Q1 and Q3). Verify if the treatment of outliers is justified and documented.
common_errors: Failing to define thresholds for identifying outliers
Arbitrarily removing outliers without statistical justification
Confusing measurement errors with genuine outliers

rules.title: Verify normalization of histograms
rules.description: Normalized histograms represent probability distributions and should integrate to 1. Ensure that students normalize the histogram if presenting it as a probability density function.
rules.check_logic: Check if the sum of the histogram bin heights multiplied by bin widths equals 1 for normalized histograms. Verify that bin widths are consistent or appropriately accounted for.
common_errors: Presenting unnormalized histograms as probability distributions
Using inconsistent bin widths without adjusting bin heights
Incorrectly calculating the total area under the histogram

rules.title: Check for sampling bias in data collection
rules.description: Ensure that the dataset used for analysis is representative of the population being studied. Identify and address any potential sampling biases that could affect the validity of the results.
rules.check_logic: Check if the sampling method is described and justified. Verify that the sample size is sufficient and that the data is not skewed due to selection bias or other systematic errors.
common_errors: Using a sample that is not representative of the population
Failing to account for systematic errors in data collection
Ignoring the impact of small sample sizes on statistical reliability

topics.name: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.title: Correct Equation Selection for Hypothesis Testing
rules.description: Ensure the use of the correct statistical equation for hypothesis testing, such as z-tests, t-tests, chi-squared tests, based on the data characteristics and sample size.

tags.topic: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.check_logic: Ensure the choice of statistical test aligns with the data type (continuous, categorical), sample size, and distribution assumptions (e.g., normality for t-tests).
common_errors: Using a t-test for large samples when z-test should be used
Applying chi-squared test on continuous data without categorization
Using parametric tests without verifying distribution assumptions

rules.title: Coordinate System Integrity
rules.description: In an experiment, ensure all measurements are consistent with the stated coordinate system. This often applies to direction conventions or sign conventions relevant to measurements like velocity or displacement.

tags.topic: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.check_logic: Check if all reported measurements maintain consistency in sign and direction relative to the declared coordinate system. Verify transformations between coordinate systems are explicitly stated and correctly applied.
common_errors: Inverting sign for vector components
Applying multiple systems without transformation explanations
Misinterpreting coordinate system origin or axes orientation

rules.title: Verification of Geometric Constraints
rules.description: When designing experiments, ensure any geometric constraints imposed by the setup are adhered to, such as alignment of optical components in a laser experiment.

tags.topic: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.check_logic: Check if the setup conforms to geometric constraints like parallel alignment, correct angular displacement, or specified distances between components.
common_errors: Ignoring beam diameter impacting optical alignment
Misalignment of equipment leading to errors in measurements
Failure to account for thermal expansion affecting alignment

rules.title: Application Validity Conditions
rules.description: Ensure the laws applied within the experimental design hold under the given conditions, such as assuming linear response for small perturbations.

tags.topic: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.check_logic: Verify if the application conditions (e.g., small angle approximation, ideal gas conditions, linearity assumptions) are satisfied before applying specific laws. Document any deviations and their potential impact on results.
common_errors: Using small angle approximation for angles >15 degrees
Applying ideal gas law without low density considerations
Assuming linear response in a nonlinear regime

rules.title: Dimensional Consistency Verification
rules.description: Ensure all equations and calculations used in the experiment are dimensionally consistent, adhering to the principle that physical laws must hold regardless of unit systems.

tags.topic: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.check_logic: Check the dimensional consistency of all derived equations and ensure units match expected dimensions when substituting specific values. Verify unit conversions are correctly applied.
common_errors: Mismatch in units leading to erroneous dimension analysis
Incorrect conversion between unit systems
Failure to verify derived equations for dimensional consistency

rules.title: Selection of Appropriate Test Statistic
rules.description: Choose the appropriate test statistic for evaluating hypotheses based on the experimental design and data type, such as ANOVA for comparing more than two groups.

tags.topic: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.check_logic: Ensure the test statistic matches the structure of hypothesis, data type, number of groups or conditions, and experimental design (e.g., paired vs unpaired data).
common_errors: Confusion between one-way and two-way ANOVA
Inappropriate use of tests for paired vs unpaired data
Using parametric tests without verifying assumptions like homogeneity of variance

rules.title: Comprehensive Error Analysis
rules.description: Include detailed error analysis in experiment design, accounting for systematic, random, and human-induced errors.

tags.topic: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.check_logic: Verify if error analysis covers all possible error sources, quantifies their impact, and includes strategies for mitigation or acknowledgment. Ensure error propagation is calculated where applicable.
common_errors: Ignoring human measurement error in precision experiments
Failure to account for environmental variations impacting results
Omitting error propagation in derived quantities

rules.title: Sampling Strategy Verification
rules.description: Ensure the sampling strategy is appropriate for the experimental goals, data type, and population characteristics.

tags.topic: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.check_logic: Verify that the sampling method (e.g., random, stratified, systematic) aligns with the experimental objectives and minimizes bias. Check if the sample size is sufficient for statistical power.
common_errors: Using a biased sampling method leading to unrepresentative data
Insufficient sample size for detecting meaningful effects
Failure to account for population heterogeneity in sampling

rules.title: Control Variable Management
rules.description: Ensure all relevant control variables are identified and managed to isolate the effect of the independent variable.

tags.topic: Design of Experiments and Hypothesis Testing

rules.check_logic: Verify that control variables are explicitly stated, consistently maintained, and monitored throughout the experiment. Check for unintended confounding variables.
common_errors: Failure to identify critical control variables
Inconsistent application of control conditions
Overlooking confounding variables impacting results

rules.title: Validate correct unit conversions
rules.description: Ensure that proper unit conversions are applied when switching between different unit systems (e.g., SI and CGS).
rules.check_logic: Verify that all quantities are consistently converted using accurate conversion factors (e.g., 1 m = 100 cm).
common_errors: Incorrectly converting units, such as using an inverse factor (e.g., 1/100 instead of 100)
Mixing unit systems without applying conversion factors
Failing to square or cube unit conversions for area or volume (e.g., 1 m^2 ≠ 100 cm^2)

rules.title: Verify correctness of derived dimensions
rules.description: Ensure that derived quantities (e.g., velocity, force, energy) are expressed correctly in terms of fundamental dimensions (M, L, T).
rules.check_logic: Validate that the derived dimensions reflect the expected relationships, such as velocity = L/T, force = M·L/T^2.
common_errors: Misidentifying the dimensions of a derived quantity (e.g., treating energy as L·T instead of M·L^2/T^2)
Confusing related quantities (e.g., mistaking force for momentum)

rules.title: Verify scaling relations using dimensional analysis
