Also flag logs with dimensional arguments (e.g., ln R) lacking a ratio. 3) Velocity and G-scaling sanity: Flag results that increase with positive powers of v (e.g., v or v^2) rather than the expected 1/v^2 dependence, and results with only one power of G or lacking M^2, unless explicitly justified by a different regime. 4) Integration measure validation: When the derivation constructs the encounter count, require dN = 2π n b db v Δt (or equivalent). Flag if the measure omits b db or v Δt (e.g., using dN ∝ n db), which typically produces linear dependence on the outer cutoff. This rule will catch errors such as deriving F_DF ≈ 2π G M ρ v^2 R (dimensionally inconsistent and linearly dependent on R) instead of the correct logarithmic dependence in the form F_DF ∝ (G^2 M^2 ρ / v^2) ln(b_max/b_min), up to order-unity distribution factors.

rules.title: Chandrasekhar dynamical friction: missing 1/v^2 factor
rules.description: This rule verifies that any expression for the Chandrasekhar dynamical friction drag force on a massive body moving through a stellar background includes the required inverse-square velocity dependence and passes a dimensional consistency check. Trigger when the solution references 'dynamical friction', 'Chandrasekhar', 'F_DF', or a drag force on an SBH moving in a galaxy and presents a formula proportional to G^2 M^2 ρ times a Coulomb logarithm (ln Λ, ln(R/b_min), ln(R/b_1), etc.). Checks: (1) Parse the force expression and compute the net power of the speed v; the expected scaling is net v^{-2} (equivalently v^{-3} times v in the direction of motion). If the formula lacks any explicit v-dependence or the net power is not -2, flag an error 'Missing 1/v^2 in dynamical friction'. (2) Dimensional check: G^2 M^2 ρ lnΛ alone has units of M·L^3·T^{-4}; a force must have units M·L·T^{-2}. If the provided expression does not include a factor of 1/v^2 (or an equivalent velocity dependence that produces the correct units), flag. (3) Allow dimensionless velocity-distribution factors (e.g., [erf(X) − (2X/√π) e^{−X^2}] with X = v/(√2 σ)); these must multiply the 1/v^2 dependence, not replace it. (4) Accept minor variations in numerical prefactor (e.g., 4π vs. order-unity constants) and in the definition of lnΛ as long as the argument is a ratio of lengths. Examples to flag: F_DF = −4π G^2 M^2 ρ lnΛ (no v term), or F_DF ∝ G^2 M^2 ρ ln(R/b_1) with v^0. Expected correct form: F_DF ≈ −4π G^2 M^2 (ρ / v^2) lnΛ times a dimensionless function of v/σ, directed opposite to v.

rules.title: Negative squared speed indicates setup/sign error, not physical impossibility
rules.description: This rule checks derivations where the speed is obtained from integrating Newton’s second law in 1D (e.g., m v dv/dx = F(x)) or from energy/work relations, producing an expression for v^2(x). The verifier will: (1) Locate any expression of the form v^2 = f(x) (or 2K/m = f(x)) and evaluate its sign over the physically reachable interval defined by the initial condition and intended endpoint. (2) If v^2(x) < 0 at any point that lies on the proposed trajectory (including at region boundaries in piecewise-defined forces), it flags a violation. A negative v^2 is non-physical and indicates a setup error such as an incorrect force sign, wrong integration limits, or misuse of the constant of integration, rather than a physical barrier. (3) For attractive forces toward decreasing x (e.g., gravity toward the origin), the rule checks that the sign of F(x) is consistent with the coordinate direction: F(x) should be negative when x increases away from the attractor, and v^2 derived from m v dv/dx = F(x) or from v^2 = (2/m)(W + C) must remain ≥ 0 along the path. (4) In piecewise force problems, the rule enforces continuity of energy at the boundary: the v^2 computed at the boundary must be non-negative; interpreting a negative v^2 at the boundary as meaning the particle cannot reach it is flagged as a logical error. The rule advises rechecking force direction, potential/work signs, integral limits, and constants of integration whenever v^2 becomes negative.

rules.title: Verify Newton’s Second Law for the Center of Mass
rules.description: The total external force acting on a system of particles equals the mass of the system multiplied by the acceleration of its center of mass. This applies to systems where forces are clearly identified as internal or external.
rules.check_logic: Verify if F_ext = M*a_cm, where F_ext is the vector sum of all external forces, M is the total mass of the system, and a_cm is the acceleration of the center of mass.
common_errors: Forgetting to distinguish between internal and external forces.
Incorrect calculation of total mass (M) of the system.
Omitting acceleration components in vector form.

rules.title: Conservation of Linear Momentum
rules.description: If the net external force acting on a system of particles is zero, the total linear momentum of the system remains constant.
rules.check_logic: Verify if the vector sum of external forces is zero (F_ext = 0). If true, check whether the initial total momentum of the system equals the final total momentum.
common_errors: Neglecting to check for external forces.
Incorrect calculation of momentum (P = mv for each particle).
Not accounting for vector nature of momentum.

rules.title: Check Torque and Angular Momentum Relationship
rules.description: The rate of change of angular momentum of a system about a point is equal to the net external torque about that point.
rules.check_logic: Verify if dL/dt = τ_ext, where L is the angular momentum and τ_ext is the net external torque.
common_errors: Using incorrect pivot point for calculation of torque.
Confusing internal and external torques.
Ignoring rotational inertia in angular momentum calculations.

rules.title: Confirm Validity of the Center of Mass Motion Equation
rules.description: The center of mass motion equation assumes that the system is not relativistic and that the particles within the system do not experience significant relativistic effects.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the velocities involved are much less than the speed of light (v << c) and that there is no significant mass variation due to relativistic effects.
common_errors: Applying the center of mass motion equation to a relativistic system.
Neglecting mass variation in cases where particles are added or lost.

rules.title: Ensure Proper Use of Sign Conventions and Coordinate Systems
rules.description: The choice of coordinate system and sign conventions must be consistent throughout the analysis of a system of particles.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all forces, displacements, velocities, and accelerations are resolved into the same coordinate system, and that consistent signs are assigned based on the chosen convention.
common_errors: Mixing coordinate systems without clear transformation.
Inconsistent sign conventions for vector components.
Incorrect resolution of forces into components.

rules.title: Account for Constraints in the System
rules.description: Geometric and kinematic constraints (e.g., rigid body motion, inextensible strings, etc.) must be properly incorporated into the equations describing the system.
rules.check_logic: Verify if constraint equations are included (e.g., for rigid bodies, relative distances between particles remain constant) and check their impact on the system.
common_errors: Neglecting to include the constraint forces in the free-body diagram.
Incorrectly defining or solving constraint equations.
Overlooking constraints in motion due to rigid connections or links.

rules.title: Dimensional and Unit Consistency Check
rules.description: Ensure that all quantities in dynamic equations have consistent units and dimensions (e.g., force in Newtons, mass in kilograms, acceleration in m/s²).
rules.check_logic: Verify that equations balance dimensionally and that units are consistent across all terms.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units (e.g., mass in grams instead of kilograms).
Forgetting to convert velocities or accelerations into standard units before substitution.
Mismatched units in torque and angular momentum.

rules.title: Verify Conservation of Energy in the System
rules.description: If no non-conservative external forces (e.g., friction) do work, the total mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) of the system should remain constant.
rules.check_logic: Check if the work done by non-conservative forces is zero. If true, ensure that the initial and final mechanical energy are equal.
common_errors: Ignoring the work done by non-conservative forces like friction or air resistance.
Incorrectly calculating potential energy for systems with multiple particles.
Omitting rotational kinetic energy for systems involving rotation.

rules.title: 非标准色散关系加速度校验
rules.description:
触发条件：题目给出非二次型动能公式 K(p) 或色散关系 E(k) 时
检查逻辑：必须先由 v = dK/dp 求出速度与动量函数，再利用 F = dp/dt 和 a = dv/dt = (dv/dp) * F 进行链式求导，不可直接套用 F=ma。
rules.check_logic: 必须先由 v = dK/dp 求出速度与动量函数，再利用 F = dp/dt 和 a = dv/dt = (dv/dp) * F 进行链式求导，不可直接套用 F=ma。
rules.trigger: 题目给出非二次型动能公式 K(p) 或色散关系 E(k) 时

rules.title: 各向异性/准粒子动力学分量分解
rules.description:
触发条件：涉及准粒子在电磁场中运动且 K-p 关系包含线性项或高次项
检查逻辑：需将速度矢量 v 表示为动量矢量 p 的函数 v = (dK/dp) * (p/|p|)，对时间求导时需注意方向导数产生的向心项或附加加速度项。
rules.check_logic: 需将速度矢量 v 表示为动量矢量 p 的函数 v = (dK/dp) * (p/|p|)，对时间求导时需注意方向导数产生的向心项或附加加速度项。
rules.trigger: 涉及准粒子在电磁场中运动且 K-p 关系包含线性项或高次项

rules.title: Minimal speed to reach any heliocentric orbit equals Earth escape speed (do not include Sun potential)
rules.description: Scope: Problems asking for the minimal launch speed from Earth to "reach/enter any heliocentric (solar) orbit". Correct modeling criterion: it is sufficient to escape Earth's gravity; once unbound from Earth, the spacecraft automatically has a heliocentric orbit because it inherits Earth's orbital velocity around the Sun. Therefore, the minimal required speed at radius r from Earth's center is v_m = sqrt(2 μ_E / r) (neglecting atmosphere and Earth's rotation unless specified). After escape, the craft is bound to the Sun without needing additional Sun-related energy conditions. Flag as a modeling error if the solution: (1) sums Earth and Sun gravitational potentials or specific energies at launch, e.g., uses E = 1/2 m v^2 − GM_E m / r − GM_S m / R_ES and imposes E ≥ 0 to justify entering a heliocentric orbit; (2) introduces GM_S (Sun’s parameter) or Earth–Sun distance R_ES in the minimal-speed condition for merely achieving any heliocentric orbit; (3) requires positive heliocentric specific energy (escape from the Sun) instead of Earth escape; (4) derives expressions like v_m ≈ sqrt(2 (μ_E / r + μ_S / R_ES)) or otherwise makes v_m depend on μ_S for this task. Acceptable reasoning indicators: uses Earth-specific orbital energy ε_E = v^2/2 − μ_E/r and sets ε_E ≥ 0 (parabolic escape), cites v_esc,Earth = sqrt(2 μ_E / r), and may note that the post-escape heliocentric velocity is Earth's orbital velocity plus small excess, ensuring a bound heliocentric orbit. Exceptions: If the problem explicitly requires a specific heliocentric orbit energy (e.g., transfer to a specified ellipse) or escape from the Sun, then Sun terms are relevant and this rule does not apply.

rules.title: Plumb-line tilt must be derived from the horizontal component of centrifugal acceleration (vector-sum model)
rules.description:
This rule verifies modeling of the vertical deviation of a plumb line on a rotating Earth. It enforces that the plumb line aligns with the direction of the resultant effective acceleration (true gravity plus centrifugal), not via a force balance along the plumb line or by equating radial gravity to the full centrifugal magnitude. The rule checks the following:
- The solution must decompose the centrifugal acceleration at latitude λ into components: radial component ω^2 R cos^2(λ) (reduces the radial gravity) and horizontal equatorward component ω^2 R sin(λ) cos(λ) (produces the tilt).
- The tilt angle α must be obtained from the ratio of these components, e.g., tan(α) = [ω^2 R sin(λ) cos(λ)] / [g0 − ω^2 R cos^2(λ)]. For small angles, the acceptable approximation is α ≈ (ω^2 R / g0) sin(λ) cos(λ).
- It flags errors where the entire centrifugal term ω^2 R cos(λ) is used as the tilting (horizontal) component, or where equations of the form mg cos(α) = m ω^2 R cos(λ) or mg_eff cos(α) = m ω^2 R cos(λ) appear (indicative of balancing forces along the plumb line or using the wrong component).
- It flags formulas for α(λ) that lack the sin(λ) factor (e.g., α ∝ cos(λ) only), or any derivation that maximizes α at λ = 0° (equator) or λ = 90° (pole) rather than at λ = 45° (where sin(λ) cos(λ) is maximal).
- It requires that the stated maximum deviation occur at λ = 45° and, if a numerical value is provided, be consistent with α_max ≈ (ω^2 R) / (2 g0) under the small-angle approximation.
Rationale: The plumb line aligns with the net effective gravity vector; the tilt is set by the horizontal (equatorward) component of the centrifugal acceleration relative to the net radial component. Using the full centrifugal magnitude or balancing forces along the plumb line leads to incorrect latitude dependence and maximum location.

rules.title: Elastic bounce on vertical surface: vertical motion continuity and minimum speed
rules.description: This rule verifies solutions for projectile problems that include a perfectly elastic collision with a vertical surface (e.g., a frictionless backboard, negligible ball size). It checks that the solution respects the kinematic invariants of an elastic bounce on a vertical wall: (1) only the horizontal component of velocity reverses sign at impact (v_x+ = -v_x-), while the vertical component remains unchanged (v_y+ = v_y-), and the speed magnitude is preserved; (2) the vertical motion is treated as continuous across the collision and depends only on the total flight time T = t1 + t2; (3) the horizontal segment times before and after the bounce are determined by the same horizontal speed magnitude (|v0 cosθ|), i.e., t1 = x1/(v0 cosθ) and t2 = x2/(v0 cosθ), with identical |cosθ| magnitude pre/post bounce; and (4) the minimum initial speed is derived from the vertical displacement equation y_f = y_i + v0 sinθ (t1 + t2) − (1/2) g (t1 + t2)^2, coupled with the horizontal timing constraints, rather than assumed to be larger due to the presence of the bounce. The rule flags solutions that: (a) assert or conclude that the bounce inherently increases the minimum speed compared to a direct shot without performing the vertical kinematic analysis over total time; (b) modify the vertical component at the collision (change magnitude or sign) for a vertical wall; (c) introduce energy loss despite a stated perfectly elastic collision; (d) use different horizontal speed magnitudes before and after the bounce without justification; or (e) fail to sum t1 and t2 in the vertical motion when computing minimum speed.

rules.title: Elastic collision consistency with restitution and energy claims
rules.description: This rule checks for contradictions between claims of elastic collisions and the use of a coefficient of restitution or energy-loss statements. It enforces that if a solution states that collisions are elastic (e.g., uses phrases like 'elastic collision(s)' or 'perfectly elastic'), then: (1) the coefficient of restitution e, if specified or implied in formulas, must be equal to 1 within a small tolerance (e.g., |e − 1| < 1e-3); (2) there should be no claims of kinetic energy loss per collision or statements like 'kinetic energy is lost' during those collisions; and (3) velocity update formulas should not use e ≠ 1 (e.g., v_after = −e v_before with e < 1). The rule flags violations when: (a) collisions are labeled elastic while e is provided as a numeric value not equal to 1 (including expressions like sqrt(1/2) ≈ 0.707); (b) the text includes both 'elastic collisions' and an explicit or implicit claim of energy loss during each collision; or (c) energy-conservation statements for each collision are made while simultaneously using or computing with e < 1 or e > 1. Conversely, if e < 1 (inelastic) or e > 1 (superelastic) is used, the solution must not claim kinetic energy is conserved in each collision. This rule is intended to catch modeling inconsistencies such as stating 'collisions are elastic' and then using e = sqrt(1/2), or asserting conservation of kinetic energy while computing per-collision energy losses.

rules.title: Missing 2π factor when converting ring circumference stretch to radial stretch
rules.description: Checks solutions involving an elastic ring/hoop of natural radius a and stiffness k (k defined for the ring's circumference) to ensure the change in circumference ΔL = 2π(r − a) is used when expressing elastic force or energy in terms of the ring radius r (often denoted x). Common errors treated as violations: (1) Using F_el = k (r − a) instead of F_el = 4π^2 k (r − a); (2) Using U_el = (1/2) k (r − a)^2 instead of U_el = (1/2) k [2π(r − a)]^2 = 2π^2 k (r − a)^2; (3) In problems where vertical equilibrium relates the surface slope to elastic force (e.g., a ring resting horizontally on a surface of revolution), deriving f'(r) = −(k/mg)(r − a) instead of the correct f'(r) = −(4π^2 k/mg)(r − a); (4) Deriving a paraboloid/profile y = C − α (r − a)^2 with α missing the factor 2π^2, i.e., α = k/(2mg) rather than α = 2π^2 k/mg. Detection heuristic: when the context contains an elastic ring/hoop with stiffness k and natural radius a, and the solution expresses elastic force/energy directly in terms of (r − a) without any 2π factors (tokens like 2π, 2*pi, 2 pi, or π^2 in the coefficient), flag as a likely omission unless the author explicitly defines k as a radial stiffness (i.e., k_r such that U = (1/2) k_r (r − a)^2 and F = k_r (r − a)). The rule specifically flags coefficients off by a factor of 4π^2 in force relations and by 2π^2 in the integrated potential/profile relations, catching errors like y = C − (k/(2mg))(x − a)^2 instead of y = C − (2π^2 k/mg)(x − a)^2.

rules.title: Disallow phantom elastic potential energy terms (rope/pulley not elastic)
rules.description:
Checks energy-method setups to ensure elastic potential energy is assigned only to declared elastic elements (springs) and not to inextensible ropes or inertial components.
- Parse the problem statement to identify the set of elastic elements and their stiffnesses (e.g., springs with constants k, 2k). Record the count and labels of springs.
- Inspect the user’s potential energy U expression. Verify that U_elastic is a sum of quadratic terms 1/2 * k_i * x_i^2 only for the identified springs; flag any additional quadratic elastic term not mapped to a declared spring or elastic component (e.g., a rope or pulley).
- If the rope is described as inextensible/massless (or otherwise non-elastic), ensure no term of the form 1/2 * K_rope * x^2 appears; flag such terms as modeling errors.
- Ensure rotational components (e.g., pulley with moment of inertia) appear only in kinetic energy, not in potential energy. Flag any 1/2 * I * ω^2 mistakenly placed in U.
- Cross-check effective stiffness: for symmetric motion where both springs extend by the same displacement y, the total elastic potential must equal 1/2 * k * y^2 + 1/2 * (2k) * y^2 = (3/2) * k * y^2. Flag any effective stiffness exceeding the sum implied by the declared springs (e.g., an incorrect (7/2) * k * y^2 arising from a fictitious third spring).
- Also verify coordinate mapping consistency: if the solution asserts x1 = x2 = y by symmetry, ensure no additional independent x3 appears without a corresponding physical spring.
This rule triggers when the energy method includes fictitious elastic terms (e.g., a third 1/2 * 2k * x^2 term for a rope) or otherwise inflates the elastic potential beyond what the physical springs justify.

rules.title: Closed ring: use circumference extension ΔL = 2π(R − a), not radius change
rules.description: Checks derivations involving an elastic ring (closed circular loop) with natural radius a and stiffness k. The rule verifies that Hooke-type relations for elastic energy and tension use the change in circumference ΔL = 2π(R − a), rather than the change in radius R − a. It flags solutions that write elastic energy or tension as U_e = (1/2) k (R − a)^2 or T = k (R − a) without an explicit and correct redefinition of the stiffness to absorb the 2π factor (e.g., k' = k (2π)^2 or k_eff = EA/L0 with L0 = 2πa). Acceptable forms include U_e = (1/2) k (ΔL)^2 with ΔL = 2π(R − a) and T = k ΔL = 2πk(R − a). The rule also checks consistency statements: if k is defined as force per unit circumference extension (N/m), tension must be T = k ΔL and energy U_e = (1/2) k (ΔL)^2; using ΔR directly without the 2π factor leads to incorrect scaling and should be flagged.

rules.title: Continuous rope through frictionless guides: account for all loaded segments and correct elongation mapping
rules.description:
Scope: Problems with a single elastic rope running through frictionless carabiners/pulleys, anchored at one end and attached to a climber at the other. The rope has multiple taut segments (e.g., ground-to-carabiner length H and carabiner-to-climber length L) made of the same material and cross-section. Check the following modeling requirements and flag violations:

1) Uniform tension and strain across segments: Under frictionless guides and a continuous rope, each taut segment carries the same tension T. With uniform rope (same E and A), stress is equal in each segment, so strain is equal: ε = T/(EA). Flag if the solution assigns different tensions or strains to segments without friction or material changes.

2) Strain energy must include all loaded segments: The elastic energy is stored in every segment under tension. For a uniform rope, the total loaded length is (H + L), and the effective axial stiffness is k_eff = EA/(H + L). Correct energy expressions must integrate over the entire loaded length, e.g., U = ∫ (σ ε/2) dV over both segments, or equivalently U = (1/2) T · Δl_total with Δl_total = ε (H + L). Flag if the solution computes strain energy using only the climber-side segment length L (e.g., k = EA/L or U ∝ L only) while other segments are clearly taut.

3) Correct kinematic mapping of fall distance to rope elongation: The climber’s additional fall distance due to rope stretch equals the elongation of the climber-side segment only: Δy_climber = Δl_lower = ε·L. The total rope extension is Δl_total = ε (H + L) and is not equal to the climber’s displacement. Flag if the solution equates the climber’s fall distance to the total rope extension, or uses an unphysical relation such as ΔL = H − L or any difference of the geometric segment lengths to represent elastic elongation.

4) Consistency checks: When energy balance or force-displacement relations are used, ensure that terms involving EA, stiffness, or strain reference the sum of all taut lengths (H + L) when computing total rope energy or effective stiffness, and reference only L when relating the climber’s displacement to rope stretch. Flag if this consistency is violated.

This rule detects modeling errors where only one segment’s stretch is considered, where elongation is tied to geometric differences like H − L, or where tension/strain is not treated uniformly across segments in a continuous, frictionless rope system.

rules.title: Require energy balance and correct tension relation in elastic fall with acceleration limit
rules.description: This rule checks solutions to problems where an elastic rope (with a given or referenced stress–strain curve) arrests a fall under a specified maximum acceleration. The rule flags two classes of errors: (A) using only a local force balance to determine the allowable fall length without a work–energy analysis, and (B) incorrect sign or form in the force balance relating tension and acceleration. Specifically: (1) If the solution attempts to compute the maximum safe rope length L (or fall distance) solely from Newton’s second law at an instant (e.g., sets mg − T = m a_max or similar) and does not equate the gravitational potential energy lost during the fall to the elastic energy stored in the rope (via integrating stress vs. strain or referencing the area under the stress–strain curve), flag the solution. Acceptable forms include statements like m g Δh = ∫ T(x) dx, using the work–energy theorem, or explicitly summing elastic energy in all loaded rope segments. (2) If the solution derives the maximum tension from the acceleration limit using mg − T = m a_max or T = mg − m a_max, or produces T < mg (e.g., T = 4 m g for a_max = 5 g), flag as a sign/logic error. The correct instantaneous relation when upward acceleration magnitude is a_max is T − mg = m a_max ⇒ T = m (g + a_max). (3) For setups with frictionless carabiners and multiple rope segments sharing the same tension, the solution must account for total elastic energy as the sum over all stretched segments; if this is omitted when determining L, flag the solution. The rule triggers on the absence of energy/work keywords or integrals (e.g., no mention of energy, work–energy, potential energy, elastic energy, area under stress–strain, ∫T dx) combined with reliance on a single force equation to set L, and on any occurrence of mg − T = m a_max or T = mg − m a_max in this context.

rules.title: Elastic collision relative-velocity consistency
rules.description: For any solution that claims a perfectly elastic, 1D collision between two bodies, check the use of the relative-velocity reversal v1' - v2' = -(v1 - v2). The verifier will: (1) compute v1 - v2 using the stated signs and magnitudes; if velocities are opposite in sign (e.g., v1 = +v and v2 = -v), require v1 - v2 = v - (-v) = 2v, not 0; flag if simplified to 0 or to v - v. (2) flag any conclusion v1' = v2' while simultaneously asserting v1 ≠ v2 (i.e., nonzero pre-collision relative speed), since v1' - v2' must be nonzero whenever v1 - v2 ≠ 0. (3) flag misuse where center-of-mass or a common falling speed is substituted for individual lab-frame velocities in the relation. This rule detects algebraic sign errors and misapplication of the elastic relative-velocity constraint that incorrectly yields equal post-collision velocities or zero relative speed after collision despite a nonzero pre-collision relative speed.

rules.title: Verify Hooke's Law Application
rules.description: Hooke's Law states that the restoring force (F) is proportional to the displacement (x) within the elastic limit of the material, given by F = -kx, where k is the spring constant. This applies only when the material is within its elastic limit.
rules.check_logic: Verify that F = -kx is applied correctly, ensuring the material deformation is within the elastic limit. Confirm that the spring constant (k) is appropriate for the material and that the negative sign is used to indicate the restoring direction.
common_errors: Using Hooke's Law beyond the elastic limit.
Forgetting the negative sign in F = -kx indicating the restoring direction.
Incorrect or mismatched units for k, x, and F.

rules.title: Verify Stress and Strain Calculations
rules.description: Stress is the force per unit area (σ = F/A), and strain is the relative deformation (ε = ΔL/L). These quantities are related through the elastic modulus (E) as σ = Eε.
rules.check_logic: Ensure stress and strain are calculated using the correct definitions. Verify that the relationship σ = Eε holds for the given material and that the elastic modulus used matches the material's properties.
common_errors: Confusing stress and strain definitions.
Incorrectly calculating cross-sectional area in stress formula.
Using the wrong elastic modulus for the material.

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional and Unit Consistency
rules.description: The units of force, displacement, spring constant, stress, strain, and elastic modulus must be consistent. For example, [k] = N/m, [σ] = N/m², [ε] is dimensionless, and [E] = N/m².
rules.check_logic: Verify that all quantities have consistent units in equations, particularly when converting between systems (e.g., SI to CGS). Ensure that strain is treated as a dimensionless ratio.
common_errors: Using strain with units instead of a dimensionless ratio.
Mixing up units of stress and elastic modulus.
Failing to convert units of force or displacement when required.

rules.title: Check for Geometric Constraints in Deformation
rules.description: Ensure that the deformation (strain) does not exceed the elastic limit or lead to unrealistic geometrical results. For example, strain should remain small (ε << 1) for linear elasticity to be valid.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the strain calculated is within reasonable bounds for the material, typically less than a few percent for most solids. Confirm that the deformation does not imply unrealistic geometry or exceed the elastic limit.
common_errors: Calculating strain values that imply large deformations beyond the elastic limit.
Ignoring the geometric implications of length changes in strain calculations.

rules.title: Verify Hooke's Law Validity Conditions
rules.description: Hooke's Law applies only within the elastic limit of a material. Beyond this limit, plastic deformation occurs, and the relationship between stress and strain is no longer linear.
rules.check_logic: Check that the stress or strain does not exceed the yield point of the material. Verify that the linear relationship σ = Eε holds only within the elastic region and that the material is not undergoing plastic deformation.
common_errors: Applying Hooke's Law to materials undergoing plastic deformation.
Using the elastic modulus (E) for non-linear regimes.

rules.title: Verify Elastic Potential Energy Calculation
rules.description: The elastic potential energy stored in a spring is given by U = 1/2 kx², where x is the displacement from the equilibrium position.
rules.check_logic: Ensure U = 1/2 kx² is correctly used, with consistent units (energy in joules). Confirm that the displacement used is the extension or compression from equilibrium, not the total length.
common_errors: Neglecting the 1/2 factor in the energy formula.
Using the wrong value for displacement (e.g., total length instead of extension).
Mismatched units for k and x leading to incorrect energy units.

rules.title: Check Sign Conventions for Forces and Displacement
rules.description: The sign convention for forces and displacements in Hooke's Law is critical. The restoring force opposes displacement, leading to a negative sign in F = -kx.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the direction of the restoring force is opposite to the direction of displacement and that the negative sign is correctly applied in F = -kx.
common_errors: Omitting the negative sign in Hooke's Law.
Incorrectly assigning force direction relative to displacement.

rules.title: Validate Material Properties Consistency
rules.description: Ensure the correct material constants (spring constant k, elastic modulus E, yield strength, etc.) are used and are consistent with the given material.
rules.check_logic: Cross-check the values of material constants with standard values provided or the context of the problem. Ensure that external factors like temperature or pressure are considered if they affect material properties.
common_errors: Using incorrect values for spring constants or modulus of elasticity.
Failing to account for temperature or other conditions affecting material properties.

rules.title: Verify Behavior Under Dynamic Loading
rules.description: Hooke's Law and elasticity principles assume static or quasi-static conditions. Under dynamic loading, additional factors like damping and resonance may need to be considered.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the problem context involves static or quasi-static conditions. If dynamic loading is present, verify that appropriate corrections (e.g., damping coefficients) are applied.
common_errors: Applying static elasticity principles to dynamic scenarios without considering additional effects.
Ignoring resonance or damping in dynamic systems.

rules.title: 均匀伸缩连续体动能建模
rules.description:
触发条件：物体均匀形变（应变 ε）且已知质量 m 和长度 L 求动能
检查逻辑：建立速度场 v(x) = x * (dε/dt)，其中 x 为距形变中心的距离，对 (1/2) * (m/L) * v(x)^2 dx 从 -L/2 到 L/2 积分。
rules.check_logic: 建立速度场 v(x) = x * (dε/dt)，其中 x 为距形变中心的距离，对 (1/2) * (m/L) * v(x)^2 dx 从 -L/2 到 L/2 积分。
