rules.check_logic: 必须拆解为两个阶段：1. 下球与地面碰撞速度反向；2. 速度向上的下球与速度向下的上球发生弹性碰撞。
rules.trigger: 出现“两球叠放”、“自由落体”、“与地面弹性碰撞”等描述时

rules.title: Correct spring-constant indexing for forces in a linear molecule (1D chain)
rules.description: This rule verifies that the Hookean force expressions (or equivalent equations of motion) for a linear chain of N masses m_i connected by N−1 springs with constants k_1...k_{N−1} are modeled with the correct spring-constant indexing and without double-counting at the endpoints. It expects the chain topology where spring k_j connects atom j to atom j+1, and no external springs or fixed supports. Checks: (1) For interior atoms i = 2...N−1, the force must be F_i = −k_{i−1}(x_i − x_{i−1}) − k_i(x_i − x_{i+1}) = k_{i−1} x_{i−1} − (k_{i−1}+k_i) x_i + k_i x_{i+1}. The rule flags if: (a) the same spring constant is used for both neighbors (e.g., F_i = −2 k_i x_i + k_i x_{i−1} + k_i x_{i+1}); (b) coeff(x_i) equals −2·k_i (or −2·k_{i−1}) instead of −(k_{i−1}+k_i); (c) coeff(x_{i−1}) equals k_i instead of k_{i−1}; (d) coeff(x_{i+1}) equals k_{i−1} instead of k_i. (2) For the first atom i = 1, the force must be F_1 = −k_1(x_1 − x_2) = −k_1 x_1 + k_1 x_2. The rule flags if: (a) an extra −k_1 x_1 term is added (double-counting), yielding −2 k_1 x_1 + k_1 x_2; (b) any term with k_0 or a second spring on atom 1 appears. (3) For the last atom i = N, the force must be F_N = −k_{N−1}(x_N − x_{N−1}) = −k_{N−1} x_N + k_{N−1} x_{N−1}. The rule flags if: (a) an extra −k_{N−1} x_N term is added (double-counting), yielding −2 k_{N−1} x_N + k_{N−1} x_{N−1}; (b) any term with k_N or a second spring on atom N appears. Implementation notes: Parse the user’s force/EOM expressions into linear combinations of x_{i−1}, x_i, x_{i+1} with coefficients that are symbolic functions of k_j. Compare coefficients to the expected pattern above; flag on any mismatch. This rule catches modeling errors where the left/right spring constants are incorrectly indexed or endpoint forces are double-counted.

rules.title: Misclassifying θ̈ ∝ sinθ·θ̇ (or θ·θ̇) as linear/SHM under small-angle approximation
rules.description: This rule verifies the correctness of linearization and classification of equations of motion that contain multiplicative state–velocity terms. It triggers if a solution derives or uses an equation of the form q̈ = k·f(q)·q̇ (common examples: θ̈ = k·sinθ·θ̇, θ̈ = k·cosθ·θ̇, ẍ = k·x·ẋ), and then: (a) applies small-angle/small-displacement approximations (e.g., sinθ ≈ θ, cosθ ≈ 1) and claims the resulting ODE is linear or first-order linear in the state, or (b) treats the system as simple harmonic motion (uses SHO terminology/solutions), or (c) solves it using linear time-invariant methods (e.g., assumes exponential/sinusoidal solutions with constant coefficients). The checker flags this because such equations remain nonlinear after small-angle approximations: products like q·q̇ or f(q)·q̇ are not linear in the dependent variable; linear ODEs cannot contain products of the state and its derivative, and their coefficients must depend at most on time. The rule also flags statements that interpret terms proportional to q̇ or q·q̇ as a restoring torque/force (implying oscillation) rather than (state-dependent) damping/anti-damping. Correct linearized second-order form near equilibrium must be q̈ + a(t) q̇ + b(t) q = g(t) with coefficients independent of q and q̇; any residual multiplicative q·q̇ indicates nonlinearity.

rules.title: Consistent small-oscillation linearization and constraint-respecting EOM
rules.description: This rule verifies that equations of motion (EOM) for constrained rolling or oscillating systems are derived consistently from a well-defined model and that the linearization to lowest order in small quantities is respected. The solution must: (1) start from a clear Lagrangian or Newton–Euler formulation with stated constraints (e.g., rolling without slipping, near-vertical plane, CM moving at approximately constant speed V) and show how the EOM follow (Euler–Lagrange or force/torque balance); (2) when the text states 'retain terms to the lowest order of small quantities,' include only first-order terms in the declared small variables and their derivatives; mixed products of small quantities (e.g., y·θ, ẏ·θ̇, θ̈·y) are considered higher order and must be omitted unless an explicit scaling argument is provided that makes such products first order; (3) avoid free-fall CM equations like ÿ = −g when constraints imply near-constant height or small oscillations about equilibrium—gravity must enter via potential energy leading to linear restoring terms, not an unbalanced constant acceleration; (4) ensure coefficients in the linearized EOM are time-invariant and depend only on parameters such as V, g, geometry, and inertias, consistent with the assumption of constant forward speed; and (5) prohibit ad hoc mixed terms or forms not traceable to the stated model. The rule flags solutions that present inconsistent EOM (e.g., ÿ = −g under near-vertical rolling) or include higher-order/mixed terms without derivation despite a claimed first-order linearization.

rules.title: Hydrostatic equilibrium must use local density (via dM/dr), not average interior density
rules.description: Checks spherically symmetric, self-gravitating fluid/gas solutions that employ hydrostatic equilibrium or Poisson/continuity relations. The rule requires that the local density ρ(r) be related to the cumulative mass M(r) by the mass-continuity relation dM/dr = 4π r^2 ρ(r). It flags as a modeling error any use of an average interior density (e.g., ρ(r) = 3 M(r) / (4π r^3) or any proportional form κ·M(r)/r^3) in local differential equations, such as dP/dr = −G M(r) ρ(r) / r^2 or ∇²Φ = 4π G ρ. Trigger conditions: (a) ρ(r) defined or substituted as M(r)/(volume inside r) when appearing in a local balance (hydrostatic equilibrium, Poisson equation, or virial integrals); (b) omission or violation of dM/dr = 4π r^2 ρ(r) when both M(r) and ρ(r) are used; (c) integration of the pressure gradient or potential with ρ(r) replaced by an average interior density. The correct usage requires ρ(r) = (1 / (4π r^2)) dM/dr. This rule catches and prevents nonlocal averaging in place of the required local density, which yields incorrect pressure profiles and energy relations.

rules.title: Missing loss-of-contact condition on curved surface (N=0 / v^2κ = g·n)
rules.description: This rule verifies that, in problems involving a particle constrained on a smooth curve z(y) under gravity (e.g., a parabolic bowl z = y^2/(2k)), the solution explicitly models loss of contact when the initial speed exceeds the critical value (v0 > vh or “critical speed” mentioned). The rule flags solutions that compute the maximum height using conservation of energy alone without introducing and using a detachment condition. Required checks: (1) The solution must state and use a loss-of-contact criterion: normal force N = 0, or equivalently that the required normal (centripetal) acceleration equals the normal component of gravity, such as v^2/R = g cos(α), v^2 κ = g / sqrt(1 + (z')^2), or N = m(g / sqrt(1 + (z')^2) − v^2 κ). Here κ is the curvature of the curve along the path, with an acceptable explicit form κ(y) = z''(y) / (1 + (z'(y))^2)^(3/2) and R = 1/κ; α is the local slope angle with tan(α) = z'(y) and cos(α) = 1 / sqrt(1 + (z')^2). (2) The detachment location y* must be determined by solving the loss-of-contact condition together with the speed along the surface (e.g., from energy: v(y)^2 = v0^2 − 2 g (z(y) − z0), for frictionless motion). (3) After detachment, the motion must be treated as free-flight (projectile) with initial state given by the tangent velocity at y*, and the maximum height must be computed from this ballistic phase. The rule flags an error if any of these elements are omitted or if the gravitational normal component is not projected correctly (e.g., missing the 1 / sqrt(1 + (z')^2) factor). This check is triggered by the presence of phrases like “v0 > vh”, “critical speed”, “loss of contact”, or by contexts where contact may be lost due to insufficient normal force, and it ensures that modeling accounts for the transition from constrained motion to free-flight.

rules.title: Lift/Magnus force must be perpendicular to free-stream
rules.description: This rule verifies the stated direction of the lift (Magnus) force for spinning bodies in a uniform flow. According to Kutta–Joukowski/Magnus effect, the lift force is perpendicular to the free-stream velocity (and perpendicular to drag). In problems where the free stream or translational motion is horizontal, the lift should be vertical. Flag as an error if a solution: (a) claims lift acts horizontally or along the flow, (b) includes lift in the horizontal force balance instead of the vertical balance, or (c) omits lift from the vertical force balance when a spinning body in a uniform flow is present. Typical trigger phrases include "lift acts horizontally", "Magnus force is horizontal", or vertical equilibrium written only as buoyancy equals weight while separately assigning lift to the horizontal direction.

rules.title: Declared mass must be used consistently in dynamics and energy
rules.description:
Checks that the mass specified in the problem statement is propagated consistently through all equations of motion and energy expressions.

What it enforces:
- Extract the declared mass expression M_decl from the prompt (e.g., "mass 2m", "mass M0", or a numeric value). If the mass is given as a scaled symbol (e.g., 2m), treat that entire expression as the mass.
- Kinetic energy: verify that any expression of the form T = (1/2)·(…)·v^2 uses (1/2)·M_decl as the coefficient of v^2 (including vector/multi-DOF forms). Flag if T = (1/2)·m·v^2 or any coefficient not equal to M_decl appears.
- Newton’s second law (all coordinate systems): verify that the mass multiplying acceleration is M_decl. Examples:
  - Cartesian: M_decl·a_x = F_x, M_decl·a_y = F_y, …
  - Polar: M_decl·(r¨ − r·θ˙^2) = F_r and M_decl·(r·θ¨ + 2·r˙·θ˙) = F_θ.
  - Momentum definitions: p = M_decl·v (and generalized momenta in Lagrangian formulations) must use M_decl.
- Lagrangian/Hamiltonian: L = T − V must use T with M_decl; Hamiltonian kinetic term must also use M_decl. Any use of a different mass symbol or missing scale factor is flagged.
- Late substitution patching: if derivations proceed with a different mass (e.g., m) and only at the end replace m → 2m without re-deriving intermediate steps, flag as inconsistent usage.

Allowed patterns:
- If the solution explicitly defines a new symbol and equates it to the declared mass early (e.g., "Let M = 2m" or "Let m (hereafter) denote the object’s mass = 2m0"), subsequent consistent use of that symbol passes.

Triggers typical of this error:
- Problem states mass is 2m, but equations use T = (1/2)·m·v^2, a = F/m, or m·(r¨ − r·θ˙^2) = F_r.
- Mismatch between mass used in radial/tangential equations and the specified mass.

Scope:
- Single-particle mechanics in any coordinate system; applies to Newtonian, Lagrangian, and Hamiltonian treatments.
- Excludes cases where reduced mass is explicitly introduced and correctly defined; if reduced mass is used, it must be explicitly tied to M_decl.

rules.title: Mass–Volume–Density Unit Consistency and Factor-of-10 Check
rules.description: This rule verifies that a computed mass for a rectangular object (e.g., a microscope slide) is consistent with its density and geometric dimensions, and flags common factor-of-10 errors caused by incorrect unit conversion or decimal placement. The verifier should: (1) Extract density ρ, length L, width W, and thickness t used by the student; ensure all dimensions are converted to SI units (meters), with particular attention to millimeters (1 mm = 1×10^-3 m) and micrometers. (2) Compute the SI volume V_ref = L·W·t. (3) Compute the expected mass m_ref = ρ·V_ref. (4) If the student provides a mass m_student or uses it implicitly (e.g., via F_g = m g), infer m_student and compute the ratio r = m_student / m_ref. (5) Flag an error if r deviates significantly from 1 and is indicative of a decimal slip: r ∈ [8,12] or r ∈ [0.08,0.12] (±20% tolerance around a factor of 10). Optionally, flag if r ∈ [80,120] or [0.008,0.012] to catch ×100 errors. (6) Also check that downstream quantities (e.g., gravitational force mg, viscous balance) use a consistent mass; if the inferred mass from mg differs from m_ref by the same factor ranges, flag the propagation. This rule targets errors where volume or unit conversion (e.g., treating 0.80 mm as 0.008 m instead of 0.0008 m) leads to a mass off by one order of magnitude, which then contaminates subsequent numeric results.

rules.title: Mass flow rate must include velocity; detect conflation of specific volume with velocity
rules.description: This rule verifies correct application of the continuity equation for steady 1D flow and checks for notation conflation between velocity and specific volume. It inspects any derived expression for mass flow rate μ and enforces that μ = ρ A v_vel, where v_vel is the flow velocity and A is cross-sectional area. If density is expressed via specific volume ν (units m^3/kg), the expression must be μ = A v_vel / ν. The rule flags as errors: (1) μ expressions missing a velocity factor (e.g., μ = ρ A or μ = A/ν), (2) μ expressed with a symbol v that has been defined as specific volume (m^3/kg) but used as velocity in μ = ρ A v, or vice versa, (3) any μ expression that is dimensionally inconsistent with kg/s (e.g., m^2/(m^3/kg) = kg/m). The rule specifically detects cases where the same symbol (commonly 'v') is declared as 'specific volume' and later used as 'velocity', or where ρ = 1/ν is substituted and the velocity term is dropped, yielding μ = A/ν. It requires distinct symbols or unambiguous unit annotations for velocity and specific volume and performs a dimensional check to ensure the final μ has units of mass per time.

rules.title: Misuse of Newton’s second law on massless connectors and improper pulley coupling
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that treat massless, inextensible connectors (rope or spring segments) as independent dynamical elements by applying Newton’s second law to them or by assigning them an 'effective mass'. Typical erroneous forms include equations like T − kx = m_eff * a, T1 − kx = m_eff * y¨, T2 − 2kx = m_eff * y¨, or equating a spring force directly to a pulley inertia term such as kx = (I/R^2) * y¨ (e.g., kx = (1/2) M * y¨). For a massless rope segment, F = m a does not apply with nonzero m; tension along any straight massless segment is uniform, and the net force on such a segment must be zero. Any tension difference can only arise across a rotating pulley and must be related through the torque equation I * α = (T2 − T1) * R with the kinematic constraint α = a/R (no slip). Valid equations of motion should be written for massive components (e.g., the bar: sum of external forces = m_bar * y¨) and for the pulley via torque balance, not for the rope/spring segments themselves. The rule triggers if the solution assigns mass or effective mass to the rope/spring, applies F = m a to rope segments, or bypasses the torque relation by directly tying spring force to the pulley’s rotational inertia.

rules.title: Disallow constant-acceleration modeling in mass–spring systems with applied force
rules.description:
This rule checks solutions for incorrect modeling of a mass attached to a linear spring (Hooke's law) when a constant external force is applied. Specifically, it flags cases where the acceleration is treated as constant (e.g., a = F/m) or kinematic equations for uniform acceleration are used, while the spring is engaged. The correct equation of motion during the forcing interval is m*x'' = F - k*x (or equivalently x'' + (k/m) x = F/m), implying acceleration depends on displacement and is not constant.

The rule triggers when:
- The problem context includes a spring with constant k connected to the moving mass, and an external force F acts along the spring axis for a finite time.
- The solution asserts a = F/m, uses F = m a with only the applied force F (omitting the spring force -k x), or applies constant-acceleration kinematic formulas (e.g., x = x0 + v0 t + 0.5 a t^2, v = v0 + a t) during a period where the spring is stretched/compressed.

Expected correct modeling:
- Include the spring force in the net force: m*x'' = F - k*x during the forcing interval, and m*x'' + k*x = 0 after the force is removed, with continuity of x and v at the switch.
- Recognize the shifted equilibrium x_eq = F/k and that the motion under constant F is oscillatory about x_eq, not uniformly accelerated.

Allowed exceptions (must be explicitly justified in the solution):
- k = 0 (no spring), or the spring is slack/not engaged so -k x = 0 throughout the interval.
- A limiting argument confined to an infinitesimal time where x ≈ 0 and the spring force is rigorously demonstrated negligible; this cannot be used to determine a finite duration.

Detection patterns to flag:
- Statements like "a = F/m" without a spring term in a spring–mass context.
- Use of phrases "constant acceleration" or "uniform acceleration" for the forced motion with a spring present.
- Application of constant-acceleration kinematics while k ≠ 0 and displacement is nonzero.

If any flagged pattern appears without a valid exception, the solution fails this rule.

rules.title: Improper assumption of constant-speed circular turn under bounded acceleration when minimizing time
rules.description: Checks for solutions to minimum-time direction-change problems with a magnitude-limited horizontal force/acceleration (e.g., friction μg) that incorrectly constrain the motion to a constant-speed circular arc (purely normal/centripetal acceleration). Triggers if: (1) the problem asks for minimum time (or time-optimal) to change direction with initial and final speeds specified and a bound on available force/acceleration, and (2) the solution assumes speed is constant throughout the maneuver and/or states that friction provides only centripetal acceleration, and (3) the solution uses circular-motion relations such as a_c = v^2/R, ω = a/v, R = v^2/a, s = RΔθ, or t = Δθ/ω to compute the time. Such modeling is suboptimal because with a norm-bounded acceleration, the time-optimal strategy is to use the full available acceleration with both tangential and normal components to change the velocity vector directly in velocity space (straight-line Δv at rate |a|max), allowing speed to vary during the maneuver and only matching the required final speed at the end. The rule flags: mentions of 'centripetal acceleration' or 'circular arc' combined with 'constant speed' for a minimum-time reorientation; calculations that enforce a_t = 0 or equate friction solely to centripetal demand; time computed as t = (Δθ) v / |a|max or via R = v^2/|a|max without demonstrating optimality. The rule expects acknowledgment that the acceleration direction is a free control up to its magnitude limit and that using tangential components can reduce time; typical correct reasoning references Δv magnitude (e.g., t_min = ||v_final − v_initial|| / |a|max) rather than constant-speed circular motion.

rules.title: Unjustified parameter assignment in collision/energy models
rules.description: This rule checks for the introduction of specific parameter values or modeling assumptions that are not supported by the problem statement or by prior derivations. It scans the solution for first-use assignments of key physical parameters—such as masses, coefficient of restitution e, collision type (elastic/inelastic), friction presence, or geometric constraints—and verifies that each assignment is either (a) explicitly stated in the problem, or (b) logically derived from previously established equations/constraints. The rule flags: (1) assuming equal masses (m1 = m2) without textual evidence; (2) assigning a numeric value to e (e.g., e = sqrt(1/2)) without justification; (3) declaring collisions as 'elastic' while using e < 1, or otherwise mixing inconsistent collision models; (4) any numeric substitution for undefined parameters that affects quantitative outcomes (e.g., number of collisions, energy loss percentage, velocities). It further ensures that if an answer depends on an unspecified parameter, the solution keeps the parameter symbolic and expresses results in terms of that parameter or explicitly states the need for additional data. Violations are raised when the solution’s conclusions (e.g., maximum collision count under a 40% energy-loss cap) rely on arbitrarily chosen or unsupported parameter values.

rules.title: Moment of inertia for a thin square wire frame about an in-plane central axis (through midpoints of opposite sides)
rules.description: Checks that when a solution models a homogeneous thin square wire frame (perimeter loop) of mass m and side length l rotating about a smooth axis lying in the plane of the frame and passing through the midpoints of two opposite sides, the moment of inertia used is I = (1/6) m l^2. Rationale: the two sides parallel to the axis contribute (m/4)(l/2)^2 each (total m l^2/8), and the two sides perpendicular to the axis contribute 2 × [ (m/(4l)) ∫_{-l/2}^{l/2} y^2 dy ] = m l^2/24, summing to m l^2/6. The rule triggers if, under these geometric conditions, the solution uses incorrect inertia values such as m l^2/8 (counting only the parallel sides), m l^2/12 (solid plate value or misapplied rod formula), m l^2/24 (counting only the perpendicular sides), or any other coefficient not equal to 1/6 within algebraic equivalence. Preconditions to apply: text indicates a square wire frame (loop, perimeter, slender sides) with uniform mass distribution; axis is in the plane of the frame and passes through the midpoints of two opposite sides (i.e., along the line joining those midpoints). Exceptions: do not apply if the object is a solid plate, if the axis is out of plane, through a vertex, through the center perpendicular to the plane, or otherwise differs from the stated geometry. The verifier should extract the used I expression and compare its coefficient with 1/6; if mismatch beyond minor symbolic algebra, flag and report that the correct inertia for this geometry is I = (1/6) m l^2.

rules.title: Moment of inertia for two point masses connected by a massless rod
rules.description: When the system is explicitly described as two identical point masses m connected by a rigid rod of length ℓ whose mass is negligible, and rotation is about the center of mass around an axis perpendicular to the rod, the correct moment of inertia is I = m ℓ^2 / 2 (equivalently, I = 2 m (ℓ/2)^2 or I = μ ℓ^2 with μ = m/2). The verifier should flag solutions that: (1) use uniform-rod formulas such as I = (1/12) M ℓ^2 (about the rod’s center) or I = (1/3) M ℓ^2 (about an end), (2) include the rod’s mass in I despite the rod being stated as massless, or (3) give any expression for I proportional to m ℓ^2 with a coefficient different from 1/2 when m denotes the mass of each point particle. This rule targets modeling errors where the inertia of a point-mass dipole is incorrectly replaced by that of a continuous rod.

rules.title: Correct moment of inertia for square wire frame about in-plane central axis
rules.description: This rule verifies the moment of inertia used for a homogeneous square wire frame (loop) of side length l and total mass m, rotating about an axis lying in the plane of the frame that passes through the center (through the midpoints of two opposite sides) and is parallel to one side. For this geometry, the correct moment of inertia is I = (m l^2) / 6. Derivation (for reference): model the frame as four slender rods of mass m/4 each; two rods parallel to the axis each contribute (m/4)(l/2)^2 = m l^2 /16, totaling m l^2 /8; two rods perpendicular to the axis each contribute (m/4)(l^2/12) = m l^2 /48, totaling m l^2 /24; sum = m l^2 (1/8 + 1/24) = m l^2 /6. The verifier should: (1) Trigger when the solution describes a square wire frame/loop with uniform mass on the sides and an in-plane axis through the midpoints of opposite sides (or equivalently, an axis through the center parallel to one side). (2) Check the moment of inertia value used for rotational dynamics. (3) Flag a calculation error if the solution uses any k != 1/6 in I = k m l^2, especially common incorrect values such as 1/3 (rod about end), 1/12 (single rod about center), 1/8, or values appropriate to a solid plate instead of a wire frame. (4) Optionally cross-check downstream results: if the linearized equation of motion or natural frequency ω uses the incorrect I (e.g., producing a factor of 3 instead of 6 in coefficients proportional to BI/m for this setup), flag the result as inconsistent with I = m l^2 / 6. The rule does not apply to solid square plates or to axes not in the plane or not through the center.

topics.name: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.title: Verify rotational kinetic energy formula
rules.description: The rotational kinetic energy is given by the formula: KE_rot = (1/2)Ic9�b2, where I is the moment of inertia and c9 is the angular velocity. This equation applies to rigid bodies in rotation about a fixed axis.

tags.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.check_logic: Ensure that the rotational kinetic energy is calculated using KE_rot = (1/2)Ic9�b2, and verify that I (moment of inertia) and c9 (angular velocity) are correctly identified, calculated, and used.
common_errors: Forgetting the (1/2) factor in the equation
Using linear velocity (v) instead of angular velocity (c9)
Incorrectly calculating or omitting the moment of inertia (I)

rules.title: Apply the parallel axis theorem correctly
rules.description: The parallel axis theorem states that I_total = I_cm + Md�b2, where I_cm is the moment of inertia about the center of mass, M is the mass of the object, and d is the distance from the axis of rotation to the center of mass.

tags.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.check_logic: Verify if the moment of inertia for an axis not passing through the center of mass is calculated using the parallel axis theorem. Ensure accurate values for d (distance) and M (mass) are used, and confirm that I_cm is correctly determined.
common_errors: Omitting the Md�b2 term when shifting the axis of rotation
Using the wrong distance (d) between the center of mass and the rotation axis
Confusing I_cm with I about the given axis

rules.title: Check perpendicular axis theorem application
rules.description: The perpendicular axis theorem states that for a planar object, I_z = I_x + I_y, where I_z is the moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to the plane, and I_x and I_y are about axes in the plane. This is valid only for thin, planar objects.

tags.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.check_logic: Ensure the perpendicular axis theorem is applied only to thin, planar objects. Verify that I_x and I_y are correctly calculated and summed to determine I_z, and confirm that the axes intersect at a single point.
common_errors: Applying the theorem to non-planar or 3D objects
Incorrectly summing I_x and I_y
Using the theorem when axes do not intersect at a single point

rules.title: Verify units of moment of inertia
rules.description: The moment of inertia (I) has the SI unit kg�b7m�b2, derived from the formula I = a mr�b2, where m is the mass and r is the distance. Consistency of units is critical in calculations.

tags.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.check_logic: Confirm that the final unit of I is kg�b7m�b2. Verify that all inputs (mass in kilograms, distance in meters) are in correct units, and ensure that the distance is squared (r�b2) when summing terms in I.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for mass or distance
Failing to square the distance (r�b2) when summing terms in I
Using inconsistent units (e.g., grams instead of kilograms)

rules.title: Check rotational energy conservation
rules.description: Rotational energy is conserved if there are no external torques acting on the system. This applies to isolated systems or systems with purely conservative internal forces.

tags.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.check_logic: Verify if external torques are zero. If yes, ensure the total rotational energy remains constant over time. Confirm that friction or other non-conservative forces are absent.
common_errors: Ignoring external torques that do work on the system
Assuming rotational energy conservation in the presence of friction
Confusing conservation of rotational energy with conservation of angular momentum

rules.title: Ensure correct sign convention for torque
rules.description: Torque (c4) is defined as c4 = r �d F = rFsin�3b8, where the direction is determined using the right-hand rule. Positive torque typically corresponds to counterclockwise rotation, and negative torque to clockwise rotation.

tags.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.check_logic: Confirm that the torque sign is determined using the right-hand rule and is consistent with the chosen coordinate system. Verify that the angle �3b8 is correctly used in c4 = rFsin�3b8.
common_errors: Reversing the sign convention for clockwise and counterclockwise torques
Neglecting the angle �3b8 in c4 = rFsin�3b8
Forgetting to use the cross product properly

rules.title: Verify geometric constraints in rotational systems
rules.description: In rotational mechanics, constraints like fixed radii or rigid body rotations must be respected. For example, all points on a rigid rotating disk have the same angular velocity but different linear velocities.

tags.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.check_logic: Ensure that angular velocity (c9) is constant across the rigid body and that linear velocity (v = rc9) is calculated appropriately for different points. Confirm that rigid body assumptions are not violated.
common_errors: Assuming linear velocity is the same for all points on a rigid body
Failing to account for the dependency of linear velocity on radius (v = rc9)
Applying non-rigid body assumptions to rigid systems

rules.title: Perform dimensional analysis for rotational energy equations
rules.description: The equations for rotational energy and moment of inertia must be dimensionally consistent. For example, KE_rot = (1/2)Ic9�b2 should result in units of energy (kg�b7m�b2/s�b2).

tags.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.check_logic: Verify that each term in the rotational energy equation has compatible dimensions, and the final result has dimensions of energy (kg�b7m�b2/s�b2). Ensure that I and c9 are expressed in consistent units.
common_errors: Omitting or miscalculating the square of c9 in KE_rot = (1/2)Ic9�b2
Using inconsistent units for I or c9
Failing to check that the final energy has units of kg�b7m�b2/s�b2

rules.title: Verify angular momentum conservation
rules.description: Angular momentum is conserved in a system if there are no external torques acting on it. This principle applies to both rigid bodies and systems of particles.

tags.topic: Moment of Inertia and Rotational Energy

rules.check_logic: Ensure that external torques are zero. If so, verify that the total angular momentum (L = Ic9) remains constant over time. Check that changes in I or c9 are consistent with conservation.
common_errors: Ignoring external torques that affect angular momentum
Assuming angular momentum conservation in the presence of friction or other non-conservative forces
Failing to account for changes in I or c9 when analyzing the system

rules.title: Zero-momentum final state assumed with nonzero initial momentum
rules.description: This rule detects kinematic models that violate linear momentum conservation by assuming a final state with zero total momentum (e.g., products "at rest relative to each other" or a "single system at rest") while the initial state has nonzero net momentum. The verifier scans for: (1) an initial beam/target description where only one incoming particle carries momentum (e.g., a beam particle with momentum p_b and a stationary target), yielding nonzero initial total momentum; and (2) a final state described as having zero net momentum without any additional outgoing particles, recoil body, radiation, external field, or other momentum sink. If both conditions are present, the rule flags a modeling error because an isolated system cannot reduce nonzero momentum to zero. The rule also flags inconsistent particle bookkeeping where a named particle is used as the stationary initial target and simultaneously declared as part of a final bound composite at rest without specifying a mechanism that carries away the excess momentum. Exemptions: the rule does not trigger if the initial total momentum is explicitly zero (e.g., equal and opposite beams) or if an external agent or additional products are clearly identified to take the recoil. This rule is particularly applied to threshold/kinematics derivations; a correct setup must use a well-defined multi-particle initial state and conserve total four-momentum in all frames.

rules.title: Mass transfer between coaxial rotors must use angular-momentum flux and constant source speed
rules.description:
This rule verifies modeling in problems where mass is transferred from one rotating body (A) to another (B) via ejection through holes, with flight time neglected and no external torques. The correct approach is: (1) treat the source rotor’s angular velocity as constant (ω_A(t) = ω_0) unless an explicit, correctly computed tangential torque on A is present; (2) determine the target rotor’s motion from the angular-momentum influx carried by the transferred mass. The verifier checks for the following:

- Context detection: two coaxial rotors; mass initially on A is ejected at rate k and sticks to B; time of flight ignored; no external torque stated.
- Source rotor modeling: flag if the solution makes ω_A(t) an unknown function or varies ω_A(t) without introducing and correctly evaluating a nonzero torque on A. Under the given assumptions, ω_A(t) must remain ω_0.
- Momentum-flux relation: require that the angular momentum delivered to B satisfies L_in(t) = ∫_0^t k a^2 ω_A(τ) dτ. With ω_A(τ) = ω_0, this reduces to L_in(t) = k t a^2 ω_0, valid only for t ≤ M_0/k. Flag if this flux is missing or replaced by an ad hoc differential relation not derived from the mass flux and sticking condition.
- Target rotor inertia and solution form: require I_B(t) = I_B0 + b^2 m_s(t), with m_s(t) = k t and I_B0 matching the cylinder model (solid: (1/2) M_b b^2; thin hoop: M_b b^2). Enforce I_B(t) ω_B(t) = L_in(t), which yields ω_B(t) = (a^2/b^2) [k t / (I_B0/b^2 + k t)] ω_0 (for t ≤ M_0/k). Flag if the solution instead tries to determine both ω_A(t) and ω_B(t) from a single global conservation equation I_A(t) ω_A(t) + I_B(t) ω_B(t) = const without a correct momentum-flux balance, or if it assumes rigid coupling between A and B.
- Boundary and consistency checks: verify inclusion of the transfer window t ≤ M_0/k; check limiting behavior consistent with the above expression.

The rule is triggered by any of the following: introducing ω_A(t) as an unknown without torque analysis, using only a global angular-momentum conservation to solve for two unknown angular velocities, or omitting the explicit angular-momentum flux to B proportional to k a^2 ω_0.

rules.title: Unbounded velocity growth from internal collisions (momentum conservation violation)
rules.description: Trigger when a solution for an isolated multi-body system (e.g., slider + box) undergoing repeated internal collisions asserts that one body’s velocity after the n-th collision grows linearly with n or by a fixed increment per collision (patterns like u_n = n*c, u_n = u_0 + n*Δu, or textual claims such as "the box’s velocity increases by e v0 each time") without any external impulse. For closed systems with finite masses and coefficient of restitution e in [0,1], total momentum must remain constant. Therefore, per-collision updates must satisfy m1*v1_n + m2*v2_n = constant for all n. If the proposed sequence implies |m1*v1_n + m2*v2_n| depends on n (e.g., grows unbounded as n increases), flag the step as a momentum conservation violation. This rule is intended to catch reasoning that accumulates a constant velocity increment per collision, leading to unphysical momentum growth (such as u_n = n*e*v0), especially in analyses of repeated collisions inside a box or between coupled bodies where all interactions are internal.

rules.title: Momentum sign convention and mass positivity in 1D inelastic impacts
rules.description: This rule validates conservation of linear momentum setups for co-linear (1D) perfectly inelastic impacts (e.g., missile warhead + satellite). It checks for physically impossible outcomes that typically arise from incorrect sign conventions or using speeds instead of signed velocities. The verifier should: (1) Require all masses and any solved mass ratio (m, M, m/M) to be nonnegative; flag if m < 0, M < 0, or m/M < 0. (2) If a post-impact velocity v_f is computed from a momentum equation, verify that v_f lies between the two pre-impact velocities v1 and v2: min(v1, v2) ≤ v_f ≤ max(v1, v2). Equivalently, |v_f| ≤ max(|v1|, |v2|). Flag if v_f is outside this range (e.g., v_f greater than both pre-impact speeds), which indicates misassigned velocity directions. (3) Detect use of magnitudes in place of signed velocities in the linear momentum equation—e.g., forms like m·|v1| + M·|v2| = (m+M)·|v_f| or any use of v^2 in a momentum balance—and flag as erroneous. This rule catches cases where algebra yields negative mass values or unbounded final speeds due to incorrect momentum setup and direction handling.

rules.title: Incorrect use of momentum/COM conservation under external horizontal friction
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that apply conservation of total linear momentum or a fixed center-of-mass (COM) condition to a chosen system while the problem explicitly introduces external horizontal forces (e.g., slab–ground friction, velocity-proportional drag). Detection criteria: (1) The problem or the solution text indicates nonzero external horizontal friction/drag acting on the system (phrases like "with friction", "friction proportional to velocity", or any external horizontal force on the slab). (2) The solution asserts momentum conservation or COM invariance for the same system, e.g., statements such as "no external horizontal force", "total momentum conserved", "p_final = p_initial", "dp/dt = 0", "COM stays fixed", or uses relations like m*x_child + M*x_slab = constant (often set to 0) to determine displacements/velocities. (3) The solution reuses frictionless COM-based results (e.g., deriving slab displacement from m*x_child + M*x_slab = const together with a relative displacement constraint) in a frictional case, or concludes the same displacement as the frictionless case without modeling the external impulse F_ext or COM equation M_total*a_COM = F_ext. Exception: Do not flag if the solution explicitly expands the system to include the Earth/ground and accounts for the Earth's momentum/impulse or motion (i.e., external impulse is modeled within an enlarged isolated system). The rule is intended to catch logical inconsistencies such as using COM constraints derived for isolated systems in scenarios where external friction is present.

rules.title: Equate object and moving boundary positions in impact problems
rules.description: This rule verifies correct modeling of contact time when an object detaches from a moving/accelerating system (e.g., an elevator) and later contacts a part of that system (floor/ceiling). The impact time must be obtained by equating the inertial-frame positions of the object and the moving boundary: y_obj(t) = y_bound(t), where y_obj(t) = y0_obj + v0_obj*t + 0.5*a_obj*t^2 and y_bound(t) = y0_bound + v_platform*t + 0.5*a_platform*t^2. Alternatively, in the accelerating platform frame, the relative motion must use initial relative velocity v_rel0 = 0 and include the pseudo-acceleration: a_rel = g − a_platform (with consistent sign convention), so for an upward-accelerating platform the magnitude is g + a_platform; the drop across a fixed internal gap H is H = v_rel0*t + 0.5*a_rel*t^2 = 0.5*(g + a_platform)*t^2. Flag solutions that: (a) treat the boundary as stationary in space by setting the object's displacement equal to the initial gap H (e.g., y_obj(t*) = −H) without modeling y_bound(t); (b) compute time using only free-fall distance H = 0.5*g*t^2 or y = v0*t − 0.5*g*t^2 when the platform has nonzero velocity/acceleration; (c) in the platform frame, omit the pseudo-acceleration or use an incorrect sign/magnitude for a_rel (e.g., using g − a_platform for an upward-accelerating platform without proper sign handling); (d) produce different impact times in different frames. The verifier should check for inclusion of boundary motion terms (v_platform*t and 0.5*a_platform*t^2) or, equivalently, the correct relative-acceleration formulation. Absence or mis-signing of these elements indicates the error.

rules.title: Missing inter-contact forces in equilibrium of multi-contact rods
rules.description:
This rule checks solutions for rigid bodies with multiple contacts (ground, wall, and an inter-rod contact with friction) to ensure all contact forces are included in force and torque balances. Trigger conditions:
- The problem statement specifies a contact between two rods with a given friction coefficient (μ_c). If the solution does not introduce variables for both the normal and tangential (friction) components at this inter-rod contact, flag an error.
- Vertical force balance for a rod sets the ground normal equal to the weight (e.g., N_A = mg) while the setup includes any potential vertical interaction at the inter-rod contact; such an equation indicates omission of vertical components from the inter-rod force.
- Horizontal force balance equates wall normal to ground friction (e.g., N_B = f_A) without accounting for horizontal components from the inter-rod contact force.
- Torque balance about a contact point yields a wall reaction of the form N_wall = (mg cos θ)/(2 sin θ) (or structurally similar ratios involving only mg and geometry), with no terms arising from the inter-rod contact force; this indicates missing torque contributions.
- Final angle/inequality conditions (e.g., cot θ ≤ k μ_A or cot α ≤ k μ_A for some constant k) that do not involve μ_c are flagged, since the inter-rod friction coefficient must influence the equilibrium condition.
The rule is intended to catch incorrect torque relations and force balances that arise from omitting contact forces and misapplying geometry in multi-contact equilibrium problems.

rules.title: Incorrect neutral-buoyancy assumption with dynamic lift/pressure forces
rules.description: Flags solutions that enforce neutral buoyancy (Fb = Mg or ρV = M) to obtain vertical equilibrium when the problem context includes rotation/motion that implies additional vertical forces (e.g., Magnus lift or pressure-difference forces) and when given parameters make neutral buoyancy numerically false. Check for any of the following in the solution: (a) explicit equations Fb = Mg, ρVg = Mg, or ρV = M; (b) textual claims such as "neutrally buoyant" or "buoyancy balances weight" used to justify horizontal motion. Then: 1) If the problem provides mass M, fluid density ρ, and object volume V (or geometry sufficient to compute V), compute M_nb = ρV. If |M - M_nb|/M > 5%, flag the solution as a modeling error for assuming neutral buoyancy inconsistent with data. 2) If the setup mentions spinning/rotation, Magnus effect, or "do not neglect pressure differences," require the vertical force balance to include a dynamic lift/pressure term L_v: Fb + L_v - Mg = 0. If the solution omits L_v in the vertical force balance (i.e., uses Fb = Mg) or misclassifies lift as purely horizontal when vertical equilibrium is required, flag the solution. This rule is intended to catch detours that simplify by neutral buoyancy instead of correctly balancing buoyancy plus lift against weight.

topics.name: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.title: Verify Correct Form of Newton's Second Law
rules.description: Newton's Second Law states that the sum of the forces acting on an object must equal the mass of the object times its acceleration (ΣF = ma). This fundamental equation applies to any object with mass under the influence of forces.

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: Ensure that the sum of forces is expressed as ΣF = ma, where 'm' is the object's mass and 'a' is its acceleration. Verify that all forces acting on the object are included in the summation.
common_errors: Mistaking weight for mass
Incorrectly isolating the acceleration component
Missing force components in the sum

rules.title: Ensure Consistent Sign Convention in Coordinate Systems
rules.description: Whenever forces and accelerations are resolved into components along coordinate axes (e.g., x, y), it is essential to maintain consistent sign conventions (e.g., right and up are positive).

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: Verify that forces and accelerations align with the chosen coordinate system sign conventions throughout the problem. Ensure that the positive and negative directions are clearly defined and consistently applied.
common_errors: Inconsistent sign usage for forces along different axes
Not defining the positive direction
Switching axes without redefining direction

rules.title: Check Vertical Geometric Constraints
rules.description: Geometric constraints can enforce conditions like an object must remain on a surface. For vertical scenarios, tension in a rope or normal force on a surface typically counteracts weight.

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: Ensure that the normal force or tension balances vertical forces as per the defined constraint (e.g., no net vertical acceleration if stationary on a surface). Verify that the forces satisfy the geometric constraints of the problem.
common_errors: Neglect of normal forces when an object is on a surface
Incorrect calculation of tension
Ignoring constraints like fixed surfaces or ropes

rules.title: Confirm Conditions for Newton's Laws Application
rules.description: Newton's Laws can only be applied in inertial frames of reference where no acceleration or rotation affects the observer, and forces must be real at macroscopic scale.

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: Check if the problem defines or implies an inertial reference frame. If the frame is non-inertial, ensure pseudo-forces are included to account for the effects of acceleration or rotation.
common_errors: Applying laws without considering inertial frames
Forgetting to account for pseudo-forces in non-inertial reference frames
Misidentifying the frame of reference

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency for Forces
rules.description: In mechanics, forces must be measured in units consistent with mass times acceleration (e.g., Newtons in SI units). Dimensional analysis ensures all terms in an equation balance correctly.

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: Verify that all force and acceleration terms have units consistent with Newtons (kg·m/s²) in SI. Ensure that unit conversions, if any, are correctly applied.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for mass or acceleration
Inconsistent unit usage among different force components
Forgetting to convert units when necessary

rules.title: Check Action-Reaction Force Pairs
rules.description: Newton's Third Law states that for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction, meaning forces always occur in pairs between two interacting bodies.

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: Verify that every force has a corresponding equal and opposite reaction force, typically between two interacting bodies in isolation. Ensure that the forces act on different objects and are of the same magnitude but opposite in direction.
common_errors: Forgetting to include or identify reaction forces
Misidentifying action-reaction force pairs
Confusing internal forces with action-reaction pairs

rules.title: Differentiate Between External and Internal Forces
rules.description: For solving and analyzing systems with Newton's Laws, it's crucial to identify external forces acting on a system as distinct from internal forces acting among components in the system.

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: Differentiate and correctly label external forces versus internal forces in system analysis. Ensure that only external forces are included in the equations of motion for the system as a whole.
common_errors: Confusing internal with external forces
Neglecting to include external forces in equations of motion
Incorrectly summing internal forces in system-level analysis

rules.title: Analyze Friction Forces
rules.description: Frictional forces oppose the relative motion or tendency of motion between two surfaces in contact. Static friction prevents motion up to a maximum value, while kinetic friction acts during motion.

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: Verify that frictional forces are correctly identified and calculated using the appropriate coefficients of friction (static or kinetic). Ensure that static friction does not exceed its maximum value (μsN).
common_errors: Using the wrong coefficient of friction
Exceeding the maximum static friction force
Neglecting frictional forces in the analysis

rules.title: Verify Net Force for Equilibrium
rules.description: For an object in equilibrium, the net force acting on it must be zero. This applies to both static equilibrium (no motion) and dynamic equilibrium (constant velocity).

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: Ensure that the sum of all forces acting on the object is zero in both the horizontal and vertical directions. Verify that there is no net acceleration.
common_errors: Forgetting to include all forces in the summation
Incorrectly resolving forces into components
Assuming equilibrium without verifying net force

rules.title: 平方阻力运动方程标准化
rules.description:
触发条件：物体在恒定重力场中受与速度平方成正比的阻力（f = kv^2）
检查逻辑：检查运动方程是否形如 dv/dt = g - (k/m)v^2，并确认其解析解是否包含 tanh 函数形式。

tags.topic: Newton's Laws and Free Body Diagrams

rules.check_logic: 检查运动方程是否形如 dv/dt = g - (k/m)v^2，并确认其解析解是否包含 tanh 函数形式。

rules.title: Misapplication of wall boundary conditions at non-boundary locations
rules.description: Flag solutions that enforce impermeable-wall boundary conditions (no-penetration: v·n = 0) at points not on the wall. The no-penetration condition must be satisfied on the wall surface(s) only; it does not constrain the velocity at interior points or at singularities (e.g., vortex filaments) that are merely near the walls. In method-of-images arguments, images are chosen to enforce v·n = 0 on the boundary; this does not imply that the velocity at the real filament/source has zero normal components relative to the walls. Trigger when the solution claims statements such as 'the velocity components perpendicular to both walls are zero at the filament' or any equivalent inference applying wall boundary conditions at the filament or other interior locations. Also verify that superfluid/ideal flow boundary treatment distinguishes no-penetration from no-slip (no-slip does not generally apply); only v·n = 0 on the wall should be enforced. The rule checks that boundary conditions are applied on the correct geometric set (the boundary surfaces), not at interior points unless the object is explicitly at the boundary.

rules.title: Check node/antinode positions for fixed-right, driven-left string (steady-state)
rules.description:
Applies to a taut 1D string of length L with wave speed u, driven transversely at x=0 with y(0,t)=A0 cos(ω t), and fixed at x=L (y(L,t)=0), ignoring attenuation, in steady state. Expected spatial dependence is proportional to sin[k(L−x)] with k=ω/u, giving y(x,t)=A0 [sin(k(L−x))/sin(kL)] cos(ω t). Nodes satisfy sin[k(L−x)]=0 → x_n=L−nπ/k=L−nπu/ω (within 0≤x≤L). Antinodes satisfy k(L−x_a)=(2ℓ+1)π/2 → x_a=L−(2ℓ+1)π/(2k)=L−(2ℓ+1)πu/(2ω).
This rule flags: 
- Any classification that does not include x=L as a node, or that labels x=L as an antinode.
- Claims that x=0 is an antinode without qualifying resonance; x=0 is an antinode only if sin(kL)=±1 (i.e., kL=(2m+1)π/2). Otherwise, x=0 is neither a node nor necessarily an antinode of the standing-wave spatial factor.
- Node lists that follow x_n = nπu/ω or nπ/k anchored at x=0 (e.g., nodes at x=0, πu/ω, 2πu/ω, …) instead of x_n = L − nπu/ω anchored at the fixed end.
- Antinode lists that place antinodes at both ends (x=0 and x=L) or at x=0 and x=L simultaneously, which contradicts the fixed-end boundary.
- Use of a single traveling wave (e.g., y=A0 cos(ω t − kx) or setting only one of f or g nonzero) to infer standing-wave nodes/antinodes; the steady-state solution must be a superposition yielding the sin[k(L−x)] spatial factor and must satisfy both boundary conditions.
- Spatial forms like sin(kx) or cos(kx) that do not satisfy y(L,t)=0 and y(0,t)=A0 cos(ω t). Algebraically equivalent forms are allowed (e.g., sin[k(L−x)] ≡ sin(kL)cos(kx) − cos(kL)sin(kx)), but the implied node set must match x=L−nπu/ω and antinodes must match x=L−(2ℓ+1)πu/(2ω).
The verifier should: (1) parse the student’s standing-wave expression and check y(L,t)=0 and y(0,t)=A0 cos(ω t); (2) if node/antinode coordinates are provided, test whether they satisfy sin[k(L−x)]=0 and k(L−x)=(2ℓ+1)π/2 with k=ω/u; (3) flag if boundary classifications at x=0 or x=L are incorrect or if the node/antinode sequences are anchored at x=0 instead of x=L.

topics.name: Non-inertial Reference Frames and Pseudo Forces

rules.title: Apply pseudo force in non-inertial frames
rules.description: In a non-inertial reference frame, an additional pseudo force must be introduced to account for the observed motion. The pseudo force is given by F_pseudo = -m * a_frame, where m is the mass of the object and a_frame is the acceleration of the non-inertial frame.

tags.topic: Non-inertial Reference Frames and Pseudo Forces

rules.check_logic: Verify if a pseudo force has been correctly added with the magnitude (-m * a_frame) and direction (opposite to the frame's acceleration).
common_errors: Omitting the pseudo force in calculations.
Using incorrect magnitude or sign for the pseudo force.
Confusing the pseudo force direction with the frame acceleration direction.

rules.title: Modify Newton's second law in non-inertial frames
rules.description: Newton's second law (F_net = m * a) must be modified in a non-inertial reference frame by including the pseudo force. The equation becomes: F_net + F_pseudo = m * a_observed.

tags.topic: Non-inertial Reference Frames and Pseudo Forces

rules.check_logic: Ensure that the pseudo force is included in the net force equation, and the observed acceleration is used in calculations.
common_errors: Using the inertial acceleration instead of the observed acceleration.
Failing to add the pseudo force term in the net force equation.

rules.title: Ensure correct sign convention for pseudo force
rules.description: The pseudo force always acts opposite to the acceleration of the non-inertial reference frame. This sign convention must be adhered to for correct results.

tags.topic: Non-inertial Reference Frames and Pseudo Forces

rules.check_logic: Check if the pseudo force direction is opposite to the acceleration of the reference frame.
common_errors: Assigning the pseudo force in the same direction as the reference frame's acceleration.
Inconsistent application of sign conventions in calculations.

rules.title: Account for geometric constraints in non-inertial frames
rules.description: In problems involving non-inertial frames, any geometric constraints (e.g., objects on inclined planes, pendulum motion) must also include the effects of pseudo forces.

tags.topic: Non-inertial Reference Frames and Pseudo Forces

rules.check_logic: Verify that pseudo forces are included when analyzing forces and accelerations along constrained paths.
common_errors: Ignoring pseudo forces when applying geometric constraints.
Incorrect resolution of pseudo forces along the constrained directions.

rules.title: Include Coriolis force in rotating reference frames
rules.description: In rotating reference frames, the Coriolis force must be included. It is given by F_coriolis = -2m(ω × v), where ω is the angular velocity of the frame and v is the velocity of the object relative to the rotating frame.

tags.topic: Non-inertial Reference Frames and Pseudo Forces

rules.check_logic: Ensure that the Coriolis force is included with the correct magnitude and direction using the cross product formula.
common_errors: Forgetting to include the Coriolis force in rotating frames.
Using incorrect cross product order for ω and v.
Incorrectly calculating the magnitude or direction of the Coriolis force.

rules.title: Include centrifugal force in rotating reference frames
rules.description: In a rotating reference frame, the centrifugal force must be included. It is given by F_centrifugal = -mω²r, where r is the radial distance of the object from the axis of rotation.

tags.topic: Non-inertial Reference Frames and Pseudo Forces

rules.check_logic: Verify that the centrifugal force is included with the correct magnitude and direction (outward from the axis of rotation).
common_errors: Omitting the centrifugal force in rotating frames.
Using the wrong direction for the centrifugal force (should be radially outward).
Incorrectly calculating the radial distance or angular velocity.

rules.title: Ensure dimensional consistency in pseudo force equations
rules.description: In equations involving pseudo forces, ensure that all terms have consistent dimensions. For example, pseudo force should have units of force (e.g., Newtons in SI).

tags.topic: Non-inertial Reference Frames and Pseudo Forces

rules.check_logic: Check that the dimensions of all terms in the pseudo force equation are consistent (e.g., mass × acceleration results in force).
common_errors: Using incorrect units for mass or acceleration in pseudo force calculations.
Adding terms with inconsistent dimensions (e.g., mixing force and acceleration).

rules.title: Misuse of angular momentum conservation in non-central-force/constraint systems
rules.description: Flags solutions that assert conservation of angular momentum (e.g., "L is constant", "m r × v = const", or formulas like L = m v0 y0) about a fixed point or the 'center/vertex of a bowl' in problems where the forces are not central and the net external torque about that point is nonzero. Typical contexts include a particle sliding on a track/surface (parabolic bowl z = f(y), bead on wire/rail, rollercoaster) under uniform gravity and normal/contact forces. The rule triggers when: (1) the solution invokes angular momentum conservation to relate states at different positions without explicitly proving that the net external torque about a fixed inertial origin is zero; (2) the problem geometry lacks rotational symmetry about the claimed axis/origin (e.g., 2D track z = y^2/(2k)), and constraint/normal forces generally do not act along the radius to that origin; (3) gravity is present as a uniform field (g), which produces torque about arbitrary fixed points; (4) the solution uses expressions like L = m v r or L = m v0 y0 about an arbitrary origin to deduce speeds/heights. Exceptions: do not flag if the solution clearly identifies a fixed inertial origin and demonstrates zero net external torque about it (e.g., all forces are central to that origin), or if the conservation is applied to a system with true rotational symmetry and central forces. Guidance: In these track/bowl problems, mechanical energy (with appropriate constraint conditions) may be conserved if no dissipation is present, but angular momentum about an arbitrary fixed point is not.

rules.title: Enforce rolling-without-slipping and gyroscopic coupling in fast-rolling ring/disk models
rules.description: Scope: Any solution modeling a ring/hoop/wheel/disk rolling on a plane near upright orientation, especially with 'rolling without slipping', 'fast rolling', 'gyroscopic stability', or 'minimum speed for stability'. Checkpoints: 1) Nonholonomic rolling constraint: The solution must explicitly impose v_contact = 0 (no slip), or an equivalent velocity relation linking the center-of-mass velocity to angular velocities and orientation (e.g., v_cm = ω × r_contact→CM). Treating δx, y, θ, φ (or similar) as independent generalized coordinates without these velocity constraints is incorrect. 2) Translational–rotational coupling: The kinetic energy or kinematics must exhibit mixed terms arising from the rolling constraints (coupling between CM motion and rotations). A separable T = (1/2) m v_cm^2 + (1/2) I ω^2 with no cross-velocity terms, or equations of motion that decouple translation and rotation, should be flagged. 3) Gyroscopic terms in linearized EOM: For small oscillations about a steady rolling state, the linearized equations must contain skew-symmetric (gyroscopic) terms proportional to the steady speed or spin (e.g., terms linear in V, φ̇, or ω) that couple tilt and spin/yaw. Absence of such terms indicates missing nonholonomic coupling. 4) Frequency and stability dependence on speed: The small-oscillation frequency Ω and the stability criterion must depend on the steady speed V (or spin rate). If Ω is independent of V, or V_min is not obtained from the characteristic equation including gyroscopic terms, flag the solution. 5) Method: The derivation must use Lagrange–d'Alembert with nonholonomic constraints or correctly substitute the rolling kinematic relations into velocities before forming T and the equations of motion; applying unconstrained Euler–Lagrange on independent variables for this system is a modeling error. The verifier should flag solutions failing any of these checks.

rules.title: Incorrect static vertical force balance during rotating rod motion
rules.description: Checks for the misuse of static vertical force balance (e.g., N = mg or N = mg cosθ) in problems where a rigid rod pivots/falls about a contact point on horizontal ground. In such dynamic scenarios, the center of mass has vertical acceleration, so ΣF_y ≠ 0 and the normal force must satisfy N − mg = m a_y. For a uniform rod of length ℓ pivoting about its bottom end, the CM vertical acceleration is a_y = −(ℓ/2)(θ'' sinθ + θ'^2 cosθ). The rule flags a solution if, while analyzing a rotating/tilting/falling rod (mentions of θ varying, nonzero θ' or θ'' or use of torque/rotation equations), it contains any of the following: (1) Equations setting N = mg cosθ or N = mg; (2) Statements asserting ΣF_y = 0 or "no vertical acceleration"; (3) Treating the normal force as a component of weight (e.g., using mg cosθ as the ground normal) or computing friction f_s = μ_s N with N obtained from static balance in a dynamic rotation context. The correction requires using N − mg = m a_y with the appropriate kinematics of the center of mass.

rules.title: Incorrect floor normal when mass is internally suspended
rules.description:
Checks problems where a box/container of mass M rests on a horizontal floor with friction and an internal mass m is attached to the box via a string/rod (e.g., a pendulum at angle θ with tension T). Flags solutions that model the floor normal force on the box as N = (M + m) g, N = Mg + mg, or use friction limits μ(M + m)g, ignoring that the internal mass’s weight is transmitted to the box via the joint force. Correct modeling requires the floor normal to equal the box’s weight plus the vertical component of the attachment force on the box (and any other external vertical loads), e.g., N = Mg + T cos θ when the box has no vertical acceleration. Detection criteria:
- Context includes: (i) a box on a horizontal surface with friction; (ii) an internal mass m suspended/attached to the box (string/rod), with an angle θ and/or tension T referenced.
- Any equation or statement sets N to (M + m) g or Mg + mg, or sets friction to μ(M + m) g, without including a vertical component of the attachment force (e.g., T cos θ) acting on the box.
- N or friction is modeled independent of θ (e.g., constant Mg + mg) while θ ≠ 0 is discussed.
- Specifically flags use of mg (from the internal mass) inside N when there is no contact of m with the floor/box base and no explicit joint-force vertical component in N.
Allowed forms (examples): N = Mg + T cos θ; N − Mg − T cos θ = 0; N = Mg + F_attach,vertical. Disallowed forms (examples): N = (M + m) g; N = Mg + mg; f_max = μ(M + m) g, unless accompanied by a justified joint-force substitution that reduces to an equivalent expression. The rule also checks special angles: at θ = 90°, N should reduce to Mg (not Mg + mg). This rule aims to prevent treating the internal mass’s weight as directly supported by the floor instead of through the attachment’s vertical force component.

rules.title: Do not modify total normal force due to in-plane spin on a horizontal surface
rules.description: Checks solutions where a body slides on a horizontal surface while spinning about a vertical axis (ωr ≪ v) and ensures the total normal force is not altered by rotation. Flag as incorrect if the solution: (a) claims that the total normal force N depends on angular speed (e.g., N = mg + f(ω) or N = mg + m ω^2 r), (b) attributes a change in friction magnitude μN to a rotation-induced change in N via a 'centrifugal' effect, or (c) computes N by integrating dm·ω^2·r or similar horizontal fictitious/centrifugal forces. In such setups, with no vertical acceleration, the vertical force balance requires N = mg (or N = mg adjusted only for vertical components of other external forces or inclines). Rotation about the vertical axis may redistribute contact pressure around the ring but does not change the total normal force. Any change in the net friction force arises from the distribution and direction of local slip velocities v_rel = V + ω × r over the contact, not from a change in N. The rule allows N to vary only if the solution explicitly includes vertical acceleration, surface inclination/curvature causing vertical components, aerodynamic/other vertical forces, or geometric lift/tilt that alters vertical equilibrium. It also flags mixing of inertial-frame analysis with fictitious centrifugal forces to modify N in a purely horizontal, steady-contact case.

rules.title: Do not alter total normal force using spin/centrifugal arguments in planar sliding with Coulomb friction
rules.description: Scope: Rigid body sliding on a flat horizontal surface under Coulomb friction (constant μ), with no vertical acceleration and small superposed rotation (ω r << v). The verifier checks that the total normal force N is determined by vertical force balance and is not modified by the body's spin. Checks performed: (1) Vertical equilibrium: Require N ≈ mg (or mg minus any explicitly modeled vertical forces) whenever the motion has no vertical acceleration and the surface is horizontal. Flag any dependence N = N(ω, v, r) introduced without vertical dynamics (e.g., adding ΔN terms due to rotation). (2) Centrifugal misuse: Flag use of centrifugal/centripetal arguments to change the total normal load in an inertial-frame contact problem on a flat surface. Internal rotational effects may redistribute pressure but must not change ∑p dA = N = mg. (3) Friction magnitude modeling: If the solution modifies the magnitude of the net friction force via F_fric = μ (mg + ΔN(ω,...)) to account for spin, flag as incorrect; spin should instead affect the distribution of frictional stress and frictional torque via the local slip velocity, not the total N. (4) Dimensional sanity: Flag any ΔN expression whose units are not force (e.g., terms like m ω^2 r^2 / v, m ω r, etc.). (5) Correct approach expectation: For spinning sliders, require that rotational effects be modeled by integrating local friction stresses over the contact (e.g., ring) using the local relative slip speed v_rel(φ) = |v + ω × r(φ)| to obtain net force/torque, while keeping ∫p dA = N = mg. (6) Allowed exceptions: Do not flag if the solution explicitly and consistently models scenarios that can change N (inclined/curved surfaces, vertical acceleration, aerodynamic lift, velocity-dependent normal load, or non-Coulomb friction with stated assumptions). The presence of terms labeled ‘centrifugal’ or explicit ΔN(ω,...) on a flat, horizontal, non-accelerating contact without such exceptions triggers this rule.

rules.title: Verify equation of motion consistency for coupled systems
rules.description: Ensure that the equations of motion for each oscillator in the coupled system are correctly derived using Newton’s second law or the Lagrangian method. The coupling force should be properly included.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the second-order differential equations correctly include restoring forces, coupling forces, and damping (if specified). Ensure that the spring constants, masses, and displacements match the problem setup and that the coupling force is derived based on relative displacements.
common_errors: Omitting the coupling force in the equations of motion.
Incorrect sign for the restoring force or coupling terms.
Forgetting to account for the displacement of both masses in the coupling term.

rules.title: Check validity of superposition principle
rules.description: In normal modes, displacements are assumed to be linear combinations of eigenfunctions. This principle applies only when the system is linear and the coupling forces follow Hooke's Law.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem setup specifies linear restoring forces and that no nonlinear terms (e.g., cubic or higher-order terms) are introduced in the equations of motion. Verify that the coupling forces are proportional to displacement.
common_errors: Using superposition principle in a nonlinear system.
Including cubic or higher-order terms in the coupling or restoring forces, which invalidates normal mode analysis.

rules.title: Verify normal mode frequencies are correctly determined
rules.description: The frequencies of the normal modes are the eigenvalues of the system matrix derived from the equations of motion. These must be calculated correctly using a determinant or matrix diagonalization technique.
rules.check_logic: Check that the determinant of the matrix (Mω² - K) is set to zero for eigenvalue calculation. Ensure that the square root of eigenvalues is taken to find angular frequencies and that the units of mass and spring constants are consistent.
common_errors: Forgetting to set the determinant to zero.
Incorrectly calculating the eigenvalues of the system matrix.
Using incorrect units or dimensions for mass or spring constants, leading to wrong frequency values.

rules.title: Check adherence to sign conventions for displacement and force directions
rules.description: Ensure that all displacements, forces, and coupling terms follow a consistent sign convention. For example, a displacement to the right should correspond to a positive restoring force to the left.
rules.check_logic: Verify that force terms in the equations of motion have the correct signs based on the chosen coordinate system and direction of displacement. Ensure consistency across all oscillators in the system.
common_errors: Using inconsistent sign conventions for different oscillators.
Forgetting to reverse the sign of the force when the displacement is in the opposite direction.
Ignoring the effect of the coupling spring, leading to mismatched signs in the coupling term.

rules.title: Verify proper application of initial conditions
rules.description: Initial conditions (initial displacements and velocities) should be applied consistently to solve for the time-dependent motion of the system. These conditions determine the amplitudes and phases of the modes.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the initial conditions are substituted into the general solution correctly to solve for constants of integration. Verify that the initial conditions are applied to all oscillators in the system.
common_errors: Forgetting to apply initial conditions to both oscillators in a coupled system.
Incorrect substitution of initial displacement or velocity values into the general solution.
Mistaking the initial phase for initial velocity or vice versa.

rules.title: Check geometric constraints in coupled oscillator systems
rules.description: Some systems have geometric constraints (e.g., fixed total length of a string or rod). These constraints must be incorporated into the equations of motion.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the sum of displacements satisfies the geometric constraint, if specified (e.g., x1 + x2 = constant for a fixed-length system). Ensure that the constraint is used to reduce the number of independent variables in the system.
common_errors: Ignoring the geometric constraint altogether.
Misinterpreting the constraint equation, leading to incorrect coupling terms.
Forgetting to reduce the number of independent variables based on the constraint.

rules.title: Check dimensional consistency of all terms
rules.description: Ensure that all terms in the equations of motion and derived quantities (frequencies, displacements) have consistent dimensions. For example, frequencies must have dimensions of [T^-1].
rules.check_logic: Verify unit consistency in each term of the equations of motion. Check that frequencies are derived with proper units based on the spring constant and mass. Ensure that all derived quantities maintain dimensional consistency.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for spring constants (e.g., N/m vs. N/mm).
Forgetting to convert mass or displacement units, leading to incorrect frequency calculations.
Failing to ensure all terms in the equation of motion are dimensionally consistent.

rules.title: Verify mode orthogonality
rules.description: In coupled oscillation systems, the eigenvectors (modes) should be orthogonal with respect to the mass matrix. This property arises from the symmetry of the system.
rules.check_logic: Check that the dot product of eigenvectors (using the mass matrix as a weighting factor) is zero for distinct modes. Ensure that the system matrix is symmetric or Hermitian, as required for orthogonality.
common_errors: Incorrectly calculating the eigenvectors, leading to loss of orthogonality.
Omitting the mass matrix in the orthogonality check.
Assuming orthogonality in a non-symmetric or non-Hermitian system, where it may not hold.

rules.title: Verify energy consistency in normal modes
rules.description: The total energy of the system should be conserved in the absence of damping. The energy should be correctly distributed among kinetic and potential components for each mode.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the total energy (sum of kinetic and potential energy) remains constant over time for undamped systems. Verify that the energy expressions for each mode are consistent with the displacements and velocities.
common_errors: Forgetting to include both kinetic and potential energy terms.
Incorrectly calculating the potential energy due to coupling forces.
Failing to verify energy conservation in undamped systems.

rules.title: 耦合振动系统周期检查
rules.description:
触发条件：涉及小车-摆锤或多质点耦合系统的简谐运动周期计算
检查逻辑：检查是否考虑了系统的质心运动约束。对于水平无外力系统，等效摆长应修正为 l' = l * M / (M + m)，周期公式应符合 T = 2π * sqrt(l' / g)。
rules.check_logic: 检查是否考虑了系统的质心运动约束。对于水平无外力系统，等效摆长应修正为 l' = l * M / (M + m)，周期公式应符合 T = 2π * sqrt(l' / g)。
rules.trigger: 涉及小车-摆锤或多质点耦合系统的简谐运动周期计算

symbolic_hint.canonical: T = 2 * pi * sqrt((M * l) / ((M + m) * g))

rules.title: 内力系统合力与质心守恒检查
rules.description:
触发条件：题目要求分析系统内力关系及位移的物理意义时
检查逻辑：验证所有内力之和是否为零 (ΣF_i = 0)，并确认位移加权和 (Σm_i x_i) 是否对应质心守恒或动量守恒。

rules.title: 拉格朗日方程小角化简时机

rules.title: 链式多体系统边界受力校验
rules.description:
触发条件：处理 N 个物体由 N-1 个弹簧连接的线性链式模型时
检查逻辑：检查端点物体（1和N）是否只受一个弹簧力，中间物体受两个弹簧力，且力的大小应正比于相邻位移差 (x_i - x_{i±1})。
