rules.title: Atmospheric static pressure at a free-discharge outlet must be imposed
rules.description: Checks that solutions impose the correct outlet boundary condition for a liquid flow discharging freely to the atmosphere (e.g., fully open valve r = R, negligible downstream restrictions or losses). Detection logic: 1) Identify problem statements indicating a free outflow to air/atmosphere (keywords such as "discharge to atmosphere", "free jet", "fully open valve", r = R, outlet to air, no back-pressure) in liquid flow (water/ρ0 given, bulk modulus B for liquid, nonviscous/1D assumptions). 2) Map outlet variables: pressure at the outlet plane just inside the pipe/valve (aliases: P0, P_out, pressure at valve/exit section). 3) Required boundary condition: the static pressure at the outlet section equals ambient atmospheric pressure, i.e., P_out = P_a (P_atm). 4) Verify the student solution uses this boundary condition when applying Bernoulli/energy equations; acceptable forms include setting P0 = P_a explicitly or substituting P_a for the outlet static pressure term. 5) Flag errors if any of the following are detected: (a) The outlet/static pressure is left as an unknown (e.g., P0) and solved from Bernoulli without imposing P0 = P_a. (b) The outlet/static pressure is set to a value different from atmospheric (e.g., reservoir pressure P_h or P_h + ρ g h) despite free discharge. (c) The solution treats atmospheric pressure as a stagnation pressure at the outlet or mixes dynamic head into the static outlet boundary (e.g., using P0 + (1/2)ρv0^2 = P_a as a boundary condition). (d) The outlet boundary condition is entirely omitted while determining steady P0 and v0 for a fully open valve. 6) Exceptions: Do not apply or flag if the problem explicitly specifies a downstream back-pressure different from atmospheric (submerged outlet, pressurized receiver), gas flow or choked conditions, cavitation, or if P0 refers to a location not at the outlet plane (e.g., upstream entrance) and the outlet boundary is correctly applied elsewhere. Purpose: Prevent modeling errors where free-outlet atmospheric boundary conditions are not enforced, leading to incorrect expressions for outlet static pressure and subsequent velocity/pressure calculations.

rules.title: Open-outlet static pressure must match ambient; reject constant dynamic-pressure offset
rules.description: This rule checks solutions for open ducts/chimneys exhausting to the atmosphere (or any large reservoir) to ensure correct outlet boundary conditions are applied. It flags models that treat the internal static pressure as the ambient hydrostatic pressure plus a constant dynamic-pressure offset along the height. Specifically, trigger an error if the solution asserts any of the following patterns without enforcing p_internal(exit) = p_ambient(exit): (a) p_flow(z) = p_ambient(z) + (1/2)·rho·v(z)^2, (b) p_flow(z) = p_ambient(z) + (1/2)·rho·(B/A)^2, (c) p_flow(z) − p_ambient(z) = const > 0 attributed to dynamic pressure. In an open chimney/pipe that discharges freely to atmosphere, the static pressure at the exit plane must equal the ambient static pressure at that elevation; any derivation implying a nonzero static overpressure at the outlet is physically inconsistent with the boundary condition. Implementation notes: (1) Detect uses of Bernoulli that yield p(z) = C − (1/2)·rho·v(z)^2 − rho·g·z and then set C by reference to ambient to obtain a uniform static offset relative to p_ambient(z); (2) Compare the predicted p_flow(h) to p_ambient(h). If they differ by a dynamic term or any nonzero constant, flag as an error; (3) Accept only models that either explicitly state p_internal(h) = p_ambient(h) or whose expressions reduce to zero static pressure difference at the outlet. Rationale: Dynamic pressure is part of the total head along a streamline, not a static pressure add-on to ambient. For a free discharge into a quiescent atmosphere (v_outside ≈ 0), the exit static pressure equals the ambient static pressure, not p_ambient + (1/2)·rho·v^2.

rules.title: Crustal P-wave velocity plausibility check
rules.description: When a solution estimates the P-wave speed in the Earth's crust from seismogram arrival times and station distances, verify plausibility against typical crustal values. Implementation guidance: (1) Confirm the context indicates a crustal path (e.g., hypocenter depth ≤ 35 km or medium explicitly stated as crust). (2) If distance and depth are provided, use hypocentral distance d = sqrt(epicentral_distance^2 + depth^2); otherwise use the stated path length but record uncertainty. Ensure unit consistency (km and s) when computing v = d / t. (3) Compare the reported velocity to the expected crustal P-wave range ~5–6.5 km/s; use an acceptance band of 4.5–7.5 km/s to allow for variability. (4) If v is outside this band (e.g., v < 4.5 km/s such as 2.25 km/s, or v > 7.5–8 km/s for crust), flag the result as implausible and likely due to incorrect inputs or modeling. (5) Additionally flag if no explicit sanity check against typical crustal P-wave speeds is documented. Provide remediation hints: verify arrival-time picking (use arrival minus origin time), correct path length (hypocentral vs epicentral), time reference consistency (UTC vs local), and unit conversions.

rules.title: Max height after loss of contact is z0 + v0^2/(2g), independent of bowl parameter
rules.description: Scope: Problems involving a frictionless particle sliding in a parabolic bowl z = y^2/(2k) with a stated/assumed loss-of-contact condition when v0 > vh, where vh = sqrt(g k). Check: If the solution treats the case v0 > vh (explicitly or implicitly), it must: (1) transition from constrained motion to free-flight projectile motion after separation, and (2) yield a maximum height z_max satisfying z_max - z0 = v0^2/(2 g), i.e., z_max = z0 + v0^2/(2 g). This result must be independent of the bowl parameter k and any geometric coordinates of the surface. Flag as a conceptual error if any of the following are detected: - The final expression for z_max contains k (or depends on surface geometry) when v0 > sqrt(g k). - The solution continues to enforce the surface constraint beyond the separation point (e.g., using the track equation to determine the apex) when v0 > sqrt(g k). - The maximum height is not equal to v0^2/(2 g) above z0 (e.g., extra factors, missing 1/2, dependence on k, or incorrect g dependence). - Misuse of the critical speed (e.g., using vh ≠ sqrt(g k)) to justify a k-dependent maximum height. Implementation notes: Apply this rule only if the problem or solution states v0 > vh or an equivalent inequality implying loss of contact. Accept algebraic equivalents such as z_max - z0 = v0^2/(2 g) or z_max = z0 + v0^2/(2 g); constant mass factors must cancel. Reject answers in which symbol k appears in the final z_max for the v0 > vh case.

rules.title: Parabolic-trajectory relations used with nonzero speed at infinity
rules.description: Flags solutions that invoke parabolic orbit assumptions (e = 1 or specific orbital energy = 0) or parabolic-only formulas when the speed at infinity v_infinity is explicitly nonzero. Detection logic: 1) Confirm the solution states or computes v_infinity > 0 (e.g., a numeric value like 9300 m/s or text indicating nonzero speed at infinity). 2) If condition (1) holds, check for any of the following parabolic indicators: a) Textual claims such as 'parabolic trajectory', 'parabola', 'eccentricity = 1'. b) Setting specific orbital energy to zero (epsilon = 0). c) Using the periapsis relation r_p = h^2/(2 mu) without the (1 + e) denominator present in the general conic form r_p = h^2/(mu (1 + e)). d) Using impact-parameter or gravitational-focusing expressions derived from the parabolic case, such as b = sqrt(2 mu R) / v_infinity or b_max^2 = 2 mu R / v_infinity^2 (omitting the geometric R^2 term in the hyperbolic result). Here mu = G (M + m), R is the target radius or closest allowed distance, h is specific angular momentum. If v_infinity > 0 and any parabolic indicator is present, flag a concept error: the trajectory is hyperbolic (e > 1), not parabolic, and parabolic relations are inappropriate.

rules.title: Parallel-axis consistency: center-to-edge distance for a hexagonal prism
rules.description: Checks that the distance used between the centroidal axis and an edge axis (center-to-edge/apothem/lever arm) is consistent with the given moments of inertia via the parallel-axis theorem. Detection logic: (1) Identify a regular hexagonal prism with side length a and given moments of inertia I about the central axis and I' about an edge axis. (2) Compute the required shift distance d_required from the parallel-axis theorem: d_required^2 = (I' - I) / M. For the provided values I = (5/12) M a^2 and I' = (17/12) M a^2, d_required = a. (3) Parse the student solution for any stated or implied center-to-edge distance used in kinematics/impact/torque (terms like 'apothem', 'inradius', 'center-to-edge distance', 'pivot shift', lever arm to the edge contact). (4) If the student uses d_est such that d_est^2 ≠ (I' - I) / M (beyond a small tolerance), flag an error. Specifically flag common misstatements like d_est = a/√3 or d_est = (√3/2) a when used as the center-to-edge distance in this context, because the given I and I' imply d_required = a. (5) Also check consistency in downstream uses: if the lever arm for torque, angular momentum, or impact calculations is taken as a/√3 (or any value not matching d_required) for edge contact, flag the step as geometrically inconsistent. Rationale: For this problem, the parallel-axis relation determines the effective center-to-edge distance; using an incorrect apothem leads to wrong kinematics and angular momentum results.

rules.title: Illegal zero-final-momentum assumption with single-beam initial state
rules.description: Checks solutions in lab-frame setups with a single incident beam and a stationary target for momentum-conservation violations caused by asserting a zero-total-momentum final state. The rule flags cases where: (1) the initial state is described as one beam particle with nonzero lab momentum (e.g., 'beam', 'E_b', 'p_b', 'target at rest', 'stationary target'), typically with p_initial = p_b != 0; (2) the final state is asserted or used as having zero total momentum in the lab (e.g., 'final system at rest', 'p_final = 0', 'proton and delta at rest relative to each other', 'form a single system at rest'); and (3) no additional momentum-balancing element is introduced (no mention of a second counter-propagating beam/head-on geometry, no additional emitted/recoil particle, no external agent). Also flags the related modeling error of enforcing E_initial = E_final without a consistent momentum balance. Guidance: In single-beam + stationary-target problems, the lab-frame final state generally carries the initial net momentum. At threshold, particles are at rest only in the center-of-mass (CM) frame, not necessarily in the lab. The correct procedure is to use the invariant s = (p1 + p2)^2; for a beam particle 1 on a stationary target 2, s_lab = m1^2 + m2^2 + 2 m2 E_b. At threshold, set s = (sum of final rest masses)^2 and solve for the requested energy (e.g., E_p) before applying small-E_b approximations. The rule triggers on textual/math cues of nonzero p_initial together with p_final = 0 (or equivalent phrasing) absent any counter-beam or extra particle, and suggests using the invariant-mass method instead.

rules.title: Use hypocentral raypath length (not epicentral distance) for body-wave velocity
rules.description: This rule verifies that, when computing P- or S-wave velocity using v = d/t from seismogram arrival times, the distance d reflects the hypocentral straight-line path (or appropriate raypath) and not merely the horizontal epicentral distance. Checks: (1) If a nonzero source (hypocenter) depth h is given or inferable, and the solution uses the surface/epicentral distance Δ (station–epicenter horizontal distance) as d without accounting for h, flag a modeling error. (2) For a homogeneous medium and direct body-wave, require d ≈ L = sqrt(Δ^2 + h^2). Compute the relative discrepancy: err = |L − d|/L; if err > 0.05 (5%), flag. (3) If h/Δ < 0.1 and the solution justifies that the depth is negligible, allow using Δ only if err ≤ 0.05. (4) If the solution explicitly models ray bending in a layered medium and computes travel time via an integral along the ray (or provides a hypocentral/raypath distance), do not flag. Example trigger: Δ = 22.5 km, h = 15 km → L ≈ 27.1 km; using d = 22.5 km yields err ≈ 17% → flag. This rule targets the common modeling error of ignoring source depth, which underestimates path length and biases velocity/time calculations.

rules.title: Require geometric justification of height drop when pivot/length changes (pin/peg pendulum)
rules.description:
This rule checks energy-based solutions in pendulum problems where a pin/peg changes the effective pivot or length mid-motion. If conservation of energy is used to compute speed/tension at a point after the pivot changes, the solution must explicitly justify the gravitational height drop (delta h) with correct geometry. The rule flags solutions that: 
- Assert delta h = L or E_initial = mg L without explaining why the vertical drop from the initial horizontal release to the lowest point about the pin equals the original string length. An acceptable justification is a two-segment argument: descend alpha*L from O to the pin at A, then (1 - alpha)*L from A to the new lowest point, giving alpha*L + (1 - alpha)*L = L. 
- Use h = L(1 - cos theta) without identifying the correct pivot and effective length (e.g., using the original L instead of the post-pin length (1 - alpha)*L) or without specifying theta relative to the appropriate pivot. 
- Omit phase segmentation (before vs. after pin contact) or another equivalent geometric derivation (e.g., computing vertical coordinates relative to the same reference) to connect the initial horizontal position to the final position about the pin. 
The rule requires explicit, consistent geometric reasoning for delta h that matches the stated pivot and length at each phase. If such justification is missing or inconsistent, the solution is flagged as a logic error in the energy calculation.

rules.title: Pendulum gravitational potential must use U(θ) = mgL(1 − cosθ) at lowest-point zero
rules.description: Checks solutions for a pendulum or a point mass on a rigid string/rod of length L in uniform gravity where the angle θ is measured from the vertical. When the gravitational potential energy is referenced to the lowest point (θ = 0), the correct expression is U(θ) = mgL(1 − cosθ). The rule flags the following issues: (a) stating U(θ) = mgL cosθ, −mgL cosθ, mgL sinθ, or any form lacking the additive constant needed to satisfy U(0) = 0 when the lowest point is the zero level; (b) asserting U(0) = 0 while using U(θ) = mgL cosθ (internal inconsistency); (c) using energy conservation to derive speed or tension but pairing it with an incorrect absolute U(θ) expression without explicitly defining and consistently using a different zero level. The rule also checks that energy differences are computed as ΔU = mgL(1 − cosθ) when the lowest point is the reference. If a solution derives v^2 = 2gL(1 − cosθ) but previously defined U(θ) = mgL cosθ without mentioning an additive constant or a different reference level, it is flagged as a potential-sign/zero-reference error.

rules.title: Pendulum dynamics: Tension has no tangential component
rules.description:
Checks solutions of constrained circular motion (pendulum, mass on string/rod) for improper use of tension in the tangential direction. Flags the following patterns:
- Any equation that uses a tangential component of tension, e.g., "T sinθ = m a", "T sinθ = m a_t", "horizontal component of T equals tangential acceleration", or similar, where a or a_t is the tangential acceleration.
- Statements that resolve forces into horizontal/vertical and then set the tangential equation using a component of T (e.g., treating T sinθ as the driving force along the path) in an ideal, frictionless, massless-string system.
- During motion at general angle θ, setting vertical force balance T cosθ = mg (implying static vertical equilibrium) without explicitly restricting to the lowest point or static conditions.
Correct reference relations:
- Tangential equation (ideal pendulum, no tangential nonconservative forces): m a_t = −mg sinθ (plus any explicit tangential forces such as friction/air drag if present). T does not appear in the tangential balance.
- Radial equation: T − mg cosθ = m v^2/L (or m a_r), i.e., tension acts purely along the string (radially). The rule triggers when the solution violates these decompositions by assigning T a tangential component or enforcing vertical equilibrium during motion.

rules.title: Specify angle reference when pivot/length changes (pendulum with pin)
rules.description: Checks that any angular coordinate (e.g., θ) used in height/energy/centripetal expressions is explicitly tied to a specific pivot and length, especially when a pin/peg changes the effective pivot and string length. The rule flags solutions that: (1) introduce an angle θ without stating whether it is measured from the vertical about the original pivot (O) or the new pivot at the pin (A); (2) use h = L(1 − cos θ) or v^2 = 2gL(1 − cos θ) after the string catches on a pin/peg (i.e., after a change in effective radius), unless θ is explicitly defined about pivot O and restricted to the pre-contact segment; (3) switch to the effective length (1 − α)L without redefining θ or clearly stating that θ is now measured about the new pivot A; or (4) mix quantities from different pivots (e.g., using r = L in tension/centripetal terms while using h based on (1 − α)L, or vice versa) without piecewise segmentation and redefinition. Acceptance criteria: The solution must either define distinct angles for each segment (e.g., θ_O for motion about O before contact and φ_A for motion about A after contact), or clearly state that θ is redefined at the moment of contact and then consistently use the matching radius (L before, (1 − α)L after) in all energy/height/centripetal expressions. This rule applies generally to problems with constraint/pivot changes (e.g., pegs, variable length, re-hinged systems) and aims to prevent conceptual inconsistencies arising from ambiguous angle references.

rules.title: Pendulum tension computed via static vertical balance (missing centripetal term)
rules.description: Flags solutions for swinging pendulum or string-constrained circular motion that treat tension using a static vertical force balance (e.g., 'T cosθ = mg', 'T = mg cosθ', 'T_y = mg', or 'vertical equilibrium') while the mass is moving. In such cases the correct radial (along-string) equation is T − mg cosθ = m v^2 / L (or equivalents like T = mg cosθ + m ω^2 L, T = mg cosθ + m L (dθ/dt)^2). The verifier should: (1) Identify contexts mentioning pendulum/string tension with a nonzero motion state (e.g., 'swinging', angle θ at release, tangential acceleration a_t, or energy change). (2) Check if the tension is derived solely from balancing components of weight without any centripetal/radial acceleration term. (3) If tangential acceleration or motion is acknowledged (e.g., a_t = g sinθ, 'begins to swing'), then any use of vertical equilibrium for tension without an m v^2 / r term is an error. (4) Also flag conclusions that directly set T = mg or T = mg cosθ at nonzero speed unless the solution explicitly states v = 0 (static equilibrium). Expected correction: include the centripetal term and use T = mg cosθ + m v^2 / L, with v obtained from energy or angular dynamics.

rules.title: Perigee/apogee radius vs altitude consistency
rules.description: Checks that perigee/apogee conditions are imposed using radii from the central body's center, not surface altitudes directly, and that altitude and semi-major axis are not algebraically mixed. The rule flags solutions that: (1) set or compare perigee/apogee using altitude alone, e.g., r_p = 160 km or r_p < 160 km, without adding the planet's radius (correct is r_p = R_body + h_p and h_p = r_p − R_body); (2) compute perigee/apogee as r_p = a − h or r_a = a + h where h is described as an altitude above the surface or a change in altitude, which mixes a center-referenced semi-major axis with a surface-referenced quantity; (3) use inequalities like a − h < 160 km or a_INT − h < 160 km to enforce a perigee altitude constraint; (4) omit the relation r_p = a(1 − e), r_a = a(1 + e) for an elliptical post-event orbit when deriving perigee/apogee from a and e, instead replacing it with a − h; (5) state perigee altitude equals perigee radius (h_p = r_p) or treat 160 km as a radius threshold without adding R_body. The verifier should look for textual/LaTeX patterns such as 'r_p = a − h', 'r_p = 160 km', 'r_p < 160 km', 'a − h < 160 km', or similar with variables a_INT, rp, r_perigee, h, h_p, and constants like 160 km, and confirm that either (i) r_p is explicitly defined as R_body + 160 km (or R_E + 160 km for Earth), or (ii) perigee is derived via r_p = a(1 − e) with altitude subsequently computed as h_p = r_p − R_body. If these conditions are not met, flag a radius–altitude mixing error.

rules.title: Incorrect energy-only impact condition for hyperbolic flyby
rules.description: Flags solutions that determine Earth contact by equating kinetic energy at infinity to gravitational potential energy at Earth's radius (e.g., 0.5*m*v_infty^2 ≈ G*M*m/R_E) or by comparing v_infty to escape velocity at R_E, instead of using perigee geometry from specific energy and angular momentum. Correct collision criterion for fixed v_infty and impact parameter b (lever arm r) is rp ≤ R_E, where rp is the perigee computed from specific energy ε = v_infty^2/2, specific angular momentum h = b*v_infty, and gravitational parameter μ = G*(M + m). A valid solution must express rp as a function of μ and b and solve for m via μ; conditions that omit b or rely on total energy proportional to m are incorrect. The verifier should flag: (1) any impact condition of the form 0.5*m*v_infty^2 = G*M*m/R (including R = R_E), (2) statements that v_infty ≥ v_escape(R_E) or v_infty^2 ≈ 2*G*M/R_E as the impact threshold, (3) impact criteria that do not contain the impact parameter b (or equivalent angular momentum h), and (4) use of total energy m*ε rather than specific energy ε and h to compute closest approach.

rules.title: Complete case enumeration for repeated positions under periodic sampling (bounce in gravity)
rules.description: This rule verifies that a solution to problems involving a ball in vacuum undergoing 1D vertical motion under gravity with an elastic bounce at the bottom and photographed at equal time intervals T considers the full set of conditions under which the ball appears at the same position in every photo. Specifically, the solution must: (1) derive or explicitly state the oscillation period P of the motion starting from rest at height H, with P = 2 * sqrt(2H/g); (2) enumerate boundary photo positions y_A = 0 (bottom) and y_A = H (top) as valid cases where identical positions occur in every photo, and correctly link them to sampling via T = P (or integer multiples of P) producing repeated top or bottom positions; and (3) include the general interior case 0 < y_A < H, showing that identical positions can also occur when T equals the intra-cycle symmetric time between the two passes at the same height y within a period, with a correct expression equivalent to Δ(y) = 2 * [sqrt(2H/g) - sqrt(2(H - y)/g)], and noting that T = Δ(y) (or integer multiples thereof) yields the same position in every photo. The rule flags solutions that only compute free-fall time/impact speed without connecting T to P or Δ(y), or that ignore any of the special cases (bottom y_A=0, top y_A=H) or the interior-case family 0<y_A<H. It also requires mapping the observed repeated-position condition to possible pairs (H, y_A) via T = P or T = Δ(y), ensuring completeness of the solution set.

rules.title: Powered acceleration limited to actuator/rail length; projectile motion thereafter
rules.description: This rule verifies correct phase separation between a powered acceleration region and subsequent free-flight. It applies to problems with a specified actuator/rail length D and a target separation w (e.g., a strait width). The rule checks that non-gravitational acceleration (e.g., electromagnetic force F = I L B, thrust) is applied only while the object remains within the actuator/rail length D, and that motion after leaving this region is treated as projectile motion under gravity only. It flags solutions that: 1) use w (or any distance larger than D) as the displacement for the powered phase in kinematic or energy equations (e.g., s = w in v^2 = v0^2 + 2 a s, or s = v0 t + 0.5 a t^2 with a ≠ 0 for the powered phase), 2) compute the powered acceleration time t_accel from the gap width w or set t_accel equal to the total crossing time across the gap, so that the implied powered displacement s_powered = v0 t_accel + 0.5 a t_accel^2 exceeds D, or 3) include electromagnetic/thrust forces (e.g., I L B) during the flight phase after leaving the rails to determine range or time of flight. Required structure: determine the exit speed v_exit at s = D using forces/energy on the rails, then use projectile motion with horizontal acceleration = 0 and vertical acceleration = -g to compute time of flight and range from v_exit and launch angle θ.

rules.title: Reject geometric-only h ≤ R(1−2/π) tipping condition; require torque about pivot with chain-induced lateral force and ground reaction shift
rules.description: This rule verifies the correctness of toppling criteria for a rigid pillar on rough ground with a smooth (frictionless) chain sliding over a curved top. It checks that the solution derives the toppling threshold from a moment (torque) balance about the impending pivot edge at the base, with the ground reaction shifting to that edge (normal at the opposite edge vanishes), and includes all relevant forces: (i) the pillar’s weight acting at its own COM, (ii) the chain’s weight acting at its instantaneous COM, (iii) the lateral (horizontal) and vertical components of the normal reaction transmitted by the smooth chain–pillar contact along the curved surface, and (iv) the ground reaction decomposed into normal and friction consistent with the roughness coefficient μ. The rule flags solutions that: (1) present a final toppling condition purely in geometric form h ≤ k·R (or h/R ≤ k) with a constant k≈0.36, specifically containing 1−2/π, or use the wrong inequality direction (e.g., h ≤ … where increasing h would incorrectly be said to promote tip), (2) omit the chain-induced horizontal push on the pillar in the moment balance, (3) treat the ground reaction as a single fixed upward normal at the base without shift to an edge at impending tip, (4) exclude μ entirely from the stability/slip-vs-tip discussion without justifying independence via required friction checks, or (5) misplace friction by applying f=μN at the chain–pillar interface despite it being smooth (frictionless). Acceptable solutions must either include μ explicitly in the tipping/sliding conditions or argue why the tipping threshold is independent of μ by comparing required ground friction to μ. They must also base the threshold on ΣM_about_pivot=0 at the instant of impending toppling and account for the chain’s contact-induced horizontal force on the pillar. Any occurrence of an h ≤ R(1−2/π)-type threshold, or absence of these elements, triggers a failure under this rule.

rules.title: Equal pressures across a light, frictionless mobile piston under quasi-static conditions
rules.description: Checks that solutions involving a vessel divided by a mobile (light/massless), frictionless piston under quasi-static conditions enforce equal pressures on both sides at any instant. Specifically: if the problem states a mobile piston and quasi-static (or equilibrium) process and does not introduce additional supporting forces (piston weight, spring force, friction, external pressure difference, or piston acceleration), the solution must set P_left = P_right for the initial state and throughout the process. Flags errors where the solution: (a) claims an 'initial pressure difference' across the piston, (b) assigns distinct simultaneous pressures (e.g., P1i ≠ P2i) without accounting for balancing forces, or (c) uses separate unequal pressures in ideal-gas relations to determine initial volumes. Exception: a pressure difference is acceptable only if explicitly justified by added forces or dynamics (e.g., ΔP = (m_p g + spring force + friction)/A or transient acceleration). The rule ensures mechanical equilibrium is correctly applied: for a light, frictionless piston in quasi-static conditions, the pressures must be equal at all times.

rules.title: Plumb-line deflection: missing sin(λ) projection in centrifugal component
rules.description:
Checks solutions for the vertical deviation of a plumb line due to Earth's rotation. The correct small-angle relation is tan(α) ≈ (ω^2 R / g0) sin(λ) cos(λ) = (ω^2 R / 2 g0) sin(2λ). This rule flags conceptual errors where the latitude dependence from projecting the centrifugal acceleration onto the local horizontal is omitted.

It performs the following checks:
- Formula check: If a student gives tan(α) or α proportional to (ω^2 R / g0) times a function of latitude f(λ), verify f(λ) equals sin(λ) cos(λ) (or equivalently 0.5 sin(2λ)). Flag if f(λ) is only cos(λ), only sin(λ), or any form lacking the sin(λ) cos(λ) product, e.g., tan(α) = (ω^2 R cos(λ))/g0.
- Boundary conditions: Evaluate the provided f(λ) at λ = 0° (equator) and λ = 90° (pole). Correct physics requires α(0°) = α(90°) = 0. Flag if the expression yields nonzero values at either boundary.
- Maximum location: The deviation attains its maximum at λ = 45° (since sin(λ) cos(λ) is maximized there). Flag if the stated latitude of maximum is not 45°, or if the implied maximum from the given f(λ) occurs at a different latitude (e.g., f(λ) = cos(λ) implies a maximum at 0°).
- Projection reasoning: If the solution uses the full centrifugal magnitude ω^2 R cos(λ) as the horizontal component without the necessary sin(λ) factor from geometrical projection onto the local tangent plane, flag as a concept error.

This rule is specific to plumb-line/vertical deviation problems under Earth's rotation and catches overestimates of α caused by omitting the sin(λ) factor.

rules.title: Strict inequality for crossing a repulsive potential barrier
rules.description: This rule checks whether a solution uses the correct strict inequality when determining if a particle can enter or pass through a region bounded by a repulsive potential barrier. In classical mechanics/electrostatics, crossing a barrier requires total energy E strictly greater than the barrier height V_max along the approach path; equality (E = V_max) implies zero kinetic energy at the boundary (a turning point) and no entry. The verifier should: (1) identify that the barrier is repulsive (e.g., for electrostatics, Q1·Q2 > 0; the field at the boundary points opposite to the approach; potential reference V(∞) = 0); (2) find the stated crossing condition, such as ½ M v^2 >= ΔU, E >= V_max, or v >= sqrt(2 ΔU / M); (3) if a non-strict comparator (>= or =) is used to claim entry/passage/penetration, flag a conceptual error and require a strict inequality (>, v > ...). Example: for a positively charged particle approaching a positively charged thin spherical shell of radius R with small holes, the correct pass-through condition is ½ M2 v^2 > k Q1 Q2 / R, i.e., v > sqrt(2 k Q1 Q2 / (M2 R)). Note: This rule does not apply to escape from attractive potentials (e.g., gravity), where equality corresponds to asymptotic escape and '>=' may be acceptable.

rules.title: Energy conservation: verify potential sign, continuity, and ΔU consistency
rules.description: This rule checks the use of conservation of energy when a potential energy U(x) is derived from a given (possibly piecewise) force F(x). Requirements: (1) The potential must satisfy F(x) = -dU/dx in every region of definition. Flag an error if F = +dU/dx is implied by the student’s U(x). (2) For piecewise forces, each segment’s U(x) must satisfy F = -dU/dx and the integration constants should make U(x) continuous at the boundary unless a physical discontinuity is explicitly justified. (3) The potential difference must match the work integral: ΔU = U(x_f) - U(x_i) should equal -∫_{x_i}^{x_f} F(x) dx. Flag a logic/sign error if U(x_i) = U(x_f) (or ΔU ≈ 0) while F ≠ 0 along the path, or if the two computations of ΔU disagree. (4) For start-from-rest cases, verify that 1/2 m v_f^2 = U(x_i) - U(x_f) ≥ 0. Flag an error if the computed U leads to v_f^2 ≤ 0 or v_f = 0 in a situation where the conservative force does nonzero work along the path. These checks catch incorrectly signed potentials, mischosen constants that nullify energy change, and inconsistent energy balances in piecewise fields.

rules.title: Continuity of potential for piecewise conservative forces
rules.description:
Checks that, for a one-dimensional piecewise position-dependent force F(x) (i.e., conservative in 1D), the potential energy constructed in each region is made continuous at the interface(s). Common student error: integrating F(x) separately on each side of a boundary and assigning different integration constants so that U_left(b) ≠ U_right(b) at the matching point b, which is unphysical for a conservative force and breaks energy conservation.

Trigger conditions:
- The problem or solution defines a force F(x) piecewise over intervals separated by one or more boundary points b (e.g., x ≥ a and x ≤ a) and F depends only on position.
- The student constructs potentials U_i(x) (or equivalent energy relations v^2/2 + U_i(x) = const) independently in each region.

Verification steps:
1) Identify region boundaries b where the force definition changes.
2) For each region i, compute (or parse from the student's work) the potential U_i(x) as U_i(x) = -∫ F_i(x) dx + C_i (up to an additive constant C_i).
3) For each boundary b, evaluate the one-sided limits U_left(b) and U_right(b) using the student’s chosen constants. If |U_left(b) − U_right(b)| > tolerance (e.g., numerical epsilon or symbolic non-equality), flag an error.
4) If the student uses energy conservation across multiple regions, verify that a single continuous U(x) (or a single energy constant) is used across the boundary. Detect segmented energy constants or mismatched potential zeros that imply a discontinuity at b.

Exceptions:
- Skip continuity enforcement if the force model explicitly includes an impulsive (Dirac delta) term at the boundary or a non-conservative/time-dependent interaction is stated; otherwise, continuity is required in 1D.

Error message:
"Potential energy is not continuous at the region boundary (U_left(b) ≠ U_right(b)). Integration constants must be chosen so that U is single-valued across interfaces for conservative forces. Match constants at the boundary and recompute energy/velocity."

rules.title: Potential energy from force: sign convention and piecewise continuity
rules.description:
This rule verifies that a potential energy function U(x) derived from a force F(x) uses the correct sign convention and is continuous across piecewise-defined regions. It is triggered when a solution computes U(x) from a stated F(x) or uses energy conservation with a force-derived potential. Checks performed: 
- Sign convention: Confirm that U'(x) = -F(x) on each domain. Compute the derivative of the student's U(x) and compare to -F(x). If U'(x) equals +F(x) (global sign error) or deviates by a sign on any interval, flag an error. 
- Proper integral definition: If the student writes U(x) via an integral (e.g., "U = - ∫ F dx"), verify the correct use of limits: U(x) = U(x_ref) - ∫_{x_ref}^{x} F(x') dx. Flag misuse of indefinite integrals that results in wrong sign or missing constants. 
- Reference level consistency: Identify the stated reference (e.g., U(∞) = 0 or U(a) specified). Check that the student's U(x) satisfies the reference condition on the applicable domain (e.g., for inverse-square gravitational-like F ∝ 1/x^2 with U(∞) = 0, U(x) → 0 as x → ∞ and U(x) is negative). Flag if the chosen reference is contradicted by the expression (e.g., U(x) = +C/x when U(∞) = 0 is required). 
- Piecewise continuity: For piecewise F(x), verify that U(x) constructed on each segment is continuous at each boundary point (e.g., x = a) unless a physical discontinuity is explicitly justified. Compute U_left(boundary) and U_right(boundary) from the student's expressions; if |U_left - U_right| exceeds tolerance, flag "Potential energy discontinuous at boundary". 
- Direction/sign of F: If the problem context implies a direction (e.g., attractive gravitational force toward the origin), ensure the signed F(x) used in U'(x) = -F(x) reflects that direction. If the student has used the magnitude of F(x) without sign, leading to U'(x) = +F(x), flag a sign error. 
- Energy conservation consistency check (optional sanity): Using the student's U(x), verify that energy differences used to compute speeds are physically sensible (e.g., starting from rest, the kinetic energy gain equals U(initial) - U(final); if this yields negative kinetic energy or imaginary speed due to sign errors, flag). 
This rule will catch errors such as computing U(x) with the wrong sign from a given F(x), failing to enforce U(∞) = 0 for inverse-square segments, and introducing discontinuities at piecewise boundaries by choosing inconsistent constants of integration.

rules.title: Verify Power is the Dot Product of Force and Velocity
rules.description: Power is calculated as the dot product of the force vector and the velocity vector of the object. This assumes the force and velocity are expressed in the same coordinate system.
rules.check_logic: Ensure Power P = F · v = F_x*v_x + F_y*v_y + F_z*v_z, where F and v are vectors in the same coordinate system.
common_errors: Using scalar multiplication instead of dot product
Ignoring directional components of force and velocity
Using mismatched coordinate systems for force and velocity

rules.title: Check Conservation of Energy with Dissipative Forces
rules.description: When dissipative forces like friction are present, mechanical energy is not conserved. Energy is transformed into heat or other forms of non-mechanical energy.
rules.check_logic: Verify if E_final = E_initial - work_done_by_dissipative_forces, where work_done_by_dissipative_forces accounts for friction, air resistance, or other non-conservative forces.
common_errors: Forgetting to subtract work done by friction from total energy
Incorrectly assuming mechanical energy is conserved in the presence of friction
Failing to account for all forms of dissipative forces

rules.title: Ensure Mechanical Energy Dimensional Consistency
rules.description: Mechanical energy equations must adhere to dimensional consistency, ensuring all terms relating to energy are expressed in Joules.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all energy terms have units consistent with kg·m^2/s^2 (Joules) and that unit conversions are correctly applied.
common_errors: Using conflicting units for energy calculations
Omitting proper conversion between units
Mixing incompatible unit systems (e.g., SI and imperial)

rules.title: Validate Power Calculation Over Time
rules.description: Power is the rate of energy transfer over time. For scenarios involving energy changes, power is calculated as the derivative of energy with respect to time.
rules.check_logic: Ensure P = dE/dt, where E is the total energy including potential, kinetic, and work done. Verify that the time derivative is correctly computed.
common_errors: Ignoring rate of change of energy over time
Calculating power without considering energy changes over time
Misinterpreting the derivative of energy with respect to time

rules.title: Confirm Correct Sign Convention in Calculations
rules.description: Power and energy equations are sensitive to the sign convention used in the coordinate system. Ensure consistent use of positive and negative signs based on component directions.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the sign convention is consistent across all calculations, particularly for forces and motion directions that contribute positively or negatively to power.
common_errors: Inconsistent sign usage leading to incorrect power calculation
Missing negative sign in calculations involving resistance forces like friction
Using conflicting sign conventions in different parts of the calculation

rules.title: Ensure Dynamic Conditions for Accurate Power Analysis
rules.description: Power analysis requires objects to be moving. Static cases with zero velocity should not involve power calculations linked to kinetic aspects.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that velocity v ≠ 0 for legitimate power calculation. If v = 0, ensure power is not attributed to kinetic energy transfer.
common_errors: Calculating power for static cases where object velocity is zero
Ignoring the need for motion in assessing power
Misinterpreting static forces as contributing to power

rules.title: Identify Misapplications of Frictionless Power Assumptions
rules.description: In scenarios with significant friction, assumptions that power can be transferred through frictionless work are invalid.
rules.check_logic: Verify that frictional forces are accounted for in power calculations, especially in systems where friction is non-negligible.
common_errors: Assuming frictionless conditions in a friction-present scenario
Excluding friction from work calculations leading to power
Underestimating the impact of friction on energy dissipation

rules.title: Assess Geometric Constraints in Energy Calculations
rules.description: Energy calculations involving geometric constraints such as inclines or curves must consider the modified forces and resulting work/energy changes.
rules.check_logic: Verify that geometric parameters like angle of incline, curvature, or path constraints are accounted for in energy formulations.
common_errors: Neglecting incline angles in potential energy and work calculations
Using straight path assumptions in geometrically constrained problems
Ignoring the effect of curvature on energy dissipation or work

rules.title: Validate Work-Energy Theorem Application
rules.description: The work-energy theorem states that the net work done on an object is equal to its change in kinetic energy. Ensure this principle is correctly applied.
rules.check_logic: Verify that W_net = ΔK = K_final - K_initial, where W_net is the total work done by all forces.
common_errors: Ignoring contributions of all forces to net work
Miscalculating changes in kinetic energy
Applying the theorem incorrectly in non-inertial reference frames

rules.title: Ensure Correct Reference Point for Potential Energy
rules.description: Potential energy calculations depend on the choice of a reference point. Ensure the reference point is clearly defined and consistently used.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the reference point for potential energy (e.g., height = 0) is explicitly stated and consistently applied in calculations.
common_errors: Using inconsistent reference points for potential energy
Failing to define a reference point in energy problems
Misinterpreting relative potential energy differences

rules.title: 非保守力功的独立性
rules.description:
触发条件：题目要求计算阻力做功且初末状态不完全已知时
检查逻辑：检查是否试图仅靠能量守恒方程求解两个未知数；阻力功必须通过路径积分（力对位移积分）独立计算。
rules.check_logic: 检查是否试图仅靠能量守恒方程求解两个未知数；阻力功必须通过路径积分（力对位移积分）独立计算。
rules.trigger: 题目要求计算阻力做功且初末状态不完全已知时

rules.title: 二次阻力位移积分律
rules.description:
触发条件：物体受二次阻力（-kv^2）且已知位移或寻找速度与位移关系时
检查逻辑：必须使用动力学方程 v(dv/dy) = a 进行空间积分，而非时间积分，以直接关联速度平方与位移。
rules.check_logic: 必须使用动力学方程 v(dv/dy) = a 进行空间积分，而非时间积分，以直接关联速度平方与位移。
rules.trigger: 物体受二次阻力（-kv^2）且已知位移或寻找速度与位移关系时

rules.title: Incorrect initial conditions for preloaded spring-mass system
rules.description: Checks for modeling errors in spring-mass problems where an object is already suspended (preloading) and an additional mass is added before release. Detection criteria: (1) If the problem text indicates the heavy object M was already hanging and supported while placing m (phrases like "already suspended", "supported while placing", "then released"), then at the instant of release the spring is initially stretched by M alone. (2) If the coordinate x is measured from the spring’s natural (unstretched) length, the correct initial conditions are x(0) = (M g)/k and x'(0) = 0. Relative to the new equilibrium x0 = ((M + m) g)/k, the displacement y = x - x0 must satisfy y(0) = - (m g)/k and y'(0) = 0. (3) Flag solutions that set x(0) = 0 (or state "spring at natural length at release") or set y(0) = 0 when the scenario is sequential loading (M first, then m). (4) Also flag if the equation of motion is written for the combined mass (M + m) about the natural length, (M + m) x'' + k x = 0, while simultaneously using x(0) = 0; or if equilibrium is computed as x0 = ((M + m) g)/k but the initial displacement is taken as zero rather than - (m g)/k. Rationale: The pre-stretch by M sets the initial deflection and amplitude; ignoring it yields incorrect oscillation amplitude and subsequent contact/normal-force extrema. The rule passes if the solution either uses x from natural length with x(0) = (M g)/k, x'(0) = 0, or uses y from the new equilibrium with y(0) = - (m g)/k, y'(0) = 0.

rules.title: Verify equations of motion for horizontal and vertical components
rules.description: In projectile motion, the horizontal motion is constant (no acceleration), while the vertical motion is uniformly accelerated due to gravity. The horizontal displacement is given by x = v_x * t, and the vertical displacement is given by y = v_y * t - (1/2) * g * t^2.
rules.check_logic: Ensure horizontal motion uses x = v_x * t, and vertical motion uses y = v_y * t - (1/2) * g * t^2 without errors in terms, coefficients, or signs. Confirm that g is positive in magnitude and applied with the correct sign based on the chosen coordinate system.
common_errors: Using acceleration in the horizontal motion equation
Missing the (1/2) factor in the vertical displacement formula
Incorrect sign for the gravitational term (-g * t^2)

rules.title: Check adherence to consistent sign conventions
rules.description: In projectile motion, a consistent coordinate system is required. For example, upward is typically positive and downward (gravity) is negative. Horizontal directions should also have consistent signs (e.g., +x for rightward).
rules.check_logic: Verify that gravity (g) is given a negative sign if upward is positive and that horizontal displacements/velocities are consistent with the chosen coordinate system. Ensure that all components of motion adhere to the same convention throughout the problem.
common_errors: Assigning gravity a positive value when upward is positive
Inconsistent signs for initial vertical velocity and acceleration due to gravity
Mixing up left/right or up/down conventions in calculations

rules.title: Validate range formula for horizontal displacement
rules.description: The horizontal range of a projectile is given by R = (v_0^2 * sin(2θ)) / g, assuming launch and landing heights are the same. This formula only applies under this condition.
rules.check_logic: Check that the condition of equal launch and landing heights is met before applying R = (v_0^2 * sin(2θ)) / g. If the heights differ, ensure the range is calculated using the appropriate kinematic equations.
common_errors: Using the range formula when the projectile lands at a different height than the launch height
Incorrectly substituting angle θ (e.g., using sin(θ) instead of sin(2θ))
Forgetting to square the initial velocity (v_0^2)

rules.title: Ensure correct time of flight calculation
rules.description: The total time of flight for a projectile launched and landing at the same height is given by T = (2 * v_0 * sin(θ)) / g. If launch and landing heights differ, a quadratic equation must be solved.
rules.check_logic: Verify use of T = (2 * v_0 * sin(θ)) / g only when launch and landing heights are equal. For differing heights, ensure a quadratic equation is solved for time, and confirm that the correct root of the equation is used.
common_errors: Using the symmetric time of flight formula when launch and landing heights are different
Missing the factor of 2 in the symmetric time of flight equation
Incorrectly solving the quadratic equation for unequal heights

rules.title: Verify decomposition of initial velocity into components
rules.description: The initial velocity vector (v_0) must be broken into horizontal (v_x = v_0 * cos(θ)) and vertical (v_y = v_0 * sin(θ)) components based on the launch angle θ.
rules.check_logic: Ensure horizontal and vertical velocity components are correctly calculated using trigonometric functions and the launch angle. Confirm that the angle is in the correct unit (radians or degrees) as required by the trigonometric functions.
common_errors: Using sin(θ) instead of cos(θ) for the horizontal component
Using cos(θ) instead of sin(θ) for the vertical component
Incorrect angle input (e.g., degrees instead of radians without conversion)

rules.title: Confirm correct calculation of maximum height
rules.description: The maximum height of a projectile is reached when the vertical velocity becomes zero. It is given by H = (v_0^2 * sin^2(θ)) / (2 * g).
rules.check_logic: Check that H = (v_0^2 * sin^2(θ)) / (2 * g) is used to calculate the maximum height and that the vertical velocity is zero at this point. Ensure sin^2(θ) is calculated correctly and that g is positive in magnitude.
common_errors: Incorrect use of sin^2(θ) (e.g., using sin(θ) instead of squaring the term)
Forgetting to divide by 2g
Assuming maximum height occurs at T/2 without verifying symmetry

rules.title: Perform dimensional and unit consistency check
rules.description: All equations in projectile motion must be dimensionally consistent. For example, displacement must have units of length, time must have units of seconds, and g must have units of m/s^2.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that all terms in the equations have consistent units and dimensions. For example, check that g is in m/s^2 and time is in seconds. Verify that trigonometric functions are dimensionless and that derived quantities have the correct units.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for g (e.g., cm/s^2 instead of m/s^2)
Mismatched units for displacement (e.g., mixing meters and centimeters)
Incorrect dimensional analysis leading to invalid terms in equations

rules.title: Check validity conditions for projectile motion assumptions
rules.description: Projectile motion assumes no air resistance, a constant gravitational field, and motion near the Earth's surface. These assumptions must hold for the equations to be valid.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the problem assumes no air resistance and that the motion occurs in a uniform gravitational field near the Earth's surface. Confirm that the effects of Earth's curvature or Coriolis forces are negligible.
common_errors: Ignoring air resistance in situations where it is significant
Applying projectile motion equations in non-uniform gravitational fields
Extending results to cases where Earth's curvature or Coriolis effects are significant

rules.title: Verify initial conditions for projectile motion
rules.description: The initial velocity, angle, and position must be clearly defined and consistent with the problem setup. These values are critical for accurate calculations.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the initial velocity, angle, and position are explicitly stated and used consistently in all calculations. Verify that the angle is measured from the horizontal and that the initial position is correctly incorporated into displacement equations.
common_errors: Omitting the initial position in displacement calculations
Using an incorrect reference for the launch angle
Inconsistent or undefined initial velocity values

rules.title: Projectile from elevated launch: tan(theta) substitution consistency
rules.description: When a projectile is launched from height h with initial speed v0 and lands on level ground (y=0), the time-of-flight and range relations impose a constraint on tan(theta). The verifier should check any claimed tan(theta) by direct substitution into the governing equation. Specifically, for cases where v0^2 = 2 g h, the dimensionless constraint is R/(2 h) = [t + sqrt(1 + 2 t^2)]/(1 + t^2), where t = tan(theta). The engine must compute the right-hand side using the provided t and compare to the left-hand side computed from the given R and h. If the values differ beyond a small numerical tolerance (e.g., 1e-3 relative or absolute), flag a calculation error. Additionally, if the problem states R = 2 sqrt(2) h under v0^2 = 2 g h, the unique physical solution is t = sqrt(2)/2; any other claimed value (e.g., t = sqrt(2)) must be rejected by this substitution check. This rule catches errors where a solver announces a value for tan(theta) that does not satisfy the kinematic constraint or introduces extraneous solutions during algebraic manipulation.

rules.title: Missing vertical flight-time and g-dependence in jump-off clearance problems
rules.description: This rule verifies that solutions to problems where an object (e.g., a frog) must jump off a movable platform (e.g., a frictionless lotus leaf) and clear a specified horizontal distance include the vertical projectile motion needed to set the flight time and the corresponding dependence on gravitational acceleration g and the geometry (e.g., radius R). The rule flags solutions that: (1) determine minimum work/energy or launch speed using only horizontal momentum conservation and platform recoil without modeling the vertical component of the jump; (2) present final expressions for the minimum work/energy (W_min) or required launch speed that do not depend on g and the required clearance distance/length scale (e.g., R), when the statement implies an airborne phase; (3) omit computing flight time T = 2 v_y / g (or an equivalent projectile-motion time-of-flight relation) and the horizontal relative displacement condition (relative speed × T ≥ required distance); (4) ignore the recoil-adjusted relative horizontal speed between jumper and platform when velocities are measured in the lab/water frame, i.e., failing to use u_rel = u_f (1 + m/M) derived from momentum conservation m u_f + M u_L = 0; and (5) give W_min expressions that do not have the correct dimensional dependence (e.g., lack a characteristic mgR scale or equivalent g×length factor). Trigger conditions include keywords such as “jump,” “leap,” “clear,” “minimum work,” and a movable/sliding platform; detection checks for the presence of g, the geometric distance (R or analogous), an explicit time-of-flight relation, and a recoil-based relative speed factor in the reasoning. If any of these are missing while the problem context requires airborne clearance, the solution is flagged for a modeling omission.

rules.title: Projectile double-pass time symmetry (require 1/2 factor)
rules.description: For 1D vertical motion under constant gravity, when a solution introduces two passage times at each height (e.g., A: t1, t2 with Δt_A = t2 − t1; B: t3, t4 with Δt_B = t4 − t3), the times must be symmetric about the apex time t* = v0/g: t1 + t2 = t3 + t4 = 2t*. From this symmetry, any relation formed by combining two double-pass intervals must include a factor of 1/2. In particular, the correct relation is t4 − t1 = (Δt_A + Δt_B)/2. The verifier should: (a) check that the solution enforces pair-sum symmetry (t1 + t2 = t3 + t4); (b) flag as an error any step that asserts t4 = t1 + Δt_A + Δt_B or t4 − t1 = Δt_A + Δt_B (missing the 1/2 factor); and (c) similarly flag misuse of combined intervals without the 1/2 factor in analogous relations (e.g., t_B_up − t_A_up = (Δt_A − Δt_B)/2, t_B_down − t_A_down = (Δt_B − Δt_A)/2). This rule targets calculation errors arising from ignoring time symmetry in constant-acceleration problems where points are crossed twice.

rules.title: 动量守恒下的相对位移约束
rules.description:
触发条件：系统初动量为零且物体在另一运动物体上移动一段距离
检查逻辑：检查是否利用“人船模型”位移关系：m*x1 = M*x2 且 x1 + x2 = L，或在动力学中利用相对速度合成位移。
rules.check_logic: 检查是否利用“人船模型”位移关系：m*x1 = M*x2 且 x1 + x2 = L，或在动力学中利用相对速度合成位移。
rules.trigger: 系统初动量为零且物体在另一运动物体上移动一段距离

rules.title: 镜像法处理弹性碰撞轨迹
rules.description:
触发条件：物体与垂直平面（如墙面、篮板）发生完全弹性碰撞
检查逻辑：将目标点以碰撞面为轴进行镜像对称，将折线轨迹转化为直线轨迹计算总水平位移。
rules.check_logic: 将目标点以碰撞面为轴进行镜像对称，将折线轨迹转化为直线轨迹计算总水平位移。

rules.title: 跨越障碍类最小功建模
rules.description:
触发条件：题目要求“跳出/跨越”给定尺寸物体且涉及“最小功”或“最小初速度”
检查逻辑：必须结合抛体运动方程（竖直上抛/斜抛）与目标几何尺寸（半径/高度）建立约束，不能仅靠动量守恒。
rules.check_logic: 必须结合抛体运动方程（竖直上抛/斜抛）与目标几何尺寸（半径/高度）建立约束，不能仅靠动量守恒。

rules.description:
触发条件：已知抛出高度 h、初速度 v0、射程 R 和仰角 θ
检查逻辑：利用轨迹方程 y = x*tanθ - (g*x²)/(2*v0²*cos²θ) 代入落地坐标 (R, -h) 建立关于 tanθ 的二次方程，避免复杂的根式化简。

rules.check_logic: 统一化为 tanθ 的表达形式（利用 1/cos²θ = 1+tan²θ），若直接设 x=sinθ 导致高次或根式方程，应优先考虑切化弦或弦化切。

rules.description:
触发条件：题目要求求解到达指定坐标 (x, y) 的最小初速度 v_min
检查逻辑：检查是否使用了轨迹包络线方程 v^2 = g(y + sqrt(x^2 + y^2)) 或对发射角求导，而非随意设定角度。
rules.check_logic: 检查是否使用了轨迹包络线方程 v^2 = g(y + sqrt(x^2 + y^2)) 或对发射角求导，而非随意设定角度。

rules.title: Misuse of equal-height projectile range formula with unequal heights or collisions
rules.description: Flags use of the equal-height projectile range formula R = (v0^2/g) sin(2θ) (or equivalent expressions like x = (v0^2/g) sin(2θ)) when the problem involves unequal launch/target heights or any mid-flight collision/bounce. Detection criteria: (1) The solution invokes the closed-form range relation containing sin(2θ) to compute a horizontal distance or total range. Look for symbols/phrases such as R, range, x_total, x = (v0^2/g) sin(2θ), R = v^2 sin(2θ)/g, or explicit use of sin(2θ) to get horizontal distance. (2) At least one of the following is true in the problem/solution context: (a) the initial and final heights differ (e.g., y0 ≠ yf or distinct numeric heights like 2 m vs 3.05 m); (b) the trajectory includes a bounce/collision/rebound (keywords: backboard, wall, rim, bank shot, bounce, elastic, collision, perfectly elastic); (c) multiple segments are combined into a single horizontal "range" across an impact or discontinuity. If both (1) and (2) hold, report an error: the equal-height range formula applies only to a single uninterrupted projectile arc with yf = y0 and no mid-flight impulses. The correct approach is to use full kinematics per segment (x = v cosθ t, y = y0 + v sinθ t − (1/2) g t^2) and apply appropriate collision laws at impacts, or use the general unequal-height range relations where applicable.

rules.title: Require coupled torque/constraint derivation for pulley-coupled oscillator; reject unjustified effective-model jump
rules.description:
This rule verifies that solutions to oscillation problems involving a pulley with stated radius and nonzero moment of inertia, an inextensible rope, and a mass/bar coupled to springs are derived from the correct coupled equations. It triggers when the problem text or given data includes a pulley (R specified) and inertia (I or M with I = c·MR^2), and a rope coupling to a translating body.

The rule checks for the following in the derivation:
- Presence of distinct rope tensions (T1, T2) on the two sides of the pulley and a torque balance on the pulley: I·α = (T2 − T1)·R.
- Presence of a kinematic constraint linking translational motion and pulley rotation (e.g., α = a/R or θ̇ = v/R) consistent with the rope wrapping geometry; and consistent spring extension relations for symmetric suspensions (e.g., x1 = x2 when stated).
- A force balance on the bar including spring forces and rope tensions (not just weight and a single lumped spring force).

It flags the following as errors:
- Setting T1 = T2 while I ≠ 0 and the system is accelerating, or omitting the pulley torque equation altogether.
- Omitting the kinematic constraint that couples bar motion to pulley rotation.
- Abandoning coupled-equation setup after encountering a contradiction/inconsistency and jumping to an unsubstantiated "effective mass" or "equivalent spring constant" model (detected by phrases like "effective spring", "equivalent mass/spring", or by presenting a single-DOF SHO without prior derivation from the coupled equations).
- Producing a final period expression that lacks dependence on the pulley’s inertia parameters (I, or M and R) when the problem specifies a nonzero inertia.
- Collapsing multiple springs into a single k_eff without demonstrating the symmetry/constraint relations and how the rope/spring displacements are related.

Acceptance criteria:
- The derivation explicitly includes the torque balance I·α = (T2 − T1)·R and a correct kinematic link between α and the bar’s acceleration/velocity.
- Distinct tensions (T1, T2) are used unless the solution explicitly and correctly justifies I = 0 (massless pulley) or quasi-static conditions; otherwise T1 = T2 is not assumed.
- The final period T depends on the pulley inertia (via I or M and R) and on the spring constants in a way derived from the coupled equations, not from an asserted k_eff without proof.

rules.title: Detect equal-tension assumption and wrong effective stiffness/inertia in bar–spring–pulley oscillators
rules.description: Scope: Solutions where a rigid horizontal bar is suspended by two linear springs of unequal constants (e.g., k and 2k) and an inextensible rope over a pulley with finite inertia (I = (1/2) M R^2). The bar moves vertically while remaining horizontal. The rule validates the correct coupling between spring forces, rope tensions, and pulley rotation. Checks: 1) Tension asymmetry and pulley torque: Verify that the rotational equation for the pulley uses the tension difference: I * alpha = (T2 - T1) * R. Flag if the solution assumes T1 = T2 for a massive pulley or uses torque as 2 T R, or neglects pulley torque entirely while keeping I nonzero. 2) Effective stiffness: In this configuration, the net restoring effect is not the simple sum k1 + k2 when k1 != k2. For k1 = k and k2 = 2k, the effective stiffness for the bar’s vertical motion must be k_eff = 8 k / 3. Flag if k_eff is taken as 3 k or any direct sum of k and 2k without accounting for the rope/pulley coupling and unequal tensions. 3) Pulley inertia mapping: The effective added mass contribution of the pulley to the bar’s translational DOF must include the transmission factor from bar displacement to pulley rotation; for this setup, the correct added mass is M / 9 (with I = (1/2) M R^2). Flag if the inertia contribution is taken as I / R^2 = M / 2 or any value that omits the coupling factor. 4) Final period consistency: If the final period is expressed as T = 2 pi sqrt((m + c M) / (d k)), require c = 1/9 and d = 8/3 (equivalently T = 2 pi sqrt(3 (m + M/9) / (8 k))). Flag if c != 1/9 or d != 8/3; explicitly flag the common incorrect T = 2 pi sqrt((m + M/2) / (3 k)). 5) Intermediate step patterns to flag: Statements asserting x1 = x2 leading directly to F_total = (k + 2k) x without coupling analysis; assumptions of equal rope tensions on both sides of a massive pulley; energy methods that use omega = v / R with no transmission factor and add (1/2) I omega^2 as if the rope had a single moving segment. This rule catches overestimation of stiffness and pulley inertia due to incorrect equal-tension and uncoupled-sum assumptions in coupled spring–pulley systems.

rules.title: Incorrectly treating pulley inertia as added mass and springs as simple sum when tensions differ
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that model a system with a rotating pulley (radius R, inertia I) and multiple suspension elements of unequal stiffness (e.g., springs k1 and k2) by (a) summing the spring constants as k_eff = k1 + k2 and/or (b) adding the pulley's rotational inertia to the translational mass as M_eff = m + I/R^2, without deriving the tension difference and rope kinematics. Applicability: problems where a body is supported by rope segments over a pulley and the segments attach to elements with potentially different force–displacement laws (e.g., k1 ≠ k2). Triggers: (1) The solution asserts k_eff = k1 + k2 (or F_net = (k1 + k2) x) without showing a rope-length constraint or energy/force balance that accounts for different segment displacements/tensions; (2) The solution introduces M_eff = m + I/R^2 (or any direct additive term proportional to I/R^2) without writing a pulley torque balance τ = (T2 − T1) R or an energy term (1/2) I ω^2 tied to the difference in rope-segment velocities; (3) The solution assumes T1 = T2 or omits tension difference when k1 ≠ k2 or asymmetry is present. Required to pass: The solution must explicitly derive the coupling between rope segment displacements and tensions (showing whether T1 ≠ T2), include the pulley torque/energy relation, and obtain an effective stiffness and inertia that reflect this coupling (typically k_eff ≠ k1 + k2 and the inertia contribution appears with a coefficient < 1 multiplying I/R^2 based on rope-speed relations). If k1 ≠ k2 and the final period/frequency uses k_eff = k1 + k2 and M_eff = m + I/R^2, flag as a modeling error.

rules.title: Verify antiderivative for ∫ dv/(A − B v^2) and correct hyperbolic substitution
rules.description:
This rule checks solutions that integrate the velocity ODE with quadratic resistance (e.g., dv/dt = g − α v^2, with g > 0 and α > 0). It verifies the correctness of the antiderivative and common substitutions:

- For integrals of the form ∫ dv/(A − B v^2) with A > 0 and B > 0, the antiderivative must be (1/√(A B)) artanh( (√B v) / √A ) + C, or an algebraically equivalent form such as (1/(2√(A B))) ln((√A + √B v)/(√A − √B v)) + C. Use of arctan in this case is incorrect and should be flagged unless the denominator is A + B v^2.
- If a substitution v = √(A/B) tanh(θ) is used, the transformed integrand must simplify to (1/√(A B)) ∫ dθ. Residual factors like sech(θ) after this substitution indicate an algebraic error.
- If the integral ∫ sech(θ) dθ appears, acceptable primitives include arctan(sinh(θ)) + C and 2 arctan(tanh(θ/2)) + C (and equivalent logarithmic forms). Incorrect coefficients (e.g., extra factors like 2/√(A B)) or wrong arguments should be flagged.
- The rule also checks the prefactor consistency: the coefficient multiplying the antiderivative must be 1/√(A B) for ∫ dv/(A − B v^2). Stray constants introduced during substitution or integration (such as 2/√(A B) without justification) will be reported.

This rule is designed to catch trigonometric–hyperbolic mismatches, incorrect integral identities for sech, and coefficient errors in the standard drag-limited descent integration, even if subsequent steps accidentally recover the correct final expression.

rules.title: No ascent–descent symmetry for energy loss with quadratic drag under gravity
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that claim the total energy dissipated equals twice the energy dissipated on the upward leg (e.g., E_total = 2·E_up or statements like "by symmetry the loss is the same on the way down") when quadratic drag (F_d ∝ v^2 or F_d = −k v|v|) and gravity are present. The ascent and descent are not symmetric: on ascent the object starts with nonzero speed and slows to rest; on descent it starts from rest and asymptotically approaches terminal speed. Because drag power depends nonlinearly on speed (P_drag = F_d·v ∝ |v|^3), the energy losses on the two legs are generally unequal. The verifier should trigger if a solution mentions quadratic drag or terminal velocity and then uses symmetry to double the upward dissipation without explicitly computing the downward contribution via an integral of drag power/work or justifying a true symmetry (e.g., no gravity or identical speed-magnitude profiles). The correct approach requires treating ascent and descent separately (e.g., integrating F_d·ds or P_drag over time for each leg using the appropriate equations of motion).

rules.title: Quadratic drag energy dissipation requires solving for launch and impact speeds
rules.description: Applies to vertical-motion problems with quadratic drag when terminal velocity (vt), mass (m), gravity (g), and a maximum height (h) are provided. The verifier checks that the solution carries out the solvable dynamics needed to determine the launch speed v0 and the impact speed v_impact, and uses them to compute the dissipated energy. Required steps: (1) Use the terminal-velocity relation to set the drag coefficient k = mg / vt^2. (2) For the upward phase under quadratic drag, use the integrated relation h = (m / (2k)) * ln(1 + (k v0^2) / (mg)) to obtain v0^2 = (mg / k) * (exp(2 k h / m) - 1). (3) For the downward phase starting from rest at height h, use v_impact^2 = (mg / k) * (1 - exp(-2 k h / m)). (4) When the object returns to the original launch height, compute the energy dissipated up to impact as E_diss = (1/2) m (v0^2 - v_impact^2). The rule flags solutions that: (a) omit solving for v0 and/or v_impact via the above separable ODE relations, (b) substitute vacuum formulas (e.g., v0 = sqrt(2gh), v_impact = sqrt(2gh)) or assume E_diss = mgh, zero, or the work of drag on only one segment, or (c) produce a numerical E_diss inconsistent with the above formulas by more than a configurable tolerance (default 5%). For the specific case m = 1 kg, g = 9.8 m/s^2, vt = 20 m/s, h = 30 m, the expected values are v0 ≈ 36.6 m/s, v_impact ≈ 17.6 m/s, and E_diss ≈ 516 J (acceptable tolerance ±3%).

rules.title: Closed-form requirement for radial velocity v_{n2} in dipole systems
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that fail to provide the requested normal/radial velocity component v_{n2} in a closed form tailored to the dipole problem. The verifier checks the final expression(s) for v_{n2} and triggers an error if any of the following are true: (1) The expression retains unresolved auxiliary variables such as θ̇ (angular speed), v_t (tangential speed), L (angular momentum), generic total energy E, or generic potential U(r,θ), instead of eliminating or expressing them in terms of the system’s parameters and specified initial conditions; (2) The dipole-specific field/potential is not substituted (e.g., leaving placeholders like E_n, E_t, or U(r,θ) rather than using φ(r,θ) = (1/(4πϵ0)) p cosθ / r^2 and U = qφ); (3) The final v_{n2} depends on free/undefined quantities and is not expressed solely in terms of permitted parameters (m, q, dipole moment p, ϵ0), coordinates (r, θ), and explicitly stated valid invariants/initial conditions; (4) The scenario contradicts stated non-conservation (e.g., relying on conserved angular momentum in a setup where angular momentum is not conserved) or fails to provide an alternative relation to eliminate θ̇. If the final v_{n2} expression includes any of {θ̇, v_t, L, E, U, E_n, E_t} without explicit elimination/substitution or linkage to given data, or lacks dipole-specific substitution, the solution is marked as incomplete and non-responsive to the problem’s request for a closed form.

rules.title: Incorrect use of radius of gyration (k) as a geometric distance
rules.description: This rule checks for misuse of the 'radius of gyration' by equating it to a geometric distance or using it as a rolling/contact radius. The radius of gyration for a specified axis must be defined by k = sqrt(I/M), where I is the moment of inertia about that axis and M is the mass. It depends on mass distribution and the chosen axis, not merely on distances like center-to-edge, circumradius, inradius, or contact radius. The rule flags a solution if any of the following are detected: (1) The phrase 'radius of gyration' (or synonyms: 'gyration radius', 'radius of inertia') or the symbol 'k' is explicitly set equal to a geometric dimension (e.g., 'k = a', 'k equals distance from center to edge/vertex', 'k equals the pencil radius', 'k equals the contact radius'). (2) The equation I = M r^2 is used with r described as a geometric distance (e.g., center-to-edge, circumradius, inradius, distance to contact point) without deriving r from I/M, i.e., without stating that r is k = sqrt(I/M) for the relevant axis. (3) k is used interchangeably with the rolling radius in kinematic relations (e.g., v = ω k) or impact geometry without first computing k from I and M or citing a correct known formula for k for the specified axis. (4) The radius of gyration is invoked without specifying the axis of rotation. The rule passes if the solution introduces the axis and defines k via k = sqrt(I/M), or uses a correct known expression for k for the shape and axis (derived from its moment of inertia), and does not conflate k with purely geometric distances.

rules.title: Misuse of reduced mass versus total mass in two-body Kepler relations
rules.description:
Checks for conceptual errors where the reduced mass is confused with the total mass in two-body orbital dynamics. The rule flags the following cases:
- The solution defines or refers to the reduced mass as equal to the total mass, e.g., statements like reduced mass = M1 + M2 or μ = M1 + M2.
- The solution correctly defines reduced mass as μ = M1 M2 / (M1 + M2) but then uses μ as the mass factor in Kepler-type relations that require the total mass, such as ω^2 = G μ / R^3, n^2 a^3 = G μ, v^2 = G μ / r, or GM is replaced by Gμ where μ is the reduced mass.
- The solution asserts that the relevant mass in Kepler's third law for a binary is the reduced mass rather than the total mass M1 + M2.
Rationale and correction: For two-body Keplerian motion of the relative separation, the correct mass combination in frequency/period laws is the total mass M1 + M2, i.e., ω^2 = G (M1 + M2) / R^3 and n^2 a^3 = G (M1 + M2). The reduced mass μ appears in the relative-coordinate equation μ r¨ = - G M1 M2 r / r^3 and in kinetic energy expressions, not as the gravitating mass in Kepler relations. If centripetal balance is written for a single body, the orbital radius about the center of mass must be used (r1 = R M2 / (M1 + M2), r2 = R M1 / (M1 + M2)) to recover the total-mass dependence.

rules.title: Verify relative velocity equation
rules.description: The relative velocity between two objects A and B is given by v_AB = v_A - v_B. This principle applies when the velocities are measured in the same inertial reference frame.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the relative velocity computation follows the vector subtraction v_AB = v_A - v_B, where all velocity vectors are expressed in the same coordinate system.
common_errors: Using addition instead of subtraction for relative velocity
Mixing up the order of subtraction (v_AB should be v_A - v_B, not v_B - v_A)
Using incompatible coordinate systems for velocity components

rules.title: Ensure consistency in sign conventions
rules.description: In relative motion problems, consistent sign conventions must be used for all velocity components. For example, positive x-direction is typically to the right, and positive y-direction is upward.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all velocity components adhere to the same sign convention throughout the solution, and document any justified deviations clearly.
common_errors: Inconsistent sign conventions for velocity components (e.g., mixing positive and negative directions arbitrarily)
Reversing the sign of one component without justification
Failing to adjust signs when switching to a new reference frame

rules.title: Check proper switching between reference frames
rules.description: When switching between reference frames, relative velocities must be transformed correctly using the equation v_A_in_B = v_A_in_C - v_B_in_C, where C is the common reference frame.
rules.check_logic: Verify that switching between reference frames uses the correct vector subtraction and that all vectors are expressed in the same coordinate system before transformation.
common_errors: Failing to identify the common reference frame correctly
Neglecting to subtract the velocity of the reference frame
Incorrectly assuming velocities are independent of the reference frame

rules.title: Ensure dimensional consistency in velocity calculations
rules.description: All terms in relative velocity equations must have consistent units, typically meters per second (m/s) in SI units. This ensures dimensional accuracy.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all velocity terms have the same units and dimensions before performing any operations (e.g., subtraction or addition).
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for velocities (e.g., m/s for one term and km/h for another)
Failing to convert units to a consistent system before calculations
Mixing dimensional quantities (e.g., adding a velocity and a displacement)

rules.title: Apply geometric constraints for relative motion
rules.description: In problems involving constrained motion (e.g., objects connected by a rope), the relative motion between objects must satisfy the geometric constraints imposed by the system (e.g., constant rope length).
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the relative velocities or displacements satisfy the geometric constraints (e.g., sum of displacements equals rope length).
common_errors: Ignoring the length constraint for connected objects
Incorrectly assigning relative velocities that violate the geometric constraint
Failing to consider the impact of pulleys on relative motion

rules.title: Check validity of kinematic equations for relative motion
rules.description: Kinematic equations for relative motion are valid only under uniform acceleration or constant velocity conditions in inertial reference frames.
rules.check_logic: Verify that relative motion equations are applied only in scenarios of constant acceleration or velocity, and ensure the reference frame is inertial.
common_errors: Applying kinematic equations in non-inertial frames without accounting for pseudo-forces
Using kinematic equations in scenarios with variable acceleration
Assuming all reference frames are inertial without verification

rules.title: Verify relative acceleration relationship
rules.description: The relative acceleration between two objects A and B is given by a_AB = a_A - a_B. This applies in an inertial reference frame where accelerations are measured relative to a common origin.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that relative acceleration is calculated using vector subtraction a_AB = a_A - a_B, with proper consideration of the coordinate system.
common_errors: Mixing up the order of subtraction (a_AB should be a_A - a_B, not a_B - a_A)
Neglecting to account for direction when subtracting acceleration vectors
Using non-inertial reference frames without proper adjustments

rules.title: Ensure correct calculation of relative displacement
rules.description: Relative displacement between two objects A and B is given by s_AB = s_A - s_B, where both s_A and s_B are measured from the same reference point.
rules.check_logic: Verify that relative displacement calculations use vector subtraction and that all displacements are measured with respect to the same origin.
common_errors: Using addition instead of subtraction for relative displacement
Mixing up the order of subtraction (s_AB should be s_A - s_B, not s_B - s_A)
Failing to specify or use a common reference point for displacement measurements

rules.title: Consider the impact of angles on relative motion
rules.description: In problems involving relative motion with angular components, ensure correct consideration of angles, using trigonometric relationships to resolve velocity and displacement into components.
