Detection logic: (1) Parse the derived equation of motion; if a linearized form x'' = +k x (k > 0) or equivalently x'' - k x = 0 appears, classify it as unstable. Also handle nonlinear forms x'' = +k sin(x) that are then linearized to x'' ≈ +k x near the equilibrium. (2) If the subsequent analysis uses sinusoidal time dependence (e.g., x(t) = A cos(ω t) + B sin(ω t), or claims 'simple harmonic motion' with ω = sqrt(k)), flag this as inconsistent with the unstable sign. (3) Provide corrective expectation: for x'' = +k x the general solution is exponential (e.g., A e^{sqrt(k) t} + B e^{-sqrt(k) t} or A cosh(sqrt(k) t) + B sinh(sqrt(k) t)); SHO requires the stable sign x'' + k x = 0 or x'' + k sin(x) = 0. Common context includes inverted pendulum or a rod near the upright configuration where small-angle dynamics are unstable and do not oscillate.

rules.title: Incorrect use of static equilibrium (x = F/k) to infer zero velocity in driven SHM
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that set the displacement x = F/k (force balance F = kx) to determine the instant when the mass is momentarily at rest for a mass–spring system with a constant applied force. In the equation m x'' + k x = F, x = F/k is the static equilibrium under the applied force; crossing this position corresponds to maximal speed in the shifted SHO, not zero velocity. Correctly, if the constant force is switched on at t = 0 with initial conditions x(0) = 0 and v(0) = 0, the motion is x(t) = (F/k)(1 − cos(ωt) ) and v(t) ∝ sin(ωt) with ω = √(k/m), so v = 0 at t = n π/ω (n integer). The rule triggers when a solution: (a) equates net force to zero (F = kx) to claim the object stops or uses x = F/k to find the stopping time; (b) states that the object 'returns to the equilibrium position' at t = π/ω while the constant force remains applied; or (c) conflates static equilibrium with turning points. The verifier should check that rest instants under sustained constant force occur at t = n π√(m/k) and that x = F/k is a crossing point with maximal speed, not a rest condition.

rules.title: Validate linearization for small oscillations at equilibrium
rules.description: This rule checks the logical consistency of applying the small-oscillation (harmonic) approximation. If a solution invokes small oscillations (e.g., uses T = 2π√(m/k), ω² = k/m, or states that the force is linear near the equilibrium), the verifier must find: (1) an explicitly identified equilibrium point x0 where the net force vanishes; and (2) a valid derivation of the linear coefficient k from a differentiable local model of the force or potential. Specifically, the rule requires one of the following to be shown: k = -dF/dx|_{x0} with F(x) differentiable and finite at x0, or k = U''(x0) with U(x) twice differentiable and finite at x0. The rule flags an error if the provided force/field/potential near x0 contains non-analytic or singular terms (e.g., 1/x, 1/x^2, ln x, |x|) without an explicit demonstration that such singular behavior cancels to yield a finite linear term. It also flags cases where a non-linear or divergent expression is followed by an unsupported claim of linearization (e.g., deriving F ~ 1/x and then asserting F ≈ -kx for small x) or where k is used without computing a finite derivative at the equilibrium. This catches internal inconsistencies such as attempting a Taylor expansion around a point where the function is not analytic or has a divergence, and prevents unjustified use of harmonic oscillator formulas.

rules.title: Volumetric source must be integrated to modify cross-sectional flux
rules.description: Checks continuity/conservation equations that relate mass or particle flow rate through a cross-section (e.g., ṁ = ρ v A or N˙ = n v A) to sources/sinks. If a volumetric source term α (units: quantity per volume per time, e.g., M·L^-3·T^-1 or particles·L^-3·T^-1) is added/subtracted directly to a flow rate using only the cross-sectional area A(s), i.e., terms like α·A(s), the rule flags a dimensional inconsistency because α·A(s) has units quantity·L^-1·T^-1, not quantity·T^-1. The source contribution must be integrated over a volume between two stations: Δflow = ∫_{s1}^{s2} α(s) A(s) ds (or α·A·Δs when constant), or equivalently α·V for uniform α over a known volume V. For particle-number formulations, the rule also checks that any conversion between mass and particles uses the mean particle mass μ_pp, e.g., ΔN˙ = (α/μ_pp)·V. The rule permits derivative forms d/ds(ṁ) = α(s)·A(s) (or d/ds(N˙) = α_n(s)·A(s)) but flags expressions where α·A(s) appears added to ṁ or N˙ without an explicit integral over s or multiplication by a length/volume. It performs unit consistency checks: RHS must match the units of the LHS flow rate. Example of incorrect form to flag: ṁ(s2) = ṁ(s1) + α·A(s). Correct forms to accept: ṁ(s2) = ṁ(s1) + ∫_{s1}^{s2} α(s) A(s) ds; for constant α and A, ṁ(s2) = ṁ(s1) + α·A·(s2 - s1) = α·V.

rules.title: Node/Antinode Positions Must Lie Within [0, L]
rules.description: Checks that any reported node or antinode x-positions for a finite string of length L lie within the physical domain 0 ≤ x ≤ L. The verifier should: - Determine the spatial domain from the problem statement (string along x with length L, left end at x=0 and right end at x=L). - Extract all claimed node/antinode positions, whether given as explicit coordinates (e.g., x = L/2, 3L/2) or as indexed formulas (e.g., x_n = n·λ/2, x_n = (2n+1)·λ/4). - For explicit coordinates, flag an error if any position is less than 0 or greater than L. - For indexed formulas, ensure the allowed index range is restricted so that 0 ≤ x_n ≤ L; flag an error if the solution uses unrestricted indices or lists example positions outside [0, L] (such as 3L/2, 5L/2). - If endpoints are classified (e.g., node at x=L, antinode at x=0), verify they are within the domain and consistent with boundary conditions; otherwise, focus the error on out-of-domain positions. This rule catches modeling mistakes where positions are enumerated beyond the finite string segment.

rules.title: Attempting to solve for mass after canceling it via specific energy/ang. momentum
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that algebraically eliminate the unknown mass m by using specific (per-unit-mass) forms of energy and/or angular momentum and then proceed to solve for m anyway. It targets two-body gravitational problems where the student divides the total energy E or angular momentum L by the small body's mass m (e.g., writes specific energy ε = v^2/2 − GM/r or specific angular momentum h = r v_t) and uses GM (central body only) as the gravitational parameter. Detection criteria: (1) The solution explicitly divides conservation equations by m or uses phrases like 'per unit mass' or writes ε = v^2/2 − GM/r and h = r v_t, thereby removing m from the governing equations. (2) The gravitational parameter is taken as GM instead of G(M + m) in the orbit/pericenter relations, so m does not influence the trajectory in the stated equations. (3) Despite (1)-(2), the solution later attempts to compute or isolate m (e.g., presents m = f(G, M, v_infinity, r, R_E) or a numerical mass). Any such attempt is logically inconsistent because m was eliminated from the determining equations. Optional consistency check: if the final expression claimed to be a mass has units not equal to mass (e.g., proportional to GM R / v^2), flag as dimensional inconsistency as well. Remediation hint: To solve for m correctly, the derivation must retain the two-body nature via the reduced-mass formulation and use μ = G(M + m) in the relative motion; per-unit-asteroid-mass equations with GM alone cannot constrain m.

rules.title: Missing mass/charge factor when using specific potential in energy equations
rules.description:
Purpose: Detect modeling errors where a potential defined per unit mass or per unit charge is used directly as a potential energy in energy conservation, turning-point conditions, or period calculations, without multiplying by the appropriate mass/charge factor.

Trigger context:
- The problem text explicitly states that V(r) is the potential energy per unit mass (specific potential), or uses phrases like "specific potential", "potential per unit mass", or defines an electric potential φ (per unit charge).

Checks to perform:
1) Energy conservation form:
   - If V is per unit mass, verify that total energy is written as E = (1/2) m v^2 + U(x) with U(x) = m V(x). Flag if the solution uses E = (1/2) m v^2 + V(x) or v(x) derived from v = sqrt(2(E - V)/m) instead of v = sqrt(2(E - m V)/m).
   - If φ is electric potential (per unit charge), verify U(x) = q φ(x). Flag if E = (1/2) m v^2 + φ(x) appears without q.

2) Turning point condition:
   - Turning points must satisfy E = U(x_turn). For specific potential, this is E = m V(x_turn). Flag if the turning point is obtained from E = V(x_turn) (mass/charge missing).
   - Example heuristic: For V(x) = A |x| defined per unit mass, the correct turning point is x_max = E / (m A). Flag solutions yielding x_max = E / A.

3) Force/acceleration consistency (optional corroboration):
   - For V per unit mass, force should be F = -∇U = -m ∇V and acceleration a = F/m = -∇V. Flag if the solution asserts F = -∇V (as a force) or a = -(1/m) ∇V (introducing an erroneous 1/m factor).

4) Period/mass dependence sanity check (when a period is derived):
   - If the period T is derived using energy methods with V per unit mass, ensure that any dependence on V enters via U = m V. For the linear specific potential V(x) = A|x| (A > 0), the correct period scales as T ∝ sqrt(E/m)/A. Flag expressions where T scales as sqrt(E m)/A or lacks the expected 1/sqrt(m) dependence, indicating the missing m in U.

Detection hints:
- Pattern-match phrases like "per unit mass", "specific potential", "electric potential" in the problem statement.
- Scan equations for occurrences of E, V (or φ), and m (or q). In energy expressions, require that V (or φ) is multiplied by m (or q). In turning-point equations, require E = m V (or E = q φ).
- Compare derived x_max or similar thresholds to expected forms containing 1/m when V is specific.

Flag message (suggested): "Potential is defined per unit mass/charge; use U = m V (or U = q φ) in energy and turning-point equations. The current derivation omits this factor, leading to incorrect scaling (e.g., x_max or period mass dependence)."

rules.title: Numeric determination and correct cubic for spherical cap height h_c,N
rules.description:
This rule verifies that when a problem asks to 'determine the height h_c,N' of the spherical cap of a floating sphere (melon) under specified conditions, the solution provides a numeric value and uses the correct buoyancy–geometry relation. The checker performs the following:

1) Numeric requirement: The final answer for h_c,N must be a single numeric value (with units of length) obtained by substituting the given parameters from the referenced conditions (e.g., Task 3b). Leaving h_c,N as an implicit root or as an unsolved polynomial equation is flagged.

2) Correct governing equation: If an intermediate implicit equation is presented, it must encode Archimedes’ principle and spherical cap geometry exactly as ρ_w (V_sphere − V_cap(h)) = ρ_m V_sphere, with V_sphere = (4/3)π R^3 and V_cap(h) = π h^2 (R − h/3). Equivalently, after canceling π, the cubic in h must be (1/3) h^3 − R h^2 + (4/3) R^3 (1 − ρ_m/ρ_w) = 0. Any alternative cubic or mismatch in coefficients/terms (e.g., missing h^3 term, wrong signs, or incorrect dependence on densities) is flagged as a logic/formulation error.

3) Physical admissibility: The reported h_c,N must satisfy 0 ≤ h_c,N ≤ 2R and be consistent with the density ratio: for 0 < ρ_m/ρ_w < 1, the chosen root must lie in [0, 2R] and be unique/physically relevant. Violations are flagged.

4) Condition compliance: The solution must reflect the stated assumptions (e.g., negligible friction and negligible water motion) and not introduce extraneous parameters. If the problem references prior task conditions (Task 3b), the parameter values from that task must be used, and a numerical h_c,N must be computed.

5) Reporting: Units must be provided; significant figures should be compatible with given data. Failure to compute and present the numeric height or providing only an unsolved cubic is marked as non-compliance.

rules.title: Validate spherical-cap droplet geometry (R, D, h, α)
rules.description: For a sessile droplet forming a spherical cap on a flat surface, with contact angle α measured through the liquid and contact diameter D (so a = D/2 is the contact radius) and cap height h, the geometry must satisfy: h = R(1 − cos α), a = R sin α. These imply α = 2·arctan(h/a) = 2·arctan(2h/D) and R = (a² + h²)/(2h) = (D²/4 + h²)/(2h), and also D/(2h) = cot(α/2). The verifier should check any relation a solution uses to connect R, D, h, and α against these identities. Flag a modeling error if: (1) the solution uses R expressed as proportional to cot α alongside D and h (e.g., R = (D²/(8h))·cot α or similar variants), (2) α is given as arctan(2h/D) without the factor 2, (3) R is given as D²/(8h) without the correct dependence on α, or (4) the contact angle convention is mixed (α measured through air) without converting via α → π − α. In general, if the asserted formulas are not algebraically equivalent to α = 2·arctan(2h/D) and R = (D²/4 + h²)/(2h) with a = D/2, mark the solution as using incorrect spherical-cap geometry.

rules.title: Spinning sphere impact: require 2/7 inertia factor and friction/regime dependence in horizontal distance
rules.description: This rule verifies final expressions for the horizontal distance traveled between the first and second impacts for a homogeneous solid sphere (I = 2/5 m R^2) dropped from height h with initial spin ω0 and contacting a rough floor. The correct structure arises from the frictional impulse coupling translation and rotation and must include: (1) the inertia-derived coefficient 2/7 multiplying R·ω0 (not 2/5), (2) a dependence on the stated slip/impact parameter (e.g., a dimensionless c encoding slip duration/impulse, or the kinetic friction coefficient μ_k for the slipping case), and (3) the free-fall time scale √(2h/g) (equivalently √(2gh)/g). Flag the solution if any of the following are true: (a) the coefficient on R·ω0 is 2/5 (or any value ≠ 2/7), indicating misuse of rotational inertia in the impulse/rolling relation; (b) the final distance expression omits any explicit dependence on the problem’s friction/regime parameter (c or μ_k) despite the problem distinguishing slipping vs non-slip phases; (c) the time-scale factor is not proportional to √(2h/g) (or √(2gh)/g). This catches errors like producing d ∝ (2/5) R ω0 √(2h/g) instead of the required form d ∝ (2/7) R ω0 × (2c √(2h/g)).

rules.title: Spring energy/force must use displacement from nonzero equilibrium length
rules.description:
Checks for misuse of Hooke’s law and spring potential when a system has an explicitly nonzero equilibrium/rest length (e.g., membrane thickness d0). The rule flags solutions that: (a) write the spring potential as U = (1/2) k L^2 or the spring force as F = k L using the absolute length/separation L (e.g., thickness d) instead of the displacement from equilibrium ΔL = L − L0 (or Δ = d0 − d for compression), when the problem specifies L0 ≠ 0 (e.g., d0); (b) assert or imply that the spring force is zero at full compression/collapse (L → 0) rather than at the equilibrium length L = L0; or (c) set the energy minimum at L = 0 for a standalone linear spring with given nonzero L0. Implementation hints: 1) Detect presence of an explicitly given equilibrium/rest length variable (L0, d0, x0, rest length, equilibrium thickness). 2) If found, scan the solution for spring expressions; flag if U_spring is written as (1/2) k L^2 or F_spring = k L without an accompanying shift to L − L0 or L0 − L. 3) Flag statements like "force is zero at collapse", "at d → 0 the spring force vanishes", or equivalent claims when L0 ≠ 0. 4) Optionally verify boundary conditions implied by the solution’s formulas: F_spring(L0) should evaluate to 0; if not, flag. Notes: Correct forms are U = (1/2) k (L − L0)^2 and F = −k (L − L0) (or for compression sign conventions, magnitude k |L − L0|). At 
collapse (L → 0), the force magnitude should be k L0, not zero.

rules.title: Preserve natural-length offset when converting spring work k x dx to volume form
rules.description: This rule verifies the correct handling of spring work/energy differentials when expressing them in terms of gas volume or piston displacement in systems with a spring of nonzero natural length. Specifically: (1) If a spring with natural length L0 is present and the differential spring energy/work is written as dU_s = k x dx, the variable x must represent the extension/compression relative to the natural length (Δl = l − L0), not the absolute length l. Using k l dl instead of k Δl d(Δl) is a modeling error. (2) When mapping x to an affine function of volume V or displacement (x = α V + β), the product x dx must expand to (α V + β) α dV = α^2 V dV + α β dV; dropping the constant-offset term α β dV is incorrect unless β is explicitly zero (i.e., x is already defined as extension Δl). (3) Concretely, if a derivation contains substitutions such as l = L − V/A, Δl = l − L = −V/A, then k Δl d(Δl) = (k/A^2) V dV is valid; however, rewriting k x dx with x = L − V/A to k(V − A L)/A^2 dV and then simplifying to (k/A^2) V dV by discarding the −(k/A) L dV term is an error. The verifier should flag any step where an expression of the form k(α V + β) α dV is simplified to k α^2 V dV with β ≠ 0 present upstream, or where x is used as absolute spring length instead of extension relative to the natural length.

rules.title: Verify stability threshold V_min from Ω^2(V) and correct √(gR)/2 prefactor
rules.description: This rule checks the correctness of the minimum speed for stability (V_min) in small-oscillation analyses where the angular frequency Ω depends on a translational speed V. It targets errors arising from an incorrect Ω expression or misuse of the stability criterion. The verifier will: (1) Ensure the stability condition is formulated with Ω^2 ≥ 0 (not Ω ≥ 0). (2) Recompute the stability threshold by solving Ω^2(V) = 0 and selecting the smallest positive real root as V_min*. (3) Validate dimensional consistency that V_min scales as √(g R) when gravity g and a length scale R appear in the model. (4) For the rolling ring near a vertical plane (the given context), verify the correct numerical prefactor: V_min must equal (1/2)√(g R). If the submitted V_min equals √(g R) or otherwise deviates from the 1/2 factor, flag a factor-of-two error. (5) Consistency check: substituting the claimed V_min into the submitted Ω^2(V) should yield zero; if it does not, flag an inconsistency in the derived Ω or threshold computation. This rule catches mistakes such as using Ω ≥ 0 instead of Ω^2 ≥ 0, sign errors in linearization, and missing numerical coefficients that lead to incorrect stability thresholds.

rules.title: FBD for non-attached (stacked) mass must exclude spring force and use common acceleration
rules.description:
This rule verifies the free-body diagram (FBD) and equation of motion for a mass that is in contact with another body attached to a spring (e.g., a small mass m placed atop a heavy mass M that is connected to a spring). It checks that the small/top mass m is not assigned a direct spring force and that its dynamics use the common acceleration of the contacting bodies while contact is maintained.

The rule flags an error if any of the following are detected:
- The force list/FBD for the top mass m includes a spring force term (e.g., kx, kΔx, F_spring) or any expression implying the spring acts directly on m.
- The equation of motion written specifically for m includes k, spring displacement x, or a spring-force variable; the correct 1D force balance for m must involve only gravity and the normal force: m a = m g − N (downward positive) or N − m g = m a (upward positive).
- The normal force N is omitted from m’s force balance while contact is assumed, or N is incorrectly set equal to the spring force (e.g., N = kx or N = kx − mg), implying spring acts directly on m.
- The acceleration used for m differs from the acceleration used for M during the contact phase (they must share a common acceleration while in contact).

Implementation notes:
- Parse body-specific equations; identify the equation labeled or contextually assigned to mass m.
- Search for presence of spring-related symbols (k, x_spring, Δx, F_spring) in m’s force balance; if present, flag.
- Verify inclusion of mg and N in m’s force balance; require that m’s EOM contains only these forces (with consistent sign convention).
- Extract acceleration symbols for m and M; require equality (a_m == a_M) during the contact interval noted in the solution.

Rationale:
- A spring exerts force only on the body it is attached to (here, M). The top mass m experiences gravity and the contact normal from M; its acceleration equals the common acceleration of the contacting bodies until separation. Assigning a spring force directly to m or using distinct accelerations violates correct FBD principles.

rules.title: Driven string with fixed right end: enforce standing-wave form and both boundary conditions
rules.description: For a taut string of length L along x ∈ [0, L] with transverse wave speed u, driven at the left end by y(0, t) = A0 cos(ω t) and fixed at the right end y(L, t) = 0, verify that the proposed steady-state solution: (1) satisfies both boundary conditions exactly for all t; (2) has the correct standing-wave spatial dependence. Specifically, accept solutions algebraically equivalent to y(x, t) = [A0 sin(k (L − x)) / sin(k L)] cos(ω t) with k = ω/u (overall sign allowed). Flag solutions if any of the following are detected: • The right-end boundary is not enforced (y(L, t) ≠ 0 identically). • The left-end boundary is not matched (y(0, t) ≠ A0 cos(ω t)). • The solution is expressed as a single traveling wave (e.g., y(x, t) = A0 cos(ω(t − x/u))) or sets one traveling component to zero (e.g., g = 0 in y = f(x − ut) + g(x + ut)), thereby failing to include the necessary reflected wave from the fixed end. • The spatial envelope is not proportional to sin(k(L − x)) (or an algebraically equivalent form such as −sin(kx − kL)) in the steady state. • Reported node positions are not x_n = L − nπ/k = L − nλ/2 (n ∈ ℕ₀), with a node at x = L always present. • Reported antinode positions are not x_a = L − (n + 1/2)π/k = L − (n + 1/2)λ/2. • Resonance is mishandled: if sin(kL) = 0 (i.e., kL = nπ), the denominator vanishes; flag a solution that presents a finite-amplitude formula without noting resonance or that gives incorrect node/antinode positions in this case.

rules.title: Static friction must be solved as an unknown within |f| ≤ μN; do not set f = μN unless at impending slip
rules.description: Checks that, in problems asserting rolling without slipping or static contact, the friction force is not incorrectly modeled as a constant f = μN (or f = μmg) or with a fixed direction by assumption. The verifier will: (1) Detect statements like “f = μN”, “f = μmg”, “friction equals μN”, or the use of kinetic friction while the text also claims no slip/rolling without slipping. (2) Require that static friction be introduced as an unknown f with sign to be determined, together with the inequality bound |f| ≤ μN (N possibly time/angle dependent), and that f be solved from force/torque balance and any rolling constraints (v_cm = rω, a_cm = rα). (3) Accept setting f = μN only if the solution explicitly justifies impending slip/limiting friction with a threshold argument (e.g., “at the verge of slipping”, “maximum static friction”, complementarity/slip condition). (4) Flag solutions that treat friction as constant in magnitude or direction throughout without deriving it from dynamics, especially when external forces/geometry imply f may vary with time/angle or change sign. (5) Require a post-check that the computed |f| stays ≤ μN over the assumed no-slip interval; if it exceeds μN, the model must switch to slipping/kinetic friction. This rule targets errors like setting f = μmg from the outset in rolling problems (e.g., a hoop pulled at its rim), where the correct static friction generally depends on the motion and may be zero initially or change sign.

rules.title: Static friction must be a bounded reaction, not a fixed μ_s N
rules.description:
Flag solutions that model static friction during no-slip (sticking) as a constant force equal to μ_s N rather than a reaction that adjusts up to its maximum. The correct modeling for a sticking contact is: (i) enforce zero relative motion at the contact (v_rel = 0), (ii) treat the static friction force F_s as an unknown satisfying |F_s| ≤ μ_s N and directed to prevent slip, and (iii) determine slip onset by checking whether the required friction magnitude reaches μ_s N (|F_required| = μ_s N). After slip begins, the kinetic friction magnitude should be μ_k N opposing the direction of slip.

Detection criteria (any trigger should flag):
- Textual assertions in the no-slip regime like "static friction equals μ_s N", "F_f = μ_s N when not sliding", or equivalent statements that set F_static to a fixed magnitude without an inequality or a threshold check.
- Equations or ODEs for a sticking phase that include a constant ± μ_s N term for the friction force, instead of solving for an unknown friction that enforces v_rel = 0 and checking |F_s| ≤ μ_s N.
- Absence of the inequality |F_s| ≤ μ_s N and of a stick/slip decision based on comparing the required friction to μ_s N; i.e., the solution never computes the friction needed to prevent slip nor verifies it against the static limit.

Expected correct structure:
- Sticking phase: impose v_rel = 0 (or x_dot equals the driver velocity), solve dynamics with F_s as an unknown reaction, verify |F_s| ≤ μ_s N; slip starts when the bound is met.
- Sliding phase: set |F_k| = μ_k N opposite slip direction.

This rule targets the common modeling error of treating static friction as always μ_s N during adhesion, which misrepresents the dynamics and the slip threshold.

rules.title: Static friction at threshold: forbid using Ma or a = μ_s N/M before sliding
rules.description: This rule checks solutions involving a body that is at rest with static friction and is described as 'just begins to slide', 'on the verge of motion', 'threshold of sliding', or 'impending motion'. It flags the following modeling errors: (1) Using Newton’s second law ΣF = M a for the friction-limited body at the threshold, e.g., writing T sin(θ) − f_s = M a_box or directly setting a_box = f_s(max)/M, a_box = μ_s N / M, or a_box = μ_s g. (2) Treating the body’s acceleration as nonzero while static friction is still in effect, except immediately after the threshold; at the threshold condition itself, static friction still applies and acceleration should not be used to determine f_s. The correct condition at impending motion is: static friction magnitude equals its maximum, f_s = μ_s N, and the net horizontal force on the friction-limited body balances this static friction at that instant (ΣF_horizontal = 0 for that body just before motion; at the threshold, use f_s = μ_s N to relate applied horizontal forces). The verifier should flag any step that computes acceleration from μ_s N or μ_s g, or that substitutes Ma for the friction-limited body instead of using f_s = μ_s N at the stated threshold angle or condition.

rules.title: Misapplied dynamic angular-momentum analysis in static geometry tasks
rules.description: Checks for a modeling mismatch where the problem requests a static geometric quantity (e.g., average radius, flattening, or similar) under stated approximations (e.g., equal densities, ignore interior shape change, use data from a figure) but the solution introduces time-evolution dynamics or conservation laws. The rule flags a solution if: (1) The problem text contains cues like 'average radius', 'flattening factor', 'use data from Fig.', 'assume equal densities', or 'ignore shape change' and does not mention temporal change or dynamics; AND (2) the solution uses dynamic frameworks such as conservation of angular momentum/energy or time-evolution constructs (e.g., 'initial/final angular velocity', 'ω0/ω1', 'spin-up', 'spin-down', 'period change', 'conservation of angular momentum', torques, frictional equalization) or introduces unprompted events (e.g., 'star-quake'); AND/OR (3) the solution fails to reference or apply the stated approximations (equal densities, ignore interior shape change) or to use the provided figure/data, while focusing on temporal evolution instead of computing the requested static geometric quantity. This rule is intended to catch misdirection where conservation-law dynamics are applied to a purely geometric estimation task.

rules.title: Missing static friction (stick-slip) regime in Coulomb friction modeling
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that model dry (sliding/Coulomb) friction solely as F_f = -μN·sign(v) without handling the static friction condition at v = 0 and the associated stick-slip behavior. The checker looks for the following patterns and omissions: (1) Friction is written as F_f = -μN·sign(v) (e.g., -μmg·sign(v) on a horizontal plane) and used universally in the equation of motion m x¨ = ΣF, with no piecewise definition for v = 0. (2) No explicit static friction inequality is stated, i.e., absence of a condition of the form |F_tangential_applied| ≤ μ_s N implies v = 0 and friction adjusts within |F_f| ≤ μ_s N to prevent motion; and |F_tangential_applied| > μ_s N implies slip with |F_f| = μ_k N opposing impending motion. (3) The coefficient μ is treated as a single constant without distinguishing static (μ_s) and kinetic (μ_k), or without clarifying behavior at rest even if μ_s = μ_k (the direction at v = 0 must oppose impending motion to satisfy the inequality). (4) For mass–spring on a horizontal surface, the solution lacks an explicit stick region/dead band: |kx| ≤ μ_s N (equivalently |x| ≤ μ_s N/k), and/or concludes a unique final equilibrium at x = 0, ignoring that any x in [-μ_s N/k, μ_s N/k] can be a valid rest position. (5) Equilibrium or steady-state analysis sets v = 0 and keeps the sign(v) friction term without addressing its undefined sign at zero velocity, or uses continuous ODE integration with the sign(v) term across v = 0 without switching regimes. If any of these are detected, the solution is flagged for missing the static friction regime and misrepresenting the qualitative behavior (e.g., incorrect claim that the mass settles at x = 0 rather than within the stick band).

rules.title: Incorrect lateral velocity/acceleration from projecting forward speed with steering angle
rules.description: This rule flags modeling errors in front-steered, no-slip wheeled vehicle problems (bike/tricycle/car) where the steering angle θ(t) of the front wheel is misused to obtain lateral motion by projecting the forward speed v onto a fixed lateral axis. In a nonholonomic vehicle with rear wheels aligned to the body, the CoM velocity is constrained to lie along the body axis; steering changes path curvature, not by creating an instantaneous lateral component v_y = v sinθ. Correct kinematics use the bicycle model: yaw rate ψ̇ = v · tan(θ) / L, curvature κ = tan(θ)/L, and lateral (centripetal) acceleration a_y = v² · tan(θ) / L (≈ v² · θ / L for small θ). Flag solutions that: (1) set v_y = v sin(θ) or derive a_y by differentiating v sin(θ), e.g., a_y = v cos(θ) · θ̇; (2) equate heading rate ψ̇ to θ̇ or use a_y = v · θ̇; (3) compute a_y from θ without introducing wheelbase L or equivalent turn radius R = L / tan(θ); (4) treat θ as the direction of motion relative to global axes rather than a steering angle affecting curvature. The expected formulation for lateral acceleration must depend on v² and either tan(θ)/L or 1/Rturn, not on θ̇ alone nor a simple sine projection.

rules.title: Amplitude in stick–slip driven oscillator must depend on driver speed, mass, spring, and friction difference
rules.description:
Applicability: Use this rule when the problem describes a mass–spring system driven by a plate moving at constant speed u, with normal load N and two friction regimes (static μ1 and kinetic μ2 where μ2 < μ1). The model includes parameters m, k, u, N, μ1, and μ2. Checks: 
- Extract the final expression for the amplitude A. If A does not contain u or does not contain m while both parameters are present in the model, flag an error: amplitude missing driver speed or mass. In stick–slip driven oscillators, the amplitude must depend on the driving speed and inertia. 
- If A uses only a single friction coefficient (only μ1 or only μ2) and does not involve the difference Δμ = μ1 − μ2 or an explicit conditional dependence on stick vs slip, flag an error: friction regime dependence omitted. 
- If A is of the form C·(μ N)/k (for any constant C) and is independent of u and m, flag as suspicious amplitude form: amplitude cannot be determined solely by static or kinetic friction and spring stiffness in a speed-driven system. 
- If the solution derivation switches from using μ2 to μ1 (or vice versa) in the final answer without a stated regime change or condition (e.g., the transition point between sticking and slipping), flag an error: inconsistent friction coefficient usage. Rationale: For periodic stick–slip under constant-speed driving, the amplitude depends on u, m, k, and the friction contrast (μ1 − μ2), and cannot be reduced to a function of μ and N alone.

rules.title: Stick–slip threshold must be applied in friction-driven oscillator analysis
rules.description: Applies to problems that specify distinct static and kinetic friction coefficients (μ1 > μ2) for a contact that drives a mass–spring system. The verifier checks that the solution explicitly uses the stick–slip transition criterion rather than assuming static friction is a fixed force. Required elements: (1) Static friction is treated as an adjustable force with magnitude ≤ μ1 N (not set equal to μ1 N during sticking), and the no-slip condition is stated as |F_required| ≤ μ1 N. (2) The slip onset is identified by the equality |F_required| = μ1 N. For the specific mass–spring driven by a plate moving at constant speed u, the solution must recognize that during stick the block’s velocity equals u, its acceleration is zero, and the required tangential force to maintain stick is the spring force F_required = k x; hence the transition is at |k x| = μ1 N. (3) During slip, the friction force magnitude is taken as μ2 N with sign opposing the relative motion, and the dynamics are written accordingly (e.g., m x¨ + k x = ± μ2 N). (4) The amplitude A is derived from these thresholds, showing dependence on μ1, μ2, N, and k (and noting u’s role via the stick phase), rather than ignoring the stick–slip mechanism. The rule flags solutions that: set F_static = μ1 N during stick without stating it is a variable up to μ1 N; omit the inequality/equality transition conditions (|F_required| ≤ μ1 N → |F_required| = μ1 N); fail to identify F_required = k x in the sticking phase with v_block = u; or present an amplitude independent of μ1, μ2, N, and k.

rules.title: Require explicit stress-to-force conversion (F = σ × A) when using material strength
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that conflate material strength (a stress, e.g., compressive/tensile strength) with force. In problems involving mechanical failure under load (compression/tension/shear), material 'strength' refers to a critical stress (units of pressure), not a force. The failure force must be obtained via F = σ × A, where A is the loaded cross-sectional area. The rule checks for any claim that the required/destructive force scales directly with 'strength' (e.g., F ∝ strength, F = k·strength, or F1/F2 = S1/S2) without explicitly stating the stress-to-force relation F = σ × A or without accounting for the cross-sectional area (A). It also checks that, when specimens are compared, the solution either (a) shows A is identical (same shape and size) to justify F ∝ σ, or (b) includes the area ratio: F1/F2 = (σ1/σ2) × (A1/A2). The rule further enforces dimensional consistency: force (N) must be derived from stress (Pa) times area (m²). If the solution equates or scales force with strength without mentioning area or the relation F = σ × A, it is flagged.

rules.title: Strain must be derived from stress via sigma = T/A and the provided stress–strain curve
rules.description: This rule validates the use of material strain in problems that explicitly provide a stress–strain (sigma–epsilon) graph for an elastic rope or cord. It flags solutions that: (1) introduce a numerical strain value (epsilon, epsilon_max, etc.) without first computing the rope tension at the relevant event (e.g., maximum allowed acceleration) using Newton’s second law and then converting to stress via sigma = T/A, followed by reading epsilon from the given stress–strain curve; (2) employ dimensionally or physically inconsistent relations linking geometry and strain, such as solving for the protective distance L solely in terms of H and epsilon (e.g., L = H/(1 + epsilon)), which omits dependence on mass m, gravity g, rope cross-sectional area A, and the rope’s constitutive law; and (3) treat strain from one segment to infer total motion without accounting for which rope segments actually contribute to the climber’s displacement and energy storage. The rule triggers when a stress–strain graph is mentioned in the problem but the solution (a) assigns epsilon arbitrarily, or (b) uses formulas that bypass sigma = T/A and the graph, or (c) derives L from epsilon in a way that ignores the required force/energy balance across the rope segments. Examples caught: epsilon_max set to a constant (e.g., 0.5) without graph-based justification; expressions like L = H/(epsilon_max + 1). The solution must explicitly show the chain: compute T at the acceleration limit → sigma = T/A → epsilon from the provided curve → apply correct geometric/energy relations for the stretched rope segments.

rules.title: Avoid spurious eigenfrequency quantization in boundary-driven strings
rules.description: Checks wave-on-a-string (or 1D wave) solutions where one end is driven with a prescribed motion (e.g., y(0,t)=A0 cos(ω t) or a specified velocity/force) and the opposite end has a homogeneous boundary (fixed y(L,t)=0 or free y_x(L,t)=0). Flags the following modeling errors: (1) Imposing discrete normal-mode conditions (e.g., kL=nπ, ω=nπu/L, sin(kL)=0, cos(kL)=0) as a necessary requirement for the steady-state, thereby quantizing the frequency despite an externally imposed ω. (2) Replacing the given driving frequency ω by an eigenfrequency ωn in the time factor. (3) Treating both ends as homogeneous (e.g., y(0,t)=0 or y_x(0,t)=0) instead of honoring the nonzero prescribed boundary motion at the driven end. (4) Using only a homogeneous normal-mode expansion without a particular solution matched to the boundary forcing amplitude, leading to omission of the frequency-dependent amplitude factor (e.g., 1/sin(kL) or 1/cos(kL)) and the associated resonance behavior. (5) Arbitrarily nulling one traveling-wave component to satisfy a single boundary while ignoring reflections from the other end. Correct behavior expected: the steady-state solution remains at the driving frequency ω with spatial profile satisfying both boundaries (e.g., Y(x) ∝ sin[k(L−x)]/sin(kL) for y(L)=0, or the cosine analog for y_x(L)=0), existing for arbitrary ω (except idealized divergence at resonant conditions where the denominator vanishes). The rule triggers if a solution enforces eigenfrequency conditions or removes the driving ω without deriving the amplitude ratio set by the two boundary conditions.

rules.title: Require T and g dependence in stroboscopic free-fall conditions
rules.description: This rule targets problems involving vertical 1D free-fall under constant gravity with perfectly elastic bounces and observations (photos) taken at fixed time intervals T, especially when the statement implies the ball appears at the same position in each photo. In such settings the motion has a natural period P that depends on g and the fall height H (e.g., P = 2√(2H/g)), and stroboscopic equality of positions requires a commensurability condition between T and P (e.g., T = (p/q)P) or equivalently H ∝ g T^2 times a rational factor. The rule flags solutions that provide a final constraint or expression for H (or any parameter determining the period) that: (a) omits both T and g entirely, or (b) shows T and g cancel completely without an explicit, justified limiting condition, or (c) is dimensionally inconsistent for H. Examples of violations include expressions like H = m^2 h_A or H given solely in terms of other lengths and integers with no T or g, when the problem setup includes fixed-interval stroboscopic observation. To pass, the final condition must explicitly involve T and g through combinations such as √(H/g), g T^2, or a rational multiple/ratio relating T to the motion period.

rules.title: Incorrectly constraining sampling interval to be a fraction of the period
rules.description: Checks for the conceptual error where a solution claims that identical positions in photos taken at equal intervals T require T to be a rational fraction of the motion’s period P (e.g., T = P/n or 'T must divide the cycle time'). The correct condition for repeated positions is y(t + T) = y(t) for all sampling times t. In periodic 1D motions with non-monotonic position within a cycle (such as free fall with elastic bounce or SHM), y(t) is not injective over a period, so identical positions can occur at intervals that are not simple fractions of P. Specifically, admissible T include the full period P and the intra-cycle separation Δ(y) between the two symmetric instants at the same position y (as well as combinations like kP ± Δ(y)). This rule flags solutions that: (1) assert or rely on T = P/n (or 'T divides P') as a necessary condition without deriving or invoking y(t + T) = y(t); (2) ignore the existence of two distinct times per cycle corresponding to the same position (except at turning points); or (3) omit or deny intra-cycle intervals like Δ(y) or P − Δ(y) as valid sampling intervals. When triggered, the verifier should mark a concept error and require the solver to explicitly formulate and solve y(t + T) = y(t) for the admissible T.

rules.title: Disallow rock density in subglacial hydraulic potential/no-flow condition
rules.description: Checks solutions for temperate ice-cap problems with a basal water layer to ensure the hydraulic potential and no-flow condition are formulated with the correct densities. Expected modeling: basal water pressure p_w(x) is approximately equal to the basal ice overburden, p_w(x) ≈ p_a + ρ_i g H(x) (optionally minus a small effective pressure), and the hydraulic potential is φ_w(x) = p_w(x) + ρ_w g z_b(x). The no-flow condition along x is dφ_w/dx = 0. The rule flags an error if the solution uses rock or magma density (e.g., ρ_r, ρ_m) in any of the following contexts: (1) in the expression for basal water pressure p_w(x); (2) inside the hydraulic potential φ_w(x) in place of ρ_w; (3) in the no-flow condition derived from φ_w. Acceptable forms include p_w expressed via ice overburden (ρ_i g H) plus atmospheric pressure and/or an effective pressure term N, and φ_w with ρ_w multiplying the elevation term. Trigger patterns include terms like ρ_r g H, ρ_r g h, ρ_m g H, or any ρ_{rock/magma} appearing in p_w or φ_w. Unless the problem explicitly specifies lithostatic confinement of the water by rock (which is not the case for a basal water film under an ice cap at the melting point), the presence of rock/magma density in these expressions is unjustified and should be flagged.

rules.title: Sun-impact transfers: forbid zero heliocentric/impact speed assumptions; require vis-viva/energy consistency
rules.description:
This rule targets solutions that incorrectly assume a spacecraft must reduce its heliocentric speed to zero to fall into the Sun, or that the impact speed at the Sun is zero. It enforces orbital mechanics consistency for impulsive, ballistic transfers from Earth's orbit to the Sun.

The rule flags any of the following patterns:
- Post-burn heliocentric speed explicitly set to v=0 at ~1 AU (e.g., “cancel Earth’s orbital velocity to zero relative to the Sun” or Δv = v_circ as a necessity/minimum without further justification).
- Impact (perihelion) speed at or near the Sun stated as zero/negligible, or omitted while implying zero kinetic energy at the Sun.
- Energy reasoning that ignores the Sun’s gravitational acceleration during coast (e.g., no use of vis-viva or energy conservation, or claims of coming to rest at the Sun without drag/thrust).

Required consistency checks the verifier applies:
- For a single impulsive retrograde burn at r_a ≈ 1 AU with ballistic coast to perihelion r_p (at or near the solar radius), the post-burn heliocentric speed must equal the ellipse aphelion speed given by vis-viva: v_ap^2 = μ_sun (2/r_a − 1/a) with a = (r_a + r_p)/2; this value is strictly non-zero and less than the circular speed v_circ = sqrt(μ_sun/r_a).
- The perihelion/impact speed must be computed from vis-viva/energy conservation: v_p^2 = μ_sun (2/r_p − 1/a), which yields a large value (order 10^2 km/s at the solar surface); any result near zero is inconsistent.

Heuristic numerical guards (when numbers are provided for a 1 AU departure and r_p ~ R_sun):
- Claiming minimal Δv = v_circ (~29.8 km/s) as a necessity/minimum is flagged unless the solution explicitly models continuous thrust or drag; a correct one-impulse ballistic solution gives Δv < v_circ (≈ 27 km/s) and v_ap ≈ 2–4 km/s.
- Impact speed at the Sun should be very large (typically > 300 km/s); values near zero are flagged.

Allowed exceptions:
- The solution explicitly includes continuous thrust, atmospheric/solar drag, or other non-conservative forces that justify coming to rest relative to the Sun.

In summary, the rule enforces use of vis-viva/energy conservation for heliocentric transfer orbits and rejects assumptions that set heliocentric or impact speed to zero absent explicit non-gravitational mechanisms.

rules.title: Earth-to-Sun impulsive transfer speeds via vis-viva must be ~3 km/s heliocentric and ~27 km/s Earth-frame
rules.description: Scope: Applies to problems where a spacecraft is sent to the Sun using a short impulsive burn at Earth's orbit, opposite Earth's heliocentric orbital motion, with a ballistic trajectory that just grazes the Sun (minimum-impulse case). Check: The solution must use the elliptical transfer with aphelion at Earth's orbital radius R (≈ 1 AU) and perihelion at the Sun's radius r_S, and derive the post-burn heliocentric speed at aphelion via the vis-viva relation. Required relations: a = (R + r_S)/2, v0 = sqrt(GM_sun / R) ≈ 29.8 km/s, v_S = v0 * sqrt(2 r_S / (R + r_S)), and the Earth-frame impulse magnitude v_E = v0 − v_S (opposite Earth's motion). Numeric validation (using R ≈ 1 AU and r_S ≈ 6.96e5 km): v_S must lie within [2.6, 3.2] km/s and v_E within [26.5, 27.5] km/s. Flag as incorrect if any of the following occur: (1) v_S is reported ≈ v0 (e.g., ~29–30 km/s) or is not much smaller than v0; (2) v_E is reported ≈ 0 or ≈ v0, or both speeds are claimed equal (e.g., both 29.8 km/s); (3) r_S is omitted from the orbital geometry or R is misidentified as Earth's physical radius instead of the Earth–Sun distance; (4) no use of vis-viva/energy-consistent elliptical transfer is evident; (5) frame confusion that equates Earth-frame and Sun-frame speeds. This rule is intended to catch the common calculation error of asserting both speeds are 29.8 km/s or otherwise neglecting the Sun-grazing ellipse constraints.

rules.title: Sign consistency between surface angle θ(x) and slope z'(x)
rules.description: Checks that the defined angle θ(x) of a 2D interface z(x) (no y-dependence) is consistent with the slope z'(x) given the stated orientation. If θ is defined as the angle between the surface and the horizontal measured from the +x-axis with counterclockwise positive, the correct relation is tan(θ(x)) = z'(x). Under the small-slope/small-angle approximation (|z'| ≪ 1), θ(x) ≈ z'(x) and dθ/dx ≈ z''(x). Flag any use of a sign-inverted mapping (e.g., θ = −arctan(z'), tan θ = −z', θ ≈ −z', or dθ/dx = −z'') unless the solution explicitly redefines the orientation (e.g., angle measured clockwise or from the −x-axis) and applies it consistently. Note that reliance on even functions like cos θ does not justify or mask a sign flip in θ. This rule detects concept errors where the slope–angle sign is inconsistent, which can propagate into subsequent derivations.

rules.title: Surface mass-balance must be per unit area (no extraneous dx/dA)
rules.description: Checks that the kinematic boundary condition at a free surface uses accumulation/ablation as an areal rate (units of length/time) without multiplying by geometric factors like dx or dA unless an explicit area integration is being performed. Triggers when a solution writes a mass-balance such as ρ·c = ρ·v_z(z=H)·dx, v_z(H) ∝ c·dx, or c·Δx, which incorrectly treats the accumulation rate c (m/s or m/yr) as a line or area-integrated flux. Correct usage: the boundary condition at the surface is v_z(z=H) = ±c (sign depends on convention; downward positive gives v_z = +c, upward positive gives v_z = −c), and at the bed v_z(z=0) = 0 (no penetration). Units consistency: c and v_z must both have L/T; any occurrence of c multiplied by a length or area (dx, dy, dA, width, thickness) in a pointwise boundary condition is flagged. Exception: geometric factors are permitted only when the equation explicitly represents an integral over a control surface, e.g., ∫_A c dA = ∫_A v_z dA, with both sides using the same area element. The rule also suggests verifying incompressibility application: ∂v_x/∂x + ∂v_z/∂z = 0 implies a linear v_z(z) profile under the stated separability assumptions, but the primary check is misuse of geometric factors in the surface mass-balance boundary condition.

rules.title: Zero perpendicular velocity at symmetry plane (ice divide / centerline)
rules.description: This rule verifies that solutions invoking a mirror-symmetry plane or axis (e.g., an ice divide at x = 0, centerline, mid-plane) enforce the correct boundary condition: the velocity component normal to the symmetry plane must vanish at the symmetry location. For a symmetry plane at x = 0 in Cartesian coordinates, the condition is v_x(0, z) = 0 for all z (and more generally, the normal component v_n = 0 at the plane). The rule flags the following issues: (1) The solution explicitly assigns a nonzero value to v_x at x = 0, or implies it by stating v_x is uniform/constant in x with a nonzero value; (2) The solution omits the boundary condition v_x(0, z) = 0 while using symmetry arguments (e.g., ‘flow away from the divide’) or outflow only at ±L; (3) The solution fails to recognize that symmetry requires v_x to be an odd function of x, hence v_x(0) = 0. This check applies to incompressible or compressible flows alike when a geometric symmetry plane is invoked. Trigger examples: ‘ice divide at x = 0’ + ‘v_x independent of z’ + ‘v_x = const ≠ 0’; ‘centerline symmetry’ but v_x(0) ≠ 0. If any such condition is detected, the rule reports a boundary-condition violation due to neglected symmetry.

rules.title: Include buoyancy in terminal-velocity force balance in a fluid
rules.description: This rule checks terminal-velocity calculations for an object moving vertically in a fluid to ensure the buoyant force is included in the force balance. It targets solutions using drag D = (1/2) C rho_fluid A v^2 and a gravity-driven terminal speed. Trigger conditions: (a) the problem context contains a fluid density (rho_fluid), object mass or density and volume, gravity g, and a drag model; (b) the solution sets a steady-state/terminal condition (net force = 0 or drag equals weight). Correct requirement: At terminal velocity, the drag must balance the apparent weight, not the full weight, i.e. D = m g - rho_fluid V g. Acceptable equivalent forms include D = g V (rho_object - rho_fluid), D + rho_fluid V g = m g, or using an effective weight m_eff g where m_eff = m - rho_fluid V. Error condition: Flag if the solution equates drag to weight without a buoyancy term (patterns like D = m g, m g = D, or v = sqrt(2 m g / (C rho_fluid A)) without any subtraction of rho_fluid V g or (rho_object - rho_fluid)). Additional checks: If the solution computes volume V or uses object density rho_object and fluid density rho_fluid, the buoyancy term rho_fluid V g must appear explicitly or implicitly. Exceptions: Do not flag if the problem explicitly states to neglect buoyancy. Severity note: If rho_fluid / rho_object < 0.01, record a soft modeling warning (small numerical impact) but still mark the omission as a modeling error; otherwise, record a hard error.

rules.title: Misuse of terminal velocity to constrain initial upward speed or acceleration
rules.description: Flag solutions that compare an initial upward launch speed to the (downward) terminal velocity or use terminal velocity to justify the direction of acceleration during upward motion. Terminal velocity for quadratic drag in free fall is the steady-state speed reached during downward motion when drag balances weight (mg = c*v_t^2). For an object launched upward with no upward thrust, the acceleration is always downward regardless of the initial speed; there is no upward terminal speed in this context. The rule should trigger if the solution: - States or implies that the initial speed must be greater or less than the terminal velocity to determine acceleration direction or to reach maximum height. - Uses terminal velocity to argue that the ball accelerates downward (or not) during upward motion. - Compares v0 to v_t to set conditions for the trajectory in the upward phase. Acceptable uses of terminal velocity include computing the drag coefficient (from mg = c*v_t^2) and discussing downward motion approaching v_t during descent; these should not be flagged.

rules.title: Unjustified circular-path time for minimal-direction change
rules.description: Flags solutions to minimal-time direction-change problems (constant speed, bounded acceleration/friction) that compute time as arc length of a circular segment divided by speed without a valid optimality justification. Typical pattern: use the friction limit to set a_max = μ g, infer a circular trajectory via centripetal acceleration v^2/R = a_max to get R, set arc length s = θ R for a heading change (e.g., θ = π/2), and conclude t = s/v. The rule triggers when: (1) time is obtained via t = s/v from a geometric arc (phrases like 'arc length', 'quarter circle', 'path length', 'circumference'); (2) centripetal acceleration and radius are used (e.g., R = v^2/a, v^2/R) to justify the path; and (3) there is no explicit argument that the chosen trajectory is both feasible under the acceleration bound and time-optimal (e.g., no discussion that acceleration direction is a control variable, that |a| should be held at the bound and perpendicular to velocity to maximize angular rate ω = a⊥/v, or derivation of t from velocity-vector rotation t = Δθ/ω). The rule targets the logic error of inferring minimal time from geometric path length rather than from the bounded-acceleration control required to reorient the velocity vector, even if the numerical result coincides with the correct formula.

rules.title: Correct toppling criterion: pivot at base edge and include all external forces
rules.description:
This rule verifies that a solution uses the correct criterion for the onset of toppling (tipping) of a rigid body resting on a horizontal surface. It flags solutions that: (a) determine toppling by setting the sum of torques of weights to zero (e.g., τ_p + τ_other weights = 0) or by balancing only gravitational torques; (b) compute moments about the base center rather than about a bottom edge; (c) equate 'net torque = 0' without specifying that the normal reaction shifts to a single edge (reaction at the opposite edge becomes zero) or that the resultant line of action exits the base footprint; or (d) omit applied/contact forces from interacting bodies (e.g., chains, strings, external loads) when forming the tipping moment balance.

Pass conditions:
- At incipient toppling, the ground reaction is explicitly stated to act at one bottom edge (opposite edge reaction is zero), or equivalently, the line of action of the resultant external force is stated to reach the boundary of the support base.
- The torque (moment) balance used to identify the tipping condition is taken about that edge and includes all relevant external forces on the body: its own weight, external loads, and any contact forces from attached or contacting bodies (not just weights).
- If friction is discussed, it is not misused as a fixed f = μN to compute a horizontal moment without acknowledging that the contact reaction is distributed and collapses to the edge at tipping.

Fail/flag conditions (any one triggers a flag):
- The toppling condition is written as the sum of torques of weights equals zero, or only weights appear in the criterion with no mention of ground reaction shift to an edge.
- The pivot for the tipping condition is taken at the center of the base (or an arbitrary point) instead of the bottom edge, with no justification tied to reaction shifting.
- The criterion is stated solely as 'net torque = 0' for motion onset without reference to the base of support/edge reaction.
- External/contact forces from interacting bodies (e.g., a chain on top) are omitted from the torque balance used to decide tipping.

This rule is triggered in problems that mention toppling/tipping/overturning for bodies on a support surface and ensures the solution checks the correct edge-pivot/line-of-action condition rather than an incorrect torque-of-weights balance.

rules.title: Incorrect toppling criterion via vertical-height torque and ad hoc fix
rules.description: Flag solutions that assert a tipping/toppling condition using an invalid torque or energy balance. The rule triggers if any of the following patterns are detected: (1) Gravitational moments about a prospective pivot are computed using vertical heights rather than the perpendicular (horizontal) moment arms, e.g., equations of the form m·g·(h/2 + R/2) = m·g·(R − R/π) or similar, where vertical coordinates are multiplied by weight to represent torque. For vertical weights, the correct lever arm about a ground edge is the horizontal offset of the line of action from the pivot; vertical distances are not valid moment arms. (2) The toppling criterion is asserted by equating m·g times lengths without identifying the pivot and perpendicular distances (or without using the equivalent COM-projection check that the combined center-of-mass horizontal projection crosses the support edge), i.e., a torque-free or energy-free ad hoc equality is used to claim tipping. (3) An earlier step yields an unphysical trigonometric bound (e.g., |cosθ|>1, |sinθ|>1), and instead of revising assumptions or the free-body/moment equations, the solution replaces it with an unrelated “correct approach” equality of the type in (1). As an auxiliary check, flag misuse of semicircle centroid constants: expressions like R − R/π used as a centroid distance indicate confusion (valid centroid distances are 2R/π for a semicircular arc and 4R/3π for a semicircular area). Any of these indicate mixing of vertical dimensions with torque lever arms or an unjustified patch after an unphysical result.

rules.title: Torque of vertical forces must use horizontal lever arm (no vertical height × sinθ)
rules.description: This rule verifies torque expressions for vertical forces (e.g., weight mg) about a pivot in planar problems. For any vertical force, the torque magnitude about a pivot equals F multiplied by the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the force’s line of action. In 2D with gravity vertical, this perpendicular distance is the horizontal offset of the center of mass (x-distance), not a vertical height multiplied by a trigonometric factor. The rule flags torque formulas that erroneously compute torque of mg as mg × (vertical length) × sinθ or mg × f(θ) × sinθ where f(θ) represents a vertical coordinate or arc-length-related quantity. Detection criteria: (1) Identify torque terms τ, M, or T involving mg (or m*g) and a trigonometric factor sin(·) or cos(·). (2) If the lever arm is expressed using symbols commonly denoting vertical measures (e.g., y, h, height, R when used as vertical radius/height, or any sum of vertical dimensions) multiplied by sin(·)/cos(·), and no explicit horizontal distance (x, x_COM, r_perp-to-vertical, or an expression clearly equal to the horizontal offset) is present, flag as incorrect. (3) Specifically flag patterns like τ = m g (h/… + …R…) sinθ, τ = m g (R − …cosθ) sinθ, or any mg × (vertical function of θ) × sinθ used as the torque. (4) Allowable forms include τ = m g × (horizontal distance to the weight’s line of action), or τ = m g r sinφ only when φ is explicitly the angle between r and the vertical force and r sinφ is demonstrated to equal the horizontal offset. Rationale: For a vertical force, the lever arm is purely horizontal; using vertical heights with sinθ/cosθ to construct the lever arm is conceptually incorrect and often yields wrong torque. The rule will mark such expressions as errors and recommend: compute torque as τ = m g × (horizontal distance from the pivot to the center-of-mass line of action), with sign determined by rotation sense.

rules.title: Incorrect lever-arm projection in torque when angle is measured from the vertical
rules.description: This rule checks torque calculations for rods or line segments when the angle variable is explicitly defined with respect to the vertical (e.g., 'angle with the wall'). In such cases, the perpendicular lever arm must use the correct projection of the geometry: for a rod of length l making angle θ with the vertical, the coordinates of the far end relative to the pivot are (horizontal = l·sinθ, vertical = l·cosθ), and for the center of mass they are (horizontal = (l/2)·sinθ, vertical = (l/2)·cosθ). Therefore: (1) A horizontal force (e.g., normal from a vertical wall) contributes a torque equal to F × vertical offset, i.e., F·l·cosθ (or F·(l/2)·cosθ if applied at the center), and using sinθ here is incorrect. (2) A vertical force (e.g., weight mg or normal from the ground) contributes a torque equal to F × horizontal offset, i.e., F·(l/2)·sinθ (or F·l·sinθ for an endpoint), and using cosθ here is incorrect. The verifier should parse torque expressions of the form F * length * trig(angle) and identify the force direction (horizontal vs vertical) together with the angle’s reference (vertical). It then verifies that the trig function matches the perpendicular distance: horizontal force → cos(angle_to_vertical); vertical force → sin(angle_to_vertical). The rule flags torque equations where the mapping is swapped (e.g., N_B·l·sinθ for a horizontal wall force, mg·(l/2)·cosθ for a vertical weight) or where both horizontal and vertical forces use the same trig function under an angle defined to the vertical. The same check applies for any rod with angle α to the vertical: horizontal force must pair with cosα, vertical force with sinα. If the angle is instead defined to the horizontal, the expected mapping inverts (horizontal force → sin, vertical force → cos); the verifier should use the declared angle reference to select the correct mapping before checking.

rules.title: Normal force at circular rolling contact gives no torque about the body’s center
rules.description: Checks torque balances written about the rolling body’s own central axis in problems involving a circular rigid body (e.g., a cylinder or disk) in point contact with another circular surface under pure rolling. For such contacts, the normal reaction acts along the line joining the centers and passes through the rolling body’s center of mass; therefore, its moment about that center is zero. The rule flags solutions that include a nonzero torque term attributed to the contact normal (e.g., τ_N = N · (R − r) · sinθ or similar) when the torque is taken about the small body’s center. It also flags omission of the frictional torque (which should be ±f · r) when modeling the spin equation I·α = Στ about the center. Exceptions: do not flag if the solution explicitly computes torque about a different axis (not the small body’s center), if the contact geometry is non-circular or off-axis so the normal does not pass through the center (e.g., cam profile, asymmetric deformation), or if the model states distributed contact with a resultant normal having a known offset. Applies in both no-slip and slip cases (in slip, friction is kinetic but still the only contact force producing spin torque). The verifier should parse torque equations and associated axis statements; if an N term appears in Στ_about(center of the small body), or a lever arm for N about that center is treated as nonzero, raise a modeling error.

rules.title: Correct use of vertical offset h in impulse-induced torque
rules.description: Checks that in collisions where a sphere (radius R) contacts a raised edge at height R + h above the table, the torque from the horizontal impulse J = (j_x, j_y, 0) about the sphere’s center uses the correct vertical lever arm h (not R or R + h). Specifically: (1) The position vector from the center to the contact point must be r = (0, 0, h), so the angular impulse is ΔL = r × J = (h j_x) ŷ − (h j_y) x̂. Consequently, the angular velocity updates must satisfy Δω_x = −(h/I_c) j_y, Δω_y = (h/I_c) j_x, and Δω_z = 0 (or equivalent forms consistent with this dependence). (2) Flag solutions that: use R or R + h as the lever arm multiplying j_x or j_y; omit h entirely from the torque/Δω relations when h ≠ 0 is present in the problem; or produce Δω_z terms from the horizontal impulse due to an incorrect lever arm. (3) Allow equivalent derivations (e.g., angular momentum about the contact point) provided the final dependence on h matches the above (i.e., torque scales with h and couples j_y to ω_x and j_x to ω_y with correct signs). (4) Also flag axis confusion that nullifies the h-dependent torque, such as asserting j_y = 0 solely from a statement like “no vertical impulse” when the problem defines impulses as horizontal (in the xy-plane), thereby removing the required −(h/I_c) j_y contribution.

rules.title: Torque from a force applied at a body-fixed point must depend on orientation
rules.description:
Checks for the incorrect modeling of torque as constant when a force is applied at a fixed material point of a rotating rigid body and the force direction is fixed in the inertial frame. In such cases, the lever arm relative to the chosen axis changes with the body's orientation, so the torque must depend on the angle (e.g., θ).

What the rule checks:
- Context trigger: The solution involves a planar rigid body with a defined orientation variable (e.g., θ(t)) and an external force F applied at a point located a distance r ≠ 0 from the rotation axis. The point of application is attached to the body (body-fixed), while the force direction is stated or implied to be fixed in the lab frame (e.g., a constant horizontal or vertical pull, a constant wind force, etc.).
- Correct physics requirement: The torque contribution from that force about the axis must be τ(θ, t) = (r × F)·k, whose magnitude is r F sin φ(θ, t), where φ is the angle between the radius vector from the axis to the point of application and the force direction. Therefore, unless the line of action passes through the axis or special symmetry applies, τ must depend on θ (typically as sinθ or cosθ).
- Violation pattern: The solution assigns a constant torque magnitude equal to rF (e.g., τ = Tr) or any sign-fixed constant for that force, with no dependence on θ (or time) in a scenario where the point of application rotates with the body while the force direction does not. Examples to flag include: "τ_T = Tr", "I θ¨ = Tr − ...", or any torque term from the applied force that lacks θ dependence despite the above context.

Concrete example (this problem): A string applies a constant horizontal tension T at the material point initially at the hoop's top. The radius vector to that point rotates with the hoop, so the torque is τ_T(θ) = −T r cos θ (for CCW positive). Modeling τ_T as a constant ±Tr is incorrect and should be flagged.

Exceptions to avoid false positives:
- Do not flag if the force line-of-action rotates with the body in such a way that the perpendicular moment arm remains constant (e.g., a tangential force always tangent to a rim due to a string wrapped around it that turns with the body). In such cases, a constant torque may be correct.
- Do not flag if the force passes through the rotation axis (r⊥ = 0) or if geometry explicitly yields a constant perpendicular lever arm.

Implementation hints:
- Identify presence of θ(t) and an external force described as constant in direction in the lab frame (e.g., "constant horizontal T").
- Detect modeling of torque terms as constants of the form rF, Tr, or ±c without θ dependence for forces applied at body-fixed points at radius r.
- If the text mentions attachment to a specific point on the rim/edge/top/edge of a rotating body and a constant-direction force, require θ-dependence in the torque term. If absent, raise a modeling error with a suggested correction: τ(θ) = rF sin(φ(θ)).

rules.title: No torque from forces applied at the chosen pivot point
rules.description: Checks rotational-equilibrium/dynamics equations for improper inclusion of torque from reaction forces applied at the pivot (moment reference) point. Physics principle: The torque of a force about a point lying on the force’s own line of action is zero. Therefore, when moments are taken about a contact/pivot point, any forces applied at that same point (e.g., a ground normal or ground friction at the bottom contact of a rod/ladder) must contribute zero torque and should not appear with a nonzero lever arm in the torque sum. Detection logic: (1) Identify the point about which torques are summed (from text like "about the bottom end/hinge," or from use of an end-pivot moment of inertia such as I_end = (1/3) m l^2, or notation τ_about A = I_A α). (2) Identify forces whose application point coincides with that pivot (e.g., ground normal N and static/kinetic friction f at the bottom contact; hinge reactions at a wall hinge). (3) Inspect the torque equation about that point; flag if any torque term includes these pivot reactions with a nonzero moment arm (patterns such as N·l cosθ, N·R, f·l sinθ, or any symbolically nonzero distance from the pivot). (4) Do not flag if the torque balance is explicitly taken about a different point (e.g., center of mass with I_cm = (1/12) m l^2), where such forces legitimately produce torque. Example caught: In a leaning rod problem taking moments about the bottom contact, terms like N·l cos(θ) or f_s·l sin(θ) are incorrectly included; they must be zero because the forces act at the pivot.

rules.title: Verify torque equilibrium condition
rules.description: For a system in static equilibrium, the sum of all torques acting on the system about any axis must be zero. This ensures rotational equilibrium.
rules.check_logic: Check if the sum of torques (A3A4) equals zero around the chosen axis of rotation.
common_errors: Forgetting to include all torque contributions (e.g., reaction forces or weights)
Incorrectly calculating the lever arm (distance perpendicular to the force)
Using inconsistent torque directions (e.g., mixing clockwise and counterclockwise signs)

rules.title: Verify force equilibrium condition
rules.description: For a system in static equilibrium, the sum of all forces acting on the system in each direction (x, y, z) must be zero. This ensures translational equilibrium.
rules.check_logic: Verify that A3A2F_x = 0, A3A2F_y = 0, and A3A2F_z = 0 for the system.
common_errors: Omitting a force component (e.g., friction or normal force)
Incorrectly resolving forces into their components
Using the wrong sign convention when summing forces

rules.title: Ensure consistent torque sign convention
rules.description: Torque direction follows a sign convention: counterclockwise torques are often considered positive, and clockwise torques are negative. This must be consistent throughout the solution.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all torques adhere to a consistent sign convention (e.g., CCW positive, CW negative).
common_errors: Mixing clockwise and counterclockwise signs inconsistently
Using the wrong sign convention for a specific torque

rules.title: Check pivot point selection for torque analysis
rules.description: The choice of pivot point for torque calculation can be flexible, but a strategically chosen pivot point can simplify the analysis by eliminating torque contributions from unknown forces.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the pivot point is logically selected to simplify calculations and check that torque calculations are correctly performed about this point.
common_errors: Choosing a pivot point that adds complexity unnecessarily
Omitting torque contributions about the chosen pivot point
Incorrectly assuming torque cancels at the pivot point without verification

rules.title: Ensure conditions for static equilibrium are met
rules.description: Static equilibrium assumes the system is stationary, with no net acceleration or angular acceleration. This is valid only if the system is truly at rest or moving at constant velocity.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the system is either stationary or moving at a constant velocity before proceeding with static equilibrium equations.
common_errors: Using static equilibrium equations for a system undergoing acceleration
Neglecting external influences that could induce motion

rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency in torque calculations
rules.description: Torque is represented as the product of force in Newtons and distance in meters, thus its unit is Newton-meters (N�b7m).
rules.check_logic: Ensure torque calculations maintain dimensional consistency with results expressed in N�b7m.
common_errors: Mixing incompatible units in torque calculations (e.g., using kilograms instead of Newtons)
Failing to multiply the force by the lever arm distance to calculate torque

rules.title: Verify geometric constraints in lever arms
rules.description: The lever arm is the shortest (perpendicular) distance from the axis of rotation to the force's line of action. Errors in geometry can skew torque calculations.
rules.check_logic: Verify that lever arms are correctly measured as perpendicular distances to the force's line of action.
common_errors: Using an incorrect measurement for the lever arm (not perpendicular)
Misidentifying the point of application for force leading to incorrect lever arm calculations

rules.title: Ensure correct application of static friction limits
rules.description: Static friction opposes motion up to a maximum value given by f_s �A4 �B5_s�B7N, where �B5_s is the coefficient of static friction and N is the normal force.
rules.check_logic: Verify that static friction remains within its limit �A4 �B5_s�B7N and effectively prevents motion.
common_errors: Exceeding the static friction limit in calculations
Incorrect normal force determination affecting friction calculations
Assuming static friction acts when unnecessary

rules.title: Check the angle of torque application
rules.description: Torque is maximized when force is applied perpendicular to the lever arm. The angle at which force is applied influences the torque produced.
rules.check_logic: Ensure forces contributing to torque are evaluated considering the angle of application and its effect on torque magnitude.
common_errors: Ignoring the angle between force and lever arm
Misusing trigonometric functions to resolve torque components

rules.title: 刚体倾覆临界判定准则
rules.description:
触发条件：题目要求寻找物体“开始翻倒”或“能够翻倒”的参数条件
检查逻辑：检查是否对比了倾覆力矩（通常由外力或动力学压力产生）与恢复力矩（通常由重力产生，支点选在底边边缘）。
rules.check_logic: 检查是否对比了倾覆力矩（通常由外力或动力学压力产生）与恢复力矩（通常由重力产生，支点选在底边边缘）。

rules.title: 软绳/链条动力学力矩审计
rules.description:
触发条件：软绳或链条在曲面上滑动并涉及整体平衡（如翻倒、移动）
检查逻辑：必须通过能量守恒求出速度，再利用向心力公式分析链条对接触面的法向压力分布，积分求出总力矩，而非仅看重心位置。
