rules.title: 多体接触平衡建模校验
rules.description:
触发条件：题目涉及两个或多个刚体相互接触并靠在边界（墙/地）上时
检查逻辑：必须区分‘边界接触力’与‘物体间相互作用力’。检查受力分析图是否包含交点处的法向力和摩擦力对，而非将其视为独立系统。
rules.check_logic: 必须区分‘边界接触力’与‘物体间相互作用力’。检查受力分析图是否包含交点处的法向力和摩擦力对，而非将其视为独立系统。
rules.trigger: 题目涉及两个或多个刚体相互接触并靠在边界（墙/地）上时

rules.title: 临界平衡不等式方向检查
rules.description:
触发条件：求取角度满足的平衡条件（Condition）时
检查逻辑：检查摩擦力是否处于临界状态 f ≤ μN。若预测结果仅给出等式或错误的几何关系而未引入μ，则建模失败。
rules.check_logic: 检查摩擦力是否处于临界状态 f ≤ μN。若预测结果仅给出等式或错误的几何关系而未引入μ，则建模失败。
rules.trigger: 求取角度满足的平衡条件（Condition）时

rules.title: Transient storage–flow coupling must yield a first-order ODE with exponential decay (no cancellation of dP/dt)
rules.description:
This rule checks for internal consistency when a solution combines a flow relation with a storage/compressibility relation in transient problems (e.g., reservoir depletion). Specifically, it verifies that equating the production rate from Darcy/transport (typically proportional to the pressure difference ΔP) with the storage/compressibility rate (proportional to dΔP/dt) leads to a first-order linear ODE of the form dΔP/dt = -k ΔP and thus exponential decay, rather than linear-in-time behavior. The rule flags the following patterns:
- The solution equates two expressions for q that both include a factor dP/dt and cancels dP/dt to obtain an algebraic identity between parameters (e.g., S = V0 c_o or similar), thereby eliminating the governing differential equation.
- After such cancellation, the solution still treats dP/dt (or dP_b/dt) as a constant and integrates to obtain ΔP(t) linear in time.
- Any conclusion that ΔP(t) is linear in t in a single-capacitance system with storage and flow coupling, without external forcing, instead of exponential decay.
- For half-time or depletion-time calculations in such first-order systems, the solution omits the ln(2) factor (i.e., t_1/2 must equal (ln 2) * S/k). Absence of ln(2) or linear-time scaling is flagged.
- Use of average pressure approximations (e.g., P̄ = (P_b + P_w)/2) to convert dP̄/dt into dP_b/dt followed by cancellation of dP_b/dt across both sides when equating q from storage and q from flow.
The rule triggers if any of these inconsistencies are detected, indicating the differential nature of the problem was lost (via cancellation) or the transient behavior was mischaracterized (linear instead of exponential).

rules.title: Use total system mass for translational forces and F=ma
rules.description: Checks that any translational force or acceleration equation (weight W=mg, ramp components mg sin(theta), mg cos(theta), normal force N, net force down the incline, and Newton's second law F=ma) uses the total mass of the system, not a partial mass that excludes subcomponents. Trigger this rule when the problem statement defines an object composed of multiple parts with specified masses (e.g., chassis mass M defined as excluding wheels, plus wheel masses). The verifier should: (1) parse mass definitions and identify phrases indicating exclusion (e.g., 'mass excluding the wheels', 'chassis only'); (2) compute the expected total mass M_total as the sum of all component masses; (3) scan the solution for translational equations involving gravity or normal reaction and for F=ma, and verify the mass used equals M_total (symbolically or numerically); (4) flag an error if the solution uses only the chassis mass or any subset of component masses (e.g., N = M g cos(theta), W = M g, F_down = M g sin(theta), or F_net = M a) when the motion concerns the entire bus including its wheels. This catches modeling mistakes where wheels or other components are omitted from the system mass in translational dynamics, even if the incorrect normal force is not used later.

rules.title: Turning-point velocity and kinetic energy consistency on constrained motion
rules.description: Checks solutions for internal consistency of velocity components and kinetic energy at a declared maximum height or turning point when the particle is constrained to move on a smooth curve/surface (e.g., z = f(x), parabolic bowl). The rule triggers when the context includes a geometric constraint and the solution references an extremum along the path ("maximum height", "turning point"). It enforces that at a turning point along the constraint the tangential speed is zero, hence the total kinetic energy is zero at that instant. Flags the following contradictions: (1) Claiming nonzero kinetic energy (or "purely vertical kinetic energy") at the turning point while also setting a component velocity to zero that would eliminate the stated kinetic energy (e.g., saying v_x = 0 and then v_z = 0 but still asserting nonzero KE). (2) Mixing projectile-apex logic with constrained motion: stating v_z = 0 while v_x ≠ 0 (or vice versa) at the maximum height along a surface defined by z = f(x), which implies nonzero tangential speed at a turning point; this is inconsistent with constrained turning points. (3) Using a nonzero kinetic term in the energy balance to compute the maximum height for a constrained turning point where speed must be zero. The rule is satisfied if the solution sets tangential speed to zero and uses purely potential energy at the extremum; it is violated by any simultaneous claims that imply nonzero kinetic energy or mutually inconsistent velocity component statements at that point.

rules.title: Two-body escape must use reduced mass/CM energy, not single-body KE with fixed source
rules.description:
Checks solutions to gravitational escape/unbinding problems involving two finite masses in isolation. Flags treatments that incorrectly fix one body and apply the escape criterion to a single mass's kinetic energy. Detection criteria:
- Context: Two bodies of finite mass (m1, m2) interacting only via mutual gravity; goal is escape/unbinding (e.g., E >= 0, "escape velocity").
- Potential energy is written as −G m1 m2 / r, but kinetic energy includes only one body's term (e.g., 1/2 m1 v^2 or 1/2 m2 v^2) in the total energy used for the escape condition.
- The escape threshold is computed as v = sqrt(2 G M / r) with M taken as one body’s mass, without any limiting argument (M >> m) or external anchoring.
- No mention of reduced mass, center-of-mass (CM) frame, or momentum conservation linking the two bodies’ speeds.
Rule/requirement:
- For isolated two-body gravity, the escape criterion must be applied to the relative motion with reduced mass mu = m1 m2 / (m1 + m2): E_rel = 1/2 mu v_rel^2 − G m1 m2 / r, and escape requires v_rel >= sqrt(2 G (m1 + m2) / r).
- Equivalent acceptable approach: sum both kinetic energies with momentum conservation (m1 v1 = m2 v2) to obtain the same threshold; or explicitly use CM frame.
- If the problem asks for the speed of one body (e.g., the lighter craft) at separation, it must be mapped from v_rel using momentum conservation, e.g., v1 = (m2/(m1 + m2)) v_rel and v2 = (m1/(m1 + m2)) v_rel. Directly setting that body’s speed equal to v_rel without justification is flagged.
Exceptions (do not flag):
- The solution explicitly justifies the fixed-source approximation (M >> m) and states/uses the approximation, or states that one body is externally anchored.
- The solution explicitly uses reduced mass/CM energy or an equivalent derivation that yields v_rel >= sqrt(2 G (m1 + m2) / r).

rules.title: Two-body escape must use relative energy/reduced mass, not single-body energy
rules.description: Checks gravitational escape problems involving two finite, free masses (attractor mass M and escaping mass m). Flags solutions that use the escape criterion on the escaping body alone (e.g., E = (1/2) m v^2 - G M m / r >= 0 or v_escape = sqrt(2 G M / r)) without accounting for the kinetic energy of both bodies via the reduced-mass formulation. The correct escape condition in an isolated two-body system is that the relative mechanical energy be nonnegative: E_rel = (1/2) μ v_rel^2 - G M m / r >= 0, with μ = m M / (m + M), giving v_rel >= sqrt(2 G (M + m) / r). The rule triggers if: (a) the derived threshold uses only m and M with v_escape = sqrt(2 G M / r), (b) energy is set to zero for the daughter alone without introducing μ or center-of-mass reasoning, or (c) the solution omits momentum conservation/COM treatment when M is not explicitly fixed or M >> m. Exemptions: do not flag if the problem explicitly states the attractor is fixed by external forces or M >> m is assumed and justified. For finite mass ratios (e.g., M = 4m), the expected minimal speed uses (M + m), e.g., v_min = sqrt(2 G (M + m) / r).

rules.title: Two-body circular orbit must use CM radii; no unjustified mass-sum in ω^2
rules.description: Checks derivations of orbital frequency ω for a binary (two-body) circular orbit to ensure consistent use of the center-of-mass (CM) framework. Flags the following issues: (1) Using the inter-body separation R as the orbital radius on the centripetal side for an individual mass, i.e., setting G M1 M2 / R^2 = Mi ω^2 R for i = 1 or 2 without defining the CM radii ri. For each body, the correct centripetal term is Mi ω^2 ri, with ri ≠ R in general. (2) Deriving both ω^2 = G M2 / R^3 (from body 1) and ω^2 = G M1 / R^3 (from body 2) with the same R but not concluding M1 = M2; this is internally inconsistent unless R is incorrectly used. (3) Jumping from the inconsistent single-body equations in (2) to ω^2 = G (M1 + M2) / R^3 without an explicit CM or reduced-mass derivation (e.g., without introducing r1, r2 with r1 + r2 = R and M1 r1 = M2 r2, or without invoking the relative-coordinate Kepler law). The rule requires that to obtain ω^2 = G (M1 + M2) / a^3, the solution must either: (a) use Mi ω^2 ri with ri expressed via CM relations ri = (Mj / (M1 + M2)) a and then eliminate ri, or (b) work in the relative coordinate/reduced mass and apply Kepler's third law with a being the total separation (semi-major axis). If the final result ω ∝ R^p has p = −3/2 but is reached via the inconsistent steps above, the solution is still flagged for faulty logic. This rule applies when the solution references two masses (M1, M2), a separation (R or a), and equates gravitational to centripetal forces to get ω.

rules.title: Kinetic energy of uniformly strained rod: final formula completeness and variable conformity
rules.description: Checks solutions to the thin elastic rod kinetic energy task for the following: (1) A complete, explicit final expression for kinetic energy T/K is present (e.g., starts with 'T =' or 'K =') and does not end mid-derivation, with ellipses, dangling equals, or unfinished integrals. (2) The final expression is written solely in terms of the requested variables m (mass), L (length), and the strain-rate ε̇ (time derivative of tensile strain), with no extraneous parameters such as ρ (density), A (cross-sectional area), u(x,t), ΔL, x, or unresolved integrals. (3) Proper elimination of ρ and A via m = ρ A L is performed; any residual appearance of ρ or A in the final answer is flagged. (4) Correct dependence for a uniformly strained, bending-prevented rod is enforced: T must scale as m L^2 ε̇^2 with a dimensionless numerical coefficient of 1/6, i.e., T = (1/6) m L^2 ε̇^2. Deviations in the coefficient or use of ε instead of ε̇ are flagged. (5) Dimensional consistency of the final formula (energy units: mass × (length/time)^2) is verified. This rule catches incomplete derivations, mid-expression termination during elimination (e.g., stopping at T = (1/2) ρ A ∫(ε̇^2 x^2) dx), missing final formula, failure to substitute m = ρ A L, inclusion of extraneous variables, and incorrect numerical factors.

rules.title: Uniform axial strain and linear velocity field for non-bending rod
rules.description: Applicable when the problem specifies a very thin homogeneous rod with constant cross-section, prevented from bending, and stretched symmetrically from both ends (or equivalently, axial motion with symmetry). The rule verifies that the solution enforces the kinematic constraints implied by the setup and reduces the kinetic energy to depend only on m, L, and the strain-rate dot(ε). Checks performed: (1) Modeling: The axial strain must be uniform along the rod, i.e., ε(x, t) = ε(t); solutions that retain position-dependent ε(x, t) or arbitrary u(x, t) without asserting uniformity are flagged. (2) Symmetry/zero-momentum: The velocity field must be linear in position about the rod’s center, v(x, t) = dot(ε) (x − L/2), or an equivalent origin choice (e.g., v = dot(ε) x with origin at the center) that ensures ∫ v dm = 0; solutions using constant v, arbitrary v(x), or failing to impose zero net momentum are flagged. (3) Energy form: The kinetic energy must be computed as T = (1/2) ∫_0^L ρ A v^2 dx and simplified to T = (m L^2 / 24) [dot(ε)]^2; any dependence on E, spatial profiles, ρ or A separately (instead of m), or leaving T as an unsimplified integral is flagged. (4) Output variables: The final T must be expressible solely in terms of m, L, and dot(ε); inclusion of additional material parameters in the kinetic energy indicates a modeling error. This rule catches failures to apply the uniform-strain and symmetry constraints needed to express T in the requested variables.

rules.title: Angular-momentum balance with variable moment of inertia and mass transfer at a radius
rules.description:
Checks that solutions for rotating systems with mass transferring between radii use the correct differential angular-momentum balance, including the ω dI term and the correct arrival angular momentum of the incoming mass. The rule applies when a rotating body’s moment of inertia I(t) changes because mass dm (or k dt) attaches/detaches at radius r.

The verifier will flag an error if any of the following are detected:
- The incremental angular-momentum balance is written as dL = I dω (or L' = I ω with I treated as constant) for a body whose I changes due to mass transfer. Correct form is d(I ω) = I dω + ω dI.
- For the receiving body (e.g., cylinder B), the added angular momentum from the incoming mass is modeled as dm r^2 ω_body (e.g., dm b^2 ω_B), i.e., assuming the mass instantly shares the body’s angular speed, instead of using the mass’s own arrival angular speed. Correct term is dm r^2 ω_arrival.
- The arrival angular speed ω_arrival of the incoming mass is not derived from the mass’s own angular-momentum conservation during torque-free flight between radii. In problems like sand moving from radius a on A to radius b on B, the correct relation is dm a^2 ω_A = dm b^2 ω_arrival ⇒ ω_arrival = (a^2/b^2) ω_A.
- The radius used in the angular-momentum contribution of the incoming mass is incorrect (e.g., using a on the RHS for the momentum gained by B instead of b, or using b for the momentum lost by A instead of a).

Acceptable template equations the verifier looks for:
- Receiving body at radius b: I_B dω_B + ω_B dI_B = dm b^2 ω_arrival, with dI_B = dm b^2 and ω_arrival computed from the sand’s own angular-momentum conservation (e.g., ω_arrival = (a^2/b^2) ω_A when moving from a to b).
- Donor body at radius a: I_A dω_A + ω_A dI_A = − dm a^2 ω_A, with dI_A = − dm a^2.

Equivalent expressions using k dt instead of dm are acceptable. Any omission of the ω dI term or misuse of ω_arrival/radius as described above will be marked as a logic error in angular-momentum conservation for variable-I systems with mass transfer.

rules.title: Potential energy reference mismatch when radius changes between stages
rules.description: This rule checks for incorrect definitions of gravitational potential energy (or height difference) when comparing two swing/pendulum configurations that have different pivot-to-mass distances (variable length across stages). Applicability: problems where a person changes posture on a swing (or a pendulum changes length), so that the distance from pivot to the center of mass is r_A at stage A and r_B at stage B, with r_A != r_B, and the zero potential energy is set at one of the stages (commonly the lowest point B). Correct requirement: the vertical separation between stages i and j with angles measured from the downward vertical is Δh(i→j) = r_j cos(θ_j) − r_i cos(θ_i). If the zero level is at the lowest point B with θ_B = 0, then Δh(A→B) = r_B − r_A cos(θ_A). Violation condition: flag any energy or height expression that uses h = r_i (1 − cos θ_i) or U_i − U_j = m g r_i (1 − cos θ_i) while simultaneously setting the zero potential at a stage with a different radius r_j != r_i (i.e., omitting the r_j term). Heuristic patterns to flag include: (1) presence of two radii (e.g., l and l+d) across stages; (2) a statement or equation setting U_B = 0 or 'zero potential at B'; (3) a height or energy expression for stage A relative to B of the form h_A = l (1 − cos θ_A) or ΔU = m g l (1 − cos θ_A), without any additive term involving r_B (e.g., +d when r_B = l + d). Explicit example: if r_A = l and r_B = l + d with zero at B, the correct height from A to B is h1 = l (1 − cos θ_A) + d. The rule flags cases where the +d term (i.e., dependence on r_B) is missing. Allowed exception: if r_A = r_B (no length change) or d = 0, then h = r (1 − cos θ) is valid and should not be flagged.

rules.title: Instantaneous radial length change: do not conserve mechanical energy; conserve angular momentum about pivot
rules.description:
Purpose: Detect the misuse of mechanical energy conservation across quick/impulsive changes of the distance to a pivot (variable-length pendulum/swing), such as standing/squatting on a swing or reeling a mass in/out. Rationale: During an instantaneous radial change, the interaction/constraint force acts along the rod and does work because there is radial displacement; therefore the mechanical energy of the point mass is not conserved through the event. The correct invariant for the instant is angular momentum about the pivot (exact if the external torque about the pivot is zero, e.g., at the bottom; approximately conserved if the change is impulsive elsewhere).

Flag if any of the following are found across a transition where the radius r changes (e.g., A→A′ or B→B′ in swing problems):
- The solution sets E_after = E_before for the person/point mass without including a nonzero work term from the constraint/actuator (e.g., muscle/rod/string), or states that kinetic energy/speed is unchanged solely by energy conservation.
- The solution asserts K_after = K_before or v_after = v_before at the instant of radial change based on energy conservation alone.
- The solution treats the constraint force as doing no work because it is a 'constraint', despite nonzero radial displacement during the change.

Pass conditions (do not flag) if the solution instead: (a) applies conservation of angular momentum about the pivot (m r^2 ω = const) during the instantaneous radial change, noting that at the lowest point gravity’s torque about the pivot is zero, or (b) explicitly includes the work done by the constraint/actuator during the radial change in the energy balance and does not set E_after = E_before unless that work is shown to be zero by valid reasoning.

Typical trigger phrases/contexts: 'quickly squat/stand', 'instantaneous change of length', 'shorten/lengthen string/rod', 'variable-length pendulum', 'reel in/out', combined with equations like E_A = E_A′, K_A = K_A′, or v_A = v_A′ when r changes.

rules.title: Incorrectly assuming constant proportionality when balance implies x-dependence
rules.description: Checks for solutions that treat a proportionality coefficient as a constant when the governing physics requires it to vary with position. Specifically: if a solution uses a relation of the form A(x) = β · B(x) (e.g., dP/dx = β · ρ(x)) and separately derives A(x) = f(x) · B(x) with explicit x-dependence in f(x) (e.g., from force balance in a rotating frame: dP/dx = ρ(x) · ω^2 · x, up to sign), then β must equal f(x) and therefore depend on x. The rule flags conclusions that set β to an x-independent constant (such as β = ω^2) or invoke an 'effective/average' constant without demonstrating that A(x)/B(x) is x-independent. The verifier should: (1) detect a proportionality statement A(x) = β · B(x); (2) find a derived relation A(x) = f(x) · B(x) where f depends on x; (3) if the final answer states β is constant or omits the x-dependence implied by f(x), mark as a conceptual error and recommend β(x) = f(x). Allow β to be constant only if the solution explicitly proves f(x) is constant (e.g., f'(x) = 0). Example caught: in rotating-tube hydrostatics, matching dP/dx = ρ(x) ω^2 x to dP/dx = β ρ(x) requires β(x) = ω^2 x; asserting β = ω^2 is incorrect.

rules.title: Require vector momentum conservation to include moving target’s initial momentum
rules.description: This rule checks momentum conservation statements in collision/scattering problems where the target particle is initially moving and (optionally) stops after the interaction. The correct vector conservation is p_initial_projectile + p_initial_target = p_final_projectile + p_final_target. The rule flags solutions that: (a) explicitly state the target is moving initially (e.g., mention non-zero velocity, relativistic gamma, or p_target,i ≠ 0) and that it stops after the collision (p_target,f = 0), AND (b) write momentum conservation using only the projectile terms (e.g., only photon momenta), omitting the initial target momentum vector. Typical incorrect patterns include setting p_i = p_f cos(θ) and 0 = p_f sin(θ) or otherwise forcing the transverse component to zero while θ ≠ 0 or π, which implicitly assumes the target’s initial momentum is zero. The rule requires component-wise vector equations that include the target’s initial momentum; if the perpendicular (to the initial projectile direction) component is set to zero without including the target’s initial momentum term in that component, the solution is flagged as a modeling error.

rules.title: Same-position photos in vertical bounce must use Δ(y), not just full period
rules.description:
Checks solutions for the vertical free-fall with elastic bounce (initial rest at height H) photographed at equal intervals T. The ball passes any height y in (0, H) twice per cycle (downward then upward), and the time between these two occurrences is Δ(y) = 2 * sqrt(2 * (H - y) / g). Correct reasoning for "same position in every photo" must consider Δ(y), not only the full period P = 2 * sqrt(2H / g). The rule flags solutions that:
- Imply or state that identical positions at each photo require T = P or integer multiples of P only, without considering Δ(y).
- Do not derive or use Δ(y) = 2 * sqrt(2 * (H - y) / g) for the two-pass same-height interval.
- Fail to obtain the continuous family of observed heights h_A from T via h_A = H - (g * T^2) / 8 for 0 < T <= P (with special cases: T = P -> h_A = 0, T = P/2 -> h_A = 3H/4).
- Provide only discrete positions (e.g., top or bottom) or restrict T to specific fractions of P without giving the general dependence h_A(T).

rules.title: Sign consistency for Newton’s second law in vertical fall arrest (tension vs weight)
rules.description: Checks that Newton’s second law is applied with correct sign conventions in vertical deceleration (fall arrest) scenarios involving gravity (mg, downward) and rope tension (T, upward). The rule targets the common mistake of writing mg - T = m a_max with a_max treated as a positive magnitude during deceleration, which implies a downward acceleration and leads to unphysical results (e.g., negative or sub-weight tension). What the rule verifies: 1) Context detection: The solution indicates a falling body being arrested/decellerated by a rope (keywords like fall, arrest, decelerate, rope/carabiner, stretch) with forces {mg downward, T upward}. 2) Acceleration direction: If the text describes deceleration of downward motion or explicitly states acceleration is upward (or uses an acceleration magnitude a_max at the instant of maximum rope force), then the acceleration used in the force equation must be upward. 3) Equation form check: For upward acceleration of magnitude a_max (>0), the correct relation is T - mg = m a_max, hence T = mg + m a_max. Using mg - T = m a_max with a_max > 0, or deriving T = mg - m a_max (or T = |mg - m a_max|) in this context is flagged. 4) Inequality check: In deceleration (acceleration upward), T must satisfy T > mg. Any result with T ≤ mg, T < 0, or a computed T like 4mg when a_max = 5g is flagged. 5) Axis convention consistency: If a downward-positive axis is explicitly used, then the acceleration value must be negative for upward acceleration (a = -a_max), so mg - T = m a must produce T = mg + m a_max. Using a positive a_max with mg - T = m a is flagged. The rule raises an error when the tension is computed as mg - m a_max or otherwise fails T = mg + m a_max for upward acceleration; it also flags negative tension magnitudes arising from sign errors.

rules.title: Do not set a single support normal equal to mg when other contacts can carry vertical force
rules.description: This rule checks vertical force balance statements for each rigid body in multi-contact equilibrium problems. It flags solutions that set a single support normal equal to the weight (e.g., N = mg, N_A = mg) while the body has other contacts or constraints that can transmit vertical force components. Detection logic: (1) Identify each body's vertical equilibrium equation (sum of forces in the vertical direction, or explicit statements like N = mg). (2) From the problem setup and the solution's force list, determine whether the body has any additional interactions that can produce vertical components: inter-body contacts with nonzero friction coefficient (μ > 0), friction at any contact point, oblique contact normals, tension/compression in members at nonzero angles, or any external forces with vertical components. (3) If such interactions exist and the vertical equilibrium is written as N_support = mg or omits vertical components from these other contacts, flag the solution. (4) Do not flag if the solution explicitly demonstrates that all other potential vertical components are zero (e.g., friction coefficient at the contact is zero, the contact is smooth with no tangential force, the line of action is horizontal, or geometry eliminates vertical components). Example of a violation: For a rod on the ground that also touches another rod at a frictional interface (μ_c > 0), writing N_A = mg ignores the vertical component that the inter-rod contact can carry; the correct balance must include the vertical component of the AB–CD contact reaction. This rule also catches analogous errors such as setting N = mg for a block pulled by a rope at an angle or for a body on an inclined/oblique member without accounting for vertical components of those interactions.

rules.title: Height difference from two passage time intervals must be completed and correct
rules.description: Scope: Problems where an object moves vertically under uniform gravity and passes two fixed heights A and B twice (up and down), with measured time intervals Δt_A and Δt_B between the two passages at each height, and the task is to find the height difference h = y_B − y_A (with B higher than A). What this rule checks: 1) The solution must connect the measured interval at a given height to the speed there via Δt_X = 2|v_X|/g, leading to v_A = g Δt_A/2 and v_B = g Δt_B/2. 2) The solution must use the kinematic/energy relation v^2 = v0^2 − 2 g y and eliminate v0 by subtraction to obtain v_A^2 − v_B^2 = 2 g h. 3) The final expression for h must be given solely in terms of g, Δt_A, and Δt_B, specifically h = (g/8)(Δt_A^2 − Δt_B^2), or an algebraically equivalent form. Failure conditions flagged: a) The derivation stops after stating Δt_X = 2 v_X/g or v_A = g Δt_A/2 without solving for h. b) The final answer for h contains v0, v_A, v_B, or other intermediate variables not eliminated. c) The final expression for h depends linearly on Δt_A − Δt_B or Δt_A + Δt_B (dimensionally incorrect), or uses v_A^2 + v_B^2 or an incorrect sign such that h ∝ (Δt_B^2 − Δt_A^2). d) The final expression is not algebraically equivalent to h = (g/8)(Δt_A^2 − Δt_B^2), or has unit inconsistency (h not in length units). e) Given B higher than A, the solution implies h < 0 (e.g., by reversing the difference of squares). This rule ensures the derivation is completed and the correct relation between time intervals and height difference is provided.

rules.title: Incorrect ground-level constraint at vertical-plane collision
rules.description: Checks that, for a projectile colliding with a vertical surface (e.g., a wall or backboard), the solution does not impose y(t_collision) = 0 or otherwise force the vertical position at impact to ground level unless explicitly stated by the problem. The collision time with a vertical plane must be obtained from the horizontal condition x(t_collision) = x_plane; the corresponding y(t_collision) should follow from the projectile's kinematics using the initial conditions, not from a ground-contact constraint. The rule flags solutions that: (a) set y=0 at the instant the projectile reaches the backboard/wall, (b) use the ground-impact equation y0 + v0_y * t - (1/2) g t^2 = 0 to solve for the collision time with a vertical plane, or (c) otherwise treat the vertical coordinate at a vertical-plane collision as predetermined (e.g., ground level) without explicit instruction. This prevents unphysical trajectories and modeling errors where the impact height is improperly constrained.

rules.title: Require restitution coefficient in post-impact vertical motion and flight time
rules.description: When a problem specifies a coefficient of restitution (c or e) for the ball–floor impact, any computation of the ball’s vertical motion immediately after the impact must include c. The verifier will check that: (1) The post-impact vertical speed (v_y+) is modeled as v_y+ = c * |v_y−| (upward), i.e., the normal relative velocity reverses sign and is scaled by c; equivalently, the rebound height satisfies h_rebound = c^2 * h_impact. (2) Any time-of-flight used to determine the interval until the next floor contact or the horizontal distance between impacts depends on c (e.g., t_flight = 2 v_y+/g = 2 c |v_y−|/g). (3) Final expressions for horizontal range/distance between impacts explicitly depend on c whenever the problem statement provides it. The rule flags solutions that: omit c in post-impact vertical velocity (e.g., v_y+ = |v_y−| or v_y+ = sqrt(2gh)); compute t_flight without c (e.g., t_flight = 2 |v_y−|/g or t_flight = 2 sqrt(2h/g)); or present a final horizontal distance independent of c. The check applies regardless of horizontal dynamics (e.g., frictional changes in v_x); it focuses on vertical rebound modeling with restitution.

rules.title: Vertical spring EOM must include gravity unless using equilibrium displacement
rules.description: Checks equations of motion for vertical mass–spring systems to ensure gravity is correctly included. If the coordinate x represents absolute extension from the spring’s natural length or an absolute vertical position, the net force must include the weight term (sum of masses)·g in addition to the spring force. The rule flags models that write forms like (M_total) x'' = -k x or x'' + (k/M_total) x = 0 (or algebraically equivalent) without a gravity term, unless the solution explicitly redefines the coordinate as displacement from the static equilibrium (e.g., y = x - x0 with x0 = (M_total) g / k) or clearly states that x is measured from equilibrium so gravity cancels. It also flags inconsistencies where an equilibrium extension x0 = (M_total) g / k is computed and then an EOM is written for the same variable x that omits gravity. Acceptable formulations include M_total x'' = M_total g - k x with downward positive, or M_total x'' = -M_total g - k x with upward positive, and the derived SHM form y'' + (k/M_total) y = 0 only for the shifted coordinate y. Trigger condition: gravity term missing in the vertical spring EOM and no explicit equilibrium shift or statement that the coordinate is measured from equilibrium.

rules.title: Vertical velocity continuity across elastic collision with a vertical surface
rules.description: Checks that in projectile-motion problems under uniform gravity where a ball/particle strikes a vertical, frictionless surface elastically, the vertical component of velocity immediately after impact equals the value just before impact, not the initial launch value. Specifically: if gravity acts (g ≠ 0) from launch to impact, then vy_before = vy0 − g·t_impact (with vy0 = v0·sinθ under standard sign conventions), and because the wall’s impulse is horizontal only, vy_after = vy_before. The rule flags solutions that set vy_after equal to the initial vertical component (e.g., vy_after = v0·sinθ or vy_after = vy0) or that omit the −g·t_impact term. It also checks that the time to impact is determined from horizontal kinematics (t_impact = x_wall/(v0·cosθ), assuming no air resistance), and that only the horizontal component reverses sign in an elastic, frictionless collision (vx_after = −vx_before, |vx_after| = |vx_before|). Exceptions: do not flag if the problem explicitly states gravity is neglected before impact, or if the surface is not vertical or frictionless (where vertical impulse may exist). The rule targets statements equating post-collision vertical velocity to the launch value rather than the pre-collision value.

rules.title: Vis-viva consistency and speed bounds at apogee/perigee
rules.description: This rule checks that any speed computed using the vis-viva relation is consistent with orbital mechanics at specified radii, especially at apogee and perigee. The verifier should: (1) Validate use of the vis-viva equation v^2 = μ(2/r − 1/a) for bound (elliptic) orbits (a > 0). If a solution instead uses 1/a − 2/r or any sign-swapped form, flag an error. (2) If a point is identified as apogee (r = a(1 + e), with 0 ≤ e < 1), enforce v_ap < v_circ(r_ap) = sqrt(μ/r_ap); equivalently v_ap^2 = (1 − e) · μ/(a(1 + e)) < μ/(a(1 + e)). If a computed apogee speed equals or exceeds the local circular speed, flag an error. (3) If a point is identified as perigee (r = a(1 − e)), enforce v_pe > v_circ(r_pe) = sqrt(μ/r_pe). If a computed perigee speed is less than or equal to the local circular speed, flag an error. (4) For any bound orbit segment, enforce v(r) < v_esc(r) = sqrt(2μ/r); if a solution reports v ≥ v_esc while the orbit is treated as bound (finite period T, a > 0), flag an error. (5) Enforce speed ordering for ellipses: v_pe > v_ap. If a solution gives v_ap ≥ v_pe, flag an error. These checks detect misapplication of vis-viva, sign/orientation errors, and confusion between apogee/perigee that can produce unphysical speeds (e.g., apogee speeds near GEO exceeding ~3 km/s or even the local escape speed).

rules.title: Misuse of terminal velocity with time-varying viscous drag in thin-film sliding
rules.description: Flags solutions that invoke a constant-coefficient terminal-velocity model for viscous sliding when the drag coefficient b(t) = η A(t) / Z is time- or position-dependent due to changing contact area. This rule applies to plate/slide problems with a lubricating film where the overlap area A decreases or otherwise varies during motion. It checks for the following patterns: (1) The solution treats A as a fixed full-plate area (e.g., A = L·W) instead of a function of overlap length/position/time, or never expresses A = W·ℓ(t/x). (2) The equation of motion is written as m dv/dt = mg − b v with constant b, or the solution introduces a constant terminal speed v_t = mg/b and/or an exponential approach v(t) = v_t (1 − e^(−t/τ)) with τ = m/b, despite geometric/time dependence of A. (3) The solution uses phrases such as "terminal velocity", "reaches steady speed after a long time", or presents a constant τ without justifying that b is constant. (4) In thin-film (lubrication) regimes, inertia is retained without a timescale check (e.g., estimating τ_inertial = m Z /(η A) and comparing to motion times), and no quasi-static force balance mg = η (A/Z) v(t) is applied. The rule expects either an instantaneous force balance with A(t) explicitly modeled or a justified constant-area scenario; otherwise, it flags the misuse of terminal velocity and constant-drag assumptions.

rules.title: Corner vortex image distances must be 2h0 and 2√2 h0
rules.description: This rule verifies geometric consistency when using the method of images for a vortex filament (or 2D point vortex) located at equal distance h0 from two perpendicular walls (e.g., walls at x=0 and y=0 with the vortex at (h0, h0)). It checks that the solution uses the correct image vortex positions and separations: single reflections at (-h0, h0) and (h0, -h0) are at center-to-center distance 2h0 from the real vortex, and the double reflection at (-h0, -h0) is at distance 2√2 h0. The rule flags errors where the student treats any of these separations as h0, or where velocity magnitudes/denominators are proportional to 1/h0 instead of 1/(2h0) or 1/(2√2 h0) for the corresponding image contributions. It also flags direction errors arising from incorrect vector differences, e.g., using displacement vectors (±h0, 0), (0, ±h0), or (±h0, ±h0) instead of the correct (±2h0, 0), (0, ±2h0), or (±2h0, ±2h0) when computing induced velocities. Trigger conditions: the solution references two perpendicular walls, a vortex at distance h0 from each wall (often expressed as position (h0, h0)), and applies the method of images. Detection heuristics: look for distances to images stated as h0; denominators like κ/(2π h0) or 1/h0 in image contributions; or displacement vectors to images written with components of magnitude h0 rather than 2h0. Acceptable exception: if the author redefines h0 as the full separation to the image (explicitly stating h0 = 2×distance to wall), the geometry must be consistent with that redefinition; otherwise, flag.

rules.title: Exclude self-induced singular contribution when evaluating vortex drift/velocity
rules.description: This rule checks solutions that compute the velocity (drift) of a vortex filament or point vortex at its own location. If the net velocity is assembled by summing Biot–Savart (or analogous) contributions from all vortices and includes the source’s own term (self-induced field), the solution is flagged. The self-contribution is singular (e.g., proportional to 1/r or log r as r→0) and must be excluded via a principal-value limit or renormalization; it does not determine translational drift of a straight filament. In bounded geometries (e.g., walls handled via image vortices), the vortex’s translational velocity must be determined only from external flows, image vortices, and other distinct vortices. Triggers include: (a) explicit inclusion of the real vortex in the summation used to evaluate velocity at the vortex’s position; (b) use of divergent terms like κ/(2πr)|_{r=0}, ln(0), or 1/0 to set the drift speed; (c) attributing nonzero translation of a straight filament to its self-induced velocity instead of to images/boundaries. Correction guidance: compute the velocity at the filament core as a limit excluding the self-term; when curvature is present, treat the local-induction contribution separately (binormal motion) and do not use it as global translational drift.

rules.title: Incorrect use of wheel spin ω in CoM lateral acceleration
rules.description: Flags derivations of a vehicle/tricycle center-of-mass (CoM) lateral acceleration that incorrectly combine the wheel's spin (ω) with the steering angle (θ) as if describing rim-point kinematics. Under pure rolling, ω should enter only via translational speed v = r·ω; lateral acceleration of the CoM must be based on path curvature/yaw rate (e.g., a_lat = v^2/R, a_lat = v^2·κ, or a_lat = v·dψ/dt). Trigger conditions: (1) The expression for lateral acceleration (e.g., a_y) contains ω^2 multiplied by the wheel radius r and a trigonometric function of θ, such as r·ω^2·sin(θ) or r·ω^2·cos(θ); (2) The expression includes terms like r·ddot(θ)·cos(θ) (or similar) directly contributing to a_y, indicative of rim-point acceleration components; (3) ω appears directly in a_y (especially as ω^2) rather than only through v = r·ω. If any of these patterns are detected, flag a conceptual error: mixing wheel spin with steering geometry for CoM dynamics. Acceptable forms explicitly derive a_lat from curvature/yaw rate and use ω only to compute v.

rules.title: Verify work–energy setup for anisotropic friction under rotation
rules.description:
This rule checks solutions that use the work–energy theorem for a body constrained by a rotating rod on a horizontal plane with anisotropic friction defined by Fx = −(N/|v|) μx vx and Fy = −(N/|v|) μy vy. It flags errors where friction work is computed using the magnitude |F| or a single constant μ, instead of the directional projection F·v. Expected setup for an arc displacement ds = L dφ is dW = F·dr = −N (μx cos^2φ + μy sin^2φ) L dφ, leading to the energy relation v^2(φ) + g L [ (μx + μy) φ + (μx − μy) sin(2φ)/2 ] = v0^2 (with N = m g; equivalent rearrangements accepted).

The rule triggers if any of the following are detected:
- Work integral written as W = −∫ |F| L dφ, W = −∫ μ N L dφ with μ constant, or using an incorrect angular dependence (e.g., μx cosφ + μy sinφ, or √(μx^2 cos^2φ + μy^2 sin^2φ)).
- Final v^2(φ) expression lacks the sin(2φ) term or contains only a linear φ dependence.
- Incorrect coefficients: the linear φ term must have coefficient g L (μx + μy), and the sin(2φ) term must have coefficient g L (μx − μy)/2 (up to overall sign conventions and mass factors if not divided out).
- Small-angle consistency check: if a small-φ expansion is presented, dv^2/dφ at φ → 0 must equal −2 g L μx; deviations indicate misuse of the anisotropic friction projection or incorrect path length.

This rule is intended to catch the common mistake of using the friction magnitude in the work integral and to ensure the characteristic anisotropic angular dependence (linear φ plus sin 2φ term) appears in the v^2(φ) result.

topics.name: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

rules.title: Verify correct application of the Work-Energy Theorem
rules.description: The Work-Energy Theorem states that the net work done on an object is equal to its change in kinetic energy (W_net = ΔKE). This applies to systems where forces are acting on a single object or a system of objects, without additional constraints like relativity or quantum effects.

tags.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

rules.check_logic: Ensure that the net work (sum of work done by all forces) equals the difference in kinetic energy of the object or system (KE_final - KE_initial).
common_errors: Incorrect computation of work done by individual forces.
Omission of one or more forces contributing to the net work.
Incorrect calculation of change in kinetic energy (e.g., missing 1/2 factor or squaring velocity incorrectly).

rules.title: Ensure proper use of the Conservation of Mechanical Energy
rules.description: The principle of mechanical energy conservation states that the total mechanical energy (kinetic + potential) of a system remains constant if only conservative forces (e.g., gravity, spring forces) act on it. Non-conservative forces, such as friction or air resistance, invalidate this principle.

tags.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

rules.check_logic: Verify that E_initial = E_final (KE_initial + PE_initial = KE_final + PE_final) when no non-conservative forces are present.
common_errors: Neglecting potential energy contributions for gravity or springs.
Assuming mechanical energy conservation when non-conservative forces are doing work.
Arithmetical errors in summing kinetic and potential energies.

rules.title: Account for work done by non-conservative forces
rules.description: When non-conservative forces (e.g., friction, air resistance) do work, the total mechanical energy changes. The work done by these forces is equal to the change in mechanical energy of the system (W_nc = ΔE_mechanical).

tags.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

rules.check_logic: Ensure that W_nc = (KE_final + PE_final) - (KE_initial + PE_initial), where W_nc includes work from non-conservative forces.
common_errors: Omitting the contribution of non-conservative forces.
Misinterpreting the direction and sign of work done by non-conservative forces.
Assuming conservation of mechanical energy despite non-conservative forces.

rules.title: Verify correct use of sign conventions for work and energy
rules.description: Work and energy are scalar quantities but can have positive or negative signs based on the direction of forces and displacement. Work is positive if the force component is in the direction of displacement, and negative if it opposes displacement.

tags.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

rules.check_logic: Confirm that work done by forces is calculated with correct attention to the angle between force and displacement. Check the sign of gravitational potential energy based on the chosen reference point.
common_errors: Incorrect sign for work done by opposing forces (e.g., friction).
Misinterpreting the angle between force and displacement.
Incorrect sign for potential energy due to inconsistent reference height.

rules.title: Check dimensional and unit consistency in work-energy calculations
rules.description: All terms in energy and work calculations should have consistent dimensions of energy (ML^2/T^2) and be expressed in compatible units (e.g., Joules in SI units).

tags.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

rules.check_logic: Verify that work, kinetic energy, and potential energy terms have consistent dimensions and units throughout the solution.
common_errors: Using incompatible units for mass, distance, and force (e.g., mixing grams with meters and Newtons).
Forgetting to square velocity in kinetic energy calculations.
Incorrect unit conversions (e.g., from cm to meters).

rules.title: Ensure applicability of conservation laws
rules.description: The Conservation of Energy principle or the Work-Energy Theorem applies only in classical mechanics for non-relativistic speeds and non-quantum scenarios. Mechanical energy conservation requires the absence of non-conservative forces.

tags.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

rules.check_logic: Check that the problem context does not involve relativistic speeds, quantum effects, or significant non-conservative forces when applying conservation laws.
common_errors: Applying conservation laws in scenarios with non-conservative forces without accounting for their work.
Using conservation of energy in relativistic or quantum contexts without modifications.

rules.title: Ensure geometric constraints are respected in energy calculations
rules.description: In problems involving inclined planes, pendulums, or other geometrically constrained systems, the potential energy and displacements must reflect the actual geometry of the system.

tags.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

rules.check_logic: Verify that potential energy is calculated based on the correct height, and that work calculations properly account for the displacement along the surface or path.
common_errors: Using vertical height instead of displacement along an incline.
Ignoring the geometry when calculating work done by forces.
Misrepresenting angles or distances in trigonometric calculations.

rules.title: Verify work-power relationship in dynamic systems
rules.description: Power is the rate at which work is done, and it is related to force and velocity in dynamic systems (P = F·v for constant force and velocity).

tags.topic: Work-Energy Theorem and Conservation of Energy

rules.check_logic: Ensure that power calculations appropriately relate to the work done over time or force applied at a specific velocity.
common_errors: Using incorrect formulas for power in dynamic systems.
Confusing instantaneous power with average power.
Neglecting time dependence when calculating work and power.
