If s > 1, the order does not exist; skip this rule. Else compute theta = arcsin(s) and c = cos(theta). (3) If c < 0.95 (i.e., theta is not small), then the small-angle approximation cos(theta) ≈ 1 is invalid. (4) Inspect the student's computation of Delta_theta: if they explicitly set cos(theta) ≈ 1 or if their numerical Delta_theta matches n*Delta_lambda/d within a tolerance (e.g., ±10%), flag an error. (5) Report that ignoring the cos(theta) factor underestimates Delta_theta by approximately 1/c and provide corrective guidance: recompute Delta_theta using c, Delta_theta = n*Delta_lambda / (d*c). Thresholds (e.g., c < 0.95 and ±10% tolerance) may be tuned to balance sensitivity.

rules.title: Do not infer droplet sag height/curvature from ceiling height without proper optics or geometry
rules.description:
This rule flags solutions that attempt to determine the droplet sag height h, curvature radius R, or contact angle α from the apparent image of distant room features (e.g., ceiling lights at ~3 m) without using correct geometric or optical relations. Specifically, it checks for the following:
- The solution treats the ceiling height or distance to a remote object as a direct proxy to obtain h, R, or α, or equates the measured distance to an image on paper directly to the focal length f, without applying the thin-lens/object–image relations (1/f = 1/do + 1/di) and without validating the object at infinity assumption.
- The solution uses the lensmaker formula for a plano-convex lens but omits the correct refractive index contrasts and interfaces (air–water–glass), or incorrectly models a water droplet on glass as a thin lens in air.
- The solution uses reflected images (e.g., specular reflection of ceiling lights) to deduce refractive focal length, conflating reflection with refraction.
- The solution does not account for medium transitions or appropriate sign conventions, ignoring that the effective optical power depends on n_rel and the radii of curvature of the water–air and water–glass interfaces.
- The solution fails to obtain h via spherical-cap geometry (e.g., using base diameter and curvature) or via an optical calibration that correctly incorporates object distance, image distance, and refractive indices.
This rule requires that any optical method to infer curvature or sag height must: (a) specify measured object distance do and image distance di, (b) use the correct relative refractive indices for the involved media and proper interface geometry, and (c) justify thin-lens approximations if applied. Otherwise, the method is marked as logically incoherent.

rules.title: Plane-wave E→B Prefactor Consistency (Faraday’s law)
rules.description: Checks derivations of the magnetic field B from the electric field E in homogeneous, isotropic, non-magnetic media (including evanescent waves) for consistent use of Faraday’s law. For monochromatic plane waves with fields ∝ e^{-iωt}, the correct vector relation is B = (1/ω) (k × E). The rule verifies that: (1) The scalar prefactor outside the k × E term is exactly 1/ω (or, equivalently, that any refractive-index dependence is contained within the k components), not multiplied by extra standalone factors such as n, n^2, c, or v; (2) When the solution uses v = c/n and k = ω n / c and decomposes components (e.g., k_x = k_T sin θ_T), the combination does not leave an additional global n factor multiplying E outside of k × E; (3) Intermediate expressions like B ∝ (n E_0/ω) ... are flagged unless the extra n is explicitly shown to be absorbed into k components via a clear algebraic step; (4) Any later omission of such an extra factor or ad hoc sign changes in B components without a demonstrated cross-product step (i.e., direction dictated by k × E) are flagged as inconsistent. This rule targets prefactor double-counting or unexplained sign fixes in E→B conversions, common in total internal reflection/evanescent-wave derivations.

rules.title: Mechanical–optical analogy with E=0: v ∝ n and V = −½ m v²
rules.description: This rule verifies consistency of the mechanical-optical (Fermat) analogy when a solution models light rays in a medium with position-dependent refractive index n(r) by a mass point in a conservative field with total mechanical energy E_total = 0. The rule applies when the solution defines a mechanical particle speed v(r) and a potential energy E_p(r) (or V(r)) as functions of n(r). Checks performed: (1) Speed mapping: v_mech(r) must be proportional to n(r), i.e., v_mech(r) = K · n(r) with K a position-independent constant (speed scale). Any inverse dependence (v_mech ∝ 1/n) or direct use of the physical light speed relation v_light = c/n to define the mechanical particle speed is flagged as an error. (2) Potential energy form and sign: With E_total = 0, the conservative potential must satisfy V(r) = −½ m [v_mech(r)]². Consequently, V(r) must scale as −n(r)² (up to the constant −½ m K²). If V(r) does not equal −½ m v_mech(r)², or has the wrong sign (e.g., +½ m v² or V ∝ +n²), flag an error. (3) Energy consistency: Check that T + V = 0 at each r, where T = ½ m [v_mech(r)]². If ½ m v_mech(r)² + V(r) ≠ 0, flag an error. (4) Constants handling: The proportionality constant K may absorb physical constants (e.g., c), but it must be position-independent; any dependence of K on r is flagged. This rule detects modeling mistakes where the solver confuses the mechanical analogue speed with the physical light speed (v = c/n) and/or assigns an incorrect potential energy form or sign under the E_total = 0 mapping.

rules.title: Require use of provided scattering/LCR model to partition incident power into Joule heating vs radiative losses
rules.description: This rule checks that solutions use the problem's provided scattering/absorption expressions and LCR (resonant) circuit parameters to determine how incident optical power is split between radiative losses and Joule (thermal) heating. Trigger: the problem statement includes any of the following model-specific cues: P_scat or 'scattering power', P_abs or 'absorption', LCR circuit elements (L, C, R), resonance frequency (ω0), damping/decay rate (γ), collision time (τ), Q-factor, or mention of 'radiative losses' vs 'Joule heating'. Violation conditions: (1) The solution computes incident power solely as intensity S times geometric area A (e.g., 'P_tot = S × A') and then directly equates that to heating, steam production, or temperature rise without calculating absorption/scattering via the given model. (2) The solution does not reference or use any of the provided model terms (P_scat, P_abs, σ_abs/σ_scat, L, C, R, τ, γ, Q) when determining the power available for heating at or near resonance. (3) The solution ignores the required partition between radiative and non-radiative channels (e.g., no computation of a heating fraction or branching ratio) and does not enforce energy conservation as P_in × absorption efficiency = P_heat + P_rad. Expected compliance: The solution should derive the absorbed power and the Joule-heating fraction using the provided scattering/absorption expression or LCR parameters (including τ/γ/Q), then compute heating power as P_heat = η_heat × P_abs (or equivalent), before converting to downstream quantities (e.g., steam mass rate). The rule flags solutions that bypass the provided model and assume all incident power contributes to heating.

rules.title: Evanescent wavevector normal-component sign must produce decay into the transmitted medium
rules.description: This rule verifies that, under total internal reflection, the transmitted (evanescent) field decays away from the interface into the rarer medium, and that the specified normal component of the wavevector is consistent with the chosen phasor convention. Checks: (1) Detect TIR (n1 > n2 and θ_I > θ_c = arcsin(n2/n1)), with the evanescent field in the rarer medium. (2) Identify the normal coordinate n̂ pointing into the evanescent medium (e.g., z > 0) and extract the stated normal component k_Tn of the transmitted wavevector, along with the spatial phasor dependence used for fields (E ∝ exp(+i k·r) or E ∝ exp(−i k·r)). (3) For evanescent waves, k_Tn must be purely imaginary: k_Tn = i δ with δ > 0 in the standard convention E(r) ∝ exp(+i(k·r − ωt)) when the evanescent medium occupies n̂ > 0, so that exp(+i k_Tn n) = exp(−δ n) gives decay. If the opposite phasor convention E ∝ exp(−i(k·r − ωt)) is used, the required sign flips (then k_Tn = −i δ with δ > 0 yields exp(+δ n) in the exponent of −i k_Tn n, which decays). (4) Compute the amplitude factor along the normal: for E ∝ exp(σ i k_Tn n) with σ ∈ {+1, −1}, the amplitude scales as exp(−σ Im(k_Tn) n). For n > 0 in the evanescent medium, require −σ Im(k_Tn) ≤ 0 (i.e., no growth; strict decay preferred: −σ Im(k_Tn) < 0). Flag an error if this condition is violated (growth with distance into the medium). (5) Consistency check: if k_Tn is declared (e.g., k_Tz = −i δ, δ > 0) but the field is later written with a decay factor exp(−δ z) under the same spatial phasor exp(+i k·r), flag a contradiction between the k-vector specification and the stated field dependence. This rule catches modeling mistakes where the evanescent wave’s normal k-component sign leads to amplitude growth or contradicts the decay behavior specified in the field expression.

rules.title: Correct decomposition of complex exponential for evanescent waves
rules.description: This rule verifies the algebraic handling of the field factor exp(i(k·r − ωt)) for evanescent waves under total internal reflection (n1 > n2, θI > θc). It checks the following: (1) If the transmitted normal component of the wavevector is specified as k_z = iδ with δ > 0, the field must factor as exp(i k_x x) exp(−δ z) exp(−i ω t) (or the equivalent with consistent global sign convention for time). Writing exp(+δ z) is flagged as incorrect. (2) The parallel component k_x must remain real and produce only oscillatory behavior along the interface; any real exponential factor along x (e.g., exp(α x) arising from treating sin θ_T > 1 as a real growth term) is flagged as incorrect. (3) The rule checks that the conservation of tangential k is respected: k_x in the rarer medium equals the real tangential component from the incident medium (k_x = k1 sin θI), and the evanescence appears only in the normal component. (4) If θ_T is treated as complex, the decomposition must not introduce spurious real exponentials in tangential directions; the imaginary part must correspond to decay in the normal direction away from the interface. Any manipulation that yields exp[(ω n2/c) sin θ_T x] or an incorrect sign for the z-decay when separating exp(i(k_x x + k_z z − ω t)) is flagged as a calculation error.

rules.title: Extraordinary index treated as constant / isotropic Snell’s law applied
rules.description:
Checks solutions in uniaxial crystal problems (extraordinary ray/e-ray) for improper modeling that treats the extraordinary refractive index as a direction-independent constant and applies isotropic Snell’s law. The rule flags cases where a student writes relations like "n_e sin(·) = …" using a scalar n_e, or invokes "Snell’s law for the e-ray" without introducing the direction dependence of the extraordinary index or the index ellipsoid/wave-normal surface. Detection criteria: 
- Trigger if the solution includes any of the following patterns without accompanying angle dependence or ellipsoid context: (a) an equation of the form "n_e sin α = …" or "n_e sin θ = n_o sin φ"; (b) statements implying n_e is a constant for the e-ray; (c) direct application of isotropic Snell’s law to the e-ray.
- Do NOT trigger if the solution explicitly models the extraordinary index as angle-dependent (e.g., uses n_e(θ), n_eff(θ), 1/n^2(θ) = cos^2θ/n_e^2 + sin^2θ/n_o^2 or equivalent), references the index ellipsoid/optical indicatrix/Fresnel equation, or distinguishes wave-normal vs. ray (Poynting vector) directions.
- For tasks deriving the relation between the wave-normal angle θ (to the optical axis) and the ray angle ξ (to the optical axis), verify the final functional form includes the squared index ratio. Acceptable equivalents include tan ξ = (n_o^2/n_e^2) tan θ or tan θ = (n_e^2/n_o^2) tan ξ, or a derivation consistent with the indicatrix geometry. Flag if the result reduces to tan ξ = tan θ or otherwise lacks the n_o^2/n_e^2 factor.
- Also trigger if the solution fails to mention that the e-ray direction (energy flow) is not collinear with the wave-normal in anisotropic media, when such distinction is essential to obtain the ξ–θ relationship.
This rule aims to catch modeling errors where anisotropy is ignored for the extraordinary ray, leading to incorrect functional forms for angle relations in uniaxial crystals.

rules.title: Apply Snell's Law for Fiber Entry Angle
rules.description: Snell's Law governs how light enters an optical fiber, involving the refractive indices of the core and cladding. It determines the critical angle for total internal reflection at the core-cladding interface.
rules.check_logic: Verify that n_core * sin(theta_core) = n_cladding * sin(theta_cladding). Ensure the entry angle satisfies the conditions for total internal reflection by checking if the angle of incidence is greater than or equal to the critical angle.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of critical angle
Mixing up refractive indices of core and cladding
Using incorrect sign for angles outside the defined range

rules.title: Correct Sign Convention for Fiber Alignment
rules.description: In fiber optics, the direction of light propagation is important. The coordinate system should align positively in the propagation direction and negatively upon reflection, following standard optical conventions.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the sign convention follows the agreed axis orientation, with positive along the direction of light propagation and negative for reflected directions. Verify that the coordinate system is consistently applied across calculations.
common_errors: Using the wrong axis for propagation direction
Incorrectly reflecting angles, leading to divergence issues
Misalignment of coordinate system leading to miscalculation

rules.title: Verify Fiber Core Dimension Constraints
rules.description: Geometric constraints in fiber optics include core diameter and cladding dimensions, which are crucial for guiding light through total internal reflection.
rules.check_logic: Check if the core diameter is correctly dimensioned relative to the cladding to guide light effectively through total internal reflection. Ensure the numerical aperture (NA) is consistent with the core-cladding ratio.
common_errors: Incorrect ratio of core to cladding sizes
Ignoring the minimal length scales for efficient waveguiding
Miscalculating fiber optic polygon cross-sectional constraints

rules.title: Ensure Conditions for Total Internal Reflection
rules.description: Total internal reflection requires the refractive index of the core to be higher than that of the cladding, and angles of incidence greater than the critical angle.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the refractive indices satisfy n_core > n_cladding and that the angle of incidence is greater than or equal to the critical angle. Verify that no light escapes through the cladding.
common_errors: Misidentifying pathways for light escape from fiber
Applying TIR concepts without checking refractive index inversion
Overlooking necessary angle conditions leading to leakage

rules.title: Consistent Dimensions for Fiber Optic Equations
rules.description: Ensure that dimensions and units are consistent within fiber optic equations, emphasizing the relationship between the speed of light (c), wavelength, and frequency.
rules.check_logic: Verify that units such as nm (nanometers) for wavelength and GHz for frequency are used correctly in calculations. Ensure dimensional consistency in equations like c = lambda * f and in power loss or dispersion calculations.
common_errors: Unit mismatches: nm for length, GHz for frequency
Misapplying dimensions when calculating power losses or dispersion
Ignoring dimensional consistency in intensity and power calculations

rules.title: Specify Fiber Material Properties for Application
rules.description: Different applications require fibers with specific material properties such as attenuation, dispersion, or birefringence. These must be correctly specified for accurate function.
rules.check_logic: Check if the fiber materials meet specific property requirements for the intended application. Ensure attenuation coefficients, dispersion parameters, and birefringence values are appropriate for the design.
common_errors: Failure to specify suitable materials for intended applications
Neglecting material absorption coefficients
Mistaking material properties leading to operational ineffectiveness

rules.title: Monitor Speed Limits and Dispersion in Fibers
rules.description: The speed of light propagation through different media must be monitored to address issues with dispersion and scattering.
rules.check_logic: Verify that light propagation speeds are within operational constraints. Account for dispersion impacts, including chromatic and modal dispersion, and check for pulse broadening effects over fiber lengths.
common_errors: Overlooking speed consistency checks leading to signal distortion
Neglecting dispersion impact in design calculations
Misrepresenting the pulse propagation characteristics

rules.title: Assess Bending Loss in Fiber Paths
rules.description: Bending loss occurs when fibers deviate from straight paths, introducing losses due to reduced conditions for total internal reflection.
rules.check_logic: Evaluate designs for minimal bends. Ensure that bend radii and angles do not exceed critical thresholds to avoid loss due to mode conversion or leakage.
common_errors: Excessive bending leading to degraded signal
Ignoring bend-induced mode conversion impacts
Miscalculating allowable bend radius

rules.title: Verify Mode Field Diameter for Single-Mode Fibers
rules.description: The mode field diameter (MFD) is critical for single-mode fibers, as it determines the spatial distribution of light intensity and affects coupling efficiency.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the MFD is consistent with the fiber's design specifications. Verify that coupling losses are minimized by matching the MFD with the source and detector.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of mode field diameter
Mismatch between MFD and source/detector dimensions
Overlooking MFD impact on coupling efficiency

rules.title: 光纤传播速度定义校验
rules.description:
触发条件：题目定义传播速度为轴向位移 z 与总时间 tau 之比时
检查逻辑：验证速度表达式是否为 v = z / \int (n(x)/c) ds。在梯度折射率光纤中，该速度通常与入射角有关，需通过积分比值消去路径参数。
rules.check_logic: 验证速度表达式是否为 v = z / \int (n(x)/c) ds。在梯度折射率光纤中，该速度通常与入射角有关，需通过积分比值消去路径参数。
rules.trigger: 题目定义传播速度为轴向位移 z 与总时间 tau 之比时

rules.title: 变折射率介质射线守恒律
rules.description:
触发条件：折射率随坐标连续变化（如 n=n(x)）且求路径或时间时
检查逻辑：检查是否应用了分层介质斯涅尔定律推广：n(x) * cos(phi) = C（phi为光线与对称轴夹角），这是求解轨迹方程 dx/dz 的前提。
rules.check_logic: 检查是否应用了分层介质斯涅尔定律推广：n(x) * cos(phi) = C（phi为光线与对称轴夹角），这是求解轨迹方程 dx/dz 的前提。
rules.trigger: 折射率随坐标连续变化（如 n=n(x)）且求路径或时间时

rules.title: Validate Diffraction Coordinate System
rules.description: Diffraction problems often use a specific coordinate system, typically with the aperture or obstacle centered at the origin. Ensure correct orientation relative to the incoming wavefront and observation point.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the chosen coordinate system aligns with the geometry of the problem, typically with the z-axis along the direction of light propagation. Verify that the aperture or obstacle is centered at the origin and that the observation point is correctly positioned relative to the aperture.
common_errors: Misaligning the coordinate system with the wave direction
Miscalculating angles due to incorrect coordinate setup
Failing to center the aperture or obstacle at the origin

rules.title: Verify Angular Sign Convention
rules.description: Diffraction angles must be consistent with the sign convention used, generally proceeding from normal incidence. Positive and negative angles should correlate correctly with the direction of deviation from the incident beam.
rules.check_logic: Ensure angles are measured from normal incidence, with deviation directions clearly defined (typically positive for deviations to the left and negative for deviations to the right in standard diagrams). Verify that the sign convention is consistent throughout the calculations.
common_errors: Confusing positive and negative diffraction angles
Incorrect angle measurement direction creating calculation errors
Inconsistent use of sign conventions in different parts of the problem

rules.title: Ensure Applicable Boundary and Edge Conditions
rules.description: In diffraction, boundary conditions determine how wavefronts interact with obstacles. Ensure boundary conditions at the edge of apertures or obstacles match the physical setup described.
rules.check_logic: Verify the boundary conditions applied correctly reflect the physical edges of the aperture or obstacle, such as zero field intensity at opaque boundaries. Confirm that the boundary conditions are consistent with the mathematical model used.
common_errors: Ignoring boundary effects in diffraction patterns
Inappropriately simplified edge conditions leading to inaccurate diffraction models
Applying boundary conditions inconsistent with the physical setup

rules.title: Confirm Fraunhofer Diffraction Condition Validity
rules.description: Fraunhofer diffraction applies when both source and screen are effectively at infinity regarding the aperture, typically involving plane wavefronts hitting the aperture and observed at far-field.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the condition a^2 / (λ * d) << 1 for Fraunhofer diffraction is met, indicating far-field approximation. Ensure that the aperture size, wavelength, and distance are in the same units.
common_errors: Incorrectly applying Fraunhofer conditions for near-field scenarios
Neglecting the plane and far-field conditions required for Fraunhofer diffraction
Using inconsistent units for aperture size, wavelength, and distance

rules.title: Verify Intensity Distribution Calculations
rules.description: Diffraction patterns consist of intensity distributions across observation screens. Verify mathematical models and integrals used to compute these distributions correctly describe physical phenomena observed.
rules.check_logic: Check that intensity distribution calculations incorporate the correct aperture function and utilize appropriate mathematical methods (e.g., integrals or Fourier transforms). Verify that the limits of integration and the aperture function are consistent with the physical setup.
common_errors: Using incorrect integration limits or methods in intensity calculations
Misapplying aperture functions leading to skewed intensity results
Failing to account for the physical dimensions of the aperture in calculations

rules.title: Validate Diffraction Grating Equation Application
rules.description: For diffraction gratings, ensure the grating equation is applied correctly to determine the angles of diffraction maxima. Verify that the grating spacing and wavelength are consistent with the observed diffraction pattern.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the grating equation d * sin(θ) = m * λ is used correctly, where 'd' is the grating spacing, 'θ' is the diffraction angle, 'm' is the diffraction order, and 'λ' is the wavelength. Ensure units are consistent and that the diffraction order is an integer.
common_errors: Using incorrect grating spacing or wavelength units
Misidentifying diffraction orders
Failing to account for higher-order diffraction maxima

rules.title: Two-beam interference fringe spacing under symmetric refraction must be independent of n and include a factor of 2
rules.description: This rule verifies the spatial fringe period for two coherent plane waves of equal frequency crossing at angle alpha when entering a medium, in the specific configuration where the angle bisector is normal to the interface and the beams lie in the same plane as the pipe. The correct fringe spacing along the axis in the interference plane is Delta = lambda / (2 * sin(alpha/2)), where lambda is the vacuum wavelength. The refractive index n cancels due to Snell’s law: inside the medium k = 2*pi*n/lambda and the refracted half-angle satisfies sin(alpha'/2) = sin(alpha/2)/n, so Delta = lambda_medium / (2*sin(alpha'/2)) = (lambda/n) / (2*(sin(alpha/2)/n)) = lambda / (2*sin(alpha/2)). The rule flags solutions that: 1) retain an explicit dependence on n in the final Delta (e.g., Delta proportional to lambda/n or any Delta that scales with n); 2) omit the factor of 2 in the denominator (e.g., Delta = lambda / sin(alpha/2)); 3) use the external angle alpha directly inside medium without applying refraction (e.g., Delta = lambda_medium / (2*sin(alpha/2))); or 4) compute |k1 - k2| = 2*k*sin(alpha/2) with k = 2*pi*n/lambda but fail to adjust alpha to alpha' via Snell’s law. Acceptable expressions include Delta = lambda / (2*sin(alpha/2)) or, equivalently, Delta = lambda_medium / (2*sin(alpha'/2)) with lambda_medium = lambda/n and sin(alpha'/2) = sin(alpha/2)/n. Any deviation from these forms in the stated geometry should be flagged as a conceptual error.

rules.title: Two-beam interference fringe spacing half-angle and medium check
rules.description: This rule verifies the spatial period Δ of the interference fringes formed by two coherent plane waves intersecting at angle α. The correct expression for the fringe spacing along the axis perpendicular to the bisector of the beams is Δ = λ_eff / (2·sin(α/2)), where λ_eff is the wavelength in the medium where the fringes form. If the problem specifies a refractive index n and the given wavelength λ is in vacuum, then λ_eff = λ/n; otherwise λ_eff = λ if λ is already the wavelength in the medium. The rule checks that: (1) the student uses the half-angle in the sine function and includes the factor 2 in the denominator (common mistakes: using sin(α) or omitting the factor 2); (2) any small-angle approximation uses radians (flags using degrees as radians); (3) refractive index is applied correctly to the wavelength when appropriate (flags multiplying λ by n or incorrectly leaving λ unmodified when λ is explicitly a vacuum wavelength and the pattern forms in a medium). Numerical validation: compute Δ_expected = λ_eff / (2·sin(α/2)) and compare to the student’s Δ with a tolerance of 5%. Example: for α = 4° and λ = 515 nm (with λ_eff = λ if specified as effective wavelength), Δ_expected ≈ 7.4 μm. Values near 11.35 μm are flagged as incorrect, indicative of a wrong formula (e.g., missing half-angle or incorrect medium handling).

rules.title: Misuse of critical angle and Snell’s law in graded-index fibers
rules.description: Flags solutions that treat a graded-index (GRIN) core with n(x) varying (e.g., n(x)=n1*sqrt(1-α^2 x^2)) as if guidance were governed by total internal reflection (TIR) at the core–cladding boundary. Checks for: (1) Explicit use of a 'critical angle' or 'total internal reflection at the core–cladding interface' to set ray limits or speeds in a GRIN core; (2) Snell’s-law boundary equations such as n(a)*sin(θ)=n2 or sin(θ_c)=n2/n(a), or simplifications like sin(θ_iM)=n2/n1, used to determine maximum internal angles, acceptance angles, α, or propagation speed; (3) Mixing external entrance angle in air with internal ray angle, e.g., equating an input angle θ_in in air to a boundary critical angle computed from n2/n1, or using n0 improperly in boundary TIR relations; (4) Using n(a)=n2 specifically within a Snell/TIR argument to solve for α. In GRIN fibers rays are guided by continuous refraction and the ray invariant n(x)*sin(φ(x)) is conserved; boundary TIR is not the governing mechanism. Correct approaches should employ the ray equation/eikonal method, use n(a)=n2 only to relate α via the given index profile, and, if an entrance condition is needed, relate the input angle via n0*sin(θ0)=n(x0)*sin(φ0) without invoking core–cladding TIR.

rules.title: Verify α calculation in graded-index fiber (correct squared ratio and units)
rules.description: This rule checks the calculation of the gradient parameter α in a graded-index optical fiber where the core index is n(x) = n1 * sqrt(1 - α^2 * x^2) and the cladding index at radius a is n2. The boundary condition requires n2 = n1 * sqrt(1 - α^2 * a^2), giving α = sqrt(1 - (n2/n1)^2) / a. The verifier will: (1) Recompute α_correct using the given n1, n2, and a, ensuring a is converted to SI units (meters). (2) Compare the student's α to α_correct and flag if the relative error exceeds 5%. (3) Detect the common algebraic mistake of using 1 - (n2/n1) instead of 1 - (n2/n1)^2 by checking whether (α_student * a)^2 is closer to 1 - (n2/n1) than to 1 - (n2/n1)^2; if so, flag a 'missing square in index ratio' error. (4) Enforce dimensional consistency: α must have units of inverse length; α * a must be dimensionless. Flag likely unit conversion errors if |α_student / α_correct| is within factors of 10^3 or 10^6 (e.g., treating micrometers as meters). (5) If intermediate values are provided (e.g., 1 - (n2/n1)^2 or its square root), verify their numerical correctness within 2% tolerance. This rule catches numerical slips in computing α, misuse of the squared index ratio, and unit/scale mistakes leading to order-of-magnitude discrepancies.

rules.title: Turning point in graded-index mirage must satisfy n(z_t)=b, not be assumed at layer boundary
rules.description: This rule verifies boundary-condition handling for light rays in a vertically stratified medium (mirage problems). For profiles where n^2(z)=n0^2+α z for 0≤z≤h and n^2(z)=n0^2+α h for z>h, the ray invariant b≡n(z)·sinθ(z) must be constant along the path. The turning point (where the ray is horizontal) occurs at z_t such that sinθ(z_t)=1, hence b=n(z_t). The rule flags solutions that: (1) assert or impose θ(h)=π/2 ("ray horizontal at z=h") or treat z=h as the turning point without deriving b=n(h) from initial/launch conditions; (2) set integration limits or compute distances assuming the turning point at z=h merely because the refractive index becomes constant above h; (3) fail to compute z_t from b via n(z_t)=b with n(z)=√(n0^2+α z) in 0≤z≤h; or (4) do not check the existence condition for a turning point (b≤n(h)): if b<n(h) then z_t<h; if b=n(h) then z_t=h; if b>n(h) there is no horizontal turning within the graded layer. To pass, a solution must establish b from initial conditions (e.g., b=n(z_obs)·sinθ_obs), then locate z_t by solving n(z_t)=b, rather than assuming the turning point coincides with the layer boundary.

rules.title: Incorrect Δλ–Δθ conversion for diffraction gratings
rules.description: Checks that the conversion between angular separation (Δθ) and spectral separation (Δλ) for a diffraction grating is derived from the grating equation d·sinθ = m·λ. The correct dispersion is dθ/dλ = m/(d·cosθ), so Δλ = Δθ·(d·cosθ)/m (and for small angles, cosθ ≈ 1 gives Δλ ≈ Δθ·d/m). Flags solutions that: (a) assert relations like Δλ = Δθ·cosθ, Δλ ≈ Δθ·λ, or Δθ ≈ Δλ/λ; (b) use a dispersion dθ/dλ that does not equal m/(d·cosθ); (c) produce a final Δλ expression that lacks dependence on slit spacing d and diffraction order m; or (d) infer resolving power or spectral separation from angular resolution without employing d·sinθ = m·λ. This rule targets logic errors where angular-to-spectral conversion omits the grating’s physical scaling (d, m) or uses ad hoc proportionalities.

rules.title: Detect uniform cosφ projection in skew-incidence grating equations
rules.description: Applies to reflection/transmission grating problems with oblique (skew) incidence relative to the groove direction. The rule flags solutions that model skew incidence by multiplying the in-plane grating equation with a single uniform projection factor (e.g., cosφ), such as mλ = d (sin α_i + sin β_m) cosφ or mλ = d cosφ (sin α_i + sin β_m), or by using the same azimuth angle φ for both incident and diffracted beams (e.g., mλ = d [sin α_i cosφ + sin β_m cosφ]). Correct treatment requires: (1) projecting wavevectors onto the direction perpendicular to the grooves within the grating surface, yielding separate azimuthal factors for incident and diffracted beams (sin α_i cos ψ_i and sin β_m cos ψ_m); and (2) enforcing conservation of the component parallel to the grooves (ky), i.e., sin α_i sin ψ_i = sin β_m sin ψ_m. Acceptable final forms include mλ = d (sin α_i cos ψ_i + sin β_m cos ψ_m), or equivalent expressions where ψ_m is eliminated, leading to nontrivial dependence (often square-root terms) rather than a single cosφ multiplier. The rule checks: (a) if φ appears only as a single multiplicative factor applied uniformly to the standard in-plane formula; (b) if the solution omits azimuthal angles or ky-conservation; (c) limiting-case consistency—when φ → 0, the expression should reduce to d (sin α_i + sin β_m), but for φ ≠ 0 it must not be a uniform scaling by cosφ. If any of these issues are detected, flag the solution as a modeling error in skew-incidence grating geometry.

rules.title: Distinct azimuth/projection factors for incident and diffracted beams in grating equations
rules.description: Checks grating solutions with oblique incidence for improper reuse of a single azimuth angle (e.g., φ) or a single cosine projection factor across both incident and diffracted beams. Trigger conditions: (1) The problem defines φ only for the incident beam (e.g., angle between the incident beam and the plane perpendicular to the slit/groove direction), yet the solution applies the same cos φ multiplier to both sin α_i and sin β_m terms in the grating equation (forms like m λ = d (sin α_i ± sin β_m) cos φ or equivalent). (2) The solution lacks an independent azimuth for the diffracted beam (e.g., ψ_m) or fails to state the groove-parallel component conservation (sin α_i sin ψ_i = sin β_m sin ψ_m) while still using identical projection factors for incidence and diffraction. (3) No explicit justification is provided that forces ψ_m = ψ_i (e.g., diffraction constrained to the plane perpendicular to grooves, in-plane geometry with φ = ψ_i = ψ_m = 0, or an explicitly stated symmetry/Littrow condition). If these conditions are met, flag the solution as conceptually incorrect. Guidance for correct structure: introduce separate azimuths ψ_i (often equal to the given φ) and ψ_m, enforce conservation of the tangential wavevector along the groove direction (sin α_i sin ψ_i = sin β_m sin ψ_m), and use the grating equation along the periodic direction, e.g., d[sin β_m cos ψ_m −/+ sin α_i cos ψ_i] = m λ (sign per convention). The rule aims to catch the specific error of assuming identical projection factors for incident and diffracted beams without justification in 3D grating geometry.

rules.title: Require separate azimuthal projections in skew-incidence grating equation
rules.description: Checks grating equations for reflection gratings under oblique (skew) incidence to ensure the path-difference is built from the components of the incident and diffracted wavevectors perpendicular to the grooves. For a slit density n (spacing d = 1/n), the constructive condition must be of the form m·λ = d·(sin(α_i)·cos(ψ_i) ± sin(β_m)·cos(ψ_m)), where ψ_i and ψ_m are the azimuths of the incident and diffracted beams measured from the direction perpendicular to the grooves. The rule flags solutions that: (1) use a single global factor like cos(φ) multiplying (sin(α_i) ± sin(β_m)), e.g., m·λ = d·(sin α_i ± sin β_m)·cos φ, without introducing separate azimuthal projections for incident and diffracted beams; (2) set ψ_i = ψ_m = φ or replace both cos(ψ) factors by cos(φ) without explicit geometric justification (coplanarity), or when φ is defined as the angle to the plane perpendicular to grooves; (3) omit the conservation of the component parallel to the grooves (k_parallel along grooves), which implies sin(α_i)·sin(ψ_i) = sin(β_m)·sin(ψ_m) (and, when φ is given as deviation from the plane perpendicular to grooves, correctly relates ψ_i and ψ_m to φ, e.g., cos(ψ_i) = sqrt(1 − (sin φ / sin α_i)^2) and cos(ψ_m) = sqrt(1 − (sin φ / sin β_m)^2), or an equivalent relation); (4) produce a final f(α_i, β_m, n, φ) in which the φ-dependence appears only as a single multiplicative cosine applied to (sin α_i ± sin β_m) rather than through separate projections tied to α_i and β_m. The rule accepts equivalent correct vector-form derivations and sign conventions but requires explicit, beam-specific azimuthal projections for skew incidence and reduction to the standard in-plane formula when φ = 0.

rules.title: Use focal-length-based mapping for grating dispersion onto detector
rules.description: When a problem specifies a focusing mirror or lens that projects the diffraction pattern onto a detector, the solution must relate the diffraction angle to detector position via the focal length of that element. The correct imaging/dispersion relations are: (i) y = f · tan(β) ≈ f · β for small angles, and (ii) dy/dλ = f · m / (d · cos β), derived from the grating equation mλ = d (sin α + sin β). Flag as modeling error if the solution: (a) replaces the focal length f with an arbitrary path length, screen distance, or grating length L (e.g., uses y ≈ L · θ, y ≈ D · θ, or dy/dλ proportional to L or a propagation distance), (b) ignores the focusing element entirely when mapping angle to detector coordinate, or (c) computes linear dispersion/resolution without f appearing in the mapping to pixels. Specifically, if the problem text includes a focusing mirror/lens and a detector (e.g., CCD) but the student uses L = 10 cm (grating length) or any non-focal distance in place of f to convert angles to linear positions or to dy/dλ, this rule should trigger. The rule also expects that resolving power R = mN is used for spectral separation in wavelength space and that conversion to pixel spacing uses the focal-length-based dy/dλ combined with the detector sampling; omission of the focal-length mapping constitutes the error.

rules.title: Misapplication of diffraction grating resolving power
rules.description: Flag solutions that compute the spectral resolution of a diffraction grating using an angular-resolution formula or omit the diffraction order. For a plane grating illuminated by N slits, the resolving power must be R = m·N (m = diffraction order), giving Δλ = λ/(m·N). The rule triggers if a solution: (1) uses or derives Δθ = λ/(N d) (with or without a cos term) as the resolution criterion for a grating; (2) converts that to a spectral separation like Δλ ≈ λ^2/(N d) or any Δλ proportional to λ^2 divided by N d; (3) states R = N or Δλ = λ/N (omitting m) for grating resolution; (4) presents Δλ with explicit inverse dependence on slit spacing d or total length L = N d, without the m·N resolving power; (5) invokes a Rayleigh criterion exclusively in angular form for a grating without using grating resolving power or proper angular dispersion dβ/dλ = m/(d cos β) to relate angle to wavelength. Correct formulations must include m·N, i.e., Δλ = λ/(m N), and should not replace grating resolving power with telescope/single-aperture angular formulas.

rules.title: Verify Young's Double-Slit Equation
rules.description: Ensure the equation for determining constructive and destructive interference in Young's Double-Slit experiment is correctly used: d*sin(θ) = m*λ for constructive interference and d*sin(θ) = (m+1/2)*λ for destructive interference. Here, d is the slit separation, θ is the angle to the maxima/minima, m is the order of the fringe, and λ is the wavelength.
rules.check_logic: Check if d*sin(θ) is equal to m*λ for constructive interference or (m+1/2)*λ for destructive interference. Ensure all variables are defined, consistent, and correctly substituted.
common_errors: Using m*λ for destructive interference instead of (m+1/2)*λ.
Incorrect substitution of slit separation (d) or wavelength (λ).
Forgetting to calculate the sine of the angle θ.

rules.title: Check Path Difference for Interference
rules.description: Verify that the path difference between the two waves is correctly calculated as ΔL = d*sin(θ). This path difference determines whether the interference is constructive or destructive.
rules.check_logic: Check if the path difference ΔL is computed as d*sin(θ) and used consistently in subsequent calculations. Ensure the relationship between ΔL and interference type is correctly applied.
common_errors: Path difference calculated incorrectly, e.g., using d*cos(θ) instead of d*sin(θ).
Missing or wrong sign conventions for angles in the calculation.
Not accounting for the order of the fringe (m).

rules.title: Verify Phase Shift in Thin Film Interference
rules.description: In thin-film interference, ensure that the phase shift of π (or λ/2 path difference) is correctly applied when light reflects off a medium of higher refractive index. This phase shift affects whether constructive or destructive interference occurs.
rules.check_logic: Check if a phase shift of λ/2 is added when reflection occurs at a higher refractive index boundary and validate its impact on the interference condition. Ensure the phase shifts for both reflections are correctly accounted for.
common_errors: Ignoring the phase shift when light reflects off a higher refractive index medium.
Incorrectly applying the phase shift for both reflections.
Misinterpreting the conditions for constructive and destructive interference due to phase shift.

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency in Interference Equations
rules.description: Verify that all terms in the equations for interference (e.g., d*sin(θ) = m*λ) have consistent units: d and λ should be in the same unit (e.g., meters), and sin(θ) is dimensionless.
rules.check_logic: Check that slit separation (d) and wavelength (λ) are expressed in the same units and that the sine function has no units. Ensure any unit conversions are correctly performed.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for d and λ (e.g., meters for d and nanometers for λ).
Forgetting to convert angles to radians if required for trigonometric functions.

rules.title: Validate Geometric Constraints in Young's Experiment
rules.description: Ensure that the geometric constraints of the experimental setup are adhered to, such as the screen distance (L) being much greater than the slit separation (d) for the small angle approximation (sin(θ) ≈ tan(θ) ≈ y/L) to hold.
rules.check_logic: Verify that L >> d and that the small angle approximation is applied only when θ is small (θ < 15 degrees approximately). Ensure that y (fringe displacement on the screen) and L are correctly calculated.
common_errors: Using sin(θ) ≈ tan(θ) when θ is not small.
Incorrectly calculating θ or y (fringe displacement on the screen).
Ignoring the condition L >> d.

rules.title: Validate Use of Refractive Indices in Thin Film Interference
rules.description: In thin-film interference, ensure that the refractive indices (n1, n2, n3) are correctly used to determine the effective wavelength within the medium (λ_medium = λ/n).
rules.check_logic: Check if the wavelength in the medium (λ/n) is correctly calculated using the medium's refractive index and if it is consistent with the interference conditions. Ensure the correct refractive index is used for each medium.
common_errors: Forgetting to modify the wavelength in the medium using λ/n.
Using the wrong refractive index for the medium.
Misinterpreting which medium is associated with which refractive index.

rules.title: Check Validity Conditions for Interference Equations
rules.description: Verify that the conditions for interference are met: the light source must be coherent and monochromatic, and the slits or thin film must allow for consistent path differences.
rules.check_logic: Check if the problem explicitly states or implies coherent and monochromatic light. Ensure that the slits or thin film are properly aligned and uniform. Verify that the experimental setup supports stable interference patterns.
common_errors: Attempting to use interference equations for incoherent or non-monochromatic light.
Ignoring misalignment or non-uniformity of the slits or thin film.

rules.title: Verify Sign Conventions for Path Differences
rules.description: Ensure that the path difference ΔL is correctly signed based on the geometry of the problem. The positive or negative sign of ΔL determines the type of interference (constructive or destructive).
rules.check_logic: Check if ΔL is correctly signed based on the relative path lengths of the two waves and if the sign convention is used consistently in calculations. Ensure the relationship between ΔL and interference type is clearly stated.
common_errors: Incorrectly assigning the sign of ΔL based on the geometry.
Using inconsistent sign conventions across multiple calculations.
Misinterpreting the relationship between path difference and interference type.

rules.title: Account for Multiple Reflections in Thin Film Interference
rules.description: Ensure that multiple reflections within the thin film are considered when calculating the overall interference pattern, especially for thicker films.
rules.check_logic: Verify if the problem accounts for additional phase shifts and path differences caused by multiple reflections within the thin film. Ensure that these contributions are included in the interference condition.
common_errors: Ignoring the effects of multiple reflections in thicker films.
Incorrectly summing the contributions of multiple reflected waves.
Overlooking phase shifts introduced by additional reflections.

rules.title: 介质不改变真空入射光的干涉条纹间距
rules.description:
触发条件：两束平行光以夹角 α 从真空射入平行介质板并在其中干涉时
检查逻辑：检查公式是否包含折射率 n。根据 Snell 定律，介质内波长缩短与折射角减小对条纹间距的影响正好抵消，Δ 仅取决于真空波长和入射夹角。
rules.check_logic: 检查公式是否包含折射率 n。根据 Snell 定律，介质内波长缩短与折射角减小对条纹间距的影响正好抵消，Δ 仅取决于真空波长和入射夹角。
rules.trigger: 两束平行光以夹角 α 从真空射入平行介质板并在其中干涉时

rules.title: 双光束干涉周期公式系数检查
rules.description:
触发条件：计算两束对称相交平面波的干涉条纹空间周期时
检查逻辑：确认分母为 2*sin(θ) 或 sin(α)，其中 θ 为半夹角，α 为全夹角。小角度下 Δ ≈ λ/α。
rules.check_logic: 确认分母为 2*sin(θ) 或 sin(α)，其中 θ 为半夹角，α 为全夹角。小角度下 Δ ≈ λ/α。
rules.trigger: 计算两束对称相交平面波的干涉条纹空间周期时

rules.title: 高阶干涉角余弦修正校验
rules.description:
触发条件：当干涉级数 n 较大或狭缝间距 d 与波长 λ 接近时
检查逻辑：必须先通过 sin θ = nλ/d 计算出确切的 θ 值，再代入含有 cos θ 的微分变化率公式，不可盲目使用小角近似（cos θ ≈ 1）。
rules.check_logic: 必须先通过 sin θ = nλ/d 计算出确切的 θ 值，再代入含有 cos θ 的微分变化率公式，不可盲目使用小角近似（cos θ ≈ 1）。
rules.trigger: 当干涉级数 n 较大或狭缝间距 d 与波长 λ 接近时

rules.title: 介质引入相位滞后判定
rules.description:
触发条件：在双缝干涉的一条光路中插入折射率为 $\mu$、厚度为 $w$ 的透明介质
检查逻辑：该路径光程增加 $(\mu-1)w$，在相位因子 $\cos(\phi_1 - \phi_2)$ 中，该项符号应与几何路程差 $d\sin\theta$ 相反。
rules.check_logic: 该路径光程增加 $(\mu-1)w$，在相位因子 $\cos(\phi_1 - \phi_2)$ 中，该项符号应与几何路程差 $d\sin\theta$ 相反。
rules.trigger: 在双缝干涉的一条光路中插入折射率为 $\mu$、厚度为 $w$ 的透明介质

rules.title: 显式比例常数核查
rules.description:
触发条件：题目明确给出强度与电场平方的比例系数（如 $\beta$ 或 $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 c$）
检查逻辑：检查最终表达式是否包含该常数，而非仅保留场强平方的函数形式。
rules.check_logic: 检查最终表达式是否包含该常数，而非仅保留场强平方的函数形式。
rules.trigger: 题目明确给出强度与电场平方的比例系数（如 $\beta$ 或 $\frac{1}{2}\epsilon_0 c$）

rules.title: Missing time-average factor in interference intensity (⟨cos^2⟩ = 1/2)
rules.description: Checks that intensity for superposed sinusoidal light fields is computed using a time average of the squared electric field. Specifically: (1) If a solution writes I ∝ (E1 + E2)^2 or I = β(E1 + E2)^2, it must explicitly apply time-averaging: I = β⟨(E1 + E2)^2⟩ with ⟨cos^2⟩ = 1/2. (2) For two coherent, equal-amplitude, identically polarized beams with field amplitudes E0, the final intensity must match any of the equivalent canonical forms: I = βE0^2(1 + cos Δφ) = 2βE0^2 cos^2(Δφ/2) = 4I0 cos^2(Δφ/2), where I0 = (1/2)βE0^2 is the single-beam intensity. (3) Flag results that omit the 1/2 time-average factor, such as I = 4βE0^2 cos^2(Δφ/2), I = βE0^2(2 + 2 cos Δφ), or defining I0 = βE0^2. (4) Cross-check maxima: for two equal beams, I_max must be 4I0; values like 8I0 indicate the missing time-average factor. This rule targets the common mistake of squaring amplitudes without time-averaging, which doubles the overall intensity prefactor.

rules.title: Inverse-square scaling of irradiance with distance
rules.description: Checks that any scaling of solar constant, irradiance, or radiative flux due to a change in source-to-target distance correctly applies the inverse-square law. Expected relation: F' = F0 * (r0/r)^2. If distance is expressed as r = r0(1 + f) for a fractional increase f > 0, the correct scaling is F' = F0 / (1 + f)^2. For a fractional decrease f (r = r0(1 - f)), the correct scaling is F' = F0 / (1 - f)^2. Equivalent percentage form: F' = F0 / (1 ± p/100)^2. The rule flags solutions that instead use multiplicative numerator forms such as F' = F0 * (1 - f), F' = F0 * (1 - f)^2, F' = F0 * (1 + f)^2, or any F' = F0 * (1 ± f)^n (n ≥ 1), as well as incorrect sign in the denominator for the specified direction of distance change. For small-f approximations, it validates consistency with (1 + f)^{-2} ≈ 1 - 2f + 3f^2 + …; accepts first-order truncations F' ≈ F0(1 - 2f) for f ≪ 1, but flags approximations like F' ≈ F0(1 - f) or F' ≈ F0(1 - 2f + f^2) when presented as exact inverse-square scaling or used for non-small f. Applies to problems involving the solar constant (e.g., 1370 W·m^{-2}), point-source radiation intensity, and radiative heat flux.

rules.title: Verify Laser Rate Equations
rules.description: Ensure laser rate equations for population inversion and gain are correctly applied. These equations describe the change in upper and lower laser energy levels and the gain for a laser medium.
rules.check_logic: Verify the use of rate equations: dN2/dt = N1 * B12 * ρ(ν) - N2 * B21 * ρ(ν) - N2 * A21 for the upper energy level and corresponding equations for the lower energy level.
common_errors: Omitting spontaneous emission term A21
Confusing stimulated absorption B12 with stimulated emission B21

rules.title: Check Sign Conventions
rules.description: Confirm the sign conventions used in laser optics for beam propagation and gain medium properties, which are vital for accurate direction and orientation of the laser beam.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the beam propagation direction aligns with the positive axis and gain is specified as positive, while loss is negative.
common_errors: Incorrect beam direction
Gain or loss discrepancies within cavity calculations

rules.title: Evaluate Laser Cavity Geometry Constraints
rules.description: Lasers require specific geometric arrangements to achieve resonance and feedback. Check if cavity length and mirror positioning are within acceptable tolerances for stable operation.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that laser cavity mirrors are positioned to support longitudinal modes according to L = mλ/2, where m is an integer.
common_errors: Miscounting the number of longitudinal modes
Incorrect application of boundary conditions for mirrors

rules.title: Assess Validity of Electric Field Approximation
rules.description: Laser equations rely on a coherent, monochromatic electric field approximation. Verify where this approximation holds, especially concerning the coherence length and time of the laser.
rules.check_logic: Confirm coherence time is greater than pulse duration in pulsed lasers, and coherence length is longer than cavity length for continuous-wave lasers.
common_errors: Ignoring temporal coherence limits in pulse modeling
Confusing coherence length with pulse width

rules.title: Dimensional Consistency of Laser Equations
rules.description: Ensure dimensions are consistent across laser equations, particularly for gain, intensity, and emission processes.
rules.check_logic: Verify units for population inversion densities (m^-3), gain coefficients (m^-1), and intensity (W/m^2) are consistently used.
common_errors: Mixed units for spatial density and volume
Inconsistent dimensional usage between gain and loss coefficients

rules.title: Verify Spatial Profile Calculations
rules.description: Laser beams often exhibit a Gaussian intensity distribution described by laser modes. Ensure the spatial profile calculations apply the correct mathematical form and parameters.
rules.check_logic: Use the Gaussian beam intensity profile I(r) = I0 * exp(-2 * r^2/w0^2), ensuring proper beam waist (w0) definition.
common_errors: Incorrect beam waist calculation
Omission of the factor of 2 in the Gaussian profile exponent

rules.title: Laser Threshold Conditions
rules.description: Verify the laser operates above the threshold condition, where gain exactly balances losses within the laser cavity.
rules.check_logic: Check if gain coefficient g is greater than or equal to total losses (including output coupling and intrinsic losses).
common_errors: Ignoring losses from non-ideal cavity elements
Misestimating output coupling value

rules.title: Verify mirror and lens equation usage
rules.description: The mirror and lens equation is given by 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, where f is the focal length, v is the image distance, and u is the object distance. This equation applies to both mirrors and lenses, provided the paraxial approximation holds (small angles and rays close to the optical axis).
rules.check_logic: Check if the given distances (u, v, f) satisfy the equation 1/f = 1/v + 1/u. Ensure that the paraxial approximation is valid (small angles and rays close to the optical axis).
common_errors: Forgetting to use the reciprocal values (1/u, 1/v, 1/f) and directly adding distances.
Incorrect substitution of object distance or image distance.
Applying the equation when the paraxial approximation is not valid (large angles or off-axis rays).

rules.title: Verify sign convention adherence for spherical mirrors and lenses
rules.description: The sign convention for mirrors and lenses depends on the Cartesian coordinate system: distances measured in the direction of incident light are positive, and those measured against it are negative. For concave mirrors and converging lenses, focal length is positive; for convex mirrors and diverging lenses, focal length is negative.
rules.check_logic: Check if the signs of u, v, and f are consistent with the sign convention and the type of mirror or lens provided. Verify that the sign convention is applied consistently across all calculations.
common_errors: Using the wrong sign for the focal length of convex mirrors or diverging lenses.
Reversing the sign of object distance and image distance.
Incorrectly assigning positive or negative signs to distances for specific cases.

rules.title: Validate the magnification formula usage
rules.description: The magnification (m) is given by m = -v/u for mirrors and m = v/u for lenses. It represents the ratio of the image height to the object height. This formula holds under the paraxial approximation.
rules.check_logic: Verify if the magnification formula is correctly applied, ensuring the correct formula is used for mirrors versus lenses. Confirm that the sign conventions for v and u are respected.
common_errors: Forgetting the negative sign in the magnification formula for mirrors.
Confusing the formulas for mirrors and lenses.
Improperly calculating the image or object height relative to magnification.

rules.title: Ensure geometric constraints on focal point location
rules.description: The focal point of a mirror or lens must lie at a fixed distance (f) from the mirror's pole or lens' optical center. For mirrors, this is f = R/2, where R is the radius of curvature.
rules.check_logic: Check if the focal length f is consistent with the given radius of curvature R (f = R/2). Ensure that the geometry of the optical system is consistent with the given parameters.
common_errors: Using an incorrect formula for focal length based on radius of curvature.
Confusing radius of curvature (R) with diameter or focal length directly.
Applying the formula for lenses to mirrors or vice versa.

rules.title: Validate real and virtual image criteria
rules.description: For mirrors and lenses, real images occur when light rays converge, and virtual images occur when they appear to diverge. Real images have positive image distances, while virtual images have negative image distances.
rules.check_logic: Check if the image distance (v) is positive for real images and negative for virtual images, consistent with the type of mirror or lens. Ensure that the interpretation of real and virtual images aligns with the optical system's geometry.
common_errors: Misidentifying the type of image (real or virtual) based on the sign of v.
Confusing the properties of real and virtual images for mirrors versus lenses.

rules.title: Verify ray diagram consistency with optical laws
rules.description: Ray diagrams for mirrors and lenses must follow the laws of reflection or refraction. For example, reflected rays must obey the law of reflection, and refracted rays must adhere to Snell's law at the lens surfaces.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the drawn rays follow the laws of reflection and refraction. Verify that the image location in the diagram matches the calculated one using the lens or mirror equation.
common_errors: Drawing rays that do not pass through the focal point for specific cases.
Violating the law of reflection for mirrors (angle of incidence ≠ angle of reflection).
Not using Snell's law for refracted rays at a lens surface.

rules.title: Check for spherical and chromatic aberrations
rules.description: Spherical aberration occurs when rays far from the optical axis do not converge at the same focal point. Chromatic aberration occurs in lenses due to the dispersion of light, causing different colors to focus at different points.
rules.check_logic: Verify if the optical system accounts for spherical and chromatic aberrations, especially for large apertures or wide-angle lenses. Check if corrective measures (e.g., aspherical lenses or achromatic doublets) are mentioned.
common_errors: Ignoring spherical aberration for wide-aperture systems.
Neglecting chromatic aberration in lenses with significant dispersion.
Failing to mention corrective measures for aberrations in high-precision systems.

rules.title: 区分反射与折射成像模型
rules.description:
触发条件：题目涉及液滴表面成像或利用液面作为光学元件时
检查逻辑：检查是利用光线穿过液滴（透镜折射）还是从液面弹回（面镜反射）。若为反射，焦距公式应为 f=R/2 而非透镜公式。
rules.check_logic: 检查是利用光线穿过液滴（透镜折射）还是从液面弹回（面镜反射）。若为反射，焦距公式应为 f=R/2 而非透镜公式。
rules.trigger: 题目涉及液滴表面成像或利用液面作为光学元件时

rules.title: 球冠几何参数一致性校验
rules.description:
触发条件：涉及曲率半径 R、弦长 D（直径）和接触角 α 的几何建模
检查逻辑：验证是否满足球冠基本几何关系：R*sin(α) = D/2。若公式中出现 cot(α) 且无平方项对应，需警惕维度或三角函数误用。
rules.check_logic: 验证是否满足球冠基本几何关系：R*sin(α) = D/2。若公式中出现 cot(α) 且无平方项对应，需警惕维度或三角函数误用。
rules.trigger: 涉及曲率半径 R、弦长 D（直径）和接触角 α 的几何建模

rules.title: Improper reduction of Euclidean light-path distance to axial absolute value
rules.description: Checks for incorrect simplification of Euclidean distances in light-travel-time (retarded-time) or time-of-flight geometry. Specifically, flags steps where a distance of the form r = sqrt((Δx)^2 + (Δy)^2 + (Δz)^2) or r = sqrt((x − x_obs)^2 + d^2) is reduced to |Δx|, (x − x_obs), or sqrt((Δx)^2) by discarding transverse terms (e.g., d, Δy, Δz, impact parameter b, observer offset, sinθ contributions) without an explicit, consistent justification. Trigger conditions include: (1) algebraic replacement sqrt(a^2 + b^2) → |a| or sqrt(a^2), where b^2 is nonzero or not proven negligible; (2) a nonzero perpendicular/offset parameter (d, b, y0, z0, sinθ⋅something) appears in the setup but disappears from the distance r or subsequent time-of-flight equations with no stated assumption (e.g., d = 0, θ = 0) or approximation regime; (3) angle-dependent geometry (presence of θ in the problem statement) leads to a distance expression that loses θ-dependence solely due to dropping perpendicular components; (4) inconsistency check such as r evaluated at Δx = 0 giving 0 while the setup defines a nonzero transverse separation (e.g., r(Δx = 0) should equal d, not 0). Acceptable exceptions: the solution explicitly declares and consistently applies on-axis or zero-angle conditions (d = 0 or θ = 0), or clearly states and uses a controlled approximation (e.g., d << |Δx|, small-angle) with an error estimate/order. This rule is applicable to derivations involving ellipses/ellipsoids of equal light-travel time, moving sources/observers, Liénard–Wiechert style retarded distances, or any time-of-flight constraint where perpendicular offsets are geometrically relevant.

rules.title: Use B̃ = (1/ω)(k × Ẽ); forbid (1/v)(k̂ × Ẽ) with complex k (evanescent/TIR)
rules.description: This rule verifies the construction of the magnetic field phasor for plane waves in media where the wavevector may be complex (e.g., evanescent waves under total internal reflection). The correct general phasor relation is B̃ = (1/ω)(k × Ẽ). The rule flags solutions that: (a) express B̃ (or H̃) using a unit direction vector k̂ and a speed v, i.e., B̃ = (1/v)(k̂ × Ẽ) or H̃ = (1/μ v)(k̂ × Ẽ), when any component of k is imaginary or the refraction angle is declared complex (keywords/indicators: evanescent wave, total internal reflection, sin θ_T > 1, θ_T = θ' + iθ'', k_z = iκ, cos θ_T imaginary); (b) normalize k to k̂ = k/|k| with |k| taken from a complex angle, or define v = c/n in this context; (c) introduce prefactors like n E_0/ω or E_0/v arising from k̂-normalization in evanescent/TIR scenarios. Rationale: when k is complex, k̂ and v (ω/|k| or c/n) are not physically well-defined, and using them yields incorrect amplitudes/prefactors. The verifier passes solutions that derive B̃ via B̃ = (1/ω)(k × Ẽ) (and, if needed, H̃ = (1/μ ω)(k × Ẽ)) and only allows B̃ = (1/v)(k̂ × Ẽ) in contexts where k is explicitly real, the medium is lossless, and no complex angles are introduced. The rule is triggered if the text contains evidence of evanescent/TIR conditions together with (1/v)(k̂ × Ẽ) or equivalent normalization-based formulas, or if the magnetic-field prefactor is written in terms of n/v rather than k/ω under those conditions.

rules.title: Check marginal-ray speed in parabolic GRIN fiber
rules.description: Applicable when the problem specifies a graded-index (GRIN) fiber with a parabolic core profile n(x) = n1 * sqrt(1 - α^2 x^2), cladding index n2, and asks for the propagation speed v_M of the marginal (critical-angle) ray up to the first axis crossing (with geometric optics, no dispersion). The rule verifies two things: (1) Formula consistency: compute the expected speed v_expected = 2 * c * n2 / (n1^2 + n2^2). If the reported v_M differs from v_expected by more than 3% relative error, flag a calculation error. (2) Physical bounds: the reported v_M must satisfy c/n1 ≤ v_M ≤ c/n2; if v_M exceeds c/n2 or is less than c/n1, flag a physical inconsistency. Rationale: In parabolic GRIN fibers, the transit time between axis crossings is angle-independent; the marginal-ray average speed equals 2 c n2 / (n1^2 + n2^2) and is typically close to c/n1. This rule catches overestimated speeds (e.g., v_M > c/n2) and deviations from the established GRIN timing relation.

rules.title: Mechanical–Optical Analogy: Incorrect Use of c/n as Particle Speed
rules.description: Checks solutions that use the mechanical analogy (Maupertuis’ principle) to model light rays in a graded-index medium. Flags an error if the fictitious mass point’s speed v(r) is identified with the physical speed of light in the medium (v = c/n or n = c/v with v taken as the particle’s speed). In the correct mapping, Fermat’s principle ∫ n ds corresponds to Maupertuis’ principle ∫ p ds with p = m v, so the particle’s momentum magnitude must satisfy p(r) ∝ n(r), yielding v(r) = v0 n(r) for some constant v0, not v = c/n. The rule also flags related misassignments such as p ∝ 1/n, using c/n inside mechanical energy relations (e.g., E = T + U with v = c/n), or deriving a potential U(r) that scales as +n or 1/n^2 under the E = 0 mapping (the correct E = 0 mapping implies U(r) = −(1/2) m v^2 ∝ −n^2). This rule triggers when the solution context mentions a fictitious mass point, mechanical analogy, Maupertuis’ principle, or E = 0 and simultaneously ties the particle speed or momentum to c/n or 1/n.

rules.title: Verify reverse-order target reflections in method of images (reject uniform table scaling)
rules.description: This rule checks modeling steps in billiards/optics problems solved via the method of images. For a rectangular table or cavity with corners A(0,0), B(a,0), C(a,b), D(0,b), and a specified hit order on boundaries, the correct construction is: reflect the destination point (the final pocket/target) across the listed boundaries in the reverse order of impact. Do not reflect the launch point, and do not uniformly scale the table dimensions. Algorithm: (1) Parse the specified collision sequence S = [wall_1, wall_2, ..., wall_n] where wall_1 is the first collision. (2) Initialize P_target = C(a,b). (3) For i from n down to 1, reflect P_target across wall_i using x' = 2 x_wall − x for vertical walls (x = 0 or x = a) and y' = 2 y_wall − y for horizontal walls (y = 0 or y = b). (4) Compute tan(theta)_expected = (P_target.y − A.y) / (P_target.x − A.x). (5) Compare the student’s tan(theta) and/or stated image coordinates against tan(theta)_expected and the computed image point. Flag an error if: (a) the student treats the final image as C' = ((k+1) a, (k+1) b) or otherwise uniformly scales both dimensions with the number of reflections; (b) the student reflects the wrong point (e.g., the source) or applies reflections in the forward order rather than reverse; (c) the student’s tan(theta) matches b/a or another ratio implying uniform scaling instead of the reverse-order reflection result. For the specific sequence [BC, AD] (first hit BC, then AD, then enter C), the correct image is C* = (3 a, b), giving tan(theta) = b / (3 a); any derivation producing C' = (2 a, 2 b) or tan(theta) = b / a is flagged as a modeling error.

rules.title: Turning-point invariant and correct ray slope in gradient-index mirage
rules.description:
Checks that solutions for inferior/superior mirage or stratified gradient-index ray tracing correctly use the horizontal turning-point condition and the associated invariant to derive the ray path. The rule triggers when the problem specifies a refractive index varying with height (e.g., n^2(z) = n0^2 + α z or similar) and the solution invokes Snell's law in a continuous medium. Required checks: 
- Turning point: The solution must introduce a turning height z_t where the ray is horizontal. If the angle is defined with respect to the vertical, it must state sin θ(z_t) = 1 (θ = 90°). If the angle is defined with respect to the horizontal, it must state cos θ(z_t) = 1 (θ = 0°). 
- Invariant constant: The conserved quantity must be correctly set using the turning point: n(z) sin θ(z) = n(z_t) (for vertical-angle convention) or n(z) cos θ(z) = n(z_t) (for horizontal-angle convention). Using an initial value like n0 sin θ0 or any value not tied to the turning point is flagged. 
- Ray slope: The solution must express the slope via the invariant and the local index: dx/dz = tan θ(z) = n(z_t) / sqrt(n^2(z) - n^2(z_t)) (for the vertical-angle convention), or an algebraically equivalent form for the horizontal-angle convention. Expressions for dx/dz that do not reduce to C / sqrt(n^2(z) - C^2), with C = n(z_t), are flagged. 
- Integration consistency (for linear n^2): For profiles like n^2(z) = n0^2 + α z, integrating the above slope should yield x(z) differing by a constant from (2 n(z_t)/α) sqrt(n^2(z) - n^2(z_t)). Omission of z_t in the integration or use of an inconsistent functional form is flagged. 
This rule is intended to catch modeling errors where the geometry of an inferior mirage (horizontal turning point and virtual image formation) is not encoded into the invariant and ray equation, leading to incorrect path integration and image distance estimates.

rules.title: Parabolic GRIN fiber modal speed equality check
rules.description: Context: A graded-index (GRIN) fiber with parabolic core profile n(x) = n1 * sqrt(1 - α^2 x^2), geometric optics (wave effects neglected), and no chromatic dispersion. In such fibers, meridional rays execute harmonic radial motion and the axial propagation time between successive axis crossings is independent of launch angle. Consequently, the effective axial propagation speeds for extreme-angle rays (e.g., at the maximum meridional angle) and the on-axis ray must be equal within small numerical tolerance. What to check: (1) If a solution claims or computes v_M (speed for the critical/maximum meridional angle) and v0 (on-axis speed) with a relative difference exceeding 2%, flag an error. (2) If a solution concludes v_M < v0 or v_M > v0 without explicit non-parabolic profile or dispersion effects, flag an error. (3) Cross-check absolute values: both speeds should be approximately c/n1 (within ~5%) for typical comparisons of axial advance per unit time; large deviations indicate a likely miscalculation. (4) Flag misuse of total internal reflection at the core–cladding boundary (e.g., applying n(a) * sin θ = n2 to set a 'critical' angle) to determine ray confinement in a parabolic GRIN core, since confinement is due to continuous refraction, not TIR; such steps often yield incorrect v_M and v0. Rationale: In a parabolic GRIN fiber, modal (ray) delays are equalized; any asserted inequality v_M < v0 or v_M > v0 under the stated assumptions is conceptually incorrect. For the given example values (n1 ≈ 1.500), expected speeds satisfy v_M ≈ v0 ≈ c/n1 ≈ 2.0×10^8 m/s.

rules.title: Verify Maxwell's equations in nonlinear media
rules.description: Check if the governing Maxwell's equations in nonlinear media are correctly applied. In nonlinear optics, the displacement field D includes higher-order terms of the electric field E, such as P = χ^(1)E + χ^(2)E^2 + χ^(3)E^3. These nonlinear terms are responsible for phenomena like harmonic generation and self-focusing.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the polarization terms (χ^(n)E^n) are included in the displacement field, and the wave equation is correctly derived from Maxwell's equations. Confirm that the nonlinear terms are appropriately incorporated into the wave equation derivation.
common_errors: Ignoring higher-order polarization terms (χ^(2), χ^(3)) for nonlinear processes.
Incorrectly deriving the wave equation from Maxwell's equations.
Using linear susceptibility instead of nonlinear susceptibility for nonlinear media.

rules.title: Check energy conservation in harmonic generation
rules.description: In harmonic generation, the energy of the generated harmonic wave must come from the fundamental wave. Energy conservation dictates that the sum of the energies (or frequencies) of the interacting waves remains constant.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the frequencies and energy of the generated harmonics match the sum or difference of the interacting fundamental wave frequencies. Ensure that the depletion of the fundamental wave is accounted for in energy transfer calculations.
common_errors: Mismatching the input and output frequencies in energy conservation.
Ignoring the depletion of the fundamental wave due to energy transfer to harmonics.

rules.title: Ensure phase-matching condition is satisfied
rules.description: For efficient harmonic generation or nonlinear interactions, the phase-matching condition (k1 ± k2 ± ... = kn) must be satisfied, where k denotes the wavevector of interacting waves. This ensures constructive interference and maximized conversion efficiency.
rules.check_logic: Check if the wavevectors satisfy the phase-matching condition in the given geometry and medium. Verify that material dispersion, birefringence, and crystal orientation are correctly accounted for in the calculations.
common_errors: Not accounting for material dispersion when calculating wavevectors.
Using incorrect refractive indices for the interacting frequencies.
Neglecting contributions from birefringence or crystal orientation in anisotropic media.

rules.title: Verify sign conventions for wave propagation
rules.description: In nonlinear optics, the sign convention for wave propagation direction, electric field, and polarization must be consistent. Incorrect sign conventions can lead to errors in phase-matching and energy flow calculations.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the propagation direction and polarization vectors follow the right-hand rule and are consistent with the chosen coordinate system. Confirm that the sign conventions are uniformly applied across all equations.
common_errors: Using inconsistent wavevector or polarization sign conventions across equations.
Incorrectly assigning negative signs to forward or backward propagating waves.
Ignoring handedness of coordinate systems in anisotropic or birefringent media.

rules.title: Check medium constraints for nonlinear effects
rules.description: Nonlinear optical effects like second-harmonic generation (SHG) or self-focusing require specific material properties, such as non-centrosymmetric crystal structure for SHG or a positive nonlinear refractive index for self-focusing.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the medium properties (e.g., non-centrosymmetry, nonlinear coefficients) are suitable for the observed nonlinear effect. Confirm that material absorption and saturation effects are considered at high intensities.
common_errors: Applying SHG in a centrosymmetric material.
Using incorrect or unrealistic nonlinear refractive indices.
Ignoring material absorption or saturation effects at high intensities.

rules.title: Ensure validity conditions for nonlinear equations
rules.description: Nonlinear equations assume certain conditions, such as the slowly varying envelope approximation (SVEA) and negligible depletion of the pump wave. These assumptions must hold for the equations to be valid.
rules.check_logic: Check if the intensity of the pump wave is high enough for nonlinear effects but low enough to maintain the SVEA and negligible depletion. Verify that the pulse duration and beam parameters are consistent with the assumptions.
common_errors: Violating the SVEA by using extremely short pulses.
Ignoring pump depletion in high-efficiency nonlinear processes.
Overestimating nonlinear effects in weak-field regimes.

rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency in equations
rules.description: All equations in nonlinear optics must be dimensionally consistent, particularly when dealing with nonlinear susceptibility terms (e.g., χ^(2), χ^(3)). These terms have specific units that depend on the order of nonlinearity and the electric field's units.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the units of χ^(2), χ^(3), and other nonlinear terms are correctly applied in calculations, and the resulting units match physical expectations. Confirm that the unit systems (e.g., SI or Gaussian) are consistently used.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for nonlinear susceptibility terms.
Mixing SI and Gaussian unit systems in equations.
Ignoring the unit scaling of electric fields in nonlinear interactions.

rules.title: Check self-focusing threshold intensity
rules.description: Self-focusing occurs when the intensity of a laser beam exceeds a critical threshold, determined by the nonlinear refractive index and beam parameters. Below this threshold, self-focusing does not occur.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the input beam intensity exceeds the critical self-focusing threshold for the given medium and beam geometry. Ensure that the beam parameters, such as spot size and wavelength, are correctly included in the threshold calculation.
common_errors: Miscalculating the critical intensity for self-focusing.
Ignoring beam parameters like spot size and wavelength in threshold calculations.
Predicting self-focusing in media with negligible nonlinear refractive index.

rules.title: Check group velocity mismatch in nonlinear interactions
rules.description: Group velocity mismatch (GVM) between interacting waves can limit the efficiency of nonlinear processes, especially for ultrafast pulses. GVM arises due to differences in group velocities of the interacting waves in the medium.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the group velocity mismatch is calculated and its impact on the interaction efficiency is assessed. Ensure that pulse durations and medium dispersion are considered.
common_errors: Ignoring group velocity mismatch in ultrafast pulse interactions.
Using incorrect group velocity values for the interacting waves.
Neglecting the effect of dispersion on pulse overlap.

rules.title: Verify coherence length using the wavelength and bandwidth
rules.description: The coherence length is given by L_c = c / Δν, where c is the speed of light and Δν is the spectral bandwidth. It describes the spatial extent over which a wavefront remains coherent.
rules.check_logic: Check if the coherence length L_c is calculated using the formula L_c = c / Δν, ensuring that Δν (bandwidth) is provided in units of Hz and c is in m/s.
common_errors: Using the source wavelength instead of the bandwidth in the formula
Incorrect unit conversion for spectral bandwidth
Confusing coherence length with wavelength

rules.title: Verify phase difference calculation in interferometers
rules.description: The phase difference Δϕ in an interferometer setup is given by Δϕ = (2π/λ) ΔL, where λ is the wavelength of light and ΔL is the path length difference.
rules.check_logic: Check if the phase difference is calculated using Δϕ = (2π/λ) ΔL, ensuring consistent units for ΔL (meters) and λ (meters).
common_errors: Forgetting the factor 2π in the formula
Using the absolute path length instead of the path difference
Mismatch in units for ΔL and λ

rules.title: Verify sign convention for path length difference
rules.description: In an interferometer, the path length difference ΔL is positive if the path in one arm is longer than the other and negative if shorter. This sign convention affects the interference pattern.
rules.check_logic: Check if the sign of ΔL is correctly assigned based on the physical geometry of the interferometer setup and ensure it is consistently applied in phase difference calculations.
common_errors: Using inconsistent signs for ΔL
Ignoring the sign of path length differences leading to incorrect phase difference calculations

rules.title: Ensure light sources are coherent for interference
rules.description: Interference phenomena in interferometers require coherent light sources, meaning the sources should have a fixed phase relationship and similar wavelengths.
rules.check_logic: Check that the light sources used are described as coherent and that they meet the criteria for producing an interference pattern. Verify that the coherence length of the source is sufficient for the experimental setup.
common_errors: Attempting to calculate interference without ensuring coherence
Using light sources with vastly differing wavelengths
Ignoring the coherence length of the source

rules.title: Check dimensional consistency of optical coherence equations
rules.description: Ensure that all terms in equations related to coherence (e.g., L_c = c / Δν) are dimensionally consistent. For instance, c must be in m/s and Δν in Hz to result in L_c in meters.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the units of all quantities in the equation are consistent, particularly with L_c resulting in units of length. Ensure proper unit conversions where necessary.
common_errors: Using mixed units (e.g., nm for wavelength and Hz for frequency)
Forgetting to convert bandwidth to Hz

rules.title: Ensure correct conditions for constructive and destructive interference
