rules.description: Constructive interference occurs when Δϕ = 2mπ (m is an integer), and destructive interference occurs when Δϕ = (2m+1)π. This depends on the path length difference and wavelength.
rules.check_logic: Check that the conditions for constructive and destructive interference are applied correctly using Δϕ and the appropriate equations. Verify that ΔL and λ are consistent with the calculated Δϕ.
common_errors: Misapplying constructive/destructive conditions
Using incorrect multiples of π in phase difference calculations
Confusing Δϕ with ΔL directly

rules.title: Verify Michelson Interferometer arm lengths and path difference
rules.description: In a Michelson Interferometer, the path length difference is 2ΔL due to the reflection of beams. ΔL is the difference in arm lengths.
rules.check_logic: Check that the path length difference is calculated as 2ΔL and that the arm lengths are correctly measured and substituted. Ensure that the factor of 2 is included due to the reflection.
common_errors: Forgetting the factor of 2 due to reflection
Using incorrect arm length measurements
Misinterpreting the geometry of the interferometer

rules.title: Ensure small angles for approximations in interferometers
rules.description: For many interferometer setups, small-angle approximations (e.g., sinθ ≈ θ) are used for simplicity. These approximations are valid only when θ is small (in radians).
rules.check_logic: Check if the small-angle approximation is applied and verify that θ is indeed small (e.g., θ < 10 degrees or approximately 0.174 radians). Ensure proper unit conversion if θ is provided in degrees.
common_errors: Applying small-angle approximations to large angles
Using θ in degrees instead of radians without conversion

rules.title: Verify frequency-wavelength relationship for light
rules.description: The relationship between frequency (ν), wavelength (λ), and the speed of light (c) is given by c = λν.
rules.check_logic: Check that the relationship c = λν is used correctly, ensuring consistent units (e.g., c in m/s, λ in meters, and ν in Hz). Verify proper conversions if units are mixed.
common_errors: Using inconsistent units for c, λ, or ν
Forgetting to convert wavelength from nm to meters

rules.title: Missing 1/2 factor in induced-dipole interaction energy
rules.description: Trigger when a solution models a neutral atom as an induced dipole (p = αE or references polarizability α) but writes the interaction energy as U = −p·E or U = −Re[p·E] without the required 1/2 factor. For an induced dipole, the correct energy is the work to build the dipole: U(E) = −(1/2) Re[p·E] = −(1/2) Re[α(ω)] |E|^2 for harmonic fields. In optical trapping, the time-averaged dipole potential must therefore be U_dip(r) = −[Re(α(ω)) / (2 ε0 c)] I(r), using I = (1/2) c ε0 |E|^2. Flag equations that: (a) use U = −p·E for an induced dipole, (b) omit the 1/2 factor in any equivalent expression (e.g., U = −α |E|^2 or U = −α I/(ε0 c)), or (c) fail to take the real part of α when α is complex. This rule targets conceptual errors conflating permanent-dipole energy with induced-dipole energy and ensures correct averaging and coefficients in optical dipole potentials.

rules.title: Induced dipole energy must include 1/2 factor (optical dipole potential)
rules.description: This rule checks solutions for the common factor-of-two error when computing the optical dipole (AC Stark) potential of an induced dipole in an oscillating electric field. For an induced dipole p = α(ω)E, the instantaneous interaction energy must be U_inst = -(1/2) p·E (not -p·E). After time-averaging over a monochromatic field E(t) = E0 cos(ωt), the correct potential is U_dip = -(1/4) Re[α(ω)] E0^2. Equivalently, using I = (1/2) ε0 c E0^2, the correct intensity form is U_dip = -Re[α(ω)] I / (2 ε0 c). If a phase form is used, Re[α] = |α| cos φ, so acceptable equivalents are U_dip = -(1/4) |α| E0^2 cos φ and U_dip = -[|α| cos φ] I / (2 ε0 c). The verifier should flag: (a) any explicit use of U = -p·E for induced dipoles, (b) expressions that yield U_dip = -(1/2) Re[α] E0^2 (missing the 1/2 in U = -(1/2) p·E), or (c) intensity-form results of the form U_dip = -Re[α] I / (ε0 c) or U_dip = -[α cos φ] I / (ε0 c), which are larger in magnitude by a factor of 2. The rule applies in contexts mentioning induced dipoles, polarizability α(ω), AC Stark shift, optical traps, or laser-induced potentials, and it accepts any algebraically equivalent correct form that contains the 1/4 factor with E0^2 or the 1/(2 ε0 c) factor with I.

rules.title: Apply Lensmaker's Equation for Focal Length
rules.description: The Lensmaker's Equation calculates the focal length of a lens based on its radius of curvature and the refractive index. It applies to thin lenses under the paraxial approximation.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the focal length is calculated using 1/f = (n - 1) * (1/R1 - 1/R2), where R1 and R2 are the radii of curvature of the lens surfaces, and n is the refractive index of the lens material.
common_errors: Using wrong sign for radii of curvature
Incorrect refractive index value in the equation

rules.title: Adhere to Sign Conventions for Lens Formulas
rules.description: In optics, sign conventions dictate the positive or negative assignment for distances. For converging lenses, distances measured against the direction of incident light (left to right) are negative.
rules.check_logic: Verify that object distances, image distances, and focal lengths adhere to the sign conventions based on lens type and orientation. For example, for a converging lens, focal length is positive, and for a diverging lens, it is negative.
common_errors: Incorrect sign for object distance when using lens formulas
Wrong sign in focal length application in calculations

rules.title: Calculate Magnification Correctly
rules.description: Magnification for optical instruments is defined as the ratio of the image height to the object height. Ensure calculations reflect this definition.
rules.check_logic: Calculate magnification using M = -di/do for lenses and telescopes, ensuring the negative sign indicates inverted images. For microscopes, ensure the total magnification is the product of the objective and eyepiece magnifications.
common_errors: Forgetting to include negative sign for inverted images
Misinterpreting object and image distances
Omitting the contribution of the eyepiece in total magnification for microscopes

rules.title: Maintain Geometric Alignment Constraints
rules.description: Geometric alignment in optical instruments is critical to their functioning. Ensure lenses, mirrors, and other components are appropriately aligned.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that all components of the optical instrument are aligned along the principal axis or the intended optical path. Check for tilt, decentering, or misalignment that could cause aberrations or distortions.
common_errors: Misaligned lenses causing distortion
Improper orientation of mirrors in telescopes
Failure to align the optical axis with the principal axis

rules.title: Validate Conditions for Ray Optics
rules.description: Ray optics applies when the wavelength is much smaller than the size of the optical elements, allowing simplification using geometric optics equations.
rules.check_logic: Check that the wavelength of light is significantly smaller than the aperture size or lens diameter before applying ray optics principles. If not, wave optics principles should be used instead.
common_errors: Applying ray optics to setups not satisfying wavelength-to-aperture proportion
Using ray optics equations for phenomena requiring wave optics

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency in Equations
rules.description: Optical instruments involve several dimensional quantities (distance, height, radius). Ensure units are consistent when substituting into formulas.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all quantities, especially distances, focal lengths, and radii of curvature, are in compatible units (commonly meters or centimeters) before calculations. Perform unit conversions if necessary.
common_errors: Mismatch in units between focal length and object/image distances
Ignoring conversion of units prior to mathematical operations

rules.title: Consider Eyepiece Accommodation in Telescopes
rules.description: The eyepiece of a telescope adjusts the focal points for viewing. Ensure calculations consider the influence of eyepiece characteristics.
rules.check_logic: Check if the telescope's eyepiece focal length is used correctly in image formation and determining overall magnification. Ensure the eye relief distance is accounted for in practical setups.
common_errors: Overlooking the effect of eye relief distance
Inaccurate use of eyepiece focal length causing miscalculation of magnification

rules.title: Apply Object-Image Distance Equation Correctly
rules.description: For optical instruments, the relation 1/f = 1/do + 1/di governs the relationship between object and image distances with focal length.
rules.check_logic: Verify that object distance (do) and image distance (di) are correctly placed in the equation and solved for their respective values. Ensure proper unit consistency during calculations.
common_errors: Mixing up object and image distances when substituting into the equation
Improper conversion of units resulting in incorrect solution

rules.title: Account for Optical Aberrations
rules.description: Optical aberrations such as spherical aberration, chromatic aberration, and astigmatism can affect image quality. Ensure these are minimized in design and calculations.
rules.check_logic: Check if the lens or mirror design accounts for aberrations. For chromatic aberration, verify if an achromatic doublet or similar correction is used. For spherical aberration, ensure the lens shape is optimized.
common_errors: Ignoring chromatic aberration in multi-wavelength setups
Failure to account for spherical aberration in high-precision instruments

rules.title: Consider Diffraction Limit in Resolution
rules.description: The resolution of optical instruments is limited by diffraction, which depends on the aperture size and wavelength of light.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the resolution calculation considers the diffraction limit using the formula θ = 1.22 * λ/D, where λ is the wavelength and D is the aperture diameter.
common_errors: Overestimating resolution by ignoring diffraction effects
Using incorrect aperture size in diffraction limit calculations

rules.title: Unjustified Pancharatnam phase–solid angle relation on Poincaré sphere
rules.description: Flags solutions that assert the relation between geometric (Pancharatnam/Berry) phase and enclosed solid angle on the Poincaré sphere (e.g., Ω = 2α, S = 2α, or α = ±Ω/2) without providing the required justification. The rule checks for the presence of claims linking phase to area/solid angle and requires: (1) explicit identification of a closed loop of polarization states on the Poincaré sphere; (2) confirmation that the loop is composed of geodesic (great-circle) arcs or an explanation of how the chosen path leads to the same enclosed solid angle; (3) demonstration that the phase discussed is purely geometric (dynamical phase is canceled or shown to be irrelevant); (4) a rationale or reference to the standard result that the Pancharatnam/Berry phase equals half the oriented solid angle enclosed by the loop, including sign/orientation conventions; and (5) clear definitions of α (geometric phase) and Ω/S (solid angle/area on the unit sphere). If any of these elements are missing and the relation is merely asserted, or if the factor/sign is incorrect (e.g., Ω = α), the solution is flagged.

rules.title: Check 2π consistency in λ↔ω conversion for phase/OPD
rules.description: This rule verifies that conversions between wavelength (λ) and angular frequency (ω) in phase and interference expressions correctly account for the 2π factor. The correct identities are: k = 2π/λ = ω/c, 1/λ = ω/(2π c), and π/λ = ω/(2c). The verifier scans phase expressions (e.g., Δφ, k·OPD, arguments of cos/sin in interference/intensity formulas) and flags the following incorrect substitutions: (a) using 1/λ = ω/c; (b) using π/λ = ω/c or π/λ → π·ω/c; (c) defining k as k = 2π·ω/c; (d) replacing cos(π·X/λ) by cos(π·ω·X/c) instead of cos((ω/(2c))·X); (e) replacing cos(2π·X/λ) by cos(2π·ω·X/c) instead of cos((ω/c)·X). The rule also checks fringe spacing expressions where λ is replaced by c/ω and ensures that no extra or missing 2π factor changes the scale of Δφ or the spacing. If any of these patterns are detected, the solution is flagged for incorrect λ↔ω conversion leading to phase scaling errors.

rules.title: Incorrect projection modeling for pinhole camera apparent length
rules.description: Flag solutions that model the apparent length in a pinhole camera as a projection (e.g., L_app = L' cos(theta)) or that introduce explicit dependence on the camera distance D after calibration. In a pinhole camera, image positions are determined by viewing angles (theta = arctan(x/D)), and with calibration via equidistant marks along the x-axis, a rod at rest appears with length L independent of D. The rule triggers if: (1) The formula for apparent length includes cosine/sine of a viewing angle (cos(theta), sin(theta)) or equivalent projection factors such as D/sqrt(x^2 + D^2), indicating a linear projection onto the x-axis; (2) The final expression for L_app explicitly depends on D in a way that does not cancel under the stated calibration; (3) The text claims the photograph is a projection onto the x-axis or uses 'foreshortening' to compute image length; (4) The solution uses pure Lorentz length contraction (L' = L sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)) as the image length without invoking angular mapping (arctan(x/D)) or light-time geometry relevant to pinhole imaging.

rules.title: Incorrect use of double-slit path-difference for plane-wave volumetric interference
rules.description: This rule flags modeling errors where a solution to interference of two coherent plane waves crossing in a medium treats the phenomenon as a double-slit/screen (Fraunhofer) problem. Specifically, it checks for the use of path-difference formulas such as ΔL = d sin(θ), fringe spacing s = λ L / d, or references to 'slit separation d' or a screen distance L that are not part of the setup. The correct approach for volumetric interference is to use the spatial modulation wavevector Δk = k1 − k2 and compute the fringe spacing as Λ = 2π / |Δk|. For two plane waves of equal wavelength in a medium with refractive index n and crossing angle α, an equivalent expression is Λ = λ_medium / (2 sin(α/2)), with λ_medium = λ0 / n. The rule triggers if any of the following are detected: (1) formulas or keywords indicative of double-slit/screen treatment (ΔL = d sinθ, mλ = d sinθ, s = λ L / d, references to 'slits', 'aperture separation d', 'screen distance L'); (2) introduction of variables d or L not provided by the problem; (3) statements implying far-field screen patterns rather than in-volume spatial modulation. The rule passes when the solution explicitly formulates Δk = k1 − k2, or uses Λ = 2π/|Δk| or Λ = λ_medium/(2 sin(α/2)), and recognizes λ_medium = λ0/n in media.

rules.title: Verify intensity of polarized light using Malus’s Law
rules.description: Malus’s Law states that the transmitted intensity of polarized light through an analyzer is given by I = I0 * cos²(θ), where θ is the angle between the light's polarization direction and the analyzer's transmission axis. It applies when light is linearly polarized and passes through an ideal polarizer.
rules.check_logic: Check if the intensity is calculated as I = I0 * cos²(θ), where θ is the correct angle between the polarization and transmission axes. Verify that the incoming light is linearly polarized.
common_errors: Forgetting to square the cosine term.
Using sine instead of cosine.
Using the wrong angle (e.g., complementary angle instead of θ).
Not considering whether the incoming light is already polarized.

rules.title: Verify Brewster’s angle calculation
rules.description: Brewster’s angle is the angle of incidence at which light is completely polarized upon reflection. It is given by tan(θB) = n2/n1, where n1 and n2 are the refractive indices of the two media. This applies to unpolarized or partially polarized light striking a dielectric surface.
rules.check_logic: Check if θB is calculated using tan(θB) = n2/n1, and verify the refractive indices used. Ensure the calculation is applied to dielectric surfaces and not metallic ones.
common_errors: Using sin or cos instead of tan.
Incorrect assignment of n1 and n2 (e.g., swapping media).
Applying Brewster’s law to metallic surfaces or total internal reflection conditions.

rules.title: Verify conditions for converting linearly polarized light to circularly polarized light
rules.description: Linearly polarized light can be converted to circularly polarized light using a quarter-wave plate. The condition is that the linear polarization must be at 45° to the fast or slow axis of the quarter-wave plate, and the plate must introduce a phase difference of π/2.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the polarization direction is at 45° relative to the wave plate's axis and the plate introduces a phase difference of π/2 (or λ/4). Verify the wave plate is correctly oriented and of the correct thickness.
common_errors: Not orienting the linear polarization at 45° to the wave plate axis.
Using a wave plate of incorrect thickness (not λ/4).
Confusing quarter-wave plates with half-wave plates.

rules.title: Check consistency of Snell’s Law for refracted polarized light
rules.description: Snell’s Law applies to light passing between two media: n1*sin(θ1) = n2*sin(θ2). For polarized light, this law holds when considering the angle of refraction at the boundary.
rules.check_logic: Verify if n1*sin(θ1) = n2*sin(θ2) holds true for the given angles and refractive indices. Ensure the calculation excludes cases of total internal reflection.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of sin(θ) for given angles.
Using approximate values of refractive indices without justification.
Applying Snell’s Law to cases involving total internal reflection.

rules.title: Verify Stokes parameters for describing polarized light
rules.description: The Stokes parameters (I, Q, U, V) describe the state of polarization of light. I is the total intensity, Q and U describe linear polarization, and V describes circular polarization. These parameters must satisfy physical constraints: I² ≥ Q² + U² + V².
rules.check_logic: Check if the calculated Stokes parameters satisfy I² ≥ Q² + U² + V² and if the parameters are consistent with the given polarization state. Verify the interpretation of Q, U, and V for the specific polarization type.
common_errors: Violating the inequality I² ≥ Q² + U² + V².
Misinterpreting the signs of Q, U, or V for specific polarization states.
Assigning incorrect values to Q, U, or V for circularly polarized light.

rules.title: Verify dimensional consistency of light intensity
rules.description: Intensity of light is defined as power per unit area and is measured in W/m². For polarization problems, the intensity values must have consistent units throughout calculations.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that all intensity values are expressed in W/m² and units are consistent in equations like I = I0 * cos²(θ). Verify that power and area are correctly defined if intensity is derived.
common_errors: Using arbitrary or undefined units for intensity.
Mixing up power (W) with intensity (W/m²).
Failing to check unit consistency when using derived equations for intensity.

rules.title: Verify reflection and polarization angle consistency
rules.description: According to the law of reflection, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. For polarized light, the reflected and refracted components must respect polarization principles (e.g., Brewster's angle).
rules.check_logic: Ensure the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection and verify if Brewster's angle is correctly applied for polarization. Confirm the polarization state of the reflected light is consistent with the incident light.
common_errors: Using different angles for incidence and reflection.
Mixing up angles of refraction and reflection.
Failing to check the polarization state of reflected light.

rules.title: Verify refractive index limits in polarization problems
rules.description: Refractive indices must be real, positive, and typically greater than 1 for transparent materials. Cases involving polarization require refractive indices consistent with the medium’s nature.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that refractive indices used in equations like Brewster’s Law or Snell’s Law are within physical limits (n > 1 for transparent materials). Verify the refractive index values are appropriate for the given materials.
common_errors: Using refractive indices less than 1 for transparent media.
Assigning negative or imaginary values to refractive indices in polarization problems.
Failing to justify refractive index values for unknown materials.

rules.title: Verify conditions for partial polarization of light
rules.description: Partial polarization occurs when unpolarized light becomes partially polarized upon reflection or scattering. The degree of polarization depends on the angle of incidence and the material properties.
rules.check_logic: Verify if the degree of polarization is calculated correctly based on the Fresnel equations or experimental data. Ensure the angle of incidence and material properties are considered.
common_errors: Ignoring the dependence of polarization on the angle of incidence.
Failing to account for material properties in partial polarization.
Confusing partial polarization with complete polarization.

rules.title: 球面三角形面积与立体角等价性
rules.description:
触发条件：在单位球面上讨论球面多边形面积与立体角关系时
检查逻辑：确认是否直接将球面超额（Spherical Excess）或面积S等同于该区域对球心张开的立体角Ω。
rules.check_logic: 确认是否直接将球面超额（Spherical Excess）或面积S等同于该区域对球心张开的立体角Ω。
rules.trigger: 在单位球面上讨论球面多边形面积与立体角关系时

rules.title: 庞加莱球几何相位面积关系
rules.description:
触发条件：涉及偏振态在庞加莱球上的演化路径及相位差计算时
检查逻辑：验证相位差α与球面三角形面积S是否满足S=2α的关系，注意立体角与相位移动的2倍系数。
rules.check_logic: 验证相位差α与球面三角形面积S是否满足S=2α的关系，注意立体角与相位移动的2倍系数。
rules.trigger: 涉及偏振态在庞加莱球上的演化路径及相位差计算时

rules.title: Reject constant or improperly simplified potential in optics–mechanics analogy with variable n(r)
rules.description: Applies to solutions mapping Fermat’s principle (variable refractive index n(r)) to a mechanical analog with zero total energy (E_tot = 0). The rule checks the following: (1) Position dependence: Do not cancel or divide out n(r) or n(r)^2 as if constant when n depends on position; any algebraic step that removes n(r) or n(r)^2 from both sides without explicitly assuming n is uniform must be flagged. (2) Potential form: The conservative potential energy E_p(r) must be an explicit function of position through n(r); constant forms (e.g., E_p = −(1/2) m c^2) or forms produced by cancelling n^2(r) (e.g., E_p = −(1/2) m c^2(1 − 1/n^2)) are invalid unless a derivation consistent with the eikonal/Hamiltonian mapping is provided. (3) Zero-energy consistency: With E_tot = 0, the relation (1/2) m v(r)^2 + E_p(r) = 0 must hold; v(r) must be derived from this relation and the chosen mapping, not set equal to the physical light speed c/n(r) for the mechanical mass point without justification. (4) Internal consistency: Multiple incompatible final expressions for E_p(r) in the same solution (e.g., both a constant and an n-dependent form) must be flagged. This rule detects unjustified cancellations and incorrect potential/speed relations that break the required correspondence with Fermat/Maupertuis principles in gradient-index optics.

rules.title: Incorrect ring pattern claimed for single-crystal or finite 2D grating diffraction
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that model the diffraction from a single oriented crystal (monochromatic beam, fixed orientation) or a finite rectangular 2D grating as producing continuous circular rings on a screen (powder-like pattern) instead of discrete spots. Trigger conditions: (1) The problem context indicates a single crystal with fixed orientation (e.g., cubic crystal with specified axes/orientation) or a finite N1×N2 (or N1×N2×N3) periodic array illuminated by a plane monochromatic wave at fixed incidence; AND (2) the solution asserts any of the following: (a) circular/annular rings, Debye–Scherrer rings, or an azimuthally symmetric intensity I(r) depending only on screen radius r; (b) positions given by x^2 + y^2 = const or r ∝ m λ L / (2a) (or similar), implying independence from the azimuthal angle φ; (c) a continuous locus of maxima rather than discrete indexed peaks; AND (3) the solution does not explicitly justify random orientation (powder/polycrystal) or angular averaging/rotation that would produce rings. Expected correct modeling: (i) For a single oriented 3D crystal, discrete Bragg/Laue spots at directions satisfying k_out − k_in = G with G a reciprocal lattice vector, typically indexed by (h,k,l); (ii) For a finite 2D grating, a 2D lattice of principal maxima at sin θ_x = m λ / d1 and sin θ_y = n λ / d2 with finite widths scaling as Δθ_x ≈ λ / (N1 d1), Δθ_y ≈ λ / (N2 d2) (or screen widths Δx ≈ λ L / (N1 d1), Δy ≈ λ L / (N2 d2)). Rationale: Rings arise from random crystallite orientations (powder diffraction) or azimuthal averaging, not from a single fixed-orientation crystal or finite rectangular aperture array. Exemptions: Do not flag if the text explicitly states powder/polycrystal/random orientations or intentional rotational averaging that justifies ring formation.

rules.title: Reject ad-hoc average refractive index in parabolic GRIN fiber time-of-flight; enforce isochrony
rules.description: This rule checks solutions to graded-index (GRIN) fiber problems with parabolic index profile n(x) = n1 * sqrt(1 - α^2 x^2). It flags modeling steps where the transit time or propagation speed is computed using an ad-hoc 'average' or 'effective' refractive index along the ray path (e.g., n̄ ≈ n1 * sqrt(1 - α^2 a^2/3)) without deriving the ray trajectory or performing the correct path integral. The correct method requires either: (a) deriving the ray equation in the small-angle/eikonal limit (d^2x/dz^2 + α^2 x = 0) and showing that rays are sinusoidal and the axial transit time between axis crossings is independent of launch angle (isochrony), or (b) computing time-of-flight via dt = ∫[n(x)/c] ds along the actual ray and demonstrating independence from amplitude. The rule also flags conclusions that off-axis rays in a parabolic GRIN core have different transit times or average speeds than axial rays (i.e., any claim of intermodal delay arising solely from geometry), which contradicts the isochronous property of the parabolic profile. Additional trigger: misuse of boundary Snell's law at x = a to define a 'critical angle' for internal guidance in a GRIN core instead of treating guidance as continuous refraction; using n(a) = n2 to justify an internal TIR-based average index is invalid. Indicators to flag include: explicit use of 'average/effective index' along the path, substitution of ⟨x^2⟩ by constants like a^2/3 or a^2/2 inside n(x), computing v = c/n̄ for off-axis rays, or concluding launch-angle-dependent transit time without a ray/path integral or proof of isochrony.

rules.title: Order-of-magnitude check for photon flux and radiation pressure (scientific notation exponents)
rules.description: This rule verifies that powers of ten are handled correctly when computing photon rate and radiation pressure for an isotropic light source. It applies to problems where a source of total power P emits uniformly and a small area A at distance r receives light of average wavelength λ. The engine will: (1) Recompute intensity I = P/(4π r^2); photon energy Eγ = hc/λ; photon rate to the area N_expected = (I·A)/Eγ; and radiation pressure for perfect reflection p_expected = 2I/c (or p_expected = 2N_expected·h/(λ·A), which should equal 2I/c). (2) Check that the product exponents in denominators like D = (4π r^2)·(hc/λ) are combined via exponent addition (10^a × 10^b → 10^(a+b)); mis-additions typically yield a ±1 order-of-magnitude error. (3) Flag a violation if the submitted N or p differ from the recomputed values by a factor between ~8× and ~12× (indicative of a single power-of-ten slip), or if the reported N and p are mutually inconsistent by ~10× relative to p = 2N·h/(λ·A). This catches errors where terms such as 4π×10^12 × (1.9878×10^-19) are evaluated as ~10^-7 instead of ~10^-6, which propagates to a 10× error in both photon rate and radiation pressure.

rules.title: GRIN fiber ray path must be harmonic in z; axis-crossing spacing angle-independent
rules.description: Applicable when the problem specifies a graded-index (GRIN) core with parabolic profile n(x) = n1 * sqrt(1 - α^2 x^2) (equivalently n^2(x) = n1^2 (1 - α^2 x^2)). In such media, the ray equation yields harmonic motion in the axial coordinate: x(z) = A * sin(κ z + φ) with κ = α n1, so the axial distance between successive crossings of the axis is Δz = π / (α n1), independent of launch angle. The verifier should flag the following modeling errors: (1) Any ray-path expression that omits z-dependence or treats the path as straight-line or constant, e.g., x(z) = a * sin(θi), x(z) = z * tan(θi), or piecewise linear segments with total internal reflection inside the graded core. (2) Use of boundary-only Snell's law at x = a to determine the internal ray path or turning points in the graded core (e.g., asserting a critical incident angle from n(a) sinθ = n2 to model core propagation), instead of deriving the continuous bending via the GRIN ray equation. (3) Any formula for the axial spacing between successive crossings (or the first axis crossing distance) that depends on the launch angle or amplitude A; it must be constant and equal to π / (α n1) for the stated profile. The rule aims to detect incorrect ray-path models that ignore harmonic motion in GRIN fibers and any angle-dependent axis-crossing predictions.

rules.title: Verify Rayleigh Scattering Intensity Relation
rules.description: Rayleigh scattering intensity I is proportional to 1/λ^4 where λ is the wavelength of light. This implies shorter wavelengths scatter more strongly. This relation is crucial for understanding phenomena like blue skies and red sunsets.
rules.check_logic: Verify that I ∝ 1/λ^4 in calculations involving Rayleigh scattering.
common_errors: Incorrect dependency on wavelength, e.g., 1/λ^3 or 1/λ^2
Confusing Rayleigh scattering with Mie scattering which does not follow this law

rules.title: Ensure Small Particle Size Assumption
rules.description: Rayleigh scattering applies to particles much smaller than the wavelength of light (typically particles with dimensions less than 1/10th the wavelength).
rules.check_logic: Verify that the particle size is significantly smaller than the wavelength of incident light.
common_errors: Applying Rayleigh scattering to particles larger than the wavelength
Ignoring particle size constraints leading to inaccurate scattering predictions

rules.title: Check Applicability of Low-Refractive Index Particles
rules.description: Rayleigh scattering assumes the scatterers have a refractive index close to that of their surroundings (typically air). Large differences in refractive index alter scattering behavior.
rules.check_logic: Compare particle and medium refractive indices to ensure they are nearly similar.
common_errors: Using Rayleigh theory for high refractive contrast particles
Failing to consider the medium's effect on scattering

rules.title: Verify Dimensional Consistency in Scattering Equations
rules.description: Ensure all terms in the Rayleigh scattering equation are dimensionally consistent, particularly when calculating intensity and cross-sectional areas.
rules.check_logic: Verify that intensity calculations yield dimensions of power per unit area, typically W/m².
common_errors: Incorrect units used for wavelength
Inconsistent units in scattering cross-section calculations

rules.title: Correct Sign Convention in Scattering Angle
rules.description: In Rayleigh scattering, the direction of scattered light must follow the convention that the phase angle increases from the incident direction. This affects the calculation of the scattering pattern.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that calculations related to scattering angles are performed with the correct sign convention.
common_errors: Using negative angles incorrectly
Mistaking backward and forward scattering definitions

rules.title: Evaluate Particle Velocity Relative to Light Speed
rules.description: Rayleigh scattering generally assumes stationary particles relative to the speed of light.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the particle's velocity is negligible compared to the speed of light.
common_errors: Including significant particle velocity impacts in stationary scattering models
Misinterpreting kinematic constraints leading to flawed applications

rules.title: Check Color Changes and Angles Relation
rules.description: Rayleigh scattering causes different colors to scatter at different intensities as a function of angle, affecting perceived sky color.
rules.check_logic: Ensure calculations or explanations factor in the angle-wavelength dependency.
common_errors: Ignoring angle dependency on scattering color
Failing to consider the contribution of varying wavelengths

rules.title: Ray vs wave-normal angle confusion and misuse of Snell’s law in anisotropic propagation
rules.description:
This rule detects conceptual errors when deriving the relationship between tan(ξ) and tan(θ) for the extraordinary ray in a uniaxial crystal. It flags solutions that conflate the ray (energy flow/Poynting vector) direction with the wave-normal (phase velocity) direction, or that incorrectly apply external refraction laws (Snell’s law) to an internal anisotropic propagation problem. The rule triggers if any of the following are found: 
- The solution uses Snell’s law or a sine-law relation inside the crystal to connect ξ and θ (e.g., expressions like "n_e sin θ = n_o sin φ", "Snell’s law", "refraction law"). 
- The solution introduces a third angle φ defined via φ = 90° − ξ (or complementary to ξ) and plugs it into Snell’s law or interface refraction equations. 
- θ is described or treated as an "angle of incidence/refraction" rather than as the angle between the wave normal and the optical axis. 
- ξ and θ are equated or treated as the same, or the solution fails to differentiate their physical meanings (ray/Poynting vector vs wave normal/phase velocity). 
- Ordinary and extraordinary indices (n_o, n_e) are used within an external refraction framework instead of via index ellipsoid/ray-velocity surface relations. 
Expected correct approach indicators (absence of which increases confidence of flagging): 
- Explicit recognition that θ is the wave-normal angle to the optical axis and ξ is the ray (Poynting vector) angle to the optical axis. 
- A derivation referencing the index ellipsoid, ray surface, or Fresnel equation to relate tan(ξ) and tan(θ) without using Snell’s law. 
Implementation notes: 
- Keyword triggers: "Snell", "n_e sin", "n_o sin", "angle of incidence", "φ = 90", "complementary angle", "refraction law". 
- Conceptual markers expected: "wave normal", "Poynting", "ray surface", "index ellipsoid". Absence of these combined with refraction-law usage should be flagged as a concept error: Misinterpretation of angles and misuse of refraction law in anisotropic internal propagation.

rules.title: Verify Law of Reflection
rules.description: Ensure that the angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection, measured with respect to the normal at the interface of the reflecting surface.
rules.check_logic: Verify that θ_incidence = θ_reflection, where both angles are measured from the normal to the surface. Ensure proper units (radians or degrees) are used consistently.
common_errors: Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal
Using incorrect units for angles (e.g., radians vs degrees)
Confusing angle of incidence with angle of reflection

rules.title: Validate Snell's Law
rules.description: Verify that Snell's Law (n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2)) is satisfied at the interface between two media with indices of refraction n1 and n2.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2), where θ1 and θ2 are angles of incidence and refraction measured from the normal. Confirm that trigonometric functions are applied correctly and units are consistent.
common_errors: Incorrectly identifying the media or their refractive indices
Using the wrong trigonometric function (e.g., cosine instead of sine)
Using degrees instead of radians in calculations without proper conversion

rules.title: Check Total Internal Reflection Condition
rules.description: Ensure that total internal reflection occurs only when light travels from a denser to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.
rules.check_logic: Verify that n1 > n2 and θ_incidence > θ_critical, where θ_critical = arcsin(n2/n1). Ensure that the refractive indices are valid and the critical angle is computed correctly.
common_errors: Incorrect computation of the critical angle
Attempting total internal reflection when light is traveling from a rarer to denser medium
Ignoring the condition θ_incidence > θ_critical

rules.title: Verify Sign Convention for Angles
rules.description: Ensure that all angles (incidence, reflection, refraction) are measured with respect to the normal to the surface and not the surface itself.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the reference for angle measurement is the normal to the interface. Verify consistency in angle measurement across all calculations.
common_errors: Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal
Using inconsistent reference directions for different angles
Misidentifying the normal direction in complex geometries

rules.title: Enforce Geometric Constraints for Ray Diagrams
rules.description: Verify that in ray diagrams, incident, reflected, and refracted rays obey geometric constraints such as alignment with the normal and proper angle relationships.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that reflected and refracted rays emerge from the point of incidence and maintain the correct angular relationships with the normal. Confirm that diagrams are consistent with physical laws.
common_errors: Misaligning rays with the point of incidence
Drawing rays that violate the law of reflection or Snell's Law
Incorrectly extending or tracing rays in diagrams

rules.title: Validate Physical Range of Refractive Indices
rules.description: Ensure that the refractive indices (n1, n2) are greater than or equal to 1, as they represent the ratio of the speed of light in a vacuum to that in the medium.
rules.check_logic: Verify that n1 ≥ 1 and n2 ≥ 1. Confirm that refractive indices are assigned correctly for common materials (e.g., air, water, glass).
common_errors: Using a refractive index less than 1 for a physical medium
Incorrectly assigning refractive indices for air (n ≈ 1) or vacuum (n = 1)
Failing to verify refractive indices for exotic materials

rules.title: Ensure Dimensional Consistency in Calculations
rules.description: Verify that all quantities in reflection and refraction equations (angles, refractive indices) have consistent and appropriate units.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that angles are in radians (or properly converted), refractive indices are dimensionless, and trigonometric functions are applied correctly. Ensure unit consistency throughout calculations.
common_errors: Using inconsistent angle units (degrees vs radians)
Applying trigonometric functions to values with incorrect units
Failing to confirm that refractive indices are dimensionless

rules.title: Verify Critical Angle Calculation
rules.description: Ensure that the critical angle is calculated correctly for total internal reflection scenarios.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the critical angle is computed as θ_critical = arcsin(n2/n1) and is only defined when n1 > n2. Verify that the calculation uses valid refractive indices.
common_errors: Using incorrect formula for critical angle
Attempting to calculate a critical angle when n1 ≤ n2
Failing to use valid refractive indices in the calculation

rules.title: Confusing reflection with refraction in curved liquid surfaces
rules.description:
This rule checks for conceptual inconsistency between reflection and refraction when analyzing images or bright spots formed by curved water surfaces (e.g., a water droplet on glass acting as a plano-convex lens).

It flags a solution if it satisfies any of the following:
- The student attributes an observed image/bright spot to reflection (uses terms like "reflection", "reflected image", "mirror", "specular") while using refraction-based lens relations, such as:
  - Lensmaker's formula: 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2)
  - Thin-lens equation with refractive index or explicit use of the refractive index n (e.g., n ≈ 1.33 for water)
  - Snell's law or statements that rays are "refracted" to a focus
- The student describes a setup where a curved transparent water surface produces a focused spot on a screen/paper below and calls it a reflection or a "reflected image" (focusing on a screen through the droplet is caused by refraction, not reflection).
- The student mixes mirror formulas and lens physics inconsistently, e.g.:
  - Uses refractive index (n) while claiming the mechanism is reflection (mirror focusing does not depend on n; for a spherical mirror f = R/2).
  - Uses mirror-based focal relations (e.g., f = R/2) while describing a transparent droplet lens or employing lens terminology.

Heuristics for detection (any trigger should flag):
- Co-occurrence within the same reasoning segment of at least one reflection keyword {"reflection", "reflected image", "mirror", "specular", "glint"} and at least one refraction/lens keyword {"refraction", "lens", "plano-convex", "focal length", "lensmaker", "Snell", "refractive index", "n =", "n ≈", "n (water)"}.
- Use of refractive index (e.g., n = 1.33) together with statements that the observed image is a reflection.
- Computation of curvature radius or focal length from a water droplet using a lens formula after labeling the phenomenon as reflection of a distant light source (e.g., ceiling lights).

Pedagogical note (for feedback): If the bright spot is on a screen or paper placed below/behind the droplet, the mechanism is refraction (lens). If discussing a reflected image of a distant source seen from above, the mechanism is reflection (mirror-like), which does not involve the refractive index for focal relations.

rules.title: Consistent refraction when computing fringe spacing in a medium
rules.description: Checks consistency between wavelength and crossing angle when computing the spatial period Δ of two-beam interference inside a refractive medium entered from air. Precondition: The setup states two coherent beams incident from air onto a medium of refractive index n, with symmetric incidence (angle bisector normal to the interface) and the fringe pattern formed inside the medium (e.g., in a fluid-filled pipe). Verification steps: (1) If the solution replaces the vacuum wavelength λ0 by λm = λ0/n (or uses k = 2π n/λ0) inside the medium, it must also replace the external crossing angle α by the internal angle α′ determined by Snell’s law: sin(α′/2) = (1/n) sin(α/2). Flag an error if λ/n (or k ∝ n) is used together with the unmodified external α. (2) For symmetric incidence, the correct fringe spacing along the axis perpendicular to the angle bisector is Δ = λm / [2 sin(α′/2)] = λ0 / [2 sin(α/2)], i.e., Δ is independent of n. Flag an error if the final expression or numerical result for Δ contains n (e.g., Δ ∝ 1/n or Δ ∝ n) when the geometry implies cancellation via Snell’s law. (3) More generally, flag if wavelength or wavevector magnitude is computed for the medium while angles or direction cosines are taken from the external (air) configuration, or vice versa, when evaluating Δ = 2π/|Δk_x| or equivalent fringe-spacing formulas. This rule catches the common mistake of adjusting the wavelength for the medium but failing to refract the beam angles, which yields an incorrect n-dependence in Δ.

rules.title: Light speed in material must satisfy v = c/n and be less than c
rules.description: Checks that the propagation speed of light in a non-dispersive, isotropic medium with refractive index n is computed as v = c / n (not v = c * n) and that any reported speed is less than the vacuum speed c. The verifier will: (1) scan expressions for speed variables (e.g., v, v0, v_M, v_axis) defined using c and a refractive index; flag if the expression uses multiplication by n (e.g., v = c*n, v = c*n(x), v = c*n1) or otherwise implies v increases with n; (2) validate numerical values: flag any speed > c by more than a small tolerance (e.g., 0.1%) as physically impossible; (3) for axial propagation specifically, ensure v0 ≈ c/n_axis (e.g., c/n1 in graded-index fibers); flag if v0 ≈ c*n_axis or v0 ≥ c; (4) enforce monotonicity: dv/dn < 0 for n > 1; flag statements or derivations claiming v increases with n. This rule targets conceptual mistakes leading to superluminal speeds or incorrect c–n relationships.

rules.title: Sagnac polygon derivations must use area line-integral; reject ad hoc distance sums
rules.description:
This rule verifies that derivations of the Sagnac time difference or phase shift for rotating closed-loop interferometers (circular, triangular, polygonal fiber rings) are based on the correct geometric area formulation rather than ad hoc sums of distances.

It checks the following:
- The derivation expresses the geometric contribution via the exact identity for a planar loop: the line integral ∮ (r × dl)_z equals 2A (Green/Stokes theorem), or an equivalent exact polygon area formula (e.g., A = (1/2)∑ (x_i y_{i+1} − x_{i+1} y_i) or A = (1/2)∑ (r_i × l_i)_z with properly defined oriented edge vectors).
- The final Sagnac time/phase expression depends on the enclosed area A and angular speed Ω (i.e., Δt ∝ AΩ or Δφ ∝ AΩ), not on perimeter or on sums of distances to sides unless those are rigorously shown to reproduce the area via a correct identity.
- If the solution introduces quantities like r_i defined as “distance from centroid to side i” (or similar ad hoc geometric distances) and uses relations such as ∑ r_i ≈ A/2 (or any unproven proportionality between a sum of distances and area), the derivation is flagged unless a formal proof is provided that the relation is exact and consistent with ∮ r × dl = 2A.
- Any geometric quantities used must be precisely defined with reference point, orientation, and sign conventions. Vague or ill-defined r_i (e.g., unspecified centroid, missing orientation) cause a failure.

Trigger heuristics:
- Presence of phrases like “triangular ring”, “polygon”, “distance from centroid to each side”, “sum r_i”, “∑ r_i ≈ A/2”, combined with absence of references to the area line-integral (∮ r × dl), Green’s theorem, or an exact polygon area formula.

Rationale: The Sagnac effect for a rotating loop is governed by the loop area via the exact area integral ∮ r × dl. Replacing this with ad hoc sums of distances is unjustified and typically yields incorrect or ill-defined results.

rules.title: Sagnac Δt must be independent of refractive index for a co-rotating ring
rules.description: This rule verifies the final expression for the Sagnac time difference Δt in ring interferometers (e.g., fiber-optic gyroscopes) when the optical medium co-rotates with the platform. It checks that Δt depends only on angular speed Ω, enclosed area A, and c, and is independent of the refractive index. Expected form: Δt = 4 Ω A / c^2 (or any algebraically equivalent expression with the same dependencies and units). The rule flags an error if the final Δt expression includes refractive-index symbols (e.g., n or μ), an effective light speed c' = c/n, or factors like n, μ, n^2, μ^2 anywhere in Δt. Examples to flag include Δt ∝ (A Ω)/c'^2 with c' = c/n, Δt ∝ (A Ω n)/c^2, or Δt = (4 μ^2 A Ω)/c^2. Intermediate steps may use c' = c/n, but the dependence must cancel in the final Δt for a co-rotating medium. Exception: Do not flag if the solution explicitly models a non–co-rotating medium and includes Fresnel drag terms (e.g., factors with 1 − 1/n^2) with a clear justification that the medium is stationary in the lab while the platform rotates. The rule also validates scaling and units: Δt must scale linearly with Ω and A and inversely with c^2, yielding time units.

rules.title: Sagnac time computed as L/(c_medium ± ΩR) without accounting for moving recombination point
rules.description: This rule flags solutions to rotating-ring interferometer or Sagnac-effect problems where travel times for the CW/CCW beams are modeled as the static path length divided by a naive lab-frame light speed, typically t = L / (c/μ ± ΩR). The rule checks for the following indicators: (1) In a rotating closed-loop geometry (keywords: Sagnac, FOG, ring interferometer, rotating platform), the CW/CCW beam speeds are written as c/μ ± ΩR or c/n ± ΩR and times are obtained by directly dividing the circumference or total path length by those speeds. (2) The solution does not explicitly account for the motion of the beam splitter/recombination point or the closing speed between the light and the moving detector/end-point (e.g., no discussion of the detector’s changing angular position, relative motion, or arrival condition). (3) A derived Sagnac time difference Δt for a co-rotating medium depends on the refractive index μ (or n), indicating a spurious μ-dependence; Δt for the Sagnac effect should be independent of μ for a co-moving medium. (4) Optional consistency check: if lab-frame light speeds in a moving medium are constructed via simple Galilean addition c/μ ± v without mentioning Fresnel drag or relativistic velocity addition, the model is likely incomplete. If any of these patterns are detected, the rule reports a modeling error: the solution ignores the moving recombination point and wrongly computes traversal times from a static path-length divided by c/μ ± ΩR, which can produce incorrect μ-dependent results.

rules.title: Sagnac time difference must be independent of refractive index for co-rotating closed loops
rules.description:
Scope: Applies to solutions that derive the Sagnac time delay Δt or phase shift Δφ for a rotating, closed optical path (e.g., fiber-optic gyroscope, ring resonator) where the optical medium co-rotates rigidly with the loop.

What to check:
- Final Δt expression: Verify that the derived time difference for any closed loop equals Δt = 4 Ω A / c^2 (to first order in Ω) and contains no dependence on refractive index n (μ). If n, μ, or c' = c/μ appears in the final Δt with nonzero power (e.g., Δt ∝ n, n^2, μ, μ^2), flag as incorrect.
- Final Δφ expression: Verify that the phase shift uses Δφ = 8 π A Ω / (λ c) with λ the vacuum wavelength (or an equivalent form that is independent of n). If Δφ includes explicit factors of n (e.g., Δφ ∝ n or n^2) beyond the choice of reference wavelength, flag as incorrect.
- Speed addition step: If intermediate or final beam speeds are written as v_CW = c/n + ΩR and v_CCW = c/n − ΩR (Galilean addition) or if this leads to Δt with n-dependence that is not cancelled, flag as misuse. Correct relativistic velocity addition is (u ± v)/(1 ± uv/c^2) with u = c/n, and in a co-rotating loop the n-dependence must cancel to first order, yielding Δt = 4 Ω A / c^2.
- General formulas claimed with index factors: Explicit formulas such as Δt = (4 n^2 Ω A)/c^2, Δt ∝ μ^2, or similar, are to be flagged as incorrect unless the problem explicitly states non co-rotating media or additional flow effects.

Heuristics/patterns for detection:
- Presence of n, μ, or phrases like "refractive index" multiplying ΩA/c^2 in the final Δt.
- Expressions for path traversal times of the form L/(c/n ± v) used to produce Δt ∝ n or n^2.
- Use of c' = c/μ as a lab-frame light speed and simple addition/subtraction with ΩR without the Lorentz denominator.

Exceptions (do not flag):
- Problems that explicitly involve non co-rotating media, flowing media (Fizeau-type scenarios), or measurement of group delays where stated assumptions lead to legitimate index dependence. Absent such explicit statements, enforce index-independence in co-rotating closed-loop Sagnac derivations.

rules.title: Relative-phase sign consistency with slab-induced phase shift
rules.description: Checks the sign of the phase term introduced by a dielectric slab in two-beam interference against the student's stated phase-difference convention. The rule parses: (a) which beam traverses the slab; (b) the declared optical path difference/phase added by the slab (e.g., OPD = w(μ − 1), phase = k(μ − 1)w); (c) how the student defines the relative phase Δφ (e.g., phase of beam 2 minus phase of beam 1, or vice versa, or via field expressions indicating which beam carries the extra phase); and (d) the final Δφ_total or intensity expression. It flags a conceptual error if the slab term enters Δφ with the wrong sign for the stated convention. Example: if Δφ is defined as phase(beam 2) − phase(beam 1) and the slab is in beam 1, the slab-induced phase must appear with a minus sign (−k(μ − 1)w). Using a plus sign (+k(μ − 1)w) in this convention triggers the rule. The rule also issues a warning when the student argues the sign is irrelevant because intensity uses an even function (e.g., cos²), noting that while intensity may be unchanged, consistent phase conventions are required to predict fringe shifts, phase advancement/retardation, and related phenomena (e.g., Pancharatnam phase).

rules.title: Unjustified sin–tan/slope substitution from n(z) sin(theta) invariant in graded-index media
rules.description: Checks derivations that start from the stratified-medium ray invariant n(z) sin(theta) = const and then replace sin(theta) with tan(theta) or with a path slope (e.g., dy/dx or dz/dx) without a correct geometric relation or without a quantitatively justified small-angle assumption. Flags the following patterns: (1) Transition from n(z) sin(theta) = const to statements like n(z) dy/dx = const, n(z) dz/dx = const, or n(z) tan(theta) = const, unless the angle reference is consistent and the exact trigonometric relations are used (e.g., if theta is measured from the vertical, sin(theta) = cos(phi) with phi from the horizontal, and cos(phi) = 1/sqrt(1 + (dz/dx)^2)). (2) Use of sin(theta) ≈ tan(theta), sin(theta) ≈ theta, or tan(theta) ≈ theta without explicit and quantitative justification (e.g., stating |theta| << 1 rad and verifying that the solution remains in this regime over the relevant z-range, including near turning points). (3) Mixing angle definitions (theta from vertical vs horizontal) to equate sin(theta) directly with a slope dy/dx or dz/dx. To pass, a solution must either: (a) proceed exactly from n(z) sin(theta) = p (constant), leading to n(z)/sqrt(1 + (dz/dx)^2) = p and hence (dz/dx)^2 = (n(z)/p)^2 - 1 (or the equivalent relation for the chosen coordinate conventions), or (b) if invoking small-angle approximations, clearly define the angle reference, state the approximation used, provide a quantitative bound ensuring self-consistency across the trajectory, and derive a differential equation that is the correct small-angle limit of the exact relation. The rule specifically flags derivations yielding n(z) dy/dx = const or n(z) dz/dx = const from the invariant without these justifications.

rules.title: Consistency of Snell-law invariant and angle reference in stratified media
rules.description: Checks that in a horizontally stratified medium (n = n(z)), the conserved quantity is formed with the correct angle reference and used consistently throughout the derivation. Valid invariants are n(z) sin(θ_v) = const when θ_v is measured with respect to the vertical (layer normal), and n(z) cos(φ_h) = const when φ_h is measured with respect to the horizontal. The rule flags: (1) using n(z) sin(θ) = const while defining θ as the angle to the horizontal (should be cos for the horizontal reference), or using n(z) cos(θ) = const while defining θ as the angle to the vertical (should be sin for the vertical reference); (2) inconsistent kinematic relations between the chosen angle and the ray slope, e.g., if θ is defined with respect to the vertical, then dz/dx must equal cot(θ_v) (equivalently dx/dz = tan(θ_v)); if φ is defined with respect to the horizontal, then dz/dx must equal tan(φ_h) (equivalently dx/dz = cot(φ_h)); using dz/dx = tan(θ_v) or dz/dx = cot(φ_h) is incorrect; (3) switching angle definitions mid-derivation without updating the invariant accordingly (e.g., starting with n(z) sin(θ_v) = const and later treating θ as measured from the horizontal). This rule detects misuse of the Snell-law invariant in stratified media and mismatches between angle definitions and ray-slope relations.

rules.title: Incorrectly zeroing the Snell invariant due to horizontal slope or turning point
rules.description: Checks gradient-index optics solutions (n = n(z)) that introduce the continuous Snell invariant (e.g., n(z) sin(theta_v) = C for theta measured from the vertical, or n(z) cos(theta_h) = C for theta measured from the horizontal) and then set the constant C to zero solely because the ray has a horizontal tangent, dz/dx = 0, or a turning point in z(x). The rule flags any reasoning that infers C = 0 from a zero slope or from a 'horizontal segment' without demonstrating that the angle used in the invariant equals 0 degrees. In stratified media, a horizontal ray corresponds to theta_v = 90 degrees (sin(theta_v) = 1) or theta_h = 0 degrees (cos(theta_h) = 1), so the invariant equals n at that height, not zero. The rule also flags misuse of trigonometric relations that equate sin(theta_v) or cos(theta_h) directly to dz/dx; for theta defined relative to vertical, dz/dx = tan(90° - theta_v) = cot(theta_v), and for theta relative to horizontal, dz/dx = tan(theta_h). Any step that concludes C = 0 from dz/dx = 0, 'horizontal ray', or 'turning point' without the correct angle definition and mapping will be marked as a logical error.

rules.title: Verify correct application of Snell's Law equation
rules.description: Snell's Law states that n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2), where n1 and n2 are the refractive indices of the first and second media, and θ1 and θ2 are the angles of incidence and refraction, respectively. This law applies when light passes between two transparent media.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the equation n1 * sin(θ1) = n2 * sin(θ2) is used correctly with proper substitution of values for n1, n2, θ1, and θ2.
common_errors: Using incorrect values for refractive indices (n1 or n2).
Using degrees instead of radians in trigonometric functions.
Misinterpreting θ1 or θ2 as complementary angles.

rules.title: Validate formula for critical angle
rules.description: The critical angle (θc) occurs when light is incident from a denser medium to a less dense medium, and total internal reflection occurs. The formula for the critical angle is θc = arcsin(n2 / n1), where n1 > n2.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the critical angle is calculated using θc = arcsin(n2 / n1) and that n1 > n2 is satisfied.
common_errors: Using n1 < n2 when applying the formula for critical angle.
Forgetting to use arcsin or incorrectly calculating it.
Calculating the critical angle for an incorrect medium pair.

rules.title: Check angle sign convention
rules.description: Angles of incidence and refraction are always measured relative to the normal to the interface. Positive angles should be used for both θ1 and θ2.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that θ1 and θ2 are measured relative to the normal and are positive values.
common_errors: Measuring angles from the surface instead of the normal.
Using negative angles for θ1 or θ2.

rules.title: Verify conditions for total internal reflection (TIR)
rules.description: Total internal reflection occurs only when light travels from a medium with a higher refractive index (n1) to a medium with a lower refractive index (n2), and the angle of incidence (θ1) exceeds the critical angle (θc).
rules.check_logic: Check if n1 > n2 and θ1 > θc before concluding total internal reflection.
common_errors: Applying TIR when n1 < n2.
Using TIR incorrectly when θ1 is less than or equal to θc.
Confusing TIR with refraction.

rules.title: Check physical constraints on refractive indices
rules.description: Refractive indices (n) must always be greater than or equal to 1, as n = c/v, where c is the speed of light in a vacuum and v is the speed of light in the medium.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that n1 and n2 are ≥ 1 for all calculations involving Snell's Law or the critical angle.
common_errors: Using refractive indices less than 1.
Mixing up speed of light in the medium with speed of light in a vacuum.

rules.title: Check validity conditions for applying Snell's Law
rules.description: Snell's Law is valid only for isotropic, homogeneous, and transparent media. It does not apply to scattering, absorption, or birefringent media.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the media involved are isotropic, homogeneous, and transparent before applying Snell's Law.
common_errors: Applying Snell's Law to anisotropic or birefringent materials.
Ignoring scattering or absorption effects in the medium.

rules.title: Validate geometric constraints at the interface
rules.description: The angles of incidence and refraction must satisfy the boundary geometry, such that they lie on opposite sides of the normal at the interface.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that θ1 and θ2 are measured in accordance with the boundary geometry and lie on opposite sides of the normal.
common_errors: Placing θ1 and θ2 on the same side of the normal.
Misidentifying the normal or interface geometry.

rules.title: 连续折射率梯度建模
rules.description:
触发条件：题目给出 n(z) 或 n^2(z) 随高度变化的函数关系时
检查逻辑：应使用 Snell 定律的层状变形公式 n(z)·cos(θ) = Constant（θ为光线与水平面夹角），并结合 dx = dz/tan(θ) 建立轨迹积分。
rules.check_logic: 应使用 Snell 定律的层状变形公式 n(z)·cos(θ) = Constant（θ为光线与水平面夹角），并结合 dx = dz/tan(θ) 建立轨迹积分。
rules.trigger: 题目给出 n(z) 或 n^2(z) 随高度变化的函数关系时

rules.title: 零总能量约束下的势能定义
rules.description:
触发条件：已知系统总能量 $E=0$ 且涉及动能与势能转化时
检查逻辑：验证势能表达式是否严格满足 $E_p = -T = -\frac{1}{2}mv^2$，符号必须为负。
rules.check_logic: 验证势能表达式是否严格满足 $E_p = -T = -\frac{1}{2}mv^2$，符号必须为负。
rules.trigger: 已知系统总能量 $E=0$ 且涉及动能与势能转化时

rules.title: 光学-力学类比速度映射规则
rules.description:
触发条件：题目要求将光线路径类比为质点在势场中的运动轨迹时
检查逻辑：检查是否满足 Maupertuis 原理与 Fermat 原理的等价性，即质点动量/速度应正比于折射率 $n$，而非反比。
rules.check_logic: 检查是否满足 Maupertuis 原理与 Fermat 原理的等价性，即质点动量/速度应正比于折射率 $n$，而非反比。
rules.trigger: 题目要求将光线路径类比为质点在势场中的运动轨迹时

rules.title: 蜃景临界距离判定
rules.description:
触发条件：要求计算观察者到“虚幻湖面”或蜃景起始点的距离 d
检查逻辑：需寻找光线轨迹的极值点（即 dz/dx = 0 的点），该点满足 n(z_min) = n(h)·cos(θ_h)，由此确定积分限。
rules.check_logic: 需寻找光线轨迹的极值点（即 dz/dx = 0 的点），该点满足 n(z_min) = n(h)·cos(θ_h)，由此确定积分限。
rules.trigger: 要求计算观察者到“虚幻湖面”或蜃景起始点的距离 d

rules.title: Misuse of thin-lens/lensmaker formula for a single curved liquid surface on a plate
rules.description:
Checks for solutions that model a liquid meniscus/droplet on a flat substrate (e.g., water on glass) as a thin plano-convex lens in air and apply thin-lens or lensmaker relations. This setup has only one curved refracting interface (air–liquid) followed by plane interfaces (liquid–glass, glass–air). Plane interfaces have zero optical power but do change image location due to index transitions; therefore the thin-lens model is invalid. Trigger conditions (any that apply):
- The system description involves a single curved surface of a liquid on a flat plate (keywords such as droplet, meniscus, water surface on glass, single curved interface) and the solution uses thin-lens equations: 1/s + 1/s' = 1/f, or lensmaker relations like 1/f = (n - 1)/R or 1/f = (n - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2) with R2 = ∞.
- Phrases like "plano-convex lens" or "thin lens" are used to describe a liquid surface on a plate, or f = R/(n - 1) is asserted for the surface.
- The surrounding media on the two sides of the refracting region are different (air–water–glass–air), yet the model assumes a homogeneous external medium as in standard thin-lens theory.
Required correct modeling (for acceptance):
- Use the paraxial imaging relation for a single spherical refracting surface: n1/s + n2/s' = (n2 - n1)/R, with n1, n2 the refractive indices of the incident and transmitted media, distances measured from the vertex in the appropriate media, and correct sign conventions.
- Treat subsequent plane interfaces explicitly as zero-power elements that alter the image location via index changes (e.g., apparent depth scaling across a plane interface), not as additional lens power.
- If an effective focal distance is invoked, it must be the proper single-surface focal distances f1 = -n1 R/(n2 - n1) (object-space) and f2 = n2 R/(n2 - n1) (image-space), not the thin-lens f = R/(n - 1).
Flag and request correction when a solution ignores the single-surface refraction equation, assigns a thin-lens focal length to the droplet/meniscus, or fails to account for index changes at plane interfaces in multi-layer stacks (air–liquid–glass–air).

rules.title: Misuse of thin-lens formula for a single refracting spherical surface
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that analyze imaging by a single spherical refracting interface (e.g., a water-air meniscus or droplet on glass) using thin-lens formulas instead of the correct single-surface refraction relation. The thin-lens imaging formula 1/f = 1/u + 1/v and the lensmaker equation are valid for thin lenses with two refracting surfaces and negligible thickness; they are not valid for a single refracting spherical surface between media of different refractive indices. Detection criteria: (1) The problem context indicates a single curved interface (meniscus/droplet/plano-convex cap) and objects in air (e.g., ceiling lights at ~3 m) with images observed via that interface. (2) The solution explicitly writes or invokes 1/f = 1/u + 1/v to relate object and image distances, or uses the lensmaker equation to infer focal length or radius when only one curved surface is present. (3) The solution determines R, f, or a contact angle from object/image distances without including refractive indices (n1, n2) in the imaging relation. (4) Distances are measured from an external reference (table/graph paper) rather than from the vertex of the refracting surface in the appropriate medium, or sign conventions for u, v, R are omitted/misapplied. Correct requirement: For a single spherical refracting surface between media n1 (object side) and n2 (image side), the paraxial imaging equation must be used: n1/u + n2/v = (n2 - n1)/R, with distances measured from the surface along the optical axis and proper sign conventions for R, u, and v. If a thin-lens formula is used, the solution must justify the presence of two refracting surfaces and negligible thickness; otherwise, flag as a logical/modeling error.

rules.title: Cross product sign check for k × E with E along y
rules.description: This rule verifies the algebraic signs in the cross product k × E used to obtain the magnetic field (H or B) from the electric field in TE polarization during total internal reflection. Trigger condition: the solution computes k × E where E has only a y-component (E = E_y ŷ) and the wave vector k has x and z components (k = k_x x̂ + k_z ẑ). Required component relations: (1) (k × E)_x = −k_z E_y, (2) (k × E)_y = 0, (3) (k × E)_z = +k_x E_y. The verifier should flag an error if the solution gives (k × E)_x with the same sign as k_z E_y (i.e., +k_z E_y) or (k × E)_z with the opposite sign to k_x E_y (i.e., −k_x E_y), or both. For evanescent waves where k_z is imaginary (k_z = ± i κ), ensure the imaginary unit carries the correct sign: (k × E)_x = ∓ i κ E_y depending on the chosen sign of k_z to enforce decay away from the interface; (k × E)_z must remain proportional to the real k_x E_y. Additionally, detect any later unmotivated sign reversals in these components (e.g., flipping signs to match an expected answer) unless explicitly justified by a change in coordinate orientation, swapping the cross product order (E × k instead of k × E), or redefining fields (e.g., using B vs H with consistent proportionality).

rules.title: Verify critical angle calculation
rules.description: The critical angle is determined using Snell's Law when light moves from a medium with a higher refractive index to one with a lower refractive index. The critical angle is given by sin(θ_critical) = n2/n1, where n1 > n2.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that sin(θ_critical) = n2/n1, verify that n1 > n2, and confirm that the angle is calculated in consistent units (radians or degrees).
common_errors: Swapping n1 and n2 in the formula.
Using n1 < n2, which makes total internal reflection impossible.
Forgetting to ensure angles are in radians or degrees consistently.

rules.title: Confirm Snell's Law application before total internal reflection
rules.description: Snell's Law states that n1*sin(θ1) = n2*sin(θ2). Verify that this relationship holds for angles below the critical angle.
rules.check_logic: Check if n1*sin(θ1) = n2*sin(θ2) for θ1 < θ_critical. Ensure that trigonometric functions are applied correctly and that refractive indices are accurate.
common_errors: Incorrectly applying Snell's Law when θ1 > θ_critical.
Using incorrect trigonometric functions (e.g., using cos instead of sin).
Miscalculating the angle or refractive indices.

rules.title: Verify angle of incidence exceeds critical angle
rules.description: Total internal reflection only occurs when the angle of incidence (θ1) is greater than the critical angle (θ_critical).
rules.check_logic: Confirm that θ1 > θ_critical before assuming total internal reflection occurs. Ensure the critical angle is calculated correctly beforehand.
common_errors: Assuming total internal reflection when θ1 < θ_critical.
Not calculating or verifying the critical angle before analyzing the situation.

rules.title: Check refractive index constraints for total internal reflection
rules.description: Total internal reflection is only possible if light passes from a medium with a higher refractive index (n1) into a medium with a lower refractive index (n2).
rules.check_logic: Ensure that n1 > n2. If n1 <= n2, total internal reflection cannot occur. Verify the direction of light propagation.
common_errors: Applying total internal reflection when light moves from a lower refractive index medium to a higher refractive index medium.
Neglecting to specify the direction of light propagation.

rules.title: Verify energy conservation during total internal reflection
rules.description: During total internal reflection, no energy is transmitted into the second medium, and all the light is reflected back into the first medium. This implies total reflectance.
rules.check_logic: Confirm that the transmitted intensity is zero and reflected intensity equals the incident intensity. Ensure no energy is lost during the process.
common_errors: Incorrectly assuming partial transmission occurs during total internal reflection.
Failing to equate reflected intensity to incident intensity.

rules.title: Check for phase shift during total internal reflection
rules.description: During total internal reflection, a phase shift occurs at the boundary, depending on polarization and angle of incidence. This phase shift does not affect energy conservation.
rules.check_logic: Verify that a phase shift is considered when analyzing reflected waves during total internal reflection. Ensure the phase shift is not confused with energy loss.
common_errors: Ignoring the phase shift introduced during reflection.
Confusing phase shift with energy loss, which does not occur.

rules.title: Confirm dimensional consistency in equations
rules.description: Ensure that all terms in equations related to total internal reflection have consistent dimensions or units. For example, angles should be in radians or degrees consistently, and refractive indices are dimensionless.
rules.check_logic: Verify that sin(θ), n1, and n2 are dimensionless and angle units are consistent. Ensure no unit mismatches in calculations.
common_errors: Mixing radians and degrees when calculating angles.
Using refractive indices with incorrect or inconsistent dimensions.

rules.title: Verify geometric path consistency
rules.description: The geometry of the incident and reflected rays must satisfy boundary conditions. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection during total internal reflection.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that θ_incidence = θ_reflection and that the reflected ray lies entirely within the first medium. Confirm that the geometry aligns with total internal reflection principles.
common_errors: Setting θ_incidence ≠ θ_reflection.
Placing the reflected ray in the second medium, which contradicts total internal reflection.

rules.title: Verify polarization effects during total internal reflection
rules.description: During total internal reflection, the polarization of light can affect the phase shift and intensity distribution. This is particularly important for polarized light.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that polarization effects are considered, especially for s-polarized and p-polarized light. Verify that the phase shift is calculated correctly for each polarization type.
common_errors: Ignoring the impact of polarization on phase shift.
Failing to distinguish between s-polarized and p-polarized light.

rules.title: 复数波矢实部提取规则
rules.description:
触发条件：处理全反射衰减波（Evanescent wave）或有耗介质传播时
检查逻辑：检查磁场分量是否通过 $\nabla \times \vec{E} = -\partial \vec{B}/\partial t$ 导出，并确认复数 $i$ 是否正确转化为相位差（如 $\cos$ 变 $\sin$）。
rules.check_logic: 检查磁场分量是否通过 $\nabla \times \vec{E} = -\partial \vec{B}/\partial t$ 导出，并确认复数 $i$ 是否正确转化为相位差（如 $\cos$ 变 $\sin$）。
rules.trigger: 处理全反射衰减波（Evanescent wave）或有耗介质传播时

rules.title: 电磁场横波分量相位一致性
rules.description:
触发条件：题目要求证明电场为 $\cos$ 形式而磁场包含 $\sin$ 分量时
检查逻辑：验证波矢 $\vec{k}$ 是否为复数。若 $k_z$ 为纯虚数，则磁场在该方向的分量必与电场存在 $\pi/2$ 相位差。
rules.check_logic: 验证波矢 $\vec{k}$ 是否为复数。若 $k_z$ 为纯虚数，则磁场在该方向的分量必与电场存在 $\pi/2$ 相位差。
rules.trigger: 题目要求证明电场为 $\cos$ 形式而磁场包含 $\sin$ 分量时

rules.title: Linear tan(ξ)–tan(θ) relation for extraordinary ray in uniaxial crystals
rules.description: This rule verifies derivations that relate the angle ξ (between the extraordinary ray propagation direction N_e and the optical axis) to the angle θ in a uniaxial crystal. The correct dependence is linear: tan(ξ) = (n_o^2 / n_e^2) tan(θ), under the standard convention for ξ and θ. The rule flags solutions that: (1) invoke isotropic Snell’s law for the extraordinary ray inside the crystal (e.g., equations of the form n_e sin(…) = n_o sin(…) or explicit references to Snell’s law as the primary step), because the e-ray requires the index ellipsoid/direction-dependent refractive index, not interface refraction; (2) produce a non-linear dependence of tan(ξ) on tan(θ), such as expressions containing square roots, additive terms, higher powers (e.g., tan^2(θ)), or trig mixtures beyond a constant multiple; (3) use an incorrect proportionality factor (e.g., n_o/n_e, n_e^2/n_o^2, or any factor not equal to n_o^2/n_e^2 in this context); (4) omit or replace the index-ellipsoid relation 1/n^2(ψ) = cos^2(ψ)/n_e^2 + sin^2(ψ)/n_o^2 (or an equivalent anisotropic refractive-index relation) with interface-based laws. The checker passes solutions that show tan(ξ) = C·tan(θ) with C symbolically reducible to n_o^2/n_e^2 and no extraneous functional dependence; otherwise it flags the derivation as logically flawed.

rules.title: Incorrect variational principle in optics–mechanics analogy
rules.description: Detects misuse of variational principles when mapping graded-index ray optics to an equivalent mechanical problem. The correct correspondence uses Maupertuis/Jacobi's principle at fixed energy (δ∫ p·dr) rather than the time-based Hamilton action (δ∫(T−V)dt). Checks trigger if a solution: (1) invokes Fermat's principle (least time, optical path length) and then derives mechanical equations from a time-based action ∫ L dt without explicitly enforcing fixed energy; (2) equates refractive index to speed via n = c/v and transfers this relation to the mass point speed, implying v_mass ∝ 1/n instead of identifying momentum magnitude |p(r)| ∝ n(r) (hence v_mass ∝ n(r) for fixed E); (3) fails the energy-consistency check p(r) = sqrt(2 m (E − V(r))) and V(r) = E − p(r)^2/(2 m); (4) for the specific case E = 0, does not yield V(r) = −T(r) = −(1/2) m v_mass(r)^2 or assigns the wrong sign (e.g., V = +(1/2) m v^2) or concludes v_mass = 0; (5) uses phrases like “Hamilton’s principle”, “Lagrangian”, or writes an action ∫(T−V)dt in the optics–mechanics mapping, or relies on n = c/v to deduce the mass point’s speed. Flag any of these patterns as a conceptual error in the variational mapping.

rules.title: Verify wavefront continuity equation
rules.description: Huygens' Principle states that every point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary spherical wavelets, and the new wavefront is the tangential surface to these secondary wavelets. Verify that the wavefront equation matches this principle.
rules.check_logic: Check if the secondary wavelets are drawn as spherical or plane waves (based on medium properties) and whether the tangent to these wavelets forms the next wavefront. Ensure that the wavelets are spaced consistently with the speed of propagation in the medium.
common_errors: Not drawing the secondary wavelets at all.
Incorrect tangent drawn to wavelets misrepresenting the wavefront.
Wavelets not spaced consistently with the speed of propagation in the medium.

rules.title: Check wavefront propagation speed consistency
rules.description: The speed at which wavefronts propagate depends on the properties of the medium (e.g., refractive index). Verify that the wavefront speed is consistent with the equation v = c/n, where n is the refractive index of the medium.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the wavefront spacing corresponds to v = c/n, where c is the speed of light in vacuum and n is the refractive index. Confirm that the refractive index used matches the medium described in the problem.
common_errors: Incorrect wavefront spacing relative to medium speed.
Using the wrong refractive index for the specified medium.
Forgetting that c is only valid in vacuum and not adjusting for n.

rules.title: Verify applicability of Huygens' Principle
rules.description: Huygens' Principle is valid for isotropic and homogeneous media. It cannot be directly applied to anisotropic or inhomogeneous media without modifications. Ensure that the problem context satisfies these conditions.
rules.check_logic: Check if the medium is isotropic (properties same in all directions) and homogeneous (properties constant throughout the medium). If the medium is anisotropic or inhomogeneous, verify that appropriate modifications to Huygens' Principle are applied.
common_errors: Applying Huygens' Principle to anisotropic media without justification.
Ignoring inhomogeneities in the medium that affect wavefront propagation.
Assuming medium properties are constant when they are explicitly variable.

rules.title: Verify wavefront geometry based on source type
rules.description: Wavefronts from a point source are spherical, while wavefronts from a distant source are planar. Ensure that the wavefront geometry matches the source description.
