rules.check_logic: Check if the wavefronts are spherical for point sources and planar for distant sources, or conform to any specific source geometry mentioned in the problem. Verify that the curvature of spherical wavefronts is consistent with the distance from the source.
common_errors: Drawing planar wavefronts for a nearby point source.
Incorrect curvature of spherical wavefronts.
Ignoring the wavefront geometry in calculations.

rules.title: Verify wavefront bending at boundaries
rules.description: When a wavefront passes from one medium to another, it bends according to Snell's Law. Verify that the bending of the wavefront at the boundary satisfies the relationship n1*sin(θ1) = n2*sin(θ2).
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the angles of incidence and refraction follow Snell's Law and that the wavefront orientation changes accordingly. Verify that the refractive indices used correspond to the respective media.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of refraction angles.
Ignoring the refractive index difference between media.
Wavefronts drawn at incorrect angles post-refraction.

rules.title: Check for wavefront diffraction at obstacles
rules.description: Wavefronts bend around obstacles, creating diffraction effects. Ensure that the wavefronts are drawn bending into the region of the geometric shadow when diffraction is significant.
rules.check_logic: Verify that wavefronts are not drawn as straight lines extending through an obstacle and correctly represent bending at edges. Confirm that the extent of diffraction matches the size of the obstacle and the wavelength of the wave.
common_errors: Ignoring diffraction effects entirely.
Drawing wavefronts as straight lines through the obstacle.
Incorrect representation of wave bending at sharp edges.

rules.title: Verify wavefront superposition in overlapping regions
rules.description: When wavefronts from multiple sources overlap, the resulting wavefront is determined by the principle of superposition. Ensure that the combined wavefront is correctly represented.
rules.check_logic: Check if the resultant wavefront is drawn as the constructive or destructive interference of overlapping wavefronts, depending on their phase relationship.
common_errors: Ignoring the effects of superposition in overlapping regions.
Incorrectly representing constructive or destructive interference.
Failing to account for phase differences between overlapping wavefronts.

rules.title: Unjustified n–potential relation and speed conflation leading to constant E_p
rules.description: This rule checks for incorrect optical–mechanical mappings in refractive-index gradient problems. It triggers when a solution: (1) introduces or uses an ad hoc relation of the form n(r) = sqrt[-2 E_p(r) / (m v(r)^2)] (or algebraic equivalents) without a derivation from the eikonal/Hamilton–Jacobi/Fermat framework; (2) simultaneously uses n(r) = c / v(r) and the same symbol v for both the light speed and the mass-point speed, or equates these expressions to eliminate v and obtain E_p(r) = −m c^2/2; (3) concludes that E_p(r) is a position-independent constant while n(r) was previously stated or implied to be position-dependent. The rule flags: (a) ambiguous reuse of the velocity symbol v across optical and mechanical contexts; (b) derivations that force E_p to be constant from n(r) = c/v(r), contradicting a nonuniform refractive index; and (c) unreferenced or unitless proportionality between n, E_p, m, and v that is not justified by a standard optical–mechanical analogy. If any of these conditions are met, the step is marked as a logical/consistency error.

rules.title: Detect truncated or incomplete final expressions with unresolved symbols
rules.description: This rule verifies that the final answer provided for the asked quantity is a complete, syntactically valid expression and depends only on allowed (given or explicitly defined) quantities. It flags solutions where: (1) The final expression is truncated or syntactically incomplete (e.g., ends with ellipses "...", placeholder tokens like "(truncated)", "TBD", "???", abrupt termination such as a lone operator or fraction like "1/4", unmatched parentheses/brackets/braces, or incomplete LaTeX). (2) The final expression for the target variable contains unresolved or undefined symbols (e.g., θ̇, E, Ft) that are not present in the problem’s given set or not introduced/defined earlier in the solution, and no supplementary equations are provided to determine them. (3) The solution outlines a method but never produces an explicit, computable expression for the requested quantity. Implementation notes: Identify the equation(s) presenting the final value of the requested variable; check for syntactic completeness of math tokens; collect symbols in the final expression and compare against the set of known givens/constants and previously defined symbols; flag if any extraneous or undefined symbols remain. This rule catches cases like a final line ending with an incomplete term (e.g., "... = 1/4") or expressions that retain free parameters such as θ̇ and E without definition, rendering the answer unusable.

rules.title: Flag final answers inconsistent with computed result without explicit recalculation
rules.description: Checks that the final stated numerical answer for the primary target quantity matches (within a tolerance) the latest computed value obtained in the solution. The verifier extracts intermediate computed values for the target quantity (same units or unit-converted equivalents) and compares the final declared answer to the most recent computed value. If the final answer deviates by more than 10% and there is no explicit recalculation or justification (e.g., updated parameters, introduced correction factor/efficiency, unit conversion with shown math, or documented error correction), flag a logic error. Also flags narrative-only overrides (e.g., claims of a discrepancy or intuition-based adjustment) that replace a correct computed result with a different number without supporting calculations. Example: computing a filling time of ~5 hours and then asserting 26 hours with no new computation triggers this rule.

rules.title: Self-consistency with stated approximate targets or figure-based ratios
rules.description: This rule checks for internal consistency between early stated approximate values/ratios (from figures, assumptions, or intermediate estimates) and the final numerical result for the same quantity. The verifier scans the solution for declarations such as 'assume', 'from the figure', 'approximately', '≈', '~', or bounds/targets (e.g., Q ≈ α·B), extracts the target value and any stated uncertainty, and later extracts the final reported value of Q. If the final value deviates from the earlier target beyond tolerance and no explicit justification for the change is provided, the solution is flagged. Tolerance policy: (1) If an uncertainty is explicitly stated (e.g., α ± Δα), require the final value to lie within that interval. (2) If labeled as 'approximate' or 'from figure' without uncertainty, use a default absolute tolerance of 1% of the relevant scale (for dimensionless ratios) or 1% of the referenced base quantity (for dimensional quantities). (3) If labeled as an 'assumption' used in subsequent derivations, require either adherence within tolerance or a later rationale that updates/relaxes the assumption. The rule triggers when: (a) a target ratio/value is recorded earlier, (b) a final value for the same quantity is presented (directly or normalized by the same base), (c) |Q_final − Q_target| exceeds the tolerance, and (d) no textual justification (e.g., refinement, corrected model, recalculated parameters) is found near the deviation. This detects calculation or reasoning errors where the final answer contradicts earlier figure-based or assumed ratios without explanation.

rules.title: Capillary interaction modeled as γΔA instead of force–height coupling
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that model the horizontal capillary interaction between floating objects primarily via the change in bare interface area (U = γ ΔA) under small-slope, linear-capillarity assumptions. In the regime specified by a linear meniscus profile (e.g., z(x) = -Lc tan(θ) exp(-(x-xc)/Lc)) and superposition, the leading-order two-body interaction energy must arise from coupling of the external vertical load (weight minus buoyancy and/or contact-line vertical force) to the companion meniscus height (U_int ≈ Σ_i F_i h_j(x_i)), not from ΔA alone. Detection criteria: (1) The interaction energy or force is derived solely from ΔA (or from integrating only the surface-area term) and then F = -∂U/∂L, with no source/load term (no dependence on weight–buoyancy, contact-line vertical force, or h evaluated at the other object). (2) The predicted separation dependence is inconsistent with the linear meniscus interaction (e.g., F(L) or U(L) scaling as e^{-2L/Lc} or purely polynomial rather than ∝ e^{-L/Lc} with appropriate load factors). (3) The derivation omits pressure/buoyancy/contact-line work terms and treats minimization of surface area as the sole mechanism for attraction/repulsion. This rule does not trigger if the solution first includes the leading force–height coupling and clearly identifies γΔA contributions as higher-order (small-slope, second-order) corrections.

rules.title: Capillary interaction energy must include effective vertical load and meniscus height
rules.description: This rule flags solutions to floating-body capillarity problems that incorrectly set the interaction energy (or change in gravitational potential energy) to zero on the basis that buoyancy balances weight at static equilibrium. Specifically, the rule checks that: (1) The solution explicitly accounts for the effective vertical load P carried by the interface (e.g., P = W − B_∞, the net load supported by capillarity far from the meniscus), and does not set P = 0 merely because the body is in vertical equilibrium; (2) The interaction energy between bodies is expressed in terms of the local interface elevation at the contact region, U(L) ∝ P · z(L − x_c), using the provided meniscus shape z(x) (such as z(x) = −L_c tanθ · exp[−(x − x_c)/L_c]); (3) The horizontal force is derived as F(L) = −dU/dL = −P · dz/dL, inheriting the functional dependence of z(x) (e.g., exponential decay with separation L over the effective capillary length L_c); (4) The solution does not rely solely on buoyancy/volume-displacement arguments (e.g., V_displaced or “buoyancy equals weight”) to conclude that the potential energy or the interaction force is zero or independent of separation; (5) For problems providing z(x) or L_c, the final force/energy must show dependence on z(x) and L_c; omission of these quantities, or claims like “no change in potential energy because buoyancy balances weight,” are flagged as conceptual errors.

rules.title: Cascade amplification: anode count must include per-stage leakage
rules.description: In cascaded amplification models (e.g., photomultiplier tubes) with per-stage gain δ (>1), interstage collection efficiency σ (0≤σ≤1), and initial collection η (0≤η≤1), verify that the total number of electrons collected at the terminal (anode) is computed as the sum of contributions that actually reach the anode from each stage, not as the sum of populations at intermediate stages. The expected stage model is: N₁ = η and N_{i+1} = σδ N_i for i = 1..n−1. The anode contributions must be counted as A₀ = (1−η), A_i = (1−σ)δ N_i for i = 1..n−1, and A_n = δ N_n, so that N_anode = A₀ + Σ_{i=1}^{n−1} A_i + A_n = (1−η) + Σ_{i=1}^{n−1} (1−σ)δ(σδ)^{i−1}η + δ(σδ)^{n−1}η. Flag solutions that: (a) equate the total amplified/anode electron count to η Σ_{k=0}^{n} (σδ)^k, to N_n, or to Σ_i N_i; (b) omit explicit (1−η) and (1−σ) leakage terms in the anode tally; or (c) conflate stage populations with terminal collection (e.g., modeling total anode electrons as a geometric series of (σδ)^k without per-stage leakage contributions). This rule catches modeling errors where branching losses to the anode at each stage are ignored or where intermediate-stage counts are incorrectly used as the terminal count.

rules.title: Misuse of finite-difference hydrostatic equilibrium for Pc/Tc (missing 1/2 factor)
rules.description:
Purpose: Detects the common modeling error where the hydrostatic equilibrium equation is turned into a single finite-difference balance across the whole star using central values (ΔP ≈ −Pc, Δr ≈ R, Mr ≈ M, ρr ≈ ρc), leading to Pc = (G M ρc)/R and, via the ideal gas law, Tc = (μ mH/kB) (G M / R). This ignores the r-dependence of Mr and g(r) and overestimates Pc (and Tc) by about a factor of 2 for a simple constant-density model.

Trigger context:
- The solution estimates the central pressure Pc and/or central temperature Tc of a star using hydrostatic equilibrium dP/dr = −G Mr ρ / r^2, optionally combined with the ideal gas law P = (ρ kB T)/(μ mH).

Checks (any one flags):
1) Coefficient check on Pc:
   - Compute the dimensionless coefficient C_P = (Pc R) / (G M ρc) from the student’s final expression.
   - If C_P is reported ≈ 1 (e.g., within [0.8, 1.2]) and no radial integration or profile-dependent coefficient is provided, flag as error. For a constant-density star, the correct integrated result is C_P = 1/2; using C_P ≈ 1 indicates the ΔP ≈ −Pc, Δr ≈ R, Mr ≈ M shortcut.
2) Coefficient check on Tc via ideal gas law:
   - If the student uses Pc = (ρc kB Tc)/(μ mH), form C_T = [(kB Tc)/(μ mH)] / (G M / R).
   - If C_T is reported ≈ 1 (e.g., within [0.8, 1.2]) and no justification from an explicit integration or stated density profile is given, flag as error. For a constant-density star, the consistent simple model gives C_T = 1/2.
3) Pattern-of-assumptions check (text/step detection):
   - Flags if the solution explicitly makes the joint approximations ΔP ≈ −Pc, Δr ≈ R, Mr ≈ M (or treats Mr as constant equal to M across r), and ρr ≈ ρc, then concludes Pc = (G M ρc)/R.

Rationale:
- Treating dP/dr as a finite difference with central values across the whole radius ignores that Mr ∝ r^3 (for uniform ρ) and g(r) ∝ r inside the star; integrating dP/dr for a constant-density star yields Pc = (1/2) (G M ρ)/R. The ΔP–Δr shortcut therefore overestimates Pc (and Tc) by about a factor of 2.

Notes:
- Do not flag if the student derives or cites a different coefficient arising from an explicit integration with a specified density profile (e.g., a polytrope) and the coefficient is consistent with that model.
- Tolerances ([0.8, 1.2] around unity; [0.45, 0.55] around 1/2) may be adjusted to accommodate rounding and order-of-magnitude estimates.

rules.title: Eliminate μ in central temperature for fully ionized hydrogen (μ=1/2)
rules.description: Scope: Solutions deriving a star’s central temperature T_c from hydrostatic equilibrium combined with the ideal gas law. Trigger: The problem context indicates a fully ionized hydrogen plasma or explicitly requests the final expression 'in terms of mass, radius, and physical constants only' (i.e., no composition-dependent parameters). Checks: (1) Symbol audit: Inspect the final expression for T_c (or Tc). If the mean molecular weight μ appears symbolically, flag an error: μ must be substituted with its hydrogen value μ = 1/2. (2) Coefficient audit: After enforcing μ = 1/2 and mapping m_H → m_p, the expression should reduce to T_c ≈ (G M m_p) / (2 k_B R). If the factor 1/2 is absent in the denominator, flag an error. (3) Allowed-symbol audit: Ensure the final expression contains only {G, M, R, k_B, m_p} (or m_H treated as m_p) and numeric factors; composition parameters (e.g., μ, X, Y, Z, Z̄) are disallowed. Notes: Accept m_H in place of m_p as equivalent; allow algebraic rearrangements (e.g., T_c R = G M m_p / (2 k_B)) and numeric forms of 1/2 (e.g., 0.5). This rule focuses on elimination of μ and the hydrogen-specific factor 1/2; it does not judge other order-unity structural factors.

rules.title: Misuse of measurement resolution (Δ) in constitutive laws (e.g., Ohm’s law)
rules.description: This rule flags steps where a constitutive relation (e.g., Ohm’s law V = I·R, j = σE, F = m·a, Hooke’s law F = kx, P = I^2R) is applied with an instrument resolution/uncertainty (ΔI, ΔV, Δx, σ_I, etc.) substituted for the physical variable (I, V, x, etc.) to compute an absolute physical quantity. Examples to flag: V_max = R·ΔI, R = V/ΔI, I = ΔV/R, or using ΔI directly in decay dynamics (I(t) = I0·exp(−tR/L)) as the current. Instrument precision bounds detectability (a change or uncertainty), not the instantaneous value entering the constitutive law. Unless the relation is explicitly written as an uncertainty propagation (e.g., ΔV = R·ΔI with both sides denoting changes/uncertainties) or as an inequality bounding detectability, substituting Δ-quantities to compute absolute values or limits is a logical error. The rule specifically checks: (1) any occurrence of Δ-prefixed variables or terms described as measurement 'precision', 'resolution', or 'uncertainty' used as the sole operand in constitutive laws to compute non-Δ quantities; (2) equations where the left-hand side lacks a Δ/uncertainty label but the right-hand side uses Δ-variables; (3) use of Δ-variables in time-evolution formulas (e.g., exponential decay) as if they were the state variable. When triggered, the verifier should require the solution to instead relate detectable fractional changes (e.g., ΔI/I) or perform proper uncertainty propagation, and, for resistive decay problems, use the appropriate dynamics (e.g., τ = L/R) rather than replacing I by ΔI.

rules.title: Electron number density must account for composition via μ_e
rules.description:
Flag solutions that compute electron number density or total electron count by dividing mass density or mass by the proton mass alone (e.g., n_e ≈ ρ/m_p or N_e ≈ M/m_p) without explicitly stating the composition/ionization assumptions or using the mean molecular weight per electron μ_e. The rule checks for the following:
- n_e derived from ρ or M using only m_p, or equating n_e to proton number density, with no mention of μ_e.
- Statements like "each hydrogen atom has one electron" used to justify n_e ≈ ρ/m_p without explicitly stating a pure, fully ionized hydrogen composition (μ_e = 1).
- Absence of composition/ionization factors when relating electron counts to mass (e.g., no μ_e, no ionization fraction, no mixture description).
The correct general relation is n_e = ρ / (μ_e m_p), where μ_e depends on composition and ionization (e.g., μ_e ≈ 1 for fully ionized H, ≈ 2 for fully ionized He, ≈ 1.14 for solar-like fully ionized mix). A solution is acceptable only if it either uses μ_e explicitly or clearly and explicitly states the assumption of pure, fully ionized hydrogen leading to μ_e = 1.

rules.title: Improper linear adjustment of elongation by Earth's axial tilt
rules.description: Flag solutions that algebraically add or subtract Earth's axial tilt (≈23.4–23.5°) or observer latitude to a Sun–object angular separation (e.g., greatest elongation, phase angle, or ecliptic-plane separation) to form an 'effective' angle without a proper coordinate transformation. The rule specifically checks for steps like theta_eff = theta ± 23.5°, 'adjusting elongation by tilt', or similar linear offsets applied to elongation. Correct physics: (1) Greatest elongation for an inferior planet in circular coplanar orbits is a purely orbital-geometry quantity independent of Earth's obliquity and depends only on orbital radii via the tangent condition (e.g., sin E = r_inner / r_Earth). (2) Earth's obliquity affects declination/altitude via an ecliptic-to-equatorial transformation and then horizon geometry; it does not change the Sun–planet angular separation. The rule requires that any use of obliquity appear only within a proper spherical/coordinate transformation (e.g., computing declination, hour angle, altitude) and not as a direct linear correction to elongation or inter-object angular separations. If a solution introduces an 'effective' elongation by ±23.5° (or latitude) without explicit spherical trigonometry or coordinate conversion, mark as a logic error.

rules.title: Energy unit consistency and SI presentation check (J vs eV)
rules.description: Verify that any computed energy quantity is reported in the unit requested by the problem or, if unspecified, in SI (Joules). Detection steps: (1) Parse the problem statement for an explicit unit requirement; default to Joules when none is provided. (2) Track the unit of constants used (e.g., ħ in J·s vs eV·s) and the time unit; using ħ = 6.582×10^−16 eV·s with time in seconds yields energy in eV, while ħ = 1.054×10^−34 J·s yields energy in Joules. (3) If the final answer’s unit (e.g., eV) does not match the expected unit (e.g., J), or if the unit is omitted, flag a unit presentation error and require conversion using 1 eV = 1.602176634×10^−19 J. (4) Also flag inconsistent unit labeling that contradicts intermediate dimensional analysis. Example caught: for τ = 2.4 min (converted to 144 s) using ħ = 6.582×10^−16 eV·s, the computed ΔE is in eV; if the expected unit is Joules, require conversion (e.g., ΔE ≥ 3.66×10^−37 J for the inequality form).

rules.title: Unjustified figure-dependent parameter values
rules.description: Checks for introduction of ad hoc numeric values or ratios for geometry/structure parameters that are required to be determined from provided data or a referenced figure. Trigger this rule when the problem statement instructs the solver to use a figure (e.g., to determine interior radius, flattening, crust thickness) and the solution assigns specific numbers (e.g., R_int/R_avg ≈ 0.95, 0.97; ε ≈ 0.02; r_e/r_p ≈ 1.03) without an explicit derivation or documented extraction from the figure. Indicators include: (1) use of phrases such as "assume", "take", "guess", "approximate as", or "we choose" followed by a numeric value for a required figure-dependent parameter; (2) lack of citation of the figure axes/coordinates, interpolation, or a formula linking the parameter to given quantities; (3) changing a guessed parameter mid-solution (e.g., using 0.95 then 0.97) without justification; (4) employing numeric geometry values not stated in the problem data and not derived from physical relations provided. To pass, the solution must show how the parameter is obtained: either (a) by reading off the figure with specified axis values and interpolation, or (b) by deriving from given equations and inputs. Any unreferenced or speculative numeric parameter in place of required figure-based data should be flagged.

rules.title: Missing or inconsistent final quantitative estimate
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that fail to provide a clear, single quantitative conclusion for a scalar quantity requested by the problem (e.g., a source temperature) or that present multiple inconsistent numerical candidates without justification. Trigger this rule when all of the following hold: (1) The problem statement contains verbs like 'estimate', 'compute', 'determine', or 'find' and references a single target scalar (e.g., 'temperature T') implying a unique numeric answer or a justified single interval. (2) The solution text does not contain an explicit final assignment or concluding statement for the target variable with units (e.g., 'Therefore, T = 175 K') or a clearly justified single interval with uncertainty notation. (3) The solution text contains two or more distinct numerical candidates for the same target (e.g., multiple temperatures in K) that differ by more than 30% (or by a factor > 1.3) and are not presented as a single uncertainty interval (e.g., 'T = 170 ± 20 K' or 'T in [150,190] K') and are not justified as separate cases with specified conditions. Additional triggers: (a) The solution ends mid-derivation (e.g., trailing ellipsis or unfinished sentence/section headers) without a final numeric conclusion. (b) The solution provides disjoint ranges or disparate values (e.g., '100–200 K, 313 K, ~1000 K') for the same quantity separated by commas or 'or' without selecting or justifying a final estimate. The rule is intended to catch logic/communication errors where the solver neither commits to a final numeric result nor coherently justifies a single range with uncertainties, despite a single estimate being requested.

rules.title: Missing explicit final expression for requested quantity
rules.description: When the problem statement explicitly asks to 'find', 'compute', or 'determine' a target quantity Q (e.g., the height h), the solution must include a final, explicit expression isolating Q on the left-hand side (Q = ...) with either a numeric value or a symbolic formula in terms of the given parameters/constants. Trigger an error if any of the following are true: (1) The solution ends with only a general or intermediate relation (e.g., a conservation law such as KE_initial = KE_final + PE_final) without solving for Q; (2) The derivation terminates mid-equation (e.g., trailing operators, incomplete lines, or ellipses like '...' or notes such as 'truncated'); (3) Q appears only inside equations but is never isolated as Q = ...; (4) The purported final line contains unresolved placeholders (e.g., KE_initial, PE_final) or undefined symbols instead of substituted expressions leading to Q; (5) The final expression references undefined placeholders or meta text (e.g., '...', 'etc.', 'to be continued') or does not restrict itself to problem-given variables/constants. If these conditions are not satisfied, flag: 'Final expression for the requested quantity is missing or incomplete.'

rules.title: Missing computed change factor in final answer
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that fail to provide the requested final quantitative factor or ratio when a problem explicitly asks 'by how many times' a measured quantity changes under a specified condition (e.g., a parameter set to zero). Checks include: (1) The problem statement contains triggers such as 'by how many times', 'factor', 'ratio', 'times', or 'increase/decrease by N times'. (2) The solution must explicitly evaluate the requested case (e.g., substitute the specified parameter change like R -> 0) and present a computed factor or ratio of final to initial readings (e.g., V_final/V_initial, k = ..., 'N times'). (3) The final answer must be stated, not just a general expression or intermediate setup (e.g., giving I = E/(R + r) without computing the ratio). The rule flags solutions that stop before answering the final question, give only qualitative statements (e.g., 'the reading increases') without a numerical factor, or discuss an unrelated quantity instead of the requested ratio.

rules.title: Missing or incomplete final expression in requested variables
rules.description: This rule verifies that a physics solution concludes with a complete, explicit final expression for the requested quantity in terms of the specified parameters. It flags solutions that end mid-derivation, contain ellipses ("..."), references to truncation, or unfinished expressions. It also checks that the final result explicitly depends on all required variables (e.g., M, v, R, G, and ρ when requested) and does not retain undefined placeholders (such as lnΛ, b_min, b_max) without expressing them in terms of the given problem parameters. The rule triggers when: (1) no final formula or statement is provided for the target quantity; (2) the last presented formula omits one or more required variables or includes undefined symbols; (3) the concluding expression uses placeholders like "...", "etc.", or textual cues of incompleteness; or (4) the solution terminates with a partial definition of auxiliary quantities (e.g., a truncated expression for lnΛ) instead of a coherent final result in the requested variables.

rules.title: Water-cone radius must be derived from melt/pressure balance, not set to surface depression radius
rules.description: Flag solutions that equate the lateral extent (radius) of the subglacial water body/cone to the radius of the surface depression without a derivation from physical constraints. The verifier should detect assignments or implicit substitutions such as R_w = R_surface, r_w = R, or r_w = 500 m, and the use of a surface-depression radius in water-cone volume formulas (e.g., V_cone = (1/3)π r^2 h with r taken from a surface feature). To avoid flagging, the solution must explicitly determine the water-region boundary using hydrostatic pressure balance (e.g., ρ_w g h vs. ice overburden/rock pressure), melt/energy balance (latent heat plus conduction to define melt-rate distribution), and mass/volume continuity. If the geometry of the water accumulation is taken directly from surface geometry parameters without these governing equations, mark as a modeling error: the water region dimensions are set by melting geometry and hydrostatic balance, not by the surface depression radius.

rules.title: Unjustified non-ideal factors under stated ideal assumptions
rules.description: Flag solutions that introduce efficiency, loss, correction, or other non-ideal factors not provided or derivable from the problem when the statement specifies idealized behavior or supplies complete data. The rule checks for: (1) Explicit ideal assumptions in the prompt (e.g., ideal gas law, incompressible/inviscid fluid, neglect losses/friction/leakage, steady state), or complete sets of state variables/constants (e.g., saturated vapor pressures, temperatures, density, atmospheric pressure, geometric parameters). (2) Presence in the solution of extraneous parameters such as efficiency (η), loss factors, real-world imperfections, heat loss, friction/drag/head loss, leakage, calibration constants, or generic multiplicative coefficients introduced without derivation from given quantities. (3) Adjustments to computed results using such factors (e.g., multiplying or dividing by an assumed percentage) without data from the problem or a justified derivation. The verifier should flag these inclusions unless the problem explicitly requests accounting for non-idealities or provides their values, or the student derives them from provided information. Example trigger: a dehumidification/condensation calculation using saturated vapor pressures and ideal gas law where the student adds an assumed device efficiency to modify the condensation rate or time, despite no efficiency data being given.

rules.title: Incorrect inequality assertion between computed quantities
rules.description: This rule checks for logical consistency in stated inequalities (e.g., greater/less than) between computed numeric quantities in a solution. It parses claims such as "A is less than B", "A < B", "greater than", "smaller/larger", and similar phrases, retrieves or evaluates the corresponding numeric values (including units where applicable), and verifies that the claimed inequality matches the actual numerical comparison. If units are present, it converts both quantities to compatible units before comparing. If the claim contradicts the evaluated relation (for example, stating 266000 < 7000 when 266000 > 7000), the rule flags an error. The rule also guards against sign/magnitude confusion: if the text explicitly refers to magnitude/absolute value, it compares |A| and |B|; otherwise, it compares signed values. A tolerance may be applied for near-equality claims; otherwise, clear contradictions are reported.

rules.title: Density substitution and dimensional consistency in interparticle spacing
rules.description: This rule verifies correct use of the stellar density relation ρ = 3M/(4π R^3) when deriving interparticle spacing (e.g., electron separation d_e) from number density in a uniform-density star. Expected scaling: d_e ∝ n_e^{-1/3} and, with n_e ∝ ρ/(μ_e m_p), the spacing should reduce to d_e = (μ_e m_p/ρ)^{1/3}, independent of R and M once ρ is introduced. The verifier should: (1) Detect substitutions of ρ into expressions like d_e = (4π m_p R^3/(3M))^{1/3} and confirm that 4π/3 and R^3/M combine to yield m_p/ρ under the cube root, leaving no residual factors of R, M, or 4π/3; (2) Perform dimensional analysis to ensure the final d_e has units of length—expressions of the form d_e ∼ [(const·m_p)/ρ]^{1/3} are acceptable, while any extra multiplicative R (or powers of R) gives length^2 or higher and must be flagged; (3) Flag any result for d_e that depends linearly or nonlinearly on R after ρ has been used (spurious radius dependence), or that retains 4π/3 under the cube root after substitution; (4) Cross-check that using ρ eliminates separate M and R dependence: if both ρ and either M or R remain in the final expression for d_e, report an algebraic substitution inconsistency. This rule targets errors where density substitution is mishandled, causing incorrect scaling and dimensional inconsistency in spacing estimates.

rules.title: DC component must be time-independent and requires frequency matching
rules.description: This rule checks analyses of products of sinusoidal signals (e.g., in lock-in amplifier or mixer problems) where a 'DC component' or 'constant/low-pass output' is identified. The verifier ensures: (1) Any term labeled as DC is truly time-independent (no explicit t in its argument). Terms of the form C cos((ω_i − ω) t + φ) or C sin((ω_i − ω) t + φ) are time-dependent and cannot be called DC unless the condition ω_i = ω (Δω = 0) is explicitly imposed beforehand. (2) If Δω ≠ 0 is retained, the long-time average or low-pass filtered output must be zero; claiming a non-vanishing DC in this case is flagged. (3) If Δω = 0 is imposed, the DC term must become constant and reduce to the expected form (e.g., (V_i0 V_R0/2) cos(φ), up to notation), with the sum-frequency term removed by averaging/low-pass filtering. The rule flags logical imprecision where time-dependent difference-frequency terms are designated as 'DC' prior to stating the frequency-matching condition or performing an explicit time average.

rules.title: Final answer asserted without solving derived constraint (non sequitur)
rules.description: Flags solutions that correctly derive a constraint equation involving the target quantity (e.g., F(θ) = c) but then assert a final value for that quantity (e.g., tanθ = √2) without demonstrating how it follows from the constraint. Detection criteria: (1) Identify at least one explicit derived equation linking the target variable to given parameters. (2) Check for subsequent, logically connected steps that solve or justify the value (algebraic isolation, monotonicity/inequality reasoning, or equivalent). (3) If the solution instead references answer choices or makes a bare assertion (e.g., uses terms like 'option', 'choose', 'clearly', or jumps directly to the final value) without derivation, flag it. (4) Perform a consistency check by substituting the asserted value into the derived equation(s); if the equality does not hold within a small tolerance (e.g., absolute or relative error ≤ 1e-6), flag it. The rule captures errors such as deriving √2 = cosθ (sinθ + √(1 + sin^2θ)) and then claiming tanθ = √2 solely because it matches a multiple-choice option, without solving or validating the relation.

rules.title: Two-stage meltwater drainage and hydrostatic equilibrium requirement under temperate ice cap
rules.description: This rule verifies that solutions explicitly model the two-stage behavior of meltwater under a temperate ice cap: (1) an initial stage where meltwater at 0°C drains away until hydrostatic equilibrium is reached, and (2) a subsequent stage where water accumulates once drainage ceases. The rule flags solutions that: (a) compute the geometry (e.g., cone top height H or retained water volume) directly from melted ice volume without invoking a hydrostatic balance condition; (b) fail to write or use a pressure equilibrium relation at the water–ice/rock interface (e.g., P_water = rho_w * g * H balanced against overburden/lithostatic pressure from ice/rock, using correct densities and thicknesses); (c) do not partition the total melted mass into drained mass m' and retained mass (m_tot - m'), or implicitly set m' = 0 when outflow paths are available; (d) misuse energy accounting by ignoring that meltwater remains at 0°C during the drainage stage (i.e., latent heat for melting must be included, and no sensible heating of water above 0°C prior to equilibrium), or by equating volume melted to accumulated volume without considering early-stage loss; (e) omit a drainage criterion/statement that outflow occurs until the water column pressure can balance the overburden. Any solution that lacks an explicit two-stage description, a correct hydrostatic equilibrium equation, and a clear mass partition between produced and drained water is flagged.

rules.title: Argument-consistency for variable dependence (time vs spatial)
rules.description: This rule checks that the functional dependence of key physical quantities in a solution is consistent with how they are defined in the problem statement. Specifically: (1) If a quantity is defined as time-dependent (e.g., current I(t)), the solution must not switch to a spatial dependence (e.g., I(z)) without an explicit and justified transformation (such as defining a distributed current I(z) along the solenoid with a clear physical model, or moving to phasor/frequency domain with clear notation). (2) If a quantity is defined as spatially dependent (e.g., M(z), L(z)), the solution must not use time dependence (e.g., M(t), L(t)) unless an explicit model is provided that relates geometry to time variation. (3) The rule flags expressions where derivatives with respect to time are applied to quantities written with a spatial argument (e.g., dI(z)/dt), which is inconsistent unless I is clearly redefined as a function of both t and z with proper notation. Detection procedure: Parse the problem for declarations of functional dependence (e.g., I(t), M(z), L(z)). Scan the solution for occurrences of these symbols with mismatched arguments (I(z), M(t), L(t)) or mixed use of I(t) and I(z) without an explicit bridging statement. If any mismatch occurs without a clear, physically justified redefinition of the variable and its domain, flag a modeling/notation error. The rule aims to prevent ambiguity and misuse of variables that can lead to incorrect modeling or interpretation.

rules.title: Ambiguous symbol reuse across distinct concepts
rules.description: Flags notational ambiguity caused by reusing the same symbol (e.g., α, β, γ) for different physical or geometric quantities within a single solution. The verifier scans the text and equations for symbol introductions and context phrases (patterns like 'let α be', 'α denotes', 'define γ =', 'phase α', 'interior angle β', 'longitude γ', 'latitude e') and builds a symbol-to-concept map. Concept categories include: phase/phase difference (interference/Pancharatnam phase), spherical-triangle interior angles, polarization parameters on the Poincaré sphere (latitude e, longitude γ), amplitudes/field components, etc. If any symbol is associated with more than one concept category without explicit disambiguation (distinct subscripts/primes, e.g., α_phase vs α_triangle; or a clear statement of redefinition followed by exclusive use of the new meaning), the rule raises an error. Typical cases to flag: introducing α as the phase difference between beams, then later using α, β, γ as interior angles of a spherical triangle; or using γ both as polarization longitude and as a triangle angle. The rule is independent of numerical correctness and exists solely to ensure consistent, non-overloaded notation throughout the solution.

rules.title: Number conservation must include volume when integrating a density distribution
rules.description: This rule verifies that solutions correctly distinguish between number density and total number when using an energy distribution f(ε). If f(ε) is defined such that f(ε) dε gives the number per unit volume in the energy interval [ε, ε + dε], then ∫ f(ε) dε represents a number density (per unit volume), not a total particle count. The total number must be computed as N = ∫∫ f(ε, x) dε dV; for spatially uniform systems, N = V ∫ f(ε) dε. The verifier will: (1) Scan for statements equating N or "total number of particles" directly to ∫ f(ε) dε without a volume factor, and flag them. (2) Check number-conservation steps in problems with changing volume (e.g., adiabatic expansion/compression) and require V0 ∫ f0(ε) dε = V ∫ f1(ε) dε; it will flag any use of ∫ f0 dε = ∫ f1 dε as a conservation law. (3) Perform unit consistency: ∫ f dε must have units of number density; equating it to a dimensionless total count is invalid. (4) When normalization constants (e.g., κ) are updated under number conservation, ensure the normalization scales with volume as needed (for uniform systems, κ1 should reflect V0/V if only normalization changes); it will flag κ1 = κ0 when volume changes and the solution claims number conservation by keeping ∫ f unchanged. This rule applies to any distribution defined per unit volume (energy distributions, phase-space distributions) to detect conflation of density with total number.

rules.title: Missing numeric final results for requested quantities
rules.description: Checks that a solution provides explicit numeric values (with appropriate units) for all quantities the problem explicitly asks to calculate (e.g., radius of curvature R and contact angle α). The rule first identifies target outputs from the problem text by matching verbs such as 'calculate', 'compute', 'determine', 'find' and associated quantity names/symbols (e.g., 'R', 'α', 'radius of curvature', 'contact angle'). It then scans the solution for corresponding numeric assignments. A valid result must include digits and, when applicable, units (e.g., 'R = 12 mm', 'α ≈ 35°'). The rule flags as errors any solutions where: (a) the final answers for the requested quantities are absent; (b) the quantities are only expressed symbolically or as formulas (e.g., 'R = f(n_w, h, d)') without numeric evaluation; or (c) placeholders or incomplete markers are present (e.g., '...', 'TBD', 'to be determined', 'approx using lensmaker's formula' without numbers). For angle outputs, expects degrees or radians; for lengths, expects a length unit (m, cm, mm). This catches incomplete calculations where the method is described but no numerical results are produced.

rules.title: Unjustified override of computed result
rules.description:
This rule checks for consistency between quantitatively derived values in the solution and the final reported answer. It flags cases where a student computes a numeric result for the target quantity (e.g., a ratio, speed, energy, etc.) using stated assumptions and formulas, but later reports a different final value without an explicit and numerically demonstrated correction or change of assumptions.

Detection criteria:
- Identify the most recent computed numeric value for the asked quantity (e.g., phrases like "we get", "thus", "=", "≈", "so the ratio/value is") and the final stated answer.
- Compute the relative difference between the derived value and the final answer. If the difference exceeds a tolerance (e.g., 5%), check for an explicit justification that would legitimately change the value (such as: stated units conversion with numbers shown, corrected constants with recomputation, correction of a specific earlier mistake followed by recalculation, or a documented model change with updated equations and numbers).
- If no such explicit and quantitative justification is present between the derivation and the final answer, flag the solution for an unjustified override of the computed result.

Examples of justifications that prevent triggering: "We used the wrong specific heat; using c=4.18 kJ/kg·K and recalculating gives 7.41→7.60" with the recalculation shown; or "Converted minutes to seconds: t=2 min = 120 s, recomputing yields ...". Non-acceptable justifications: changing the final numeric answer without recalculation, citing an expected/known answer, or vague statements like "approximately" without linking to a new computation.

Scope: Applies to all physics topics where a numeric derivation precedes a final numeric answer (e.g., thermodynamics heating curves, kinematics, energy/momentum problems). The rule is tolerant to minor rounding differences but flags substantial discrepancies not supported by clear, quantitative reasoning.

rules.title: Excessive rounding of standard constants leading to biased final result
rules.description: This rule checks whether a solution’s numerical result is noticeably biased due to the use of overly rounded standard constants or inputs, despite a correct physical method. It is intended for problems where the result depends on standard atmospheric/thermal constants (e.g., buoyancy with ideal-gas air). Detection procedure: (1) Parse the constants and inputs used by the student (e.g., ρ_air, R_specific for dry air, p0, g, temperatures) and identify their significant figures. (2) Compare these to canonical precise values from the verifier’s reference table (e.g., R_air = 287.058 J/(kg·K), g = 9.80665 m/s², p0 = 1.01325×10^5 Pa, ρ_air at 20 °C ≈ 1.2041 kg/m³). (3) Recompute the target quantity using the student’s stated method but replacing rounded constants with canonical precise values while keeping problem data unchanged. (4) Compute the relative deviation between the student’s numerical result and the recomputed result. (5) Trigger a precision/rounding warning if either: relative deviation > 1% or, for temperature outputs, absolute deviation > 1 K. (6) Additionally flag if multiple rounded constants (≤3 significant figures) are used and their combined effect causes the deviation threshold to be exceeded. The rule does not mark a conceptual error when the governing equations/logic are correct; it specifically labels the discrepancy as a rounding/precision issue and suggests carrying more significant figures or using canonical constants to avoid bias.

rules.title: Boundary value claimed as optimal without model-based optimization
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that declare an 'optimal' value equal to a stated constraint bound (upper or lower) without performing any optimization or using the governing physical relations. Applicable to problems that explicitly require choosing an optimal parameter (e.g., antenna length s, resonance condition, switching threshold) based on circuit or wave dynamics. The verifier checks: (1) whether the final chosen value exactly matches a constraint limit mentioned in the problem; (2) whether the solution derives or cites an objective/optimality criterion (e.g., quarter- or half-wavelength, resonance/impedance matching, instability threshold) and uses the relevant model equations; (3) whether the solution computes the dependent physical quantity that determines the optimum (e.g., oscillation frequency from circuit parameters R, C, and nonlinear element characteristics) and maps it to the target variable; (4) whether a monotonicity or boundary-optimality justification is provided (e.g., showing the objective is monotonic over the feasible interval). If the answer equals a bound and the solution lacks both a derived criterion and a calculation tying parameters to the optimum (or lacks monotonicity analysis), the rule marks a logic error: 'constraint bound taken as optimal without analysis.' This catches cases like setting s to the maximum allowed length solely due to the constraint, instead of determining s from wavelength/frequency or resonance determined by circuit parameters.

rules.title: Unjustified order-of-magnitude rounding (magnitude jump > ×2)
rules.description: Checks for logical consistency when converting a computed numerical estimate to an order-of-magnitude (OOM) answer. If a solution computes a value X from the stated physical model/inputs and then reports a final OOM value Y, the rule flags cases where max(Y/X, X/Y) > 2 and there is no explicit justification (e.g., stated uncertainty range, revised input parameters, or a clearly specified rounding convention). Acceptable conventions are: (a) rounding X to one significant digit; or (b) rounding to the nearest power of ten on a log10 scale. The rule specifically targets statements like “since it’s an order-of-magnitude estimate, we can round to …” followed by a jump to a larger decade without revising assumptions (e.g., reporting 10 h after computing ~3–4 h). To pass, either the rounding must follow a declared, consistent criterion, or the solver must adjust and justify physical inputs to support the new magnitude.

rules.title: Consistency of computed value with stated order-of-magnitude/rounding
rules.description: This rule checks that any later restatement of a previously computed numerical quantity (same variable and units) as an approximate or order-of-magnitude value is consistent with the computed value. The verifier identifies a computed numeric result (e.g., E ≈ 3.3 meV) and then scans nearby text for an approximate claim using cues such as '~', '≈', 'about', 'roughly', 'of order', or 'order-of-magnitude'. It flags a discrepancy if: (a) the ratio between the computed value and the stated approximate value is outside [0.5, 2] (i.e., differs by more than a factor of 2); or (b) the stated value purports to be a one-significant-digit rounding but is not the nearest one-digit rounding of the computed value. The rule also requires unit consistency when comparing values. Larger deviations are allowed only if the text explicitly justifies a change (e.g., states changed parameters, new assumptions, or intent to quote a power-of-ten scale, using phrases like 'assuming...', 'due to...', 'changing...', 'using...', 'neglecting...', 'to within an order of magnitude'). Example caught: computing ~3.3 meV and then concluding '~1 meV' without justification.

rules.title: Require explicit branch selection for variables defined via max/min
rules.description: When a problem defines an intermediate variable using a max/min operator (e.g., v_L = max(v, v0) and ω = v_L/h), any substitution of that variable in a solution must be accompanied by an explicit determination of which branch applies. The solution should state and justify the inequality (e.g., v ≥ v0 or v ≤ v0) or perform a case split before setting v_L equal to v, v0, or an unknown critical value v_c. This rule flags solutions that directly set v_L = v_c (or v_L = v, v0) without discussing its relation to the other argument(s) of the max/min, especially when deriving thresholds (e.g., skin depth δ = d) where the resulting expression implies a relation like v_c > v0. The check passes if the solution includes a clear inequality or parameter-based reasoning (e.g., given h/d = 10 ⇒ v_c > v0 ⇒ v_L = v) to select the correct branch; otherwise it fails.

rules.title: Conflating twilight duration with geometric visibility time
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that determine how long a planet is visible after sunset by invoking twilight length or sky brightness, instead of using purely geometric constraints (elongation, hour angle, horizon crossing). The rule targets problems that assume idealized geometry (no atmosphere unless explicitly stated) and seek the maximum time a planet remains above the horizon after sunset. Triggers: (a) The solution uses terms such as "twilight", "civil/nautical/astronomical twilight", "dusk", "sky brightness", "longer twilight at high latitudes" to compute or justify the duration of post-sunset visibility; (b) The final duration is made to depend on latitude specifically via twilight length or sky brightness; (c) There is no accompanying computation of geometric quantities such as elongation (e.g., θ ≈ arcsin(R_inner/R_earth) for inner planets), hour-angle differences between the Sun and planet, projection of elongation onto the horizon (involving declination/ecliptic tilt), or explicit horizon-crossing time. The rule assumes the correct approach is to use the planet–Sun angular separation (elongation) and convert the corresponding hour-angle difference into time via Earth’s rotation rate, possibly accounting for declination/ecliptic geometry, and that twilight/sky brightness does not alter the geometric time the planet remains above the horizon. Exceptions: Do not flag if the problem explicitly requests detectability relative to a brightness threshold, defines twilight categories to be used, or instructs to include atmospheric scattering/sky brightness in the visibility criterion. The rule is violated if twilight duration is used to extend or limit the visibility time without a geometric horizon-crossing analysis.

rules.title: Verify point-vortex velocity normalization matches stated circulation
rules.description: Checks that the normalization of the 2D point-vortex velocity field is consistent with the circulation convention stated in the problem. Detection logic: (1) Parse the problem statement to identify the circulation convention for a single vortex filament, i.e., whether it states ∮ v·dl = 2π κ or ∮ v·dl = κ. Set Gamma_expected accordingly. (2) In the solution, locate any asserted point-vortex velocity expressions, either as a vector field v(r) ∝ e_z × (r − r0)/|r − r0|^2 or as tangential speed v(d) ∝ 1/d with coefficients involving κ and possibly 2π. (3) Compute the implied circulation from the candidate field around a circle of radius d: Gamma_field = v_t(d) × 2π d. For v(r) = A × (e_z × (r − r0))/|r − r0|^2, the tangential speed at radius d is A/d, so Gamma_field = 2π A. (4) Require A = Gamma_expected/(2π). Therefore, if the problem states ∮ v·dl = 2π κ, the correct normalization is A = κ, yielding v(d) = κ/d and v(r) = κ (e_z × (r − r0))/|r − r0|^2. If the problem states ∮ v·dl = κ, the correct normalization is A = κ/(2π), yielding v(d) = κ/(2π d). (5) Flag an error when the coefficient A in the solution does not satisfy A = Gamma_expected/(2π), e.g., the presence of an extra 1/(2π) factor when the problem uses ∮ v·dl = 2π κ, or the absence of 1/(2π) when the problem uses ∮ v·dl = κ. This catches incorrect numerical factors in point-vortex velocity fields and ensures consistency between circulation quantization and velocity normalization.

rules.title: Disallow ad hoc fluid compressibility and V–P relations when model specifies rock compressibility storage with Darcy flow
rules.description: Flag solutions that introduce oil/fluid compressibility (e.g., c_o) or linear volume–pressure relations (e.g., V = V0(1 − c_o ΔP)) when the problem already specifies storage via rock compressibility c_r and provides/implicitly requires Darcy’s law for linear flow. Specifically, trigger if any of the following occur: (1) c_o (or generic fluid compressibility) appears in place of, or in addition to, c_r in the storage term when the given storage equation is q = −2 φ L^2 c_r h dP̄/dt; (2) the solution derives q from an ad hoc volume–pressure linearization rather than coupling the provided storage equation to Darcy’s linear flow q = (2 k h / μ L)(P_b − P_w) (or an equivalent Darcy expression); (3) an independent V–P relation is asserted that is not stated or derived from the given model assumptions; (4) the storage equation is mislabeled as Darcy’s law or replaced by a compressibility-based volume balance unrelated to the specified c_r. Rationale: In this setup, pore-volume change is governed by rock compressibility c_r, and depletion dynamics must come from coupling that storage relation with Darcy flow. Introducing fluid compressibility or unsupported V–P laws constitutes an inconsistent model change and should be flagged.

rules.title: Receiver without a clock cannot measure reception time or signal delay
rules.description: Flag a conceptual error when a solution claims that a receiver lacking an internal clock or synchronization to the transmitter time scale can directly measure the reception time t or the signal time-of-flight Δt = t − t_i. In such setups (e.g., GNSS-like problems), the only time provided by the signal is the emission timestamp t_i and the satellite position at t_i; the receiver cannot know t or Δt_i without a local clock referenced to the same time system. The correct formulation must treat the reception time (or receiver clock bias) as an unknown to be solved simultaneously with position using range equations (e.g., c · (t − t_i) = |r − r_i| for multiple satellites). This rule should trigger if the problem statement specifies the receiver has no clock or is unsynchronized, yet the solution asserts: (a) the receiver measures Δt_i directly, (b) the receiver knows the exact reception time t, or (c) the receiver infers time-of-flight from signal content alone without introducing an unknown reception time/clock bias and solving for it.

rules.title: Missing or incomplete final expression for requested quantity
rules.description: This rule verifies that a solution provides a complete, explicit final expression for the specific quantity requested by the problem (e.g., maximum height z_max). The verifier should: 1) Identify the target quantity Q from the prompt (e.g., phrases like 'maximum height', 'z_max', 'h_max', or 'z at the apex'). 2) Check that the solution contains an explicit equation of the form Q = expression or an equivalent definitive statement yielding Q. 3) Ensure the expression is syntactically complete (no dangling operators, unmatched parentheses/brackets, or truncated symbols), contains no ellipses '...' or unfinished variables (e.g., 'v0^2 y_{'), and does not end mid-derivation. 4) Verify that the final expression uses only the variables allowed by the prompt for the answer (e.g., only v0, z0, g, k if specified) and fundamental constants; it must not depend on undefined or intermediate variables (e.g., y_max, y, v_h) unless those are explicitly permitted by the problem statement. 5) Confirm that the final statement uniquely identifies a single value for Q (not just conditions, inequalities, or a procedure). Failure modes this rule flags include: the derivation stops without yielding Q; the final line references Q but lacks '=' or a complete right-hand side; presence of placeholders like 'TBD', '...', or 'to be continued'; reliance on symbols not defined or not allowed in the requested form; or expressions that are syntactically incomplete.

rules.title: Sun altitude at sunset/sunrise must be ~0° (or −0.833° apparent)
rules.description:
Checks for misuse of the solar altitude formula at the events of sunset or sunrise. At geometric sunset/sunrise, the Sun’s center altitude h equals 0°. For apparent sunset/sunrise (including refraction and the solar disk), h ≈ −0.833°. The rule flags solutions that compute or assert a nonzero solar altitude at 'sunset' or 'sunrise' using declination and latitude only (e.g., h = −arcsin(sin ε · sin φ) or h = arcsin(sin φ · sin δ), or the general relation sin h = sin φ sin δ + cos φ cos δ cos H with H omitted or set incorrectly) and then use that value to infer times or geometry. Detection criteria:
- The text references 'sunset', 'sunrise', or 'at the moment of sunset/sunrise' and provides a numeric altitude for the Sun with |h| > 1° (outside the acceptable 0° geometric or ≈ −0.833° apparent range).
- The solution uses an altitude expression depending only on latitude φ and declination δ (or axial tilt ε) to represent the Sun’s altitude specifically 'at sunset/sunrise', without solving for the hour angle H that satisfies h = 0°.
- Pattern examples to flag: h = −arcsin(sin(tilt) · sin(latitude)); h = arcsin(sin φ sin δ) at sunset; or any computed h at sunset/sunrise not within [−1.5°, +1.0°] of 0°, unless explicitly justified as apparent −0.833°.
- Also flag if the incorrect altitude value is used to determine time intervals after sunset (e.g., the time until Venus sets).
The correct approach at sunset/sunrise is to set h = 0° (or use h ≈ −0.833° for apparent definitions) and, if needed, solve the hour angle from sin h = sin φ sin δ + cos φ cos δ cos H.

rules.title: Ambiguous symbol reuse causing dimensional/role conflicts
rules.description: Checks for reuse of the same symbol with conflicting meanings or dimensions within a solution (e.g., using R both as the universal gas constant and as a geometric radius). Detection logic: (1) Build a symbol usage map across the solution by parsing equations, limits of integration, and textual declarations. (2) Infer each symbol’s role/dimensions from context using pattern heuristics: examples include n R T, p = n R T, or U = (3/2) n R T implying R is the universal gas constant; expressions like ∫_0^R ..., 'radius R', 'outer radius R', or units of length imply R is a geometric radius. (3) If the same symbol is inferred to belong to more than one incompatible role category (thermodynamic constants {R, k_B, N_A}, gravitational constants {G}, geometric variables/lengths {r, R, L}, etc.), flag an error. (4) Additionally, flag derived expressions that mix the conflicting interpretations, such as internal energy U containing factors of 1/R while R is also used in n R T (gas constant), or using R as an integration bound after defining R as a constant in the ideal gas law. This rule aims to prevent ambiguous notation that leads to logical contradictions and dimensional inconsistency; it requires that each distinct physical quantity be assigned a unique symbol consistent with its role and units throughout the derivation.

rules.title: Symmetry-derived equality must not be replaced by a different ratio without explicit derivation
rules.description: This rule checks for internal logical consistency when a solution uses symmetry to assert equality between two physical quantities and later claims a non-unit ratio between the same quantities without a clear, quantitative bridge. The verifier scans for an initial statement such as "by symmetry" or equivalent reasoning that concludes A = B (or a ratio A/B = 1). It then looks for subsequent assertions that A = k·B with k ≠ 1 (e.g., A = (1/3)·B) applied to the same defined quantities. If the later change in ratio is not accompanied by explicit derivation steps—such as application of governing laws (e.g., Maxwell's equations, conservation/continuity relations), boundary-condition analysis, geometric/topological modifications, or quantified coupling arguments—the solution is flagged as inconsistent. The rule also flags the introduction of new physical effects (e.g., "shielding", "screening") not specified in the problem statement unless they are quantitatively modeled or justified by referenced properties and equations. Scope: general physics (e.g., magnetism, circuits, mechanics, fluids) where symmetry implies equal partitioning or equality. Trigger conditions: (1) symmetry-based equality claim; (2) later non-equal numeric ratio for the same variables; (3) absence of an explicit derivation or changed assumptions bridging the two claims.

rules.title: Missing explicit time dependence in requested quantity
rules.description: Purpose: Flag solutions that fail to provide a requested quantity as an explicit function of time. Trigger: The problem statement includes phrases like "as a function of time", asks for X(t), or requests a time relationship (e.g., V_PQ(t)), but the solution's final expression for the requested quantity does not explicitly depend on t. Check details: 1) Parse the task to confirm time dependence is requested (keywords: "as a function of time", "X(t)", "time relationship", "time evolution"). 2) Inspect the final provided expression(s) for the requested quantity. If they are left in terms of intermediate variables (e.g., angle θ, angular velocity θ̇, flux Φ) without solving for the state variable as a function of time (θ(t), Φ(t), etc.), mark as incomplete. 3) Acceptable resolutions include: an explicit closed-form V(t); a piecewise V(t); or a solved differential equation yielding θ(t) (or the relevant state variable) with applied initial conditions, then substitution to obtain X(t). 4) Not acceptable: reporting general induction/kinematic formulas like V = B l^2 sin(θ) θ̇ or V = dΦ/dt without deriving θ(t) (or Φ(t)) from dynamics and initial conditions; giving parametric dependence on θ and θ̇ while never expressing θ as a function of t; or omitting the use of provided initial time t0 and orientation/connection state. Example of a violation: The solution ends with V_PQ = B l^2 sin(θ) θ̇ for a rotating loop when the problem asks for V_PQ(t), without deriving θ(t) via rotational dynamics and initial conditions.

rules.title: Consistency of error bars for symmetric ranges under linear proportionality
rules.description: This rule verifies that when a solution assumes a linear proportionality between two quantities (e.g., μ ∝ Δz in a Stern–Gerlach analysis) and the observed range is symmetric about a central value, all equivalent methods of computing the uncertainty yield the same error bar. Checks performed: (1) Symmetry and linearity: If Q ∝ X is used and X_min, X_max are symmetric around X_0, then Q_min = k·X_min, Q_max = k·X_max with k = Q_0/X_0. The correct uncertainty must satisfy δQ = (Q_max − Q_min)/2 = |Q_max − Q_0| = |Q_0 − Q_min| and δQ/Q_0 = δX/X_0. Any student's δQ that deviates from these values beyond a small tolerance (e.g., relative error > 1%) is flagged as a logic/calculation error. (2) Method consistency: If the student presents multiple methods (e.g., 'half-range' vs 'deviation from central value') for the same symmetric, linear case, their numerical δQ results must agree within tolerance; disagreement indicates misuse of symmetry or proportionality. (3) Scientific notation sanity: Normalize reported values to standard scientific notation (coefficient in [1,10)). For operands of similar order (e.g., Q_min, Q_max ~ 10^−23), the half-range δQ should have an exponent one order smaller (≈10^−24). If the reported δQ exponent/magnitude is inconsistent with the operands (e.g., using 10^−23 instead of 10^−24 for a half-range), flag an exponent-handling error. (4) Full-range vs half-range: If the student erroneously uses the full range (Q_max − Q_min) as the error bar when a symmetric error bar is requested, flag the discrepancy. This rule catches errors where symmetric ranges under linear mappings must produce identical uncertainty estimates, but the student’s result differs due to arithmetic, exponent, or methodological mistakes.

rules.title: Use of undefined/misinterpreted symbol and unrelated domain formulas
rules.description: This rule verifies that symbols/parameters used in a solution are defined within the problem context and that any optimization or calculation involving them is grounded in the system described. It flags cases where a variable (e.g., s) is assigned a meaning not established by the problem (such as interpreting s as an antenna length) and where formulas from an unrelated physical domain are introduced without justification. Specifically, for circuit problems (e.g., RC networks with nonlinear I–V elements), the rule flags the introduction of electromagnetic wave/antenna heuristics and relations (e.g., 'antenna', 'wavelength', 'quarter-wavelength', 'half-wavelength', 'λ = c/f', 'speed of light') unless the problem explicitly mentions antennas or radiation. It also flags optimizing a parameter by appeal to these heuristics instead of tying it to quantities and dynamics derivable from the circuit (e.g., frequency set by R, C, and the nonlinear element’s I–V characteristics). The rule triggers if: (1) a symbol is used or optimized without being defined by the problem or explicitly defined by the solver; (2) the solution invokes EM wave propagation relations in a pure circuit context; or (3) the proposed optimization is not justified by equations or reasoning based on the given circuit components and their dynamics.

rules.title: Require surface tension in vertical force balance for floating objects at interfaces
rules.description: This rule checks solutions to problems involving objects floating at a liquid–air interface when surface tension or capillarity is explicitly relevant (e.g., γ given, capillary length L_c mentioned, contact angle θ defined, or a deformed meniscus curve provided). The solution must include the vertical component of surface tension at the contact line in the static equilibrium (vertical force) balance, in addition to buoyancy. Flag as an error if the equilibrium is modeled by weight = buoyancy alone (e.g., ρ_object V_object g = ρ_fluid V_displaced g) without any γ-dependent term or contact-angle dependence. Specific triggers: (1) The force balance or immersion-depth determination omits any term involving γ, θ, or the contact line perimeter (e.g., F_γ ≈ γ × 2π r_c × sinθ or cosθ), and relies solely on Archimedes’ principle to set V_displaced or h; (2) The solution computes V_displaced = (ρ_object/ρ_fluid) × V_object or similar to fix the immersion geometry while γ appears nowhere in the balance; (3) Previously provided relations linking θ and material parameters (e.g., cosθ = f(ρ), capillary length effects, Young–Laplace considerations) are ignored when establishing equilibrium. The rule is intended to catch modeling errors where surface tension’s vertical contribution is overlooked in capillarity problems, which invalidates subsequent interaction force estimates (e.g., meniscus-mediated horizontal forces).

rules.title: Incorrect adjustment of elongation by axial tilt or latitude for visibility duration
rules.description: Checks solutions that compute the maximum post-sunset (or pre-sunrise) visibility duration of an inner planet (e.g., Venus) in a simplified coplanar, circular-orbit model. In this model, the fundamental time separation is determined by the planet’s greatest elongation and Earth’s uniform rotation rate (~15° per hour). The rule flags the following errors: (1) Defining an 'effective' angular separation by subtracting Earth’s axial tilt (≈23.5°) or the observer’s latitude (φ) from the elongation, e.g., θ_eff = θ − 23.5°, θ_eff = θ − φ, or similar; (2) Computing the visibility duration as (θ − Δ)/ω where Δ is Earth’s tilt or latitude and ω ≈ 15°/h; (3) Asserting that axial tilt or latitude directly reduces the maximum time Venus is visible after sunset in the coplanar/circular assumption without a proper projection to hour angle via spherical astronomy (declination/altitude effects may influence horizon crossing but do not warrant a simple subtraction from elongation). The rule triggers when a solution claims that tilt/latitude linearly diminishes elongation or visibility time, or mixes ecliptic and equatorial angles by naive subtraction. Acceptable approaches must base the first-order time estimate on elongation alone (θ/15° per hour) unless a justified hour-angle projection is explicitly derived.

rules.title: Incorrectly equating melt/intrusion volume to surface depression volume
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that assume the volume of a magma/rock intrusion or the volume of melted ice equals the geometric volume of a surface depression (e.g., a cone) without an energy/mass balance. Examples include statements or equations like V_intrusion = V_depression, V_melt = V_depression, or computing melted mass via m_melt = rho_i * V_depression. In temperate ice-cap problems, the depression reflects vertical motion and density contrasts (rho_i ≠ rho_w), not a one-to-one volume match. To pass, the solution must (a) derive melt mass/volume from an energy balance using available heat (Q_in) and material properties (latent heat, specific heat) before relating to geometry, and (b) acknowledge density differences between ice and water when converting mass to volume. The verifier should detect any direct use of the surface-depression volume to infer intrusion or melt volume/mass, or any equality between volumes of distinct physical domains (surface depression vs subsurface intrusion) without justification via energy and mass conservation.

rules.title: Correct method-of-images for a vortex in a 90° corner (three images with specific signs)
rules.description: This rule verifies the correct application of the method of images for a 2D point vortex or straight vortex filament near two perpendicular impermeable walls (a quarter-plane/90° corner). For an incompressible, inviscid, irrotational flow (e.g., superfluid helium) with no-penetration boundary conditions v·n = 0 on both walls (x = 0 and y = 0), a single real vortex of circulation Γ located at (x0, y0) with x0 > 0, y0 > 0 must be complemented by three image vortices: (1) at (−x0, y0) with circulation −Γ, (2) at (x0, −y0) with circulation −Γ, and (3) at (−x0, −y0) with circulation +Γ. This construction is the minimal image set that enforces zero normal velocity on both walls. The verifier should flag a modeling error if any of the following is detected in a solution that uses the method of images in a corner: (a) fewer than three image vortices are used, (b) the diagonal image at (−x0, −y0) is omitted, (c) incorrect sign assignment to any image (i.e., not the pattern −Γ, −Γ, +Γ), or (d) the resulting velocity field fails the boundary conditions (nonzero v·n on x = 0 or y = 0 when evaluated). When the task involves induced velocities (e.g., computing the initial velocity v0 of the filament), the rule also checks that the summation includes contributions from all three images with the correct signs. Equivalent constructions (e.g., complex potential formulations or harmonic corrections) are acceptable only if they yield v·n = 0 on both walls; otherwise, the solution is flagged.

rules.title: Consistent Z and mass scaling in Bohr radius and energy for hydrogen-like ions
rules.description: Checks that, for hydrogen-like ions analyzed via Bohr theory, the nuclear charge Z and (reduced) mass scaling are applied consistently and with the correct powers in both the ground-state radius and energy. Expected scaling from hydrogen (n=1) to an ion with charge Z and orbiting particle mass m' (using electron mass m_e as reference) is: r1' = r1_H * (m_e / m') * (1 / Z) and E1' = E1_H * (m' / m_e) * Z^2, with the energy remaining negative. The rule performs the following validations: (1) Extract the implied scaling factors s_r = r1' / r1_H and s_E = |E1'| / |E1_H| from the solution (symbolic or numeric). (2) Verify exponent correctness: radius must include Z to power -1 and mass to power -1; energy must include Z to power +2 and mass to power +1. Flag if the radius omits the 1/Z factor, uses Z^0, or uses an incorrect power (e.g., Z^+1 or Z^2), and likewise flag if the energy omits Z^2 or uses the wrong mass dependence. (3) Cross-consistency check: given correct Bohr scaling, s_r_expected = (m_e/m')/Z and s_E_expected = (m'/m_e)*Z^2. If either provided factor deviates from its expected value beyond tolerance (e.g., >2% for numeric answers), flag. Additionally, if the product s_r * s_E does not equal Z within tolerance, flag for inconsistent application of Z between radius and energy (e.g., Z included in energy but missing in radius). This rule specifically catches errors like computing E' with Z^2 and m'/m_e while computing r' only with m_e/m' (omitting the 1/Z), or applying the same mass or Z power to both r and E. The rule accepts either m' or the reduced mass μ where appropriate, but enforces the opposite mass dependence for r (inverse) and E (direct), and the correct Z powers (-1 for r, +2 for E).

rules.title: Natural linewidth from lifetime: use Γ ≈ ħ/τ, not ΔE·Δt ≥ ħ/2 with Δt = τ
rules.description: This rule verifies the correct method for estimating the energy uncertainty (natural linewidth) of an unstable/radioactive state from its decay time. It should trigger when the problem context includes keywords such as radioactive isotope, decay time, mean lifetime (τ), half-life (t1/2), energy uncertainty, or natural linewidth. Checks: (1) If the solution uses the Heisenberg energy-time inequality ΔE·Δt ≥ ħ/2 and substitutes Δt = τ (or Δt = t1/2) to compute ΔE = ħ/(2τ), flag a conceptual error. The inequality provides only a lower bound and underestimates the typical width by about a factor of 2. (2) The expected relation for exponentially decaying states is Γ ≈ ħ/τ; if half-life t1/2 is given, the correct conversion is τ = t1/2 / ln(2). (3) Numerical validation: After proper unit conversion to seconds, compare the reported ΔE to ħ/τ. If the reported value is within ~10% of ħ/(2τ) while deviating by >20% from ħ/τ, flag the solution. (4) Unit consistency: Verify use of ħ ≈ 6.582×10^-16 eV·s or 1.054×10^-34 J·s and correct conversion of time units (minutes/hours to seconds). (5) Accept solutions that explicitly use Γ = ħ/τ and identify ΔE ≈ Γ; minor rounding differences are allowed. This rule catches the common misuse of the Heisenberg inequality for decay widths and enforces the linewidth–lifetime relation derived from the exponential decay's Fourier transform.

rules.title: Misuse of ħ/2 in energy–time uncertainty for decay width
rules.description: Checks solutions that compute the energy uncertainty from a radioactive decay time or lifetime. For unstable states, the physically relevant quantity is the natural width Γ = ħ/τ (not ΔE = ħ/(2Δt) from treating ΔE·Δt ≥ ħ/2 as an equality). The rule triggers if: 1) Context mentions decay time/lifetime/mean life/radioactive isotope. 2) The solution writes the inequality ΔE·Δt ≥ ħ/2 and then explicitly sets ΔE = ħ/(2Δt), or uses the literal factor 'ħ/2' to compute ΔE. 3) Numerical check: parse the time (convert to seconds) and compute Γ_expected = ħ/τ. If a reported ΔE is present and the ratio r = ΔE / Γ_expected satisfies 0.45 ≤ r ≤ 0.55, flag a half-width (1/2 factor) conceptual error. 4) Convention consistency: if the solution uses the h-based estimate (ΔE ≈ h/τ), it must be labeled as an order-of-magnitude estimate; otherwise, if r lies in the 5.6–7.0 range (≈2π mismatch), flag inconsistent constant choice. Notes: This rule targets factor-of-two and 2π convention errors specific to decay widths; minor rounding differences are ignored.

rules.title: Non-parabolic dispersion: require v = ∇_p K and dp/dt = q(E + v×B); flag use of F = m a or p = m v
rules.description: Scope: Problems that specify a quasiparticle with non-parabolic dispersion K(p) (e.g., K = p^2/(2m) + α p or any K(p) ≠ p^2/(2m)). Check that the solution uses the correct kinematics and dynamics for quasiparticles. Required modeling: (1) Velocity must be obtained from the dispersion via v = ∇_p K (for isotropic K(p): v = dK/dp · p̂), not from p = m v. (2) The equation of motion must be written for momentum: dp/dt = q(E + v × B), and acceleration computed as a = dv/dt derived from v(p(t)). Flag as error if any of the following appear: (a) The solution invokes Newton's second law in the form F = m a to directly compute acceleration components; (b) The solution assumes p = m v or treats m as the inertial mass linking F and a; (c) The solution sets a_x = qE/m and a_y = 0 solely from F_x = qE, F_y = 0 without deriving v from K(p) and differentiating v with respect to time; (d) The solution does not reference or use ∇_p K, dK/dp, or group velocity to obtain v. Rationale: For K(p) with non-parabolic terms (e.g., K = p^2/(2m) + α p), v ≠ p/m; the correct dynamics use dp/dt from the external fields and a follows from dv/dt, which can include transverse components even when force has no transverse component. Using F = m a or p = m v in this context is a modeling error that can miss perpendicular acceleration.

rules.title: Misuse of effective mass and p=mv in non-quadratic dispersion
