rules.description: Trigger this rule when a problem specifies a quasiparticle with a non-quadratic dispersion K(p) (e.g., K = p^2/(2m) + α p) and the solution treats dynamics using p = m v or F = m a (or defines an ad hoc scalar m_eff) instead of the correct dp/dt = F and v = ∂K/∂p. Specifically, flag if any of the following are detected: (1) The solution assumes p = m v or v = p/m without deriving v from v = ∂K/∂p; (2) The solution uses Newton’s second law as F = m a with the given m (or a scalar "effective mass") when K(p) is not purely quadratic; (3) An "effective mass" m_eff is defined by differentiating K with respect to v, or by first substituting p = m v into K(p) and then differentiating, yielding expressions like m_eff(v,α) that mix v and α and ignore that K is a function of p; (4) The final acceleration components (e.g., a_x = qE/m, a_y = 0) or velocity expressions do not depend on α even though α appears in K(p); (5) The solution states or implies v = p/m or v = dK/dp = p/m, omitting the α term. Rationale: For isotropic K(p), the correct kinematics are v = ∂K/∂p and dynamics use dp/dt = F; acceleration must be obtained via the chain rule a = (d v/d p)·F (plus directional curvature terms), and a scalar F = m_eff a is generally invalid unless K is strictly quadratic.

rules.title: Use mean lifetime (τ) not half-life (t1/2) in energy–time uncertainty/width
rules.description: Checks that when computing energy uncertainty or decay width from a radioactive decay time, the solution uses the mean lifetime τ, not the half-life t1/2, unless explicitly stated. The relevant relations are ΔE·Δt ≳ ħ/2 or Γ = ħ/τ (up to convention). If the problem supplies a half-life, the solver must convert via τ = t1/2 / ln 2. The rule flags solutions that: (1) take Δt = t1/2 directly (e.g., convert minutes to seconds and plug in as Δt) without a τ = t1/2/ln2 step; (2) define τ as the given half-life; (3) use ΔE = ħ/(2 Δt) or Γ = ħ/τ with Δt or τ numerically equal to the quoted half-life; (4) treat ambiguous wording like "decay time" as Δt without clarifying whether it is the mean lifetime and without applying the ln 2 conversion. Detection hints: look for presence of uncertainty/width formulas (keywords: ΔE, Γ, hbar/ħ, energy-time uncertainty) combined with time inputs labeled or described as "half-life", "half life", "t1/2", "T1/2", or ambiguous "decay time"; check whether ln 2 appears in the mapping between the given time and the lifetime. Passing conditions: the solution either (a) explicitly states the given time is the mean lifetime τ, or (b) converts a provided half-life using τ = t1/2/ln 2 (or equivalently t1/2 = τ ln 2) before substituting into ΔE or Γ.

rules.title: Adiabatic work sign and population constancy in two-level Otto cycles
rules.description:
Checks the expressions for work on the adiabatic legs (B→C and D→A) of a two-level quantum Otto cycle for sign consistency and population constancy. Expected physics: for an adiabatic step with no heat (Q=0) and fixed level populations (p1 constant), the internal energy change is ΔU = p1·(E_final − E_initial). With the convention ΔU = Q − W (W is work done by the system), the work must satisfy W = −ΔU = p1·(E_initial − E_final).
The rule performs the following:
- Convention detection: If the solution states ΔU = Q − W or explicitly says W is work done by the system, enforce W_step = −ΔU_step on adiabats. If it states ΔU = Q + W or W is work done on the system, enforce W_step = +ΔU_step. If no convention is stated, default to W as work done by the system (ΔU = Q − W).
- Adiabatic leg checks (B→C and D→A): Require Q=0, p1 constant across the leg (p1B = p1C; p1D = p1A). Validate that the reported work uses the constant population value for that leg and the correct energy difference direction per the detected convention.
- Error patterns to flag under the default/by-system convention: expressions like W_BC = p1B·(E1C − E1B) or W_DA = p1D·(E1A − E1D), i.e., W written as +ΔU. More generally, flag whenever W_step + ΔU_step ≠ 0 on an adiabatic leg given Q=0.
- Population consistency: Flag if a changing population is used within an adiabatic leg or if p1 is taken from a different state that is not equal by constancy (e.g., mixing p1B with p1C inconsistently without asserting p1B = p1C).
This rule targets and flags the common sign mistake where the adiabatic work is written as +ΔU (work on the system) while the solution claims to report work done by the system. It also ensures the correct use of constant populations across adiabatic steps.

rules.title: Acceleration with non-parabolic K(p): enforce dp/dt=F and dimensional consistency
rules.description: This rule verifies acceleration derivations for quasiparticles when the kinetic energy depends nonlinearly on momentum (e.g., K(p)=p^2/(2m)+α p). The checker enforces use of the momentum equation dp/dt=F and the velocity definition v=∇_p K, and performs dimensional analysis on any introduced 'effective mass' or acceleration formulas. It flags the following errors: (1) Using F=ma directly to obtain a_x=qE/m and a_y=0 without accounting for the non-quadratic dispersion (presence of an α p term). (2) Introducing an ad-hoc effective mass m_eff that mixes dimensions of velocity and mass (e.g., any form where terms like v^2 and α m are added/subtracted, such as m_eff=m v^2/(v^2+α m)); m_eff must have units of mass. (3) Expressing transverse acceleration as a geometric factor times qE/m_eff (e.g., a_y ∝ tanθ·qE/m_eff) without deriving it from v=∇_p K and dp/dt=F; specifically, any a_y depending solely on F/m_eff rather than on α and the momentum direction is flagged. (4) Failing to provide explicit lab-frame components a_x and a_y that are dimensionally [length·time^-2] and depend on qE, α (with units of velocity), and the current momentum (p or p_x, p_y). The checker expects to see: dp/dt=qE x̂; v=(dK/dp) p̂, with dK/dp=p/m+α; and acceleration obtained via the chain rule a=dv/dt, which yields nonzero transverse terms proportional to α. Any solution not using this framework or producing dimensionally inconsistent expressions is marked incorrect.

rules.title: Do not set transverse acceleration to zero from zero transverse force under non-parabolic dispersion
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that, in problems where a non-parabolic (non-quadratic) dispersion K(p) is specified (e.g., K = p^2/(2m) + α p, band/quasiparticle contexts), conclude component-wise that a = F/m or that a_y = 0 solely because F_y = 0. In systems with non-parabolic dispersion, the correct relations are F = dp/dt and v(p) = ∂K/∂p; the acceleration is a = dv/dt = (∂v/∂p)·F = (∂^2K/∂p_i∂p_j) F_j, which can produce transverse acceleration even when the external force has no component in that direction. The rule triggers if: (1) the problem statement includes a dispersion relation K(p) that is not purely quadratic in p (keywords: non-parabolic, α p term, band/quasiparticle, effective mass, group velocity), and (2) the solution applies Newton’s second law as a = F/m component-wise or states phrases like 'since F_y=0, a_y=0' without first deriving v(p) = ∂K/∂p and using a = (∂v/∂p)·F (or the effective mass tensor/Hessian of K). It is acceptable to set a ∥ F only when K ∝ p^2 (parabolic dispersion). The rule should mark as incorrect any answer that asserts a_y = 0 from F_y = 0 in such non-parabolic contexts or gives a_x = qE/m, a_y = 0 without using v(p) or the curvature of K.

rules.title: Angular circumference must use g_phi_phi only (no g_rr or g_tt factors)
rules.description: This rule verifies that when a solution computes the proper length/circumference of a circle at fixed r and θ in a diagonal, spherically symmetric spacetime metric, it uses only the angular metric component g_phi_phi and does not introduce radial (g_rr) or temporal (g_tt) factors. Scope: metrics of the form ds^2 = -A(r) dt^2 + B(r) dr^2 + r^2 dθ^2 + r^2 sin^2θ dφ^2 (including Schwarzschild-like forms A(r)=c^2 f(r), B(r)=1/g(r)). Correct principle: For a path with dt=0, dr=0, dθ=0 and varying φ, the proper line element is ds = sqrt(g_phi_phi) dφ. Therefore L = ∫ sqrt(g_phi_phi) dφ. In standard spherical coordinates g_phi_phi = r^2 sin^2θ, so ds = r sinθ dφ and L = 2π r sinθ (at θ=π/2, L = 2π r). Check implementation: 1) Detect computations labeled as circumference/arc length along φ (keywords: circumference, circle, L, ∫ dφ, φ-parameterization) with dt=dr=dθ=0 declared or implied. 2) Verify that the integrand for ds involves only sqrt(g_phi_phi); in spherical form, only r and θ (via r sinθ). 3) Flag as incorrect if the expression for ds or L includes any of the following in the integrand: A(r), f(r), B(r), g(r), factors from g_tt or g_rr (e.g., sqrt(B(r)), 1/sqrt(g(r)), redshift factors, Schwarzschild factors (1 - 2GM/(c^2 r)) or their inverses) multiplying dφ. 4) For the common metric ds^2 = -c^2 f(r) dt^2 + dr^2/g(r) + r^2(dθ^2 + sin^2θ dφ^2), explicitly enforce that L at fixed r,θ does not depend on f(r) or g(r). 5) Acceptable forms: L = 2π r sinθ; L = ∫_0^{2π} r sinθ dφ; L = ∫_0^{2π} sqrt(g_phi_phi) dφ with g_phi_phi = r^2 sin^2θ. 6) Examples to flag: L = ∫_0^{2π} r sqrt(g(r)) dφ; L = 2π r / sqrt(1 - 2GM/(c^2 r)); ds = r sqrt{g(r)} dφ; any inclusion of f(r) or g(r) in ds along φ. Rationale: g_rr multiplies dr^2 (radial distances) and g_tt multiplies dt^2 (temporal intervals); they must not appear in purely angular spatial lengths at fixed r,θ in a diagonal metric.

rules.title: Angular circumference in static spherical metrics must not include radial/time factors
rules.description: Checks solutions that compute the proper circumference of a circle at fixed radius in a static, spherically symmetric spacetime. Preconditions: The metric is diagonal and of the form ds^2 = -A(r) dt^2 + B(r) dr^2 + r^2 dθ^2 + r^2 sin^2θ dφ^2 (e.g., Schwarzschild-like). Verification: For a path with dr = 0, dθ = 0 and varying φ, the proper length element must be ds = sqrt(g_φφ) dφ = r sinθ dφ. Therefore, at θ = π/2 the circumference is L = ∮ r dφ = 2π r. The rule flags an error if (a) the final expression for L depends on A(r), B(r), f(r), g(r), or any radial/time metric functions (e.g., includes sqrt(g(r)), 1/sqrt(g(r)), or factors from g_tt or g_rr), (b) L ≠ 2π r for θ = π/2 under the stated metric, or (c) the solution exhibits internal inconsistency by first simplifying ds^2 along the φ path to r^2 sin^2θ dφ^2 (or ds = r dφ at θ = π/2) and later reintroducing extra r-dependent metric factors from other components into the angular length. This catches unjustified insertions of horizon-related factors into purely angular lengths in spherical spacetimes.

rules.title: Angular circumference must depend only on g_phi_phi, not on g_tt or g_rr near horizons
rules.description: For static, spherically symmetric metrics written in diagonal form ds^2 = -A(r) dt^2 + B(r) dr^2 + C(r) dθ^2 + C(r) sin^2θ dφ^2, any circumference at fixed r and θ must be computed solely from the angular metric component g_φφ = C(r) sin^2θ. Specifically, along a circular path at fixed r = r0 and θ = π/2 with dt = dr = dθ = 0, the line element is ds^2 = g_φφ dφ^2 and the circumference is L = ∮√g_φφ dφ = 2π √g_φφ = 2π √C(r0). Vanishing or divergence of g_tt = -A(r) or g_rr = B(r) at a horizon (e.g., A(r_h) = 0 or B(r_h)^{-1} = 0) affects radial or temporal intervals, not the angular length. The verifier should flag solutions that: (1) include factors of A(r), B(r), or their derivatives (e.g., A(r0), B(r0), A'(r0), B'(r0), or linearizations like B(r_h + ε) ≈ B'(r_h) ε) in ds or L for an angular path at fixed r; (2) argue that the circumference vanishes, diverges, or scales due to A(r) or B(r) near the horizon; or (3) replace √g_φφ by r times functions of A or B for the angular arc length. Acceptable variations include expressing √g_φφ as the areal radius R(r) if the metric is written with C(r) = R(r)^2, and Taylor expanding C(r_h + ε) itself for small ε. Do not penalize correct uses of √g_φφ only. This rule targets the specific modeling error of using horizon behavior of g_tt or g_rr to modify angular circumference.

rules.title: Beaming cone width ≈ 1/γ, not dependent on pitch angle φ
rules.description: When verifying synchrotron or relativistic emission solutions, ensure the relativistic beaming cone half-angle around the instantaneous velocity direction is stated as approximately 1/γ for γ >> 1 and is independent of the pitch angle φ. Pitch angle φ affects the rate at which the velocity direction sweeps past the observer (and thus pulse duration) via sinφ, but it does not change the beaming cone width. Flag as an error if the solution defines or uses an effective beaming angle with explicit φ-dependence, such as θ_beam ≈ sinφ/γ, θ_eff ≈ sinφ/[γ(1−β cosφ)], or θ_beam ≈ 1/[γ(1−β cosφ)] where φ is the pitch angle to the magnetic field. Also flag claims that the beaming angle scales with sinφ or cosφ. Accept formulations where θ_beam ≈ O(1)·1/γ (e.g., 1/γ, 0.5/γ) and where φ only enters timing estimates (e.g., pulse duration scaling with sinφ via the sweep rate), not the cone width.

rules.title: Incorrect ultra-relativistic approximation β ≈ 1/γ (v ≈ c/γ)
rules.description:
This rule detects misuse of the velocity–Lorentz factor relation in ultra-relativistic regimes (γ ≫ 1). It flags solutions that assert or implicitly use v ≈ c/γ, β ≈ 1/γ, or γ ≈ 1/β. Checks performed: 
- Text/Math pattern scan: Trigger if the solution contains statements or substitutions such as "v ≈ c/γ", "β ≈ 1/γ", "β = 1/γ", "γ = 1/β", or any derivation step that replaces β by 1/γ in the γ ≫ 1 limit. 
- Limit consistency check: Evaluate the implied behavior as γ → ∞. Flag if the solution leads to β → 0 or v → 0, which is inconsistent with ultra-relativistic motion (correctly, β → 1 and v → c). 
- Scaling check: If a derived quantity’s γ-dependence arises solely from the incorrect substitution β ∝ 1/γ (e.g., timescales or frequencies acquiring a 1/γ factor when the correct leading behavior should be O(1)), flag the derivation. 
- Reference relation: The correct kinematic relation is β = sqrt(1 − 1/γ^2), with the ultra-relativistic approximation β ≈ 1 − 1/(2γ^2). Use this to validate substitutions and asymptotic expansions. 
- Example heuristic (non-exhaustive): For relativistic gyro motion in a uniform magnetic field, the gyrofrequency is ω = qB/(γ m) and the period is T = 2πγ m/(qB), independent of β and pitch angle φ. If β or sin φ appears in T due to replacing v by c/γ, flag as a likely consequence of the incorrect β ≈ 1/γ assumption.

rules.title: Rigid accelerating rocket: proper separation must be constant
rules.description: This rule checks solutions that use the equivalence principle or accelerating (Rindler) frames for a rigid rocket. It flags modeling errors where the proper separation d between two fixed points in the rocket (e.g., emitter and receiver at opposite ends) is stated or treated as time-dependent in the rocket’s frame. Specifically, it triggers when: (a) the solution asserts that d decreases/increases due to the rocket’s acceleration, (b) d(t) is introduced to compute frequency shifts, or (c) a relative velocity v ≈ gΔt between endpoints in the ship’s frame is used to produce a Doppler shift. For a Born-rigid rocket, the endpoints remain at rest in the rocket frame with constant proper separation; the frequency shift should be attributed to the effective gravitational field (gravitational redshift) or, equivalently, to kinematic effects accumulated over the light-travel time in an inertial frame, not to a changing d. The rule also flags the inconsistent assumption that all points of a ‘rigid’ rocket share identical proper acceleration, which would imply changing separation; Born rigidity requires different proper accelerations along the rocket. Valid treatments should give a first-order shift Δf/f ≈ ±(g d / c^2) and avoid attributing the shift to shrinking or growing distance within the rocket frame.

rules.title: COM boost must use total four-momentum (not single-particle β, γ)
rules.description: Checks that any Lorentz boost to the center-of-momentum (COM) frame in a multi-particle initial state uses β_cm and γ_cm derived from the total four-momentum, not from a single particle’s velocity or Lorentz factor. Required formulas: β_cm = |Σ p_i| c / (Σ E_i) and γ_cm = 1 / sqrt(1 − β_cm^2), where E_i and p_i are the lab-frame energies and momenta of all incoming particles. Flags an error if the solution: (a) explicitly sets the COM boost as β = p_j c / E_j or γ = E_j / (m_j c^2) for any single particle j when more than one particle is present; or (b) uses a β_boost or γ_boost that differs from the value computed from the total four-momentum by more than a small tolerance (e.g., relative difference > 1e−3). Special attention: for two-particle collisions with one particle at rest (e.g., e− with energy E_e and momentum p_e, and e+ at rest with energy m_e c^2), the correct COM boost is β_cm = p_e c / (E_e + m_e c^2). Using β = p_e c / E_e and γ = E_e / (m_e c^2) to represent the COM boost must be flagged. Consequence: using a single-particle β, γ for the COM transformation leads to incorrect transformed photon energies and angles; the rule prevents this modeling error.

rules.title: Missing derivation: jump to known final formula in SR-based rocket problems
rules.description: Trigger when the problem statement explicitly requests a derivation (keywords: 'derive', 'show that', 'prove', 'obtain') using special relativity or specified conservation laws (e.g., 'using conservation of energy and momentum in special relativity'), but the submitted solution skips the derivation and asserts a known final result. The rule checks that the solution includes: (1) explicit setup of the relativistic conservation laws (at minimum, one momentum equation and one energy equation written with relativistic factors, e.g., p = gamma m v and E = gamma m c^2, or a 4-momentum statement), (2) intermediate algebra/differential steps connecting those equations to the target relationship (e.g., elimination of exhaust terms, relation between dm and dv, integration from Mi to M), and (3) a logically continuous sequence from setup to final expression. Flag an error if the solution presents the final relativistic rocket equation (e.g., forms involving tanh or ln(Mi/M)) or any target formula after phrases such as 'we know', 'it is known that', 'the relativistic rocket equation is', 'after some algebra/simplification', 'thus/therefore' without showing intermediate equations and manipulations. Tolerate concise derivations only if at least two nontrivial intermediate mathematical steps are shown and the conservation equations are explicitly stated. This rule is intended to catch unjustified logical jumps where a derivation is required, especially in SR rocket problems.

rules.title: Transcendental function arguments must be dimensionless (e.g., proper time in SR)
rules.description: This rule checks for dimensional consistency when a variable with physical units is used as the argument of transcendental functions (sin, cos, tan, sinh, cosh, tanh, exp, ln). Specifically: (1) If proper time τ is introduced with units of time (e.g., via ds^2 = −c^2 dτ^2), then any occurrence of sinh(τ), cosh(τ), exp(τ), sin(τ), cos(τ), ln(τ), etc., is flagged unless the argument is rendered dimensionless by an appropriate scale factor (e.g., ω τ, k x, a τ / c, t/τ0, x/L) or the symbol is explicitly declared dimensionless. (2) In relativistic uniformly accelerated motion (Rindler/hyperbolic worldlines), verify that the argument of hyperbolic functions is α τ / c (or an explicitly defined dimensionless rapidity η) rather than τ alone; examples: flag t(τ) = (c/α) sinh(τ) and accept t(τ) = (c/α) sinh(α τ / c). The rule performs unit analysis on the function argument: if the argument carries nontrivial units (time, length, etc.) and no unit-canceling factor is present, it is a violation. Exceptions are allowed only when the argument variable has been explicitly defined as dimensionless (e.g., "let η = α τ / c" and then using sinh(η)). This catches errors where dimensional quantities are used directly inside transcendental functions, ensuring consistent unit handling.

rules.title: Nonzero β^2 correction in classical vs relativistic Doppler comparison
rules.description: This rule checks solutions that compare classical and relativistic Doppler shifts for light when the speed ratio β = v/c is small but nonzero. The verifier will: (1) detect tasks that ask for the difference/error between classical and relativistic expressions; (2) compute β from the given v and c; (3) require that the comparison retains terms up to order β^2 (via series expansion or high-precision numerical evaluation). Specifically, for small β the fractional difference between the classical and relativistic results is O(β^2) and not identically zero (e.g., for wavelength with an approaching source, the magnitude of the fractional difference is approximately ½β^2). The rule flags the following: (a) conclusions of "0% error" or "no difference" when β > 0 without an explicit β^2-order analysis or an uncertainty bound; (b) comparisons that round both results to the same value using insufficient significant figures that mask an O(β^2) difference; (c) derivations that truncate at first order in β and infer equality. To pass, the solution must either present a second-order expansion in β and report the nonzero fractional error (order β^2 with an appropriate coefficient for the quantity compared), or provide numerical values with enough precision to resolve the β^2-scale difference and avoid declaring zero error.

rules.title: Require β^2 discrepancy when comparing classical vs relativistic Doppler; forbid 'zero error' claims at nonzero v
rules.description: Checks solutions that compare classical and relativistic predictions for Doppler shift (or any relativistic correction) at nonzero velocity v. Flags an error if the solution concludes 'zero error', 'exact agreement', or infers equivalence by matching only first-order terms in β = v/c. The correct reasoning is that the leading difference between classical and relativistic results appears at order β^2, and is small but nonzero for any v > 0. For longitudinal Doppler of light: lambda_rel/lambda = sqrt((1 - β)/(1 + β)) ≈ 1 - β + 0.5*β^2, whereas the classical approximation gives lambda_class/lambda ≈ 1 - β + β^2; their relative difference is ~0.5*β^2. A valid solution must either include a second-order expansion or provide an explicit error bound of order (v/c)^2 with a numeric estimate for the given v (e.g., for v = 6000 m/s, β ≈ 2e-5, so the relative difference is ~2e-10). If the solution asserts 'zero error' or compares only first-order terms to justify equivalence at nonzero v, mark it incorrect.

rules.title: Detect premature rounding that hides O((v/c)^2) differences in classical vs relativistic Doppler
rules.description: This rule checks comparisons between the classical and relativistic Doppler formulas at small beta = v/c for premature rounding and loss of second-order accuracy. Trigger conditions: (1) The solution uses or compares classical Doppler factors of the form F_class = 1/(1 ± beta) with relativistic factors F_rel = sqrt((1 ∓ beta)/(1 ± beta)), or their equivalent frequency forms. (2) The solution rounds intermediate multiplicative factors (e.g., sqrt(1 − 2 beta + ...) and 1/(1 ± beta)) to the same few significant digits (such as both ≈ 0.99998 for beta ≈ 2×10^-5) and then concludes there is no difference or reports a zero discrepancy. Verification: For beta << 1, the expected fractional difference in the wavelength factors is |F_rel − F_class|/F_rel ≈ 0.5 beta^2 (same magnitude for the frequency factors, possibly with opposite sign in the raw difference). The verifier should compute beta from the given v and c, then compute delta_expected = 0.5*beta^2. The solution must either (a) present a series expansion including the second-order term and report a nonzero discrepancy of order beta^2, or (b) perform a numerical comparison with sufficient precision to resolve O(beta^2) (i.e., keep at least −log10(beta^2)+1 significant digits in the factors; for beta = 2×10^-5 this is ≈ 10 significant digits). Flag as an error if: (i) the reported discrepancy is 0 or omitted when a comparison is made, (ii) the discrepancy magnitude differs from 0.5 beta^2 by more than an order of magnitude, or (iii) the computation shows identical rounded values for F_class and F_rel to low precision without any second-order analysis. This rule generalizes to near-cancellation cases where two models agree to first order in a small parameter: students must carry second-order terms or sufficient numerical precision to avoid suppressing true differences.

rules.title: Incorrect Doppler frame/sign for laser–atom resonance
rules.description:
Checks solutions to laser-excitation of moving atoms/ions for misuse of Doppler formulas and wrong detuning sign. Triggers when the problem context involves tuning a lab laser to drive a known atomic transition in a moving atom/ion (keywords: laser, resonance, absorption, moving ion/atom, Doppler). The rule verifies the following:

- Correct resonance framing: The solution should impose the resonance condition in the particle rest frame, f_rest = f0, and relate lab and rest-frame frequencies via the relativistic Doppler transform: f_rest = gamma (1 - beta cosθ) f_lab. For head-on counter-propagating geometry (ion and laser approach), cosθ = -1, thus f_lab = f0 / [gamma (1 + beta)]. In wavelength form: λ_lab = λ0 gamma (1 + beta). Classical limit: f_lab ≈ f0 / (1 + beta), λ_lab ≈ λ0 (1 + beta).

- Error patterns to flag:
  1) Using observer/source "observed shift" formulas (e.g., λ' = λ sqrt[(1 - beta)/(1 + beta)] or f' = f sqrt[(1 + beta)/(1 - beta)]) as the required lab laser value for resonance, without inverting to solve for f_lab that makes f_rest = f0.
  2) Labeling λ' = λ/(1 ± beta) or f' = f(1 ± beta) as the classical resonance prediction for the lab laser, instead of the correct classical resonance relations f_lab = f0/(1 ± beta) and λ_lab = λ0(1 ± beta).
  3) Detuning sign inconsistency: For head-on (counter-propagating) excitation, the required lab laser must be red-detuned relative to λ0 (λ_lab > λ0). Flag conclusions that predict blue detuning (λ_lab < λ0) for this geometry.
  4) Gamma misplacement/omission: Flag relations like f_lab = f0 gamma (1 ± beta) or λ_lab = λ0 / [gamma (1 ± beta)] as resonance conditions; the correct is f_lab = f0 / [gamma (1 ± beta)], λ_lab = λ0 gamma (1 ± beta).
  5) Wrong order of relativistic correction: Between relativistic and classical resonance predictions, the leading correction is +0.5 beta^2 (i.e., ratio ≈ gamma). Flag claims of an O(beta) difference or incorrect sign for the correction.
  6) Missing explicit resonance step: No explicit statement or use of f_rest = f0 (or equivalent) when determining the lab laser frequency/wavelength.

This rule helps catch conceptual frame mix-ups where students apply observed-shift formulas (appropriate for measuring a moving source) instead of the resonance condition for tuning a lab laser to drive a transition in a moving atom/ion, leading to incorrect sign (blue vs red) and missing gamma factors.

rules.title: Extraneous Lorentz length contraction in equal-arrival-time ellipse center
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that introduce Lorentz length contraction or dependence on object length L or the speed of light c when deriving the center position x_c of an equal-arrival-time ellipse that is explicitly requested "in terms of v, θ, t" only. Checks performed: (1) Parse the final expression provided for x_c and verify that its free-variable set is a subset of {v, θ, t} (and numeric constants). If the expression contains L, L', c, γ, or sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), flag an error. (2) Scan the derivation for explicit use of length-contraction formulas (e.g., L' = L sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), γ = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), or textual mentions of "length contraction") applied to the object's geometry; if present, flag an error. Rationale: The center of symmetry of the equal-arrival-time ellipse for a uniformly radiating linear source moving along x is determined by kinematics (v), viewing angle (θ), and the observation time t; it does not depend on the object's proper length L or relativistic length contraction, and c should not enter x_c when the prompt restricts variables to v, θ, t. Exceptions: Do not apply this rule if the problem statement explicitly requests dependence on L or c or asks for full image formation including endpoint delays; otherwise, treat any inclusion of L, c, γ, or length contraction in x_c as a modeling error.

rules.title: Misuse of point-source apparent-position or naive length contraction for ellipse center of a moving radiating rod
rules.description:
Scope: Problems asking for the center of symmetry (or geometry) of the equal-arrival-time ellipse produced by light from an extended object (e.g., a luminous rod) moving at constant velocity. 

Flag a solution if it treats the extended-object geometry using point-source apparent-position relations or naive Lorentz length contraction, instead of retarded-time conditions for the object’s endpoints.

Trigger conditions (one or more):
- The solution applies Lorentz length contraction (e.g., L' = L sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) or L/γ) as a primary step to determine the apparent shape/center without setting up light-travel-time constraints (no use of a light-cone/retarded-time equation t_obs = t_em + R/c for the endpoints or distributed elements).
- The solution uses or derives a point-emitter apparent-position formula to locate the center, e.g., x_app = v t / (1 - β cos θ) or any expression featuring division by (1 - β cos θ) for the center position.
- The final expression for the ellipse center x_c contains no dependence on the rod length L despite the problem specifying L, and there is no explicit derivation showing legitimate cancellation of L under stated limits/assumptions.
- Reliance on generic aberration or Doppler formulas to place the center, with no calculation of retarded positions for both ends (absence of solving for emission times from each end that satisfy equal arrival to the observer).

Rationale: The center of symmetry of the equal-arrival-time ellipse for an extended source must be obtained by solving the retarded-time conditions for both endpoints (or integrating along the rod) and then deducing the ellipse geometry (e.g., via the midpoint of retarded endpoint positions projected along the observation direction). Point-source apparent-position relations and naive length contraction do not yield the correct center for an extended, radiating object.

Examples of phrases/forms to flag: "we first Lorentz-contract the rod", "apparent position x_app = v t/(1 - β cos θ)", "divide by (1 - β cos θ)", using aberration to place the center without retarded-time equations.

Exception: Do not flag if the solution explicitly sets up retarded-time equations for both endpoints, solves them, and either (a) derives a center expression that properly depends on L, or (b) justifies with clear limiting arguments why L cancels in the specific regime considered.

rules.title: Equal-energy claim vs COM-to-lab boost inconsistency
rules.description: Detects internal inconsistency in two-photon (or two massless) production solutions: if the solution asserts the two photons have equal energies in the lab, but then models the center-of-mass (COM) emission as exactly along and opposite the boost direction (θ′ = 0 and θ′ = π) and applies Lorentz energy transforms E_lab = γ E′ (1 ± β), it will necessarily produce unequal lab energies for β ≠ 0. The verifier flags cases where all of the following are present: (1) an explicit claim of equal lab energies (e.g., 'E_A = E_B' or 'equal energies'); (2) an initial state with nonzero net momentum in the lab (e.g., one particle moving, the other at rest, implying β > 0 for the COM-to-lab boost); and (3) a COM-to-lab step that sets θ′ = 0/π or uses energy expressions proportional to (1 ± β). If these conditions co-occur, the solution contains a logical contradiction. The rule also flags the pattern of setting E_A = E_B = (E_total)/2 while simultaneously deriving Doppler-shifted unequal lab energies. A consistent solution must either have β = 0 (lab = COM) or choose COM emission angles not aligned with the boost so that equal lab energies in the lab are achievable.

rules.title: Four-velocity normalization must use metric components without extra sign flips
rules.description: Checks the stated normalization of a timelike four-velocity against the metric signature and components used earlier in the solution. When a diagonal metric (e.g., Schwarzschild) is specified, the normalization must be written as g_{μν} u^μ u^ν = -c^2 for the mostly-plus signature (ds^2 = -|g_tt| dt^2 + ... with g_tt < 0, spatial components > 0) or g_{μν} u^μ u^ν = +c^2 for the mostly-minus signature (ds^2 = +|g_tt| dt^2 - ...). The rule flags: (a) placing an extra minus sign in front of an already-signed metric component, e.g., writing -g_tt (u^t)^2 + g_rr (u^r)^2 = -c^2 when the metric line element has g_tt < 0 and g_rr > 0; (b) selectively flipping signs of individual terms (e.g., -g_tt, -g_rr) instead of using g_{μν} directly; (c) using an RHS sign that is inconsistent with the inferred signature from the presented metric; (d) inconsistent intermediate normalization statements even if later algebra happens to cancel the sign error. For radial motion (dθ = dφ = 0), the accepted forms are: mostly-plus: g_tt (u^t)^2 + g_rr (u^r)^2 = -c^2; mostly-minus: g_tt (u^t)^2 + g_rr (u^r)^2 = +c^2. The rule parses the metric given in the solution to infer the signature and then verifies that the normalization uses the metric components as written (no ad hoc extra minus signs) and that the right-hand side sign matches the signature.

rules.title: GPS clock GR+SR daily bias and range conversion check
rules.description: This rule verifies the first-order combined general-relativistic (GR) and special-relativistic (SR) clock rate correction for a GPS satellite and checks the correct conversion of time bias to range error. It applies when a solution estimates the daily timing/range error due to relativity for GPS. Checks performed: (1) Compute expected fractional rate difference using δ ≈ (GM/c^2)·(1/R_E − 1/r_sat) − v^2/(2c^2), with v = √(GM/r_sat). Using standard constants (G=6.674×10^-11, M_E=5.972×10^24 kg, c=2.998×10^8 m/s, R_E≈6.371×10^6 m, r_sat≈2.656×10^7 m), the target values are: δ_GR ≈ +5.3×10^-10, δ_SR ≈ −8.3×10^-11, net δ ≈ +4.5×10^-10. Flag the solution if the reported net fractional rate deviates by more than ±30% from 4.5×10^-10 without justification. (2) From δ, the daily time bias is Δt_day ≈ δ·86400 s ≈ 3.9×10^-5 s (≈ 39 μs). Flag values outside 2×10^-5–6×10^-5 s unless justified. (3) Range error must be computed using the speed of light: range_error = c·Δt_day ≈ 11.5 km. Flag any conversion that uses satellite orbital speed v (i.e., range_error ≈ v·Δt_day, typically 150–350 m/day) as conceptually incorrect. Explicitly detect this by comparing reported range error to v·Δt_day within 10% tolerance; if matched, raise an error. (4) Flag internally inconsistent outputs (e.g., simultaneously reporting ~178 m and ~12 km daily range errors) as contradictory. This rule catches misuse of v instead of c in time-to-range conversion and incorrect/implausible magnitudes for GPS relativistic clock corrections.

rules.title: Correct combination of SR and GR time dilation for GPS clocks
rules.description:
This rule verifies the logical combination of special relativity (SR) and general relativity (GR) time-dilation effects when comparing satellite and ground clocks in weak-field conditions (e.g., GPS). It expects the satellite proper-time rate relative to coordinate time to be combined multiplicatively, not via ad hoc 'gamma' ratios. Required forms:
- Satellite rate: dτ_sat/dt = sqrt(1 - 2GM/(c^2 r_sat)) * sqrt(1 - v_sat^2/c^2)
- Satellite-to-ground rate ratio: R = (sqrt(1 - 2GM/(c^2 r_sat)) / sqrt(1 - 2GM/(c^2 R_E))) * sqrt(1 - v_sat^2/c^2)
- Valid first-order expansion: R ≈ 1 + (GM/c^2)(1/R_E - 1/r_sat) - v_sat^2/(2c^2)
The rule flags solutions that:
- Express the rate ratio as γ_SR × γ_GR or γ_SR / γ_GR (mixing SR and GR via arbitrary 'gamma' factors),
- Use γ_SR = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) directly as the rate instead of its inverse (i.e., fail to use dτ/dt = 1/γ_SR = sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2)),
- Define a GR 'gamma' (e.g., γ_GR = 1/sqrt(1 - 2GM/(c^2 r))) and combine it algebraically with γ_SR,
- Add SR and GR contributions without an explicitly correct first-order fractional rate (e.g., Δ_total = Δ_SR + Δ_GR with incorrect signs; the correct weak-field fractional rate must match the expansion above),
- Omit division by the Earth-surface gravitational factor when comparing satellite to ground clocks.
Any combination not matching the multiplicative square-root factors or their consistent first-order expansion is flagged as a logical inconsistency in SR/GR mixing.

rules.title: Require velocity-based justification for Lorentz factor approximations
rules.description:
This rule flags solutions in special-relativistic, variable-mass problems (e.g., rocket/exhaust derivations using conservation of energy/momentum) that approximate Lorentz factors (γ) without explicit velocity-based justification. Specifically:
- If the solution sets the exhaust’s Lorentz factor to γ_exhaust ≈ 1 (or treats the exhaust nonrelativistically) without explicitly demonstrating u/c ≪ 1 and quantifying the resulting error (e.g., γ − 1 ≈ ½β^2), flag.
- If the solution sets the rocket’s post-ejection Lorentz factor equal to its pre-ejection value (γ_after ≈ γ_before or γ ≈ γ_i) solely because Δm is small, an infinitesimal mass is expelled, or similar mass-based reasoning, flag. γ depends on velocity, not mass; an infinitesimal mass change does not justify neglecting Δv or Δγ.
- If approximations to γ lead to degenerate conservation statements (e.g., the momentum/energy equations collapse to a trivial or contradictory equality such as 0 = Δm·u/V1), flag as likely caused by unjustified γ approximations.
Accepted justification criteria:
- The solution must state and use a velocity bound (e.g., |u|/c ≤ ε ≪ 1 or |Δv|/c ≤ ε) and demonstrate that the neglected γ-terms are of higher order than the required accuracy (e.g., O(β^2) or O(Δγ/γ)).
- Equating γ values at different stages is acceptable only if equal velocities are explicitly shown or if a quantified small Δv makes |Δγ/γ| negligible relative to the solution’s precision.
Example violations to flag:
- “γ_Δm ≈ 1 because Δm is small.”
- “Take γ ≈ γ_i; the mass change is infinitesimal.”
- “Neglect change in γ” without bounding β or Δv.
Rationale: Lorentz factors depend on velocity, not mass. Exhaust speeds and rocket speed changes can be relativistic; mass smallness alone cannot justify γ ≈ 1 or γ equality.

rules.title: Misapplication of gravitational lensing to massive-particle deflection
rules.description: Checks for conceptual mixing between relativistic light deflection (gravitational lensing) and Newtonian scattering of a massive particle. Trigger conditions: (a) The problem context or solution mentions a massive projectile (e.g., star, planet, massive body) with impact parameter b and finite speed v (keywords like 'star', 'massive', 'impact parameter', 'velocity v', or uses b1 = GM/v^2); AND (b) the solution justifies the deflection using 'gravitational lensing', 'Einstein light deflection', 'General Relativity', 'relativistic', or invokes the speed of light c; OR (c) the solution writes or cites the light-deflection formula α ≈ 4GM/(b c^2) or defines b1 using c (e.g., b1 = GM/c^2); OR (d) the solution uses the correct Newtonian formula α ≈ 2GM/(b v^2) but explicitly attributes it to gravitational lensing or relativistic light deflection. Rationale: For massive particles at speed v, the appropriate small-angle deflection is Newtonian (α ≈ 2GM/(b v^2)) derived from classical scattering, whereas gravitational lensing (α ≈ 4GM/(b c^2)) applies to photons. Flag any solution that mixes these regimes or uses lensing terminology to justify a Newtonian result.

rules.title: Gravitational/Equivalence Principle Frequency Shift Sign
rules.description: Checks the sign and physical interpretation of the first-order frequency shift for light traveling between two points in a uniformly accelerated frame or uniform gravitational field (via the equivalence principle). Context: small parameter gd/c^2 with gd << c^2 and linear approximation f_rec ≈ f_emit (1 ± gd/c^2). The rule determines direction of propagation relative to the effective field: in an accelerating rocket with acceleration +x, the effective gravitational field points toward −x (rear). If a photon travels down the field (from higher position to lower position along the field direction), it must be blueshifted: f_rec = f_emit (1 + gd/c^2). If it travels up the field (from lower to higher), it must be redshifted: f_rec = f_emit (1 − gd/c^2). The rule flags errors when a solution (a) assigns a redshift (minus sign) to downward propagation or claims the photon “loses energy going to lower height,” or (b) assigns a blueshift (plus sign) to upward propagation. For the specific setup where the rocket accelerates in +x, emitter at the right/front and receiver at the left/rear separated by distance d, the correct relation is f_alien = f1 (1 + gd/c^2). Any statement or formula contradicting this direction-dependent sign (e.g., f_alien = f1 (1 − gd/c^2) for right-to-left transmission) is flagged. The rule also checks for consistent physical language: photons lose energy climbing (upward, redshift) and gain energy falling (downward, blueshift); reversing this interpretation is marked incorrect.

rules.title: Require relative gravitational time dilation (satellite vs ground)
rules.description: When comparing clock rates between a GPS satellite and an Earth-surface clock, the gravitational redshift must be computed as a relative effect between the two radii. The correct weak-field Schwarzschild factor is the ratio sqrt(1 - 2GM/(c^2 r_sat)) / sqrt(1 - 2GM/(c^2 R_E)), or equivalently the fractional difference Δ ≈ (GM/c^2)(1/R_E - 1/r_sat). The verifier should flag solutions that: (a) apply the gravitational time dilation at the satellite radius only (e.g., use sqrt(1 - 2GM/(c^2 r_sat)) without an Earth-surface term), (b) omit the reference clock’s gravitational factor at R_E, (c) use the wrong sign for the gravitational effect (the satellite at higher altitude must tick faster than the ground clock; Δ_grav > 0 since 1/R_E > 1/r_sat), or (d) propagate position error using an absolute factor rather than the relative rate difference between the two clocks. Solutions may use either the exact ratio or the weak-field approximation with both radii present; absence of R_E or inclusion of only r_sat indicates a modeling error.

rules.title: Gravitational time-dilation/redshift sign check (Schwarzschild)
rules.description: This rule verifies the sign and magnitude of the gravitational time-dilation (redshift) factor for a clock at radius r in a Schwarzschild field. It targets solutions that compute or approximate the factor f(r) = sqrt(1 - 2 G M / (c^2 r)). Checks performed: (1) If a solution presents a single-radius gravitational factor (not a ratio between two radii), the numeric value must satisfy 0 < f(r) < 1 for any positive M and r > 2 G M / c^2. Flag an error if f(r) is reported as greater than 1 (e.g., written as 1 + δ with δ > 0). (2) Validate first-order (small-parameter) expansions: for x = 2 G M / (c^2 r) > 0, sqrt(1 - x) ≈ 1 - x/2 = 1 - G M / (c^2 r). Flag if the linear term is given with a plus sign (e.g., 1 + G M / (c^2 r)). (3) If the expansion is expressed using the Newtonian potential Φ, ensure the definition Φ = - G M / r is respected and the linearized factor is written as 1 + Φ / c^2 (which is less than 1). Flag if 1 + |Φ| / c^2 or 1 - Φ / c^2 is used. Guard against false positives: do not flag when the quantity is explicitly a ratio between two radii, such as f(r_sat)/f(r_surface), which correctly can be greater than 1 even though each individual f(r) is less than 1.

rules.title: Restrict to gravitational time dilation when requested; flag SR mixing
rules.description:
This rule verifies that a solution respects the requested scope of relativistic corrections. Applicable when the prompt explicitly asks for the general relativistic (gravitational) time dilation only (e.g., references to 'this effect' from a prior part defining gravitational time dilation). The checker should: 
- Scan the solution for inclusion of special relativistic (kinematic) time dilation terms (e.g., Lorentz factor γ = 1/sqrt(1−v^2/c^2), v/c, β, or −v^2/(2c^2) contributions to clock rates). If any v-dependent SR term is used while the prompt specifies gravitational-only, flag a modeling error. 
- Allow use of orbital mechanics (e.g., Kepler's law) to find orbital radius r; however, if velocity v is subsequently used to compute time dilation, flag. 
- Confirm gravitational-only treatment uses the weak-field expression based on potential differences: fractional rate difference Δ(dτ/dt) ≈ ΔΦ/c^2 with Φ = −GM/r, and no velocity-dependent terms. 
- If both GR and SR are legitimately requested, require correct combination in the weak-field, slow-motion limit: dτ/dt ≈ 1 + Φ/c^2 − v^2/(2c^2). If combination is attempted without this form or signs are inconsistent with altitude effects (gravitational term increases rate at higher altitude; SR term decreases), flag. 
- Numeric heuristic for GPS context: gravitational-only clock offset ≈ +45 μs/day; net combined ≈ +38 μs/day. If an answer near the net combined value is presented when gravitational-only is requested, flag as scope violation. 
This rule catches solutions that mix kinematic SR effects into a calculation that should isolate the gravitational time dilation, or that combine effects without using the correct weak-field formula.

rules.title: Relativistic gyroperiod/gyrofrequency in uniform B must be independent of β and pitch angle
rules.description:
This rule verifies the correct modeling of a charged particle’s gyrofrequency/gyroperiod in a uniform magnetic field, especially in relativistic contexts (synchrotron motion). It enforces that: 
- In the relativistic regime (explicit statements like γ ≫ 1, relativistic electron, synchrotron), the angular gyrofrequency and period must be ω_g = |q| B/(γ m) and T_g = 2π γ m/(|q| B). 
- There must be no dependence on speed (β = v/c), perpendicular speed v⊥, or pitch angle φ in ω_g or T_g. Pitch angle affects gyroradius r_L = γ m v⊥/(|q| B) = γ m β c sinφ/(|q| B), not ω_g or T_g. 
- Flag as errors any expressions for gyrofrequency/period that include β, v⊥, or sinφ (e.g., T_g ∝ γ β sinφ/(qB), ω_g ∝ qB/(m γ β sinφ), or any factor of sinφ in ω_g/T_g). 
- In a relativistic context, flag the omission of γ (e.g., using nonrelativistic ω_g0 = |q| B/m or T_g0 = 2π m/(|q| B) while asserting γ ≫ 1). 
- Dimensional sanity check: ω_g must depend only on q, B, m, and possibly γ; T_g must depend only on q, B, m, and γ. If velocity-dependent factors appear in ω_g/T_g, flag the modeling error. 
- Applicable synonyms to scan: gyrofrequency, cyclotron frequency/Larmor frequency; gyroperiod, cyclotron period.

rules.title: Small-Eb relativistic kinematics: Ep must scale as 1/Eb and use invariants
rules.description:
This rule checks solutions that determine a projectile energy Ep in terms of mp, mΔ, and a small beam energy Eb. It enforces proper relativistic 4-vector treatment and correct leading-order scaling with Eb. The rule triggers an error if any of the following are detected: 
- Ep is derived using non-relativistic kinetic-energy partitioning (e.g., reduced-mass methods) instead of invariant 4-momentum relations. Typical red flag: p_b^2 ≈ 2 μ Eb with μ = mp mΔ/(mp + mΔ). 
- The invariant mass is misused or absent. The solution should explicitly or implicitly use s = (p_p + p_b)^2 and E^2 − p^2 = m^2 (c = 1) for each particle, not sums of scalar kinetic energies. 
- The leading-order dependence of Ep on small Eb is linear or non-inverse (Ep ∝ Eb^α with α ≥ 0). In correct two-beam kinematics near threshold, Ep should scale inversely with Eb at leading order, e.g., Ep ≈ (mΔ^2 − mp^2)/(4 Eb) up to geometry/angle factors. 
- Algebraic expansions are performed on mismatched quantities (mixing rest-mass energies and kinetic energies) to obtain p_b^2 and Ep. 
Pass criteria: The derivation references or is consistent with s = (p_p + p_b)^2 and E^2 − p^2 = m^2, avoids reduced-mass kinetic-energy splitting, and yields Ep with leading 1/Eb scaling (coefficient consistent with masses, such as (mΔ^2 − mp^2)/(const × Eb)).

rules.title: Doppler in laser absorption: use absorber rest-frame transform and correct shift direction
rules.description: This rule checks Doppler-shift reasoning in laser-excitation/absorption setups where a stationary laser interacts with a moving atom/ion (the absorber). To achieve resonance, the laser frequency must be transformed into the absorber’s rest frame. The correct relation is ν_rest = γ(1 − β cos θ) ν_lab, where β = v/c, γ = 1/√(1 − β²), and θ is the angle between the ion velocity and the laser propagation direction. For counter-propagating geometry (ion moving opposite to the laser, θ = π), ν_rest = γ(1 + β) ν_lab, so the required laboratory frequency is ν_lab = ν0 / [γ(1 + β)] and the required laboratory wavelength is λ_lab = λ0 γ(1 + β), i.e., a red shift relative to the rest wavelength. The rule flags solutions that: (a) apply source-moving observer formulas (classical or relativistic) directly to the laser light, such as λ' = λ/(1 ± v/c), ν' = ν(1 ± v/c), or ν' = ν √((1 − β)/(1 + β)), instead of transforming to the absorber’s rest frame; (b) predict a blue shift (λ_lab < λ0) for counter-propagating absorption, contrary to the correct red shift; or (c) omit the Lorentz factor γ in a relativistic treatment of light absorption. The rule is triggered in contexts with keywords like 'absorption', 'resonance', 'laser spectroscopy', 'moving atom/ion', and 'stationary laser', and it verifies that the solution uses ν_rest = γ(1 − β cos θ) ν_lab (and its consequences) rather than a moving-source observer formula, with the correct sign of shift for the stated geometry.

rules.title: Require transverse light-path geometry in off-axis viewing problems
rules.description: Checks that solutions for moving radiating sources with a specified viewing angle (θ) or off-axis observer correctly include nonzero transverse separation in light-travel-time modeling. The rule triggers when the problem references an ellipse of equal-arrival-time, viewing angle θ, off-axis geometry, impact parameter, or retarded-time effects. It verifies: (1) Light-path distance is modeled with a Euclidean norm (e.g., cΔt = sqrt((Δx)^2 + (Δy)^2 + ...)) rather than a 1D simplification like Δt = |Δx|/c or ct = |x - x0|. (2) A transverse distance variable (d, y, b, R_perp, etc.) appears and is not set to zero unless the problem explicitly states θ = 0 or the observer is exactly collinear. (3) The derived quantity (e.g., center of symmetry x_c) depends on θ; flag if θ is provided in the problem but absent from the final expression or intermediate equations (e.g., no sinθ/cosθ terms or no transverse term under a square root). (4) Flags reliance solely on Lorentz length contraction (L' = L√(1 - v^2/c^2)) to explain ellipse geometry without retarded-time/light-path geometry. Failure patterns include: equations like t = |x|/c, ct = |x - x0|, explicit setting d = 0, omission of any transverse term in distance expressions, or θ appearing only as a label with no mathematical role.

rules.title: Relativistic pinhole imaging: limit checks and small-angle validity
rules.description: This rule verifies final expressions for the apparent length of a moving rod imaged by a pinhole camera (variables typically include L_app, L, v, c, D). It enforces two sanity-limit requirements and checks the justification of small-angle approximations. Checks: (1) Rest-limit consistency: Substitute v = 0 into the submitted L_app expression and require L_app(v=0) = L exactly (the problem defines L as the measured length at rest). If not equal, flag an error indicating incorrect geometry/projection or double-counting. (2) On-axis limit: Substitute D = 0 and require L_app(D=0) = L * sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) (i.e., a single Lorentz-contraction factor and no extra multiplicative constants). If the expression yields any prefactor other than 1 (e.g., 2) multiplying sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), flag a factor-of-two or projection error. (3) Small-angle approximation validity: If the solution uses approximations like tan(theta) ≈ theta or theta ≈ D/tilde{x} over an extended rod, require an explicit domain condition ensuring small angles across the entire visible portion (e.g., maximum angular span << 1 or D >> characteristic x-range/L). If such a condition is absent, or if the derived L_app violates check (1) due to D-dependent terms from unjustified small-angle use, flag a misuse of approximation. This rule is designed to catch erroneous final formulas that fail basic limiting cases and global, unjustified application of small-angle approximations.

rules.title: Frame-consistent γ usage in relativistic rocket energy conservation
rules.description: This rule flags derivations of the relativistic rocket equation that apply energy conservation with a single, shared Lorentz factor γ for multiple bodies/states, or that fail to specify and consistently use an inertial frame (typically the rocket’s instantaneous rest frame) when balancing energy. The rule checks for any energy balance written in the form γ M_i c^2 = γ M c^2 + γ Δm c^2 (or with a single γ symbol on both sides without subscripts or frame labels), or equivalent statements implying the same γ for the initial rocket, the final rocket, and the exhaust. It also flags omission of the condition γ_i = 1 for the rocket at the instant of expulsion in its rest frame, and omission of a distinct exhaust Lorentz factor γ_e associated with the exhaust’s speed relative to the rocket. The rule requires one of the following to pass: (a) conservation formulated via four-momentum in a single frame; or (b) explicit use of the instantaneous rocket rest frame with energy balance M_i c^2 = M c^2 + γ_e Δm c^2 and momentum balance consistent with the exhaust velocity relative to the rocket. It further checks that the derivation recognizes that the exhaust kinetic energy comes from the rocket’s rest-mass decrease (e.g., ΔE_exhaust = (γ_e − 1) Δm c^2 and ΔM c^2 supplies this energy). Solutions that use lab-frame γ’s without corresponding momentum terms or frame transformations, or that conflate γ’s across different bodies/states, are flagged.

rules.title: Lorentz factor consistency for moving electrons in photon–electron scattering
rules.description: This rule checks that any Lorentz factor γ assigned to an electron that is explicitly described as moving before a collision (nonzero initial momentum or speed) satisfies the relativistic bound γ ≥ 1, with equality only for v = 0. The verifier should: (1) detect contexts involving Compton or inverse Compton scattering where an initial electron is stated to be moving (e.g., p_1e ≠ 0 or v_1e ≠ 0); (2) locate any derived or asserted expression/value for that electron’s γ; (3) evaluate or simplify γ numerically or symbolically under the domain assumptions h > 0, c > 0, m_0 > 0, and wavelengths λ > 0; (4) flag an error if γ < 1, if γ ≤ 1 while the electron is described as moving, or if γ is written in a form that is strictly less than 1 under the stated domain (e.g., γ = 1 − h/(2 m_0 c λ_i)). Such outcomes are unphysical and typically indicate incorrect application of momentum/energy conservation (e.g., treating vector momentum as scalars or omitting components), which can also yield unjustified wavelength relations like λ_0 = 2 λ_i. This rule is triggered whenever a moving electron’s γ violates the bound, independent of the specific scattering angle or wavelengths used.

rules.title: Improper square-rooting of metric differentials without forming derivatives
rules.description:
Checks for non-rigorous manipulation of squared differentials derived from spacetime metrics (e.g., −c^2 dτ^2 = −c^2 dt^2 + dx^2) where a solution isolates a single differential by taking square roots (e.g., dx = c sqrt(dt^2 − dτ^2)) instead of first forming a derivative with respect to a common parameter. The rule flags cases where: 
- A metric relation involving squared differentials (dt^2, dτ^2, dx^2, etc.) is directly converted to an expression of the form d(q) = sqrt(…) mixing differentials of distinct variables.
- Square roots are taken over sums/differences of squared differentials to isolate dx, dt, or similar, without dividing both sides by a common differential (e.g., dτ^2 or dt^2) to obtain a derivative such as dx/dτ = c sqrt((dt/dτ)^2 − 1).
- Integration is attempted on an expression with raw differentials produced by such square-rooting rather than on properly formed derivatives.
The rule expects that after introducing proper time or a parameterization, subsequent steps express kinematics via derivatives (dx/dτ, dt/dτ, dx/dt) before integration. If these conditions are not met and patterns like dx = c sqrt(dt^2 − dτ^2) or dt = sqrt(dτ^2 + …) appear, the solution is flagged as a logical/differential misuse.

rules.title: Exhaust momentum sign and relativistic velocity addition consistency
rules.description: Checks momentum-balance sign conventions and exhaust velocity composition in rocket/exhaust models. Trigger conditions: (1) In any momentum conservation statement for a rocket expelling mass (recoil/propulsion), the exhaust momentum must appear with the opposite sign to the rocket’s forward momentum when the forward direction is taken as positive. Equivalently, in the instantaneous rocket rest frame before expulsion, the post-event momenta must satisfy p_rocket + p_exhaust = 0, implying p_exhaust < 0 if p_rocket > 0. Flag solutions that sum p_rocket and p_exhaust with the same sign (e.g., p_total = p_rocket + p_exhaust with both positive in the rocket’s direction). (2) For relativistic kinematics, the exhaust velocity in the lab/inertial frame must be obtained via velocity addition with a minus sign for backward exhaust: v_exhaust = (V - u) / (1 - V u / c^2), where V is the rocket velocity in the lab frame and u is the exhaust speed relative to the rocket (u > 0 defined backward). Flag use of plus-sign composition (e.g., v_exhaust = (V + u) / (1 + V u / c^2) or the Newtonian v_exhaust = V + u) unless the coordinate/sign conventions are explicitly reversed and consistently applied. (3) Detect explicit exhaust momentum modeled as p_exhaust = γ_exhaust m_exhaust v_exhaust with v_exhaust having the same sign as V, or written as γ Δm (V + u), and then added to p_rocket in the conservation equation. This rule applies in both relativistic and Newtonian limits: in the Newtonian case v_exhaust should be V - u, not V + u. The rule passes if the solution clearly assigns a negative sign or opposite direction to exhaust quantities consistent with the chosen axis and demonstrates correct velocity addition; otherwise it fails.

rules.title: Relativistic momentum of massive particles must not include division by c in SI
rules.description: Checks expressions for the relativistic 3‑momentum of a massive particle (e.g., electron) for dimensional consistency in SI. In SI units, the correct form is p = γ m v (vector), with units kg·m/s. The rule flags any momentum expressions of the form γ m v / c or γ m (v/c) that lack a compensating factor of c, which incorrectly yields units of mass (kg) rather than momentum. It also flags p = γ m β without multiplying by c (i.e., p = γ m β is incorrect in SI; p = γ m β c is correct). The rule distinguishes photon momentum (p_photon = h/λ = E/c), which is allowed to include c in the denominator, and applies only to massive particles. Context sensitivity: If the solution explicitly declares natural units (c = 1) and is consistent elsewhere (e.g., E = γ m, p = γ m v), this rule is not triggered. Indicators of SI context include use of E = hc/λ, Compton formulas with h, c, and explicit mc^2. The rule inspects the final or key stated expressions for the particle’s momentum and performs dimensional analysis; if the resulting units are not kg·m/s, it flags the error.

rules.title: Comoving vs physical number density consistency and a^-3 scaling
rules.description: Checks for confusion between comoving and physical number density in cosmology problems. The rule flags solutions that: (1) define n(t) as a physical number density (e.g., using terms like "physical number density", "n_p", or "n_phys") and then assert that "the number density in comoving coordinates remains constant" using the same variable (e.g., n(t) = n(t0)) without introducing a distinct comoving variable; (2) fail to state or use the correct scaling for physical number density with expansion, namely n_phys(t) = n_phys(t0) * [a(t0)/a(t)]^3 (equivalently n_phys ∝ a^-3) under no creation/annihilation; (3) present an explicit scaling n(t) ∝ a(t)^k with k ≠ -3 while referring to n as physical, unless n is explicitly labeled as comoving; (4) introduce both "comoving" and "physical" number density terms but omit an explicit relation connecting them, or use the same symbol for both; (5) derive radiation energy density scaling inconsistent with a^-4 (e.g., using constant n or n ∝ a^0 or n ∝ a^-2) due to incorrect number-density treatment. Detection heuristics: parse for keywords/phrases such as "comoving", "physical", "number density", "n(t)", "n_p", "n_phys", "n_comov", and statements like "remains constant" or equalities n(t) = n(t0). If a variable previously identified as physical is later claimed constant in comoving coordinates without redefining it as comoving, flag. Expected correct formulation: define a distinct comoving number density n_comov that is constant, and relate the physical number density via n_phys(t) = n_comov / a(t)^3 = n_phys(t0) * [a(t0)/a(t)]^3; for radiation energy density, require ρ_r(t) ∝ a^-4 from n_phys ∝ a^-3 and E_photon ∝ a^-1.

rules.title: Incorrect per-photon momentum change for reflection from a moving sail
rules.description: Checks derivations of radiation pressure/force on a moving mirror/sail at normal incidence. The correct lab-frame treatment for a perfectly reflecting sail moving away at speed v (β = v/c) requires: (1) Per-photon momentum change Δp_photon = p_in + p_out = (h f/c) + (h f_ref/c), with the reflected frequency f_ref = f (1 − β)/(1 + β). (2) Photon arrival rate at the sail reduced by the relative speed factor: Ṅ_hit = (P/(h f)) (1 − β). (3) Resulting force F(v) = Ṅ_hit Δp_photon = (2P/c) (1 − β)/(1 + β). The rule flags solutions that: - Use Δp_photon = 2p or 2(h f/c) when v ≠ 0 (i.e., no Doppler correction to the reflected momentum). - Introduce factors like 1/[γ(1 − β cos θ)] directly into per-photon momentum change for normal incidence (θ = 0) without a Lorentz-transform-based derivation or without using the mirror Doppler formula for f_ref; patterns such as Δp = 2p − 2p/[γ(1 − β cos θ)], Δp = 2p/[γ(1 − β)], or similar are flagged. - Apply a Doppler shift to the incident frequency but fail to use f_ref = f (1 − β)/(1 + β) for the reflected photon in the Earth frame. - Compute force using photon rate P/(h f) without the (1 − β) reduction in the Earth/source frame. - Produce a final F(v) that does not reduce to (2P/c)(1 − β)/(1 + β) for a perfect reflector (or to (P/c)(1 − β) for perfect absorption), or that fails the β → 0 limit F → 2P/c. Acceptable alternatives include frame-transform derivations that are algebraically equivalent to the above lab-frame results; all other expressions for Δp_photon or F(v) that omit the Doppler-shifted reflected frequency and/or the reduced arrival rate are flagged.

rules.title: Flag use of constant g*h/c^2 for gravitational redshift at large altitude; require potential difference
rules.description: This rule checks calculations of gravitational time dilation/redshift between two radii around a spherical mass (e.g., Earth and a satellite). It flags solutions that model the fractional rate or frequency shift as gh/c^2 with g treated as a constant (e.g., g = 9.81 m/s^2) when the altitude is not negligible relative to the body's radius. Detection criteria: (1) Identify patterns like Delta t/t = g*h/c^2, Delta f/f = g*h/c^2, or equivalents where g is a single constant and h is altitude. (2) If the context references Earth, GPS, satellites, or orbital radii, compute the correct potential difference-based shift using Delta f/f = Delta Phi/c^2 with Delta Phi = GM*(1/r1 - 1/r2), where r1 is the body's radius and r2 = r1 + h (GM and r1 can be inferred from provided values or standard Earth constants if GPS is explicitly mentioned). (3) Estimate the modeling error: E = |(g0*h) - GM*(1/r1 - 1/(r1 + h))| / |GM*(1/r1 - 1/(r1 + h))|, where g0 = GM/r1^2 if g is not provided, or the provided constant g otherwise. (4) If h/r1 > 0.01 or E > 0.01 (1% relative error), flag the solution as an incorrect modeling of gravitational redshift due to assuming constant g. Rationale: g varies as GM/r^2; the linear approximation gh is only valid for h << r1. Required correction: Use Delta f/f = Delta Phi/c^2 with Delta Phi from the gravitational potential difference, or explicitly integrate g(r) dr to obtain Delta Phi. This rule specifically targets errors like using surface g in gh/c^2 for GPS altitude; it will also catch similar constant-g approximations at non-negligible altitudes around any spherical mass.

rules.title: Incorrect use of coordinate time in hyperbolic formulas for constant proper acceleration
rules.description: This rule flags solutions to uniform proper-acceleration (Rindler motion) problems that incorrectly apply hyperbolic functions with the coordinate time t instead of the proper time τ. In special relativity, for constant proper acceleration g: (1) the hyperbolic worldline and velocity are functions of τ: t(τ) = (c/g) sinh(gτ/c), x(τ) = x0 + (c^2/g)(cosh(gτ/c) − 1), v(τ)/c = tanh(gτ/c); (2) when expressed in terms of coordinate time t, the correct forms are x(t) = x0 + (c^2/g)(sqrt(1 + (gt/c)^2) − 1), v(t)/c = (gt/c) / sqrt(1 + (gt/c)^2), and γ(t) = sqrt(1 + (gt/c)^2). The verifier should flag any of the following patterns when the problem context states 'constant proper acceleration': (a) x(t) given with cosh(gt/c) or sinh(gt/c) directly (e.g., x(t) = (c^2/g)(cosh(gt/c) − 1)); (b) v(t) expressed as c·tanh(gt/c); (c) an equation like t = (c/g) sinh(gt/c) where t appears inside the hyperbolic function argument; or more generally any use of cosh/sinh/tanh with argument proportional to g·t/c for kinematic quantities defined as functions of t. These indicate mixing of coordinate time with proper-time hyperbolic relations. Exceptions: expressions are valid if the hyperbolic arguments use τ (proper time), or if the t-dependence is through sqrt(1 + (gt/c)^2) as above. The rule should consider common symbol variants for proper time ("τ", "tau", or explicitly described as 'proper time') and only flag when t is clearly the coordinate time.

rules.title: Proper time vs. spacetime interval sign consistency
rules.description:
Checks consistency between the stated metric signature and the relation between the spacetime interval ds^2 and proper time dτ for timelike worldlines.

What it checks:
- Detects the metric signature from the given line element by inspecting the signs of the time and spatial terms (e.g., in Schwarzschild or Minkowski forms). If the coefficient of dt^2 is negative and spatial terms are positive, assume signature (-,+,+,+). If the coefficient of dt^2 is positive and spatial terms are negative, assume signature (+,-,-,-).
- Searches for an explicit relation between ds^2 and dτ (e.g., "ds^2 = ± c^2 dτ^2", "(dτ)^2 = ± (ds)^2 / c^2", or with c=1 units: "ds^2 = ± dτ^2", "dτ^2 = ± ds^2").
- Validates the sign convention:
  • For signature (-,+,+,+): require ds^2 = - c^2 dτ^2 for timelike worldlines (equivalently dτ^2 = - ds^2 / c^2; with c=1, ds^2 = - dτ^2).
  • For signature (+,-,-,-): require ds^2 = + c^2 dτ^2 for timelike worldlines (equivalently dτ^2 = + ds^2 / c^2; with c=1, ds^2 = + dτ^2).
- Flags as an error if the stated relation uses the wrong sign relative to the inferred signature (e.g., writing dτ^2 = ds^2 / c^2 while using a metric with negative g_tt).
- Optional propagation check: If the student substitutes the metric into the dτ–ds relation for radial motion (e.g., Schwarzschild with dθ=dφ=0), verify term-by-term sign consistency. For (-,+,+,+): starting from ds^2 = g_tt dt^2 + g_rr dr^2, the derived dτ^2 = - ds^2 / c^2 must yield a positive coefficient for (dt)^2 and a negative coefficient for (dr)^2 outside the horizon (r>r_s). If the resulting signs are inverted, flag.
- Handles units where c=1 by treating c^2 factors as 1.

Rationale: Students often mix metric signature conventions and the sign in the proper-time relation. This rule catches inconsistent use such as asserting (dτ)^2 = (ds)^2 / c^2 while simultaneously employing a (-,+,+,+) metric, or vice versa, and catches downstream sign errors in derived expressions.

rules.title: Inconsistent relativistic approximations for massive beams
rules.description: Flags solutions that apply contradictory or incorrect approximations in energy–momentum relations for massive particles, especially when the beam energy is stated to be small. The rule triggers under any of the following conditions: (1) The problem involves massive particles (e.g., variables like m_p, m_Δ appear) and the solution’s initial total energy omits the projectile’s rest-energy term (e.g., uses E_initial = E_b + m_Δ c^2 instead of including m_p c^2). (2) The solution claims or implies that m_p c^2 can be neglected compared to a small beam energy E_b, or otherwise treats E_b as dominating over rest energies when E_b is described as “small.” (3) The solution uses the ultrarelativistic/massless momentum relation p ≈ E/c (or |p| = E/c) for a massive particle (e.g., proton) without an explicit and correct justification that E ≫ m c^2; this includes using photon-like kinematics for a massive beam. (4) The solution mixes nonrelativistic energy expansions (E ≈ m c^2 + p^2/(2m)) with ultrarelativistic momentum relations (p ≈ E/c) within the same derivation, which is internally inconsistent. The rule checks text for mentions of small E_b alongside omission of rest-energy terms, presence of p ≈ E/c tied to massive particles, and simultaneous use of nonrelativistic and ultrarelativistic approximations. Correct treatments should retain rest energies for massive particles when E_b is small and use the relativistic relation E^2 = (pc)^2 + (m c^2)^2 or invariant methods; this rule does not enforce a specific method but flags the inconsistent approximations.

rules.title: Doppler shift for light reflected from a moving mirror/sail
rules.description: This rule verifies the relativistic treatment of photon reflection from a mirror/sail moving collinearly with the beam. In the source (lab/Earth) frame, for a mirror receding at speed v (β = v/c > 0), the reflected photon frequency must be Doppler-reduced by the two-way (incident + reflected) factor: f_ref = f * (1 - β) / (1 + β). Equivalently, the reflected photon momentum magnitude satisfies p_ref = p_inc * (1 - β) / (1 + β), and the per-photon momentum transfer to the mirror is Δp = (h/c) (f + f_ref), which is strictly less than 2 h f / c when β ≠ 0. The rule flags solutions that: (a) assert f_ref = f (or E_ref = E_inc, or p_ref = p_inc) in the Earth/lab frame for β ≠ 0; (b) use Δp = 2 h f / c for β ≠ 0; (c) give radiation-pressure force independent of v (e.g., F = 2P/c) in the lab frame for a moving mirror without any β dependence; (d) apply a one-way Doppler factor instead of the double-Doppler factor for reflection, or use the wrong sign (e.g., predict a blue shift for a receding mirror). Acceptable derivations may compute in the mirror frame and transform back; the final lab-frame reflected frequency must satisfy f_ref/f = (1 - β) / (1 + β). The rule applies to problems involving laser sails, radiation pressure, or photon momentum transfer with a moving reflective surface.

rules.title: Require relativistic Doppler (γ factor) and second-order error for light
rules.description: This rule verifies Doppler-shift modeling when electromagnetic radiation (photons/laser light) interacts with moving atoms/ions. It flags solutions that use a classical/acoustic Doppler expression for light or that fail to quantify the relativistic correction. Checks: 1) Context trigger: problem mentions light/photons/laser spectroscopy/fluorescence and Doppler shift or comparison of classical vs relativistic formulas. 2) Formula check: if the solution uses a classical form for light such as f' = f(1 ± v/c) or λ' = λ(1 ∓ v/c) or λ' = λ/(1 ± v/c) without the relativistic time-dilation factor (γ) or the equivalent square-root ratio (f'/f = sqrt((1+β)/(1-β)) or λ'/λ = sqrt((1-β)/(1+β))), flag as modeling error. 3) Error-order check: when asked to quantify the error incurred by using the classical formula, require the small-β expansion; the fractional difference between classical and relativistic for light must be O(β^2), specifically ≈ ½β^2. If the solution claims zero error, omits the γ-related correction, or reports an O(β) difference, flag. 4) Numerical check (if v and c are provided): compute β = v/c and require that the reported fractional error magnitude is ≈ 0.5*β^2 (e.g., for v = 6000 m/s, β ≈ 2×10^-5 and error ≈ 2×10^-10). If no numeric estimate is given when requested, or the estimate differs qualitatively (wrong order), flag. Rationale: For light, relativistic Doppler includes time dilation via γ; classical formulas are inappropriate, and the discrepancy with SR appears at second order in β.

rules.title: Require fractional (dimensionless) error for classical vs relativistic Doppler at v << c
rules.description: This rule verifies that, in problems comparing the classical Doppler formula for light to the relativistic Doppler formula at small speeds (v << c), the student reports the error as a fractional (dimensionless) quantity rather than as an absolute shift with units. The rule checks for the following: (1) If the student's answer presents the 'error' with units (e.g., nm or Hz) as Δλ or Δf without also providing a normalized quantity (Δλ/λ or Δf/f), flag as incorrect measure because the expected output is the fractional/relative error. (2) Compute β = v/c (using c ≈ 3×10^8 m/s unless otherwise specified). The expected fractional error between classical and relativistic predictions for longitudinal light Doppler at small β is approximately e_rel ≈ 0.5·β^2. If the reported fractional error (dimensionless or percentage) deviates by more than ~20% from 0.5·β^2, flag as a conceptual mistake. (3) If the student reports an error that scales linearly with β (e.g., ~v/c or first-order in β) instead of order β^2, flag as incorrect scaling. (4) Acceptable formats include Δλ/λ, Δf/f, or a percentage; unacceptable is only an absolute error (e.g., Δλ ≈ 1.2×10^-7 nm) without normalization. Example: for v = 6000 m/s, β ≈ 2×10^-5, the expected fractional error is ≈ 2×10^-10; reporting only the absolute wavelength error (≈ 2×10^-10 × 600 nm ≈ 1.2×10^-7 nm) should be flagged unless accompanied by the fractional value.

rules.title: Relativistic flux must include Lorentz factor when density is in comoving frame
rules.description: This rule checks continuity and flux expressions in relativistic flows (e.g., AGN jets) for correct frame transformations. If the problem states that number density n(s) or mass density ρ(s) is defined in the jet/comoving/proper frame, then any particle/number or mass flux written in the AGN/lab frame must include the Lorentz factor γ(s) = 1/sqrt(1 − v(s)^2/c^2). Expected forms: particle flux Φ_N = γ(s) n_proper(s) v(s) A(s); mass flux Φ_m = γ(s) ρ_proper(s) v(s) A(s); steady continuity implies γ(s) n_proper(s) v(s) A(s) is constant along s (absent sources/sinks). Flag errors when a solution uses n(s) v(s) A(s) or ρ(s) v(s) A(s) without γ while simultaneously indicating that n(s) or ρ(s) is measured in the jet/comoving frame, or derives continuity as n1 v1 A1 = n2 v2 A2 without γ under relativistic conditions. Do not flag if the solution explicitly redefines n or ρ as lab-frame quantities (e.g., n_lab = γ n_proper) or uses four-current notation with u^μ where the γ factor is clearly included (e.g., u^x = γ v). This rule targets missing γ factors in lab-frame fluxes derived from comoving-frame densities in relativistic contexts.

rules.title: Apparent length of a rod imaged by a pinhole camera while moving along its axis must be L/gamma and independent of camera distance
rules.description: This rule verifies solutions to problems where a pinhole camera photographs a rod moving along the x-axis and the apparent longitudinal length is read using x-axis calibration marks. The correct apparent length along the rod’s direction of motion is the Lorentz-contracted length L/gamma, with gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), and it is independent of the camera’s perpendicular offset D. The rule flags solutions that: (1) ignore light-travel-time and simultaneity-of-arrival effects (i.e., do not account for retarded emission times, or do not mention that light from different points is emitted at different times but arrives simultaneously at the shutter); (2) derive or present an apparent length that includes geometric/perspective factors or explicit dependence on D, angles, or projection scaling; (3) apply static Euclidean projection to the rod’s length without solving for emission times (e.g., scaling L or L/gamma by D-based factors); or (4) assert that the apparent longitudinal length depends on the camera distance or viewing geometry in this setup. Heuristics: in contexts containing keywords such as "pinhole camera", "rod", "moving along x-axis", "apparent length", and a parameter D, check that the final length expression equals L/sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) (i.e., L/gamma) and does not contain D or angular terms; also check for presence of concepts/phrases like "retarded time", "emission time", "t_emit = t_photo - R/c", or "simultaneity of arrival". If D appears in the final longitudinal length formula or if no light-time/arrival-simultaneity reasoning is present, flag the solution as conceptually incorrect.

rules.title: Check β expression from momentum-energy relation
rules.description: Verify that when β (v/c) is expressed in terms of momentum p and total energy E for a relativistic particle, the formula used is β = (p c)/E in SI units, or β = p/E in natural units (c = 1). Flag any occurrence where β is written with an incorrect power of c, such as β = (p c^2)/E, β = p/(E c), β = (p c)/(E c), or generally β = (p c^n)/E with n ≠ 1. Include a dimensional check: β must be dimensionless; (p c)/E is dimensionless, whereas (p c^2)/E has dimensions of speed and is invalid for β. Accept derivations via v/c only if v is correctly given as v = (p c^2)/E, which implies β = v/c = (p c)/E. Also accept natural-unit expressions with β = p/E where c is consistently omitted. Trigger an error when the written β formula contradicts these identities, even if subsequent numerical steps effectively use the correct relation.

rules.title: Correct relativistic velocity addition for light in rotating systems
rules.description:
