In these cases, the solution must be corrected to use steam tables or an appropriate EOS with the isentropic condition to determine x (and r) at the local pressure.

rules.title: Incorrect TOA energy balance: equating surface-absorbed shortwave to space-emitted longwave
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that impose a single global energy balance by directly equating absorbed shortwave at the surface to infrared emission to space, without a proper top-of-atmosphere (TOA) control volume and atmospheric layer treatment. Indicative patterns include: (1) using an incoming term proportional to α_vis * w_s * πR^2 (or similar) and an outgoing term σ T^4 * 4πR^2 multiplied by a simple infrared transmission factor (e.g., (1 − α_ir), τ_ir), (2) missing the 1/4 geometry factor that converts the solar constant to a global-mean flux (i.e., using πR^2 vs 4πR^2 without recasting to S/4), (3) treating atmospheric IR absorption as a single multiplicative attenuation on σT^4 to space instead of modeling atmospheric absorption and re-emission (upward and downward) via emissivity/absorptivity, (4) omitting planetary albedo A at TOA or conflating it with surface-only albedo, and (5) lacking separate balance equations for the atmosphere, surface, and TOA. Examples of expressions to flag: α_vis * w_s' * πR^2 = σ T^4 * 4πR^2 * (1 − α_ir), or S_in = α * w_s and S_out = σ T^4 (1 − α_ir) with no atmospheric re-emission terms. Correct formulations should use TOA balance (e.g., (1 − A) w_s / 4 = σ T_e^4 for effective temperature) and, when greenhouse effects are included, explicit atmospheric shortwave absorption and infrared emissivity with up/down IR fluxes.

rules.title: Inconsistent use of reversible adiabatic relations in irreversible processes
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that apply reversible adiabatic state/path relations to processes explicitly described as irreversible or non-quasi-static, and detects self-contradictions where a relation is declared inapplicable and then used anyway. The verifier checks for: (1) Irreversibility cues in the solution text (keywords/phrases such as: irreversible, non-quasi-static, free expansion, sudden release, rapid, throttling, Joule expansion, shock, oscillation/settling, damping/viscous losses); (2) Use of reversible adiabatic relations to connect states (patterns including: p V^γ = const, TV^(γ-1) = const, p1 V1^γ = p2 V2^γ, isentropic with γ, polytropic with n = γ); (3) Explicit contradictions (e.g., statements like “this relation is not valid for an irreversible process” followed by using that relation to compute or conclude). If items (1) and (2) co-occur, or item (3) occurs, the solution is flagged as logically inconsistent. The rule also checks mechanical equilibrium claims: if the external load and atmospheric pressure are unchanged and the solution sets p_final = p_initial, concluding α ≠ 1 (or α = 1) solely by invoking the reversible adiabatic relation is flagged unless the solver provides a correct energy-balance justification. Expected correct approach: for irreversible adiabatic setups, use the First Law with Q = 0 (including piston kinetic and potential energy terms where relevant) and enforce final mechanical equilibrium (p_final A = p_0 A + W). Do not use PV^γ = const (or related isentropic relations) unless the path is explicitly reversible/quasi-static. Any conclusion about the final height ratio α must be supported by energy and force balance, not by reversible adiabatic state relations in an irreversible context.

rules.title: Shell-level ideal gas law misuse for temperature (dimensional/μ-scaling check)
rules.description: Checks for incorrect application of the ideal gas law to a shell/parcel that yields a temperature expression with wrong molar-mass scaling or dimensional inconsistency. Trigger when the solution uses PV = nRT (locally) with n replaced by dm/μ or ρV/μ and then solves for T. The verifier must validate that the derived temperature matches one of the dimensionally correct forms: T = (μ p V)/(dm R) or T = (μ p)/(ρ R). Flag as an error if: (1) the exponent of μ in the T expression is not exactly 1 (e.g., μ² p V/(dm R) or missing μ), (2) V and dm do not appear as a ratio forming density (i.e., T expressed with dm and V separately but not reducible to μ p/(ρ R)), (3) the relation is written with p dV = nRT (using dV instead of the parcel's full V) to solve for T, or (4) a dimensional analysis of the final T formula (using SI base units for μ, p, V, dm, R) does not reduce to Kelvin. Additionally, if the system is stated to be isothermal, flag any derivation that treats T(r) as varying with local shell variables (e.g., T depending explicitly on P(r), dm(r), dV(r)) unless it reduces to the constant relation T = μ p/ρ R. This rule catches errors like T = μ² P V/(dm R), which are dimensionally inconsistent and indicate misuse of the ideal gas law at the shell level.

rules.title: Negative sign between production rate and pressure decay in depletion models
rules.description: This rule checks sign consistency between production/outflow rate and pressure decline in reservoir depletion (or any compressible storage discharge). In depletion problems where q denotes oil/gas production rate (defined positive for outflow) and pressure P (boundary or average) controls storage, mass balance requires q_out = - S dP/dt, with S > 0 the storage coefficient (e.g., S = 2 φ L^2 c_r h, or φ c_t V, etc.). The minus sign is essential: during depletion dP/dt < 0 and q_out > 0. The verifier will: (1) Identify equations of the form q = α dP/dt (or q ∝ dP/dt) where α is composed of positive storage parameters (e.g., φ, c_r or c_t, geometric factors L, h, area/volume terms) and no explicit negative sign appears. If the problem context indicates production/depletion (q > 0 by convention, no external injection), flag as a sign-convention error. (2) Check trend consistency: if the solution asserts q > 0 but derives dP/dt > 0 (or P increasing with time) during depletion, flag a sign error. Conversely, if dP/dt < 0 is used but the equation without a minus sign implies q < 0, flag. (3) Validate that S is treated as positive; introducing a negative constant to compensate the missing minus sign is not acceptable. (4) Apply to relations using boundary pressure P_b(t) or average pressure P̄(t): require q + S dP/dt = 0 (i.e., sgn(q) = - sgn(dP/dt)). Examples of incorrect forms to flag: q = φ L^2 c_r h dP_b/dt, q = C dP̄/dt (C > 0) in a depletion setting, or textual justifications like "the minus sign just indicates production" followed by its removal. Correct expectation: q = -C dP/dt so that pressure decreases over time for positive production. This rule prevents later inconsistencies such as implying P increases with time under depletion.

rules.title: Distinct specific heats for different materials unless explicitly stated
rules.description: Check calorimetry/thermal-equilibrium solutions to ensure that each physically distinct material is assigned its own specific heat capacity unless the problem explicitly states they are identical. The verifier will: (1) parse the problem text to detect distinct bodies/materials (e.g., a liquid vs. an added solid, phases with different melting points, or different substances) and any explicit statements asserting equal specific heats; (2) inspect heat-balance terms of the form m * c * ΔT in the solution and verify that the liquid and any added solid(s) use different symbols/parameters for specific heat (e.g., C_liquid vs c_solid), rather than reusing the liquid’s C for the solid by default; (3) flag a modeling error if the same specific heat symbol is applied to different materials without justification, or if the solid’s sensible heat term is written with the liquid’s specific heat; (4) in problems involving phase change at the liquid’s freezing/melting point, also verify that latent heat terms (m_f * L) are included separately from sensible heat and that the solid’s specific heat only appears in terms for its temperature change. Example trigger: an energy balance such as m C (Th − T0) + m_f L = 2 m C (T0 − Tl) where C is used for both the liquid and a different solid without an explicit statement that their specific heats are equal. The solution passes if it introduces and consistently uses a distinct symbol (e.g., c_s) for the solid’s specific heat or if the prompt explicitly states the specific heats are the same.

rules.title: Steam generation enthalpy must include sensible heating and latent heat
rules.description: When verifying solutions that compute the mass of steam produced from liquid water using an energy balance (e.g., mass flow = input power divided by energy per kg), ensure the per‑kilogram enthalpy change includes all required terms based on the initial liquid temperature Ti, the boiling temperature Tboil at the working pressure, and the final steam temperature Tout. Specifically: (1) If Ti < Tboil, the solution must include sensible heating of liquid: c_liquid · (Tboil − Ti). (2) The phase change must include latent heat of vaporization: L_vap at the appropriate pressure/boiling temperature. (3) If Tout > Tboil (superheated steam), the solution must include sensible heating of vapor: c_vapor · (Tout − Tboil). Flag a conceptual error if the energy per kg is taken as L_vap only, or if any required sensible heating term is omitted given Ti and Tout. Do not flag if Ti ≈ Tboil (within ~1 K) or Tout ≈ Tboil (within ~1 K), or if the solution uses steam tables/enthalpy data that implicitly account for these changes. This rule targets common mistakes like computing mass rate as P / L_vap when water starts below boiling or the steam exits above boiling, which overestimates production rate.

rules.title: Pressure continuity at submerged opening: gas pressure must include external hydrostatic head
rules.description: Checks modeling of pressure balance for a container with a gas above a liquid and a small opening (hole) at depth. At static equilibrium, the pressure at the hole must be equal on both sides. For the same liquid (density ρ) inside and outside, the correct balance at the hole is: P_gas + ρ g x_in = p0 + ρ g y_out, where x_in is the internal water column height above the hole and y_out is the external depth of the hole below the outside free surface. In a floating cylinder with base area A and initial submerged depth h, mass increases by ρ A x_in as water enters, so y_out = h + x_in. This yields P_gas = p0 + ρ g h, i.e., P_gas is independent of x_in. Flag solutions that: (1) set the post-leak gas pressure to P_gas = p0 + ρ g x_in, (2) make P_gas depend solely on x_in (ignoring y_out or h), or (3) omit the external hydrostatic term p0 + ρ g y_out when equating pressures at the hole. Also flag if P_gas is equated directly to p0 (atmospheric) without the ρ g h contribution. The rule verifies the presence of a correct two-sided pressure continuity equation at the opening and checks that the derived P_gas reduces to p0 + ρ g h in the floating-cylinder case.

rules.title: Insulation Boundary Consistency Check
rules.description: Checks that the student's stated thermal boundary conditions (which walls are insulated/adiabatic versus which wall is uninsulated/heat-contact) match the problem statement. Specifically: (1) Parse the problem text to identify walls marked as insulated and any exceptions (e.g., 'all walls are insulated except the left wall' implies the left wall is uninsulated/heat-contact). (2) Parse the student's solution text for assertions about insulation (e.g., 'only the left wall is insulated', 'the left wall exchanges heat', 'all other walls are adiabatic'). (3) Use synonym mapping: insulated ≈ adiabatic ≈ no heat transfer; uninsulated ≈ in thermal contact ≈ heat can flow. (4) Flag a violation if the student reverses or contradicts the exception (e.g., problem says 'except the left wall' but student says 'left wall is the only insulated wall') or otherwise misidentifies which wall allows heat transfer. This rule targets conceptual misreadings of boundary conditions that may not immediately affect subsequent calculations but indicate an incorrect physical setup.

rules.title: Misuse of eggshell conductivity for overall egg heat-flow modeling
rules.description: Verify that the thermal conductivity k used to estimate heat flow into an egg corresponds to the dominant heat-transfer path through the egg interior (water/protein, k ≈ 0.5–0.7 W/m·K). Flag a solution if: (1) k > 1.0 W/m·K is used while applying Fourier’s law across a bulk length scale (Δx comparable to the egg radius, i.e., mm–cm), and the shell is not modeled explicitly as a thin layer with its thickness; or (2) the chosen material for k is named as eggshell/calcium carbonate/ceramic (typical k ≈ 1.6–2.0 W/m·K) while the geometry and Δx correspond to the egg interior; or (3) no series thermal-resistance model (shell thickness ~0.3–0.5 mm + interior radius ~20–25 mm) and/or external convection is included. To pass, either use interior k in the 0.5–0.7 W/m·K range for bulk conduction into the egg or explicitly include the eggshell as a thin high-k layer in series with the interior (and convection if applicable). This rule targets modeling errors where the thin, higher-conductivity shell is incorrectly treated as controlling the overall heat transfer, inflating J.

rules.title: Missing critical-temperature criterion in fuse/thermal cutoff derivations
rules.description:
Checks that, when determining a fuse blowing current or any thermal-failure threshold with radiative (or other) cooling, the solution explicitly ties the threshold to the material’s critical/failure temperature (e.g., melting point) and uses it in the heat-balance equation. Specifically:
- If the problem involves a fuse or thermal cutoff and provides a heat-loss law P_loss ∝ S (T^4 − T_env^4) (or similar), the solution must state that blowing/failure occurs when the conductor reaches its melting (or specified critical) temperature T = T_m, and must use T_m (not an arbitrary or steady unknown T) in the threshold condition.
- The heat-balance at threshold should be written conceptually as I^2 R = k S (T_m^4 − T_env^4) (k may include emissivity/σ and constants); leaving T generic or equating T to T_env at threshold is flagged.
- The conclusion should attribute the threshold current to material properties and geometry at T_m, and for a uniform cylindrical fuse wire cooled by surface radiation, recognize/capture the cancellation of length via R ∝ L and S ∝ L (i.e., the blowing current is independent of the exact length). Claiming a length dependence due to not fixing T = T_m is flagged.
- Acceptable synonyms for T_m include melting point, fusing temperature, critical temperature, failure temperature. Failure to reference such a critical temperature or to use it in the balance is flagged as a conceptual error.

rules.title: Conduction length scale must reflect dominant thermal resistance in heating of bulk solids
rules.description: This rule checks whether a solution estimating heat inflow J into a solid object (e.g., an egg in boiling water) uses an appropriate conduction length scale for the dominant thermal resistance. Trigger conditions: (a) the solution models heat inflow with Fourier’s law q = k * ΔT / Δx and multiplies by surface area to get J, and (b) the object is bulk-sized (characteristic dimension L_char ≥ 10 mm). The rule flags an error if Δx is taken as a thin shell or wall thickness that is much smaller than the object size (Δx ≤ 0.05 * L_char) without justification that the shell dominates the resistance. Justifications that prevent flagging include: (1) explicit series-resistance modeling showing R_shell >> R_internal (e.g., k_shell/k_core ≤ 0.1 or L_shell comparable to L_char), (2) convective boundary modeling indicating external convection dominates (e.g., using J = h * A * ΔT and demonstrating small Biot number), or (3) a Biot number analysis with Bi = h * L_char / k_core ≤ 0.1 supporting a lumped-capacitance approach. In typical boiling-water heating of an egg, h is large (hundreds to thousands W/m^2K) and Bi >> 0.1, so the dominant resistance is internal conduction over a length scale comparable to the egg radius (≈ 20–30 mm), not the ~0.5 mm eggshell. If the solution uses Δx equal to a thin shell thickness and omits internal conduction or Biot analysis, flag as a modeling error likely to overestimate J by one to two orders of magnitude.

rules.title: Thermal Conductivity Dimension Consistency
rules.description: Verify that any variable identified as thermal conductivity (e.g., k, k_sm, κ, lambda, or labeled 'thermal conductivity') has base dimensions M^1 L^1 T^-3 Θ^-1. If units are given as W m^-1 K^-1, expand W as J s^-1 and J as M L^2 T^-2, yielding k ≡ M L T^-3 Θ^-1. Flag an error if the stated or derived dimensions differ (such as using L^-3, L^-2, or L^0), or if W is incorrectly expanded (e.g., treating W as M L^2 T^-2). This rule also distinguishes thermal conductivity from thermal diffusivity (k/(ρ c)), which has dimensions L^2 T^-1; conflating the two should be flagged.

rules.title: Misclassification of molar/specific heat capacity as extensive
rules.description: This rule checks for conceptual errors that conflate intensive and extensive properties in thermodynamics, specifically for heat capacities. It flags solutions that: (1) explicitly state or imply that molar or specific heat capacity (e.g., C_{V,m}, C_{P,m}, c per mole or per mass) is an extensive property, or that it depends on the number of moles/amount of substance; (2) apply additivity of extensive properties directly to per-mole/per-mass quantities (e.g., writing C_{V,m,mix} = C_{V,m,A} + C_{V,m,B} or C_{V,m,mix} = n1*C1 + n2*C2 without normalizing by total moles); (3) label per-mole/per-mass heat capacities as “total” or otherwise suggest scaling with system size. Acceptable and encouraged relationships are C_V (total) = n * C_{V,m} and the mixture molar heat capacity C_{V,m,mix} = (n1*C1 + n2*C2)/(n1 + n2). The rule should flag a conceptual inconsistency even if subsequent algebra uses the correct relationships, whenever text claims that molar/specific heat capacity is extensive.

rules.title: Do not apply ideal-gas EOS or γ-relations to saturated two-phase mixtures
rules.description: This rule flags solutions that apply ideal-gas equations or ideal-gas isentropic relations to systems explicitly described as two-phase (liquid–vapor) or saturated mixtures in equilibrium. Trigger context: the solution references any of the following indicating a two-phase equilibrium: 'two-phase', 'liquid–vapor mixture', 'wet steam', 'saturated', 'equilibrium between phases', 'quality', 'dryness fraction', 'relative liquid content', or uses symbols like x (quality) or r (liquid mass fraction). In this context, the following are prohibited and will be flagged: (1) Using ideal-gas EOS to relate pressure, temperature, and density/volume of the mixture (e.g., P = ρ R T, PV = nRT, v = RT/P) for the bulk mixture; (2) Using ideal-gas isentropic or γ-based relations for the bulk mixture (e.g., Pv^γ = const, T2/T1 = (P2/P1)^((γ-1)/γ), P2/P1 = (ρ2/ρ1)^γ, a = sqrt(γ R T)); (3) Computing mixture internal energy/enthalpy/entropy as u = c_v T, h = c_p T, or s = c_p ln(T) − R ln(P) for the two-phase bulk; (4) Using a single adiabatic index γ for a wet (two-phase) steam mixture to close the state or flow relations. Rationale: a saturated liquid–vapor mixture is not an ideal gas; mixture properties must be obtained from saturated liquid/vapor values (v_f, v_g, h_f, h_g, s_f, s_g) combined by quality (e.g., v = (1−x) v_f + x v_g), with pressure tied to saturation conditions, not P = ρ R T. Exception: If the solution clearly and consistently treats the working fluid as single-phase superheated vapor (no liquid present, x = 1) or explicitly states it is outside the two-phase region, this rule does not apply.

rules.title: Do not apply ideal-gas isentropic γ-law to two-phase (liquid–vapor) mixtures
rules.description:
This rule flags solutions that use ideal-gas isentropic relations with a constant adiabatic index (γ) for systems explicitly involving phase equilibrium or two-phase (liquid–vapor) mixtures, such as saturated steam with a liquid fraction. The γ-law (e.g., Pv^γ = const, Tv^(γ−1) = const, TP^{(1−γ)/γ} = const, or any derivation based on constant cp, cv and γ) is only valid for single-phase ideal gases. In the saturated region, a water/steam mixture does not obey ideal-gas γ-law behavior; properties must be obtained from phase equilibrium and saturation relations (steam tables) along the isentropic path.

The rule checks for the following indicators in the solution:
- Problem context or solution text mentions two-phase conditions or phase equilibrium: "saturated", "liquid fraction", "quality x", "relative mass content r of liquid", "equilibrium between liquid and vapor", "wet steam", or similar.
- Use of ideal-gas isentropic relations with a constant γ: explicit statements like "Pv^γ = const", "adiabatic index γ = ..." applied to state changes, use of Tv^(γ−1) relations, Mach-number/isentropic formulas derived for ideal gases, or reliance on constant cp/cv to propagate an isentrope.
- Absence of appropriate two-phase property handling: no use of steam tables, saturation properties (hf, hg, sf, sg, vf, vg), mixture relations (e.g., s = sf + x sfg, h = hf + x hfg), or Clausius–Clapeyron-based equilibrium.

If all three indicators are present, flag a modeling error: "Ideal-gas γ-law applied to a two-phase mixture." 

Exceptions (do not flag) when:
- The solution demonstrates and documents that the state lies entirely in a single-phase region (e.g., superheated vapor with x = 1 or clearly outside the saturation dome) and justifies the ideal-gas approximation for steam at the given conditions before applying γ-law; or
- A non-ideal EOS suitable for water vapor is used with verified single-phase conditions.

Expected correct approach for two-phase isentropic changes:
- Use phase-equilibrium relations and steam tables: compute state changes along s = const via sf/sg and quality x; determine mixture properties (h, v) from hf, hg and x; and only apply γ-based relations if/after the flow is shown to be single-phase vapor where the ideal-gas model is valid.

rules.title: Unjustified equation of state or assumed density profile in force-balance problems
rules.description: Flag solutions that introduce an arbitrary equation of state (EOS) or a specific functional form for density or pressure (e.g., polytropic or ideal-gas relations) without explicit justification when the problem only requires hydrostatic/force balance to relate pressure gradient to density. Detection criteria: (1) The problem states or implies a relation of the form ∂P/∂x = β · ρ(x) (or pressure gradient proportional to density) under a known body acceleration a(x) (e.g., rotating frame with a(x) = ω^2 x), where β should be identified directly from equilibrium (β = a(x), up to sign by coordinate choice). (2) The solution assumes or derives a specific EOS or density profile that is not given or derived from stated constraints, such as P = K ρ^γ, P ∝ ρ^γ, P = ρ R T (with unspecified T), or ρ(x) = ρ0 f(x; γ, K, C), including forms like ρ(x) = ρ0 (1 + α x^2)^(-γ). (3) The solution introduces new thermodynamic parameters or constants (γ, K, n, T0, C) not present in the problem statement and uses them to compute ρ(x) or P(x) instead of determining β from ∂P/∂x = ρ a(x). (4) The solution claims an EOS is needed to find β when β follows directly from force balance. Examples to flag: mentions of 'polytropic', 'adiabatic', 'isothermal', 'P = K ρ^γ', 'P = ρ R T', or explicit profiles like ρ(x) = ρ0 (1 + ω^2 x^2 / 2C)^(-γ) in contexts where the task is only to extract β from the body acceleration. The rule does not evaluate sign conventions; it focuses on the unjustified modeling assumption that bypasses the direct equilibrium relation.

rules.title: Misuse of dQ = n C_V dT for variable-volume/piston-coupled systems
rules.description: Checks solutions that equate heat flow to n C_V dT (or dQ/dt = n C_V dT/dt) for a gas whose volume can change due to a movable piston or mechanical coupling to another chamber. Triggers when: (a) the problem statement includes a frictionless/movable/adiabatic piston or otherwise indicates variable volume or mechanically coupled chambers, and (b) the solution uses dQ = n C_V dT or Q = n C_V ΔT for a single chamber without an explicit pdV work term or without accounting for the coupled chamber's internal energy change. For a single chamber with a moving boundary, the correct first-law statement is dQ_r = dU_r + p dV_r = n C_V dT_r + p dV_r; omitting p dV_r is incorrect unless the solution justifies dV_r = 0 (e.g., rigid container or explicitly locked piston). For a two-chamber system separated by an adiabatic frictionless piston with only one wall exchanging heat, the correct overall energy balance is dQ_in = dU_l + dU_r = n C_V dT_l + n C_V dT_r; analyzing only the heated chamber requires inclusion of pdV work and the coupling to the adiabatic chamber via mechanical equilibrium. The rule flags setups that: (1) equate a conductive heat rate (e.g., via Fourier’s law, kappa A ΔT/d) directly to n C_V dT_r/dt for the heated side without p dV_r, or (2) ignore the left-chamber term n C_V dT_l when applying the first law to the whole device, or (3) fail to relate dT_l and dT_r using the adiabatic constraint on the unheated chamber (n C_V dT_l + p dV_l = 0) and common pressure via the piston. Exceptions: do not flag if the solution explicitly establishes constant volume (rigid, immovable boundary) or proves dV = 0 at the instant considered. This rule targets the common conceptual error of applying constant-volume heat capacity in processes with work and piston-mediated coupling, which leads to underestimating the effective heat capacity (missing extra terms proportional to R and gamma effects).

rules.title: Correct virial theorem usage for self-gravitating ideal gas (beta = 1/2)
rules.description: This rule verifies that solutions invoking the virial theorem for a self-gravitating monoatomic ideal gas cloud in hydrostatic/mechanical equilibrium use the fluid form of the scalar virial theorem and maintain consistent symbol definitions. Applicability: solutions referencing a self-gravitating gas/cloud, hydrostatic equilibrium, ideal gas law, pressure p(r), or the virial theorem. Required checks: (1) The virial relation must include the pressure term: 3∫ P dV + E_G = 0 for zero external (surface) pressure, or 3∫ P dV + E_G + 3 P_s V = 0 if a nonzero confining surface pressure P_s is present. Using the point-mass form 2⟨K⟩ + ⟨U⟩ = 0 without the pressure term in a fluid context is flagged as incorrect. (2) Symbol consistency: the solution must not conflate internal energy with the potential energy symbol used in the virial theorem. If U is defined as internal energy, the gravitational potential energy must be denoted distinctly (e.g., E_G or U_G), and kinetic energy in the virial theorem must be K (not temperature T). Any use of 2⟨T⟩ + ⟨U⟩ = 0 with T meaning temperature or U meaning internal energy is flagged. (3) Energy relations: for an isothermal ideal gas, the solution should use p = n k_B T to obtain ∫ P dV = N k_B T and U_int = (3/2) N k_B T = (3/2) ∫ P dV, then combine with the correct virial relation to conclude U_int = -E_G / 2 when P_s = 0, implying beta = 1/2 in U = -beta E_G. If beta differs from 1/2 in the zero external pressure case, or if the link ∫ P dV = N k_B T and U_int = (3/2) N k_B T is omitted or misapplied, flag the solution. (4) If a nonzero external pressure is explicitly considered, the solution must state the surface term and yield U_int = -(E_G + 3 P_s V)/2; failing to mention the boundary term while invoking an external confining pressure is flagged. This rule catches misuse of the point-mass virial form in fluid problems, omission of the pressure term, and symbol confusion between internal energy and gravitational potential energy.

rules.title: Verify β via virial theorem for self-gravitating monoatomic ideal gas
rules.description: This rule checks solutions that relate the internal energy U and the gravitational potential energy E_G of a self-gravitating monoatomic ideal gas cloud in stationary mechanical equilibrium. Under standard assumptions (spherical symmetry, monoatomic ideal gas, no rotation/magnetic fields, negligible external confining pressure, and no non-ideal degrees of freedom), the scalar virial theorem implies 2U + E_G = 0, hence U = -E_G/2 and β = 1/2 in U = -β E_G. The verifier should: (1) detect the presence of a claimed proportionality U = -β E_G; (2) confirm the context matches the standard assumptions (monoatomic ideal gas, hydrostatic/stationary self-gravitating cloud without additional energy reservoirs); (3) ensure the derivation employs either the virial theorem 2U + E_G = 0 or the equivalent identity 3∫p dV = -E_G together with U = (3/2)∫p dV; (4) validate the final numerical value β = 0.5 within a small tolerance. The rule flags an error if β ≠ 0.5 is stated without explicitly introducing and correctly accounting for non-standard physics (e.g., external boundary pressure work, rotation, magnetic fields, non-monoatomic degrees of freedom, or relativistic effects), or if β is derived from misapplied pressure integrals or by confusing the uniform-sphere gravitational energy coefficient (e.g., 3/5) with β. It also flags if U is misidentified (e.g., using enthalpy or pV terms instead of kinetic/internal energy) or if the derivation omits the virial relation entirely while asserting β.

rules.title: Verify Stefan-Boltzmann Law Application
rules.description: Ensure the formula for the Stefan-Boltzmann Law is correctly stated and applied: P = σAeT^4, where σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, A is the area, e is the emissivity, and T is the temperature in Kelvin.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the power emitted is calculated using P = σAeT^4, with temperature in Kelvin and consideration of emissivity. Ensure all variables are correctly substituted and calculated.
common_errors: Using incorrect formula for power emitted
Confusing temperature units (Celsius instead of Kelvin)
Neglecting the emissivity factor

rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency in Blackbody Equations
rules.description: Verify that units align correctly: Power emitted (P) should be in Watts.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the output of P = σAeT^4 has units of Watts (W). Confirm that all input variables have consistent units (e.g., area in square meters, temperature in Kelvin).
common_errors: Incorrect unit conversion leading to power not in Watts
Mismatch in units leading to incorrect calculations

rules.title: Ensure Temperature is in Kelvin
rules.description: Confirm that the temperature used in the Stefan-Boltzmann Law is in Kelvin, as this law requires absolute temperature scales.
rules.check_logic: Verify temperature input is in Kelvin before substituting into the Stefan-Boltzmann equation. If temperature is provided in Celsius, ensure it is converted to Kelvin using T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
common_errors: Using temperature in Celsius instead of Kelvin
Misconversion of temperature units

rules.title: Verify Wien's Law for Peak Wavelength
rules.description: Ensure Wien's Law is correctly applied to identify peak wavelength λ_peak = b/T, where b is Wien's displacement constant.
rules.check_logic: Verify λ_peak is calculated with λ_peak = b/T, and ensure b is correctly valued as approximately 2.898 × 10^-3 m·K. Confirm that T is in Kelvin.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation of the peak wavelength
Misapplication of Wien's displacement constant
Using temperature in incorrect units

rules.title: Check Validity of Blackbody Assumptions
rules.description: Confirm that the body assumed to be a blackbody is a perfect emitter or sufficiently close, such as stars or furnace cavities.
rules.check_logic: Assess the physical situation to ensure it meets the requirements for treating as a blackbody. Verify that the emissivity is close to 1 for near-perfect blackbodies.
common_errors: Applying blackbody equations to non-blackbody actors
Ignoring the requirement for a blackbody to be a perfect emitter

rules.title: Verify Geometric Area in Stefan-Boltzmann Calculation
rules.description: Ensure that the surface area used in calculations accurately represents the radiating object's geometry.
rules.check_logic: Confirm the surface area (A) is correctly calculated from given geometric parameters before substituting into the equation. For example, use A = 4πr^2 for a sphere.
common_errors: Incorrect calculation or assumption of surface area
Misapplying the geometry of the object in area calculations

rules.title: Validate Emissivity Value and Range
rules.description: Check that emissivity (e) is within the physical range of 0 ≤ e ≤ 1, representing a real material's emissive properties.
rules.check_logic: Confirm emissivity value is within allowable limits before using in Stefan-Boltzmann Law. Ensure emissivity is not confused with reflectivity or absorptivity.
common_errors: Using emissivity values outside the physical range
Confusing emissivity with reflectivity or other optical properties

rules.title: Correct Sign Convention for Heat Transfer
rules.description: Check that the sign convention adheres to the principle that energy emitted by radiation from the surface is considered as positive heat loss.
rules.check_logic: Verify energy flow direction and ensure heat loss is denoted correctly as a negative contribution in energy balance calculations. Confirm that heat gain is treated as positive.
common_errors: Incorrectly stating energy loss as a gain
Misunderstanding the sign convention in heat balance

rules.title: Verify Energy Density of Blackbody Radiation
rules.description: Ensure the energy density of blackbody radiation is calculated correctly using u = (4σ/c)T^4, where c is the speed of light.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the energy density u is calculated using u = (4σ/c)T^4, with T in Kelvin and c as the speed of light in vacuum.
common_errors: Incorrect formula for energy density
Using incorrect value for the speed of light
Temperature not in Kelvin

rules.title: Verify Radiative Flux Calculation
rules.description: Ensure the radiative flux (F) is calculated correctly using F = σT^4 for a perfect blackbody.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the radiative flux is calculated using F = σT^4, with T in Kelvin. For non-perfect blackbodies, ensure emissivity is included as F = eσT^4.
common_errors: Neglecting emissivity for non-perfect blackbodies
Using incorrect formula for radiative flux
Temperature not in Kelvin

rules.title: 有效截面与表面积区分
rules.description:
触发条件：计算行星（球体）吸收太阳辐射与向外辐射能量平衡时
检查逻辑：吸收功率应使用投影面积 (πR²)，辐射功率应使用全表面积 (4πR²)。检查公式中系数 4 的位置是否正确。
rules.check_logic: 吸收功率应使用投影面积 (πR²)，辐射功率应使用全表面积 (4πR²)。检查公式中系数 4 的位置是否正确。

rules.description:

检查逻辑：利用微分关系 dT/T = 1/4 * dP/P。若距离增加 f，则功率下降约 2f，温度下降约 f/2。检查近似推导是否符合此线性比例。
rules.check_logic: 利用微分关系 dT/T = 1/4 * dP/P。若距离增加 f，则功率下降约 2f，温度下降约 f/2。检查近似推导是否符合此线性比例。

触发条件：题目给出摄氏度（°C）且涉及比例、乘除或辐射定律计算时

rules.check_logic: 需确认是否为单层透明模型；若存在大气吸收，平衡方程应体现温室效应项（如分母包含 1+alpha_ir）。

rules.description:

检查逻辑：检查是否对全频域 [0, ∞] 进行积分，并确认积分常数项在指数衰减边界条件下的消去逻辑是否正确。
rules.check_logic: 检查是否对全频域 [0, ∞] 进行积分，并确认积分常数项在指数衰减边界条件下的消去逻辑是否正确。

rules.title: 天体距离变化辐射修正
rules.description:
触发条件：题目给出轨道半径或距离的百分比变化 f 时
检查逻辑：检查辐射强度修正因子是否遵循平方反比律，即 1/(1+f)^2 而非线性近似 (1-f)^2。
rules.check_logic: 检查辐射强度修正因子是否遵循平方反比律，即 1/(1+f)^2 而非线性近似 (1-f)^2。
rules.trigger: 题目给出轨道半径或距离的百分比变化 f 时

rules.title: 维恩分布幂次量纲一致性
rules.description:
触发条件：涉及 Wien 分布或 Planck 分布的变体公式时
检查逻辑：验证频率 v 的幂次与温度 T 的幂次在积分后是否满足 Stefan-Boltzmann 定律的 T^4 比例关系。
rules.check_logic: 验证频率 v 的幂次与温度 T 的幂次在积分后是否满足 Stefan-Boltzmann 定律的 T^4 比例关系。
rules.trigger: 涉及 Wien 分布或 Planck 分布的变体公式时

rules.title: Apply Carnot Efficiency Formula
rules.description: The Carnot efficiency equation is used to calculate the maximum efficiency of a heat engine operating between two thermal reservoirs. It is given by η = 1 - (T_cold / T_hot), where T_cold and T_hot are the absolute temperatures of the cold and hot reservoirs, respectively.
rules.check_logic: Calculate η using η = 1 - (T_cold / T_hot). Ensure that temperatures are in Kelvin and T_hot > T_cold.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin for temperatures
Mixing up T_hot and T_cold
Incorrect subtraction or division order
Using negative temperatures without proper conversion

rules.title: Verify Reversible Process in Carnot Cycle
rules.description: A Carnot cycle consists of four reversible processes: two isothermal and two adiabatic. The cycle is hypothetically reversible, and real engines operating on Carnot principles should approach reversibility.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the process sequence is isothermal expansion, adiabatic expansion, isothermal compression, adiabatic compression. Confirm that no heat exchange occurs during adiabatic processes and that heat exchange occurs only during isothermal processes.
common_errors: Failing to identify the correct sequence of processes
Mistaking any process as irreversible
Incorrectly labeling adiabatic processes as isothermal
Ignoring the reversibility assumption in calculations

rules.title: Check Temperature Units in Carnot Calculations
rules.description: Temperatures in thermodynamic calculations involving Carnot cycles must be expressed in absolute units (Kelvin). This ensures correct comparison and ratios in formulas.
rules.check_logic: Verify all temperatures are given in Kelvin before substitution into formulas. If temperatures are provided in Celsius, convert them to Kelvin using T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.
common_errors: Using Celsius or Fahrenheit for temperature inputs
Ignoring unit conversion entirely
Wrong conversion from Celsius to Kelvin
Failing to check for negative temperatures in Celsius

rules.title: Validate Carnot Cycle Assumptions with Ideal Gas
rules.description: Carnot engines often assume gases behave ideally in the cycle. This requires conditions where the gas's behavior approximates the ideal gas law closely.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem context or conditions denote ideal gas behavior or provide necessary conditions such as low pressure and high temperature. Verify that the ideal gas law (PV = nRT) is applicable.
common_errors: Assuming ideal behavior when conditions don't support it
Using real gas equations without context clarity
Failing to match conditions with equation assumptions
Ignoring deviations from ideal gas behavior at high pressures or low temperatures

rules.title: Efficiency Limitation Recognition
rules.description: The Carnot efficiency represents the maximum efficiency limit for any heat engine operating between two temperatures. No real engine can surpass this efficiency.
rules.check_logic: Compare calculated engine efficiency with Carnot efficiency (η_c). Report if any real engine efficiency exceeds η_c. Ensure that η_c is calculated correctly using absolute temperatures.
common_errors: Claiming real engine efficiency exceeds Carnot limit
Neglecting the efficiency definition for non-Carnot engines
Misinterpreting efficiency calculations
Failing to account for irreversibilities in real engines

rules.title: Ensure Work Done Calculations in Adiabatic Processes
rules.description: In adiabatic processes of a Carnot cycle, work done relies on pressure and volume changes, with no heat exchange occurring.
rules.check_logic: Evaluate work done using adiabatic relations: W = μ(C_vm/T)*(V_initial/V_final)^(γ-1) where applicable. Confirm that Q = 0 for adiabatic processes.
common_errors: Confusing adiabatic with isochoric processes
Using heat transfer equations in adiabatic calculations
Incorrect exponent calculation involving adiabatic processes
Failing to verify that no heat is exchanged (Q = 0)

rules.title: Verify Net Power Output Calculation
rules.description: The net power output of a Carnot engine is calculated from the net work done in one complete cycle, considering all processes.
rules.check_logic: Calculate net work as W_net = Q_h - Q_c, where Q_h is heat input and Q_c is heat output. Ensure that Q_h > Q_c and that heat values are consistent with the first law of thermodynamics.
common_errors: Incorrectly adding rather than subtracting heats
Omitting work done calculations
Confusion between input and output heat quantities
Failing to check consistency with the first law of thermodynamics

rules.title: Constrain Cycle Path in P-V Diagram
rules.description: The Carnot cycle should accurately reflect its adiabatic and isothermal paths in a P-V diagram, depicting ideal process transitions.
rules.check_logic: Ensure diagram paths are correct: isothermal paths are horizontal while adiabatic paths should curve according to pressure-temperature changes. Verify that transitions between processes are smooth and consistent with thermodynamic principles.
common_errors: Incorrectly labeling isothermal paths as vertical
Misrepresenting adiabatic curves with straight lines
Failing to respect process transitions accurately on diagrams
Ignoring the relationship between pressure, volume, and temperature in the diagram

rules.title: Verify Heat Transfer in Isothermal Processes
rules.description: During isothermal processes in the Carnot cycle, heat transfer occurs at constant temperature. The heat absorbed or released is related to the work done.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that Q = W for isothermal processes, where Q is the heat transferred and W is the work done. Verify that the temperature remains constant throughout the process.
common_errors: Failing to equate heat transfer to work done in isothermal processes
Assuming temperature changes during isothermal processes
Ignoring the relationship between heat transfer and work

rules.title: 循环过程状态量一致性
rules.description:
触发条件：处理类奥托循环（Otto Cycle）的四段式过程时
检查逻辑：检查绝热过程（等熵/等概率）与等体过程（等能级）的交替逻辑，确保 ΔU = Q + W 在每一段均闭合。
rules.check_logic: 检查绝热过程（等熵/等概率）与等体过程（等能级）的交替逻辑，确保 ΔU = Q + W 在每一段均闭合。
rules.trigger: 处理类奥托循环（Otto Cycle）的四段式过程时

rules.title: 量子热力学功热辨析
rules.description:
触发条件：题目给出 d<E> = p dE + E dp 形式的能量变化分解时
检查逻辑：需严格区分 p dE 为对外做功（能级移动）项，E dp 为热交换（布居数改变）项，注意系统做功与外界做功的符号差。
rules.check_logic: 需严格区分 p dE 为对外做功（能级移动）项，E dp 为热交换（布居数改变）项，注意系统做功与外界做功的符号差。

rules.title: Verify the differential form of the Clausius-Clapeyron equation
rules.description: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation in its differential form is written as dP/dT = L / (T * ΔV), where dP/dT is the slope of the phase boundary in a P-T diagram, L is the latent heat of the phase transition, T is the absolute temperature, and ΔV is the change in specific volume between the two phases. This relationship applies at equilibrium between two phases.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the equation is correctly structured as dP/dT = L / (T * ΔV) with all terms properly substituted.
common_errors: Incorrectly swapping ΔV and L in the equation.
Forgetting to use absolute temperature (T) in Kelvin.
Omitting ΔV or using incorrect phase volumes for ΔV.

rules.title: Confirm applicability to first-order phase transitions
rules.description: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation is valid only for first-order phase transitions (e.g., melting, boiling) characterized by a discontinuous change in entropy and volume. It does not apply to second-order transitions or continuous phase changes.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the phase transition is first-order, specifically involving latent heat.
common_errors: Applying the Clausius-Clapeyron equation to second-order phase transitions.
Failure to confirm that the phase transition involves latent heat.

rules.title: Check dimensional consistency of terms
rules.description: Ensure all terms in the Clausius-Clapeyron equation have consistent units: L in J/kg or J/mol, T in Kelvin, ΔV in m³/kg or m³/mol, and dP/dT in Pa/K. Dimensional consistency ensures the equation's validity.
rules.check_logic: Verify consistency of units for L, T, ΔV, and dP/dT throughout the equation.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin for temperature.
Mismatched units between ΔV and L (e.g., mixing specific and molar quantities).
Omitting unit conversion where necessary (e.g., from bar to Pascal).

rules.title: Verify correct sign conventions for ΔV and ΔS
rules.description: Ensure ΔV (change in specific volume) sign matches the phase transition direction. For example, during vaporization, ΔV > 0 (as gas has a larger volume than liquid). Additionally, confirm entropy change ΔS = L/T aligns with heat flow direction.
rules.check_logic: Check that ΔV and ΔS possess the correct signs based on the transition analyzed.
common_errors: Incorrectly assigning ΔV < 0 for vaporization.
Using the wrong sign for ΔS during absorption or release.
Neglecting the physical interpretation of volume changes.

rules.title: Ensure latent heat is temperature-dependent if specified
rules.description: In some scenarios, latent heat (L) can vary with temperature. If specified, ensure the correct form L(T) is used in the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.
rules.check_logic: Confirm whether L is constant or temperature-dependent, using the appropriate form.
common_errors: Assuming constant latent heat when temperature dependence is specified.
Failing to substitute the correct expression for L(T).

rules.title: Confirm the geometric interpretation on a P-T diagram
rules.description: The Clausius-Clapeyron equation describes the slope (dP/dT) of the phase boundary on a pressure-temperature (P-T) diagram. Ensure the correct identification of the phase boundary and accurate slope calculation.
rules.check_logic: Verify slope (dP/dT) accuracy for the appropriate phase boundary.
common_errors: Analyzing incorrect phase boundary (e.g., melting instead of boiling).
Misinterpreting slope direction on the P-T diagram.

rules.title: Verify entropy change relation ΔS = L/T
rules.description: Confirm that the entropy change (ΔS) during a phase transition relates to latent heat (L) as ΔS = L/T, ensuring consistent units and temperature in Kelvin.
rules.check_logic: Validate correct implementation of ΔS = L/T with consistent units.
common_errors: Neglecting Kelvin temperature conversion before calculating ΔS.
Incorrectly presuming ΔS = L without dividing by T.
Mixing units for L and T (e.g., using Celsius for T).

rules.title: Verify Energy Expression for Degrees of Freedom
rules.description: Equipartition theorem states that each degree of freedom contributes (1/2)kT to the internal energy of a system at thermal equilibrium.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the energy associated with each degree of freedom is expressed as (1/2)kT, where k is the Boltzmann constant and T is the absolute temperature. Verify that the factor (1/2) is not omitted and that the degrees of freedom are correctly identified.
common_errors: Using incorrect factor, e.g., forgetting (1/2) factor
Misinterpreting degrees of freedom count

rules.title: Check Temperature Influence on Energy
rules.description: The equipartition theorem relates the energy of a system directly to its temperature; energy per degree of freedom linearly increases with temperature.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the energy calculated by the equipartition theorem is directly proportional to the absolute temperature (in Kelvin). Ensure that no non-linear dependencies are introduced.
common_errors: Ignoring the linear dependency on temperature
Using non-absolute temperature scales

rules.title: Validate Equipartition Application Conditions
rules.description: Equipartition theorem applies to classical systems where energy is quadratic with coordinate and momentum, and assumes ideal conditions without quantum restrictions.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the system is classical, the temperature is sufficiently high to avoid quantum effects, and the degrees of freedom involve quadratic energy dependencies. Verify that quantum systems or systems with non-quadratic energy terms are excluded.
common_errors: Applying equipartition theorem to quantum systems improperly
Applying to systems with non-quadratic energy dependencies

rules.title: Verify Positive Energy Contributions
rules.description: Energy contributions from degrees of freedom should be positive as temperature and Boltzmann constant are inherently positive.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that all energy contributions calculated from kT are positive. Verify that no negative values arise due to miscalculation of temperature or incorrect sign assignment.
common_errors: Negative energy due to miscalculation of temperature or incorrect sign assignment

rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency of Energy and Temperature Variables
rules.description: The energy given by the equipartition theorem must have correct units, with kT yielding units of energy.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the units of kT align with the units of energy (e.g., Joules in SI units). Ensure that the Boltzmann constant and temperature are expressed in compatible units.
common_errors: Confusing units of temperature (Kelvin vs other scales)
Incorrect unit assignment for Boltzmann constant leading to dimensional inconsistencies

rules.title: Validate Degree of Freedom Count in the System
rules.description: The total energy contribution depends on correctly identifying the number of degrees of freedom relevant to the system being considered.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the degree of freedom count matches the physical setup of the system (e.g., 3 for translational per particle, additional for rotations and vibrations). Verify that all relevant degrees of freedom are included and none are omitted.
common_errors: Neglecting rotational or vibrational degrees of freedom
Incorrectly summing degrees of freedom across molecules

rules.title: Check Kinematic Constraints Affecting Degrees of Freedom
rules.description: Ensure the system's geometry or constraints do not limit the degrees of freedom expected from theoretical calculations.
rules.check_logic: Verify that kinematic constraints, such as fixed or constrained components, are accounted for. Adjust the effective degrees of freedom accordingly.
common_errors: Overcounting degrees of freedom by ignoring fixed or constrained components
Missing constraints that reduce effective degrees of freedom

rules.title: Evaluate Equipartition Theorem in Limiting Cases
rules.description: Assess application of equipartition theorem in edge cases such as very low temperatures where quantum effects become significant.
rules.check_logic: Check applicability of the theorem in limiting cases where classical assumptions degrade, especially as temperature approaches zero. Ensure that quantum mechanical considerations are applied when necessary.
common_errors: Using classical equipartition in regimes dominated by quantum mechanics
Ignoring quantum restrictions at low temperatures

rules.title: Verify High-Temperature Limit Behavior
rules.description: At very high temperatures, the equipartition theorem should remain valid, and quantum effects should become negligible.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the energy contributions per degree of freedom remain consistent with (1/2)kT at high temperatures. Verify that no deviations occur due to incorrect assumptions.
common_errors: Introducing quantum effects unnecessarily at high temperatures
Incorrectly modifying energy contributions at high temperatures

rules.title: Ensure First Law Equation Utilized
rules.description: The First Law of Thermodynamics states that the change in internal energy (ΔU) of a system is equal to the heat added to the system (Q) minus the work done by the system (W), expressed as ΔU = Q - W.
rules.check_logic: Verify if ΔU = Q - W is used and all variables are defined with correct signs. Ensure the equation is applied consistently across the problem.
common_errors: Using incorrect formula variants like ΔU = W - Q
Confusing heat added with heat removed

rules.title: Check Direction of Work and Heat
rules.description: In the First Law of Thermodynamics, heat (Q) added to the system is positive, and work (W) done by the system is positive.
rules.check_logic: Ensure Q and W have correct signs based on their direction with respect to the system. Verify that heat removed from the system is negative and work done on the system is negative.
common_errors: Inverting signs for heat and work
Confusing work done by the system with work done on the system

rules.title: Verify Dimensional Consistency
rules.description: The units for heat (Q), work (W), and change in internal energy (ΔU) must be consistent, typically in Joules (J) in SI units.
rules.check_logic: Ensure all terms in ΔU = Q - W are expressed in compatible units (e.g., Joules). If other units like calories are used, verify proper conversion.
common_errors: Using different units for heat and work
Mixing energy units like Joules and calories without conversion

rules.title: Apply Law to Correct System Type
rules.description: The First Law of Thermodynamics is applicable to closed systems without mass exchange across the boundaries.
rules.check_logic: Check if the system described is closed and fulfills the criteria for applying the First Law. Ensure no mass flow occurs across the system boundary.
common_errors: Applying First Law to open systems
Ignoring boundary conditions related to mass flow

rules.title: Constrain Equation for Isothermal Process
rules.description: In an isothermal process for ideal gases, the change in internal energy (ΔU) is zero, so Q = W.
rules.check_logic: Verify if ΔU = 0 is correctly applied and Q = W condition is met for ideal gas isothermal processes. Ensure the gas is ideal and the process is truly isothermal.
common_errors: Misapplying isothermal condition to non-ideal gases
Forgetting ΔU = 0 for isothermal processes

rules.title: Adiabatic Process Application
rules.description: For adiabatic processes, no heat is exchanged (Q=0), and the First Law simplifies to ΔU = -W.
rules.check_logic: Ensure Q=0 is correctly applied in adiabatic calculations and ΔU = -W is used. Verify that the process is truly adiabatic (no heat exchange).
common_errors: Incorrectly setting Q≠0 for adiabatic cases
Misunderstanding work direction for adiabatic processes

rules.title: Verify Closed Cycle Conditions
rules.description: In a closed thermodynamic cycle, the net change in internal energy is zero, so Σ(Q - W) = 0.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that calculations for cycles result in ΣΔU = 0, checking each step in the cycle. Verify that the system returns to its initial state.
common_errors: Failing to sum cycle stages correctly
Ignoring net zero change in internal energy for cycles

rules.title: Differentiate Types of Work
rules.description: Recognize different types of work (e.g., PV work) and ensure appropriate application in the First Law.
rules.check_logic: Distinguish between work types (PV work versus other forms) and apply correctly in ΔU = Q - W. Verify that the correct work expression is used for the given process.
common_errors: Confusing PV work with electrical work
Ignoring the specificity of work types in energy calculations

rules.title: Verify Heat Transfer Mode
rules.description: Ensure the mode of heat transfer (conduction, convection, or radiation) is consistent with the problem's context.
rules.check_logic: Check if the heat transfer mode is correctly identified and applied in the calculation of Q. Verify that assumptions about heat transfer are valid.
common_errors: Assuming conduction when radiation dominates
Ignoring mixed modes of heat transfer

rules.title: Account for Non-Ideal Gas Behavior
rules.description: For non-ideal gases, ensure that deviations from ideal gas behavior are considered in thermodynamic calculations.
rules.check_logic: Verify if corrections for non-ideal gas behavior (e.g., van der Waals equation) are applied when necessary. Ensure that ideal gas assumptions are not incorrectly used.
common_errors: Using ideal gas law for non-ideal gases
Ignoring intermolecular forces and finite molecular volume

rules.title: Verify heat engine efficiency equation
rules.description: The efficiency of a heat engine is given by η = 1 - (Qc/Qh), where Qh is the heat absorbed from the hot reservoir and Qc is the heat rejected to the cold reservoir. This relation assumes a cyclic process.
rules.check_logic: Check if η = 1 - (Qc/Qh) is correctly applied, ensuring Qh > Qc > 0 and all terms are positive.
common_errors: Incorrect placement of Qc and Qh in the formula.
Assigning negative values to Qc or Qh, violating the assumption of heat as a positive quantity.
Calculating η > 1, which is physically impossible.

rules.title: Validate Coefficient of Performance (COP) for refrigerators
rules.description: The COP of a refrigerator is defined as COP = Qc / W, where Qc is the heat extracted from the cold reservoir and W is the work done on the system.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that COP is calculated as COP = Qc/W, where Qc > 0 and W > 0, and verify that the result is physically meaningful (COP > 0).
common_errors: Misinterpreting the formula and using Qh instead of Qc.
Using a negative value for work done (W), which is inconsistent with the definition.
Calculating COP < 0, which is unphysical.

rules.title: Apply the First Law of Thermodynamics
rules.description: The first law states ΔU = Q - W, where ΔU is the change in internal energy, Q is the heat added to the system, and W is the work done by the system. This law must hold for any thermodynamic process.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the energy balance ΔU = Q - W is used, all terms have consistent units, and the sign convention is correctly applied.
common_errors: Forgetting to account for all forms of energy transfer (Q or W).
Incorrect sign convention for work (e.g., using W as work done on the system instead of by the system).
Ignoring ΔU when it is non-zero for non-cyclic processes.

rules.title: Check Carnot efficiency limits
rules.description: The Carnot efficiency is the theoretical maximum efficiency for a heat engine operating between two temperatures, given by η_Carnot = 1 - (Tc/Th), where Tc and Th are the absolute temperatures of the cold and hot reservoirs, respectively.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that η_Carnot = 1 - (Tc/Th) is used, with Tc < Th and temperatures expressed in Kelvin. Verify that η_Carnot ≤ 1.
common_errors: Using temperatures in Celsius instead of Kelvin.
Switching Tc and Th, leading to unphysical negative efficiency.
Calculating η_Carnot > 1, which violates the second law of thermodynamics.

rules.title: Ensure consistent sign conventions for heat and work
rules.description: In thermodynamics, heat (Q) is positive when added to the system, and work (W) is positive when done by the system. Misinterpreting these conventions can lead to incorrect calculations.
rules.check_logic: Verify that Q is positive for heat input and W is positive for work output. For refrigerators, W is positive for work done on the system. Ensure consistency across all calculations.
common_errors: Using opposite sign conventions for Q and W.
Confusing work done by the system with work done on the system.
Neglecting to check signs in cyclic processes.

rules.title: Verify compliance with the Kelvin-Planck statement
rules.description: The Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics states that it is impossible to construct a heat engine that operates in a cycle and converts all the heat absorbed into work (i.e., W cannot equal Qh).
rules.check_logic: Check if W < Qh for any heat engine operating in a cycle. Ensure that some heat is always rejected to the cold reservoir (Qc > 0).
common_errors: Assuming 100% conversion of heat to work (W = Qh).
Ignoring losses to the cold reservoir (Qc).
Violating the second law by assuming η = 1.

rules.title: Check conditions for reversible processes
rules.description: A thermodynamic process is reversible if it is quasi-static and there are no dissipative forces (e.g., friction, turbulence). Reversible processes are idealized and maximize efficiency.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that processes assumed to be reversible have no dissipative forces, occur quasi-statically, and involve infinitesimally small temperature gradients for heat transfer.
common_errors: Assuming reversibility for real-world processes with friction or turbulence.
Overlooking the need for infinitesimally small temperature gradients for heat transfer.

rules.title: Ensure dimensional and unit consistency
rules.description: In thermodynamic equations, all terms must have consistent units (e.g., Q, W, and ΔU in joules, temperatures in Kelvin). Incorrect units can cause significant errors in calculations.
rules.check_logic: Verify that all terms in equations have compatible units (joules for energy, Kelvin for temperature, etc.). Ensure proper unit conversions where necessary.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin in temperature ratios.
Mixing different energy units (e.g., joules and calories) without conversion.
Failing to convert work or heat into consistent energy units.

rules.title: Verify entropy change calculations
rules.description: The change in entropy (ΔS) for a reversible process is given by ΔS = Qrev/T, where Qrev is the reversible heat transfer and T is the absolute temperature. For irreversible processes, ΔS > Q/T.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that ΔS = Qrev/T is used for reversible processes, and verify that ΔS ≥ 0 for all processes, consistent with the second law of thermodynamics.
common_errors: Using Q instead of Qrev for entropy calculations in reversible processes.
Calculating ΔS < 0 for an isolated system, violating the second law.
Ignoring the temperature dependence of entropy changes.

rules.title: Apply Fourier's Law for Heat Conduction
rules.description: Fourier's Law states that the heat transfer rate (q) through a material is proportional to the temperature gradient and is given by q = -k * A * (dT/dx), where k is the thermal conductivity, A is the cross-sectional area, and dT/dx is the temperature gradient. This applies to steady-state, one-dimensional heat conduction.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the heat transfer rate is computed using q = -k * A * (dT/dx), that k, A, and dT/dx are correctly defined, and that the negative sign is used to indicate heat flows from high to low temperature.
common_errors: Incorrect sign: forgetting the negative sign indicating heat flows from high to low temperature.
Using incorrect or inconsistent units for thermal conductivity (k).
Forgetting to account for the cross-sectional area (A).
Misinterpreting the temperature gradient direction.

rules.title: Apply Newton's Law of Cooling for Convection
rules.description: Newton's Law of Cooling states that the convective heat transfer rate (q) is proportional to the temperature difference between the surface and the surrounding fluid: q = h * A * (T_surface - T_fluid), where h is the convective heat transfer coefficient, A is the surface area, and T_surface/T_fluid are the temperatures of the surface and fluid, respectively.
rules.check_logic: Ensure q is calculated using q = h * A * (T_surface - T_fluid), that all variables are correctly defined and evaluated, and that the temperature difference is calculated with the correct sign.
common_errors: Omitting the surface area (A) in the formula.
Using inconsistent units for the convective heat transfer coefficient (h).
Incorrectly calculating the temperature difference (e.g., wrong sign).
Applying the law when fluid motion or convection is not present.

rules.title: Apply Stefan-Boltzmann Law for Radiation
rules.description: The Stefan-Boltzmann Law states that the radiative heat transfer rate (q) from a surface is proportional to the fourth power of its absolute temperature: q = ε * σ * A * (T_surface^4 - T_surroundings^4), where ε is the emissivity, σ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, A is the surface area, and T_surface/T_surroundings are absolute temperatures (in Kelvin).
rules.check_logic: Verify that q is calculated using q = ε * σ * A * (T_surface^4 - T_surroundings^4), that temperatures are in Kelvin, and that emissivity (ε) is correctly applied.
common_errors: Forgetting to convert temperatures to Kelvin.
Mistaking emissivity (ε) as 1 when it's not explicitly stated.
Incorrectly raising temperatures to the fourth power.
Ignoring the surface area (A) in the calculation.

rules.title: Use Thermal Resistance Networks for Composite Systems
rules.description: In steady-state heat conduction across composite systems, the equivalent thermal resistance can be used to simplify the calculation. For series systems, R_eq = R1 + R2 + ...; for parallel systems, 1/R_eq = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + .... Thermal resistance is defined as R = L/(k*A), where L is the material thickness.
rules.check_logic: Ensure thermal resistance is calculated correctly for series or parallel systems, combined appropriately to find the equivalent resistance, and that all layers or paths in the composite system are considered.
common_errors: Adding thermal resistances incorrectly for parallel configurations.
Using incorrect expressions for thermal resistance (e.g., forgetting the A term).
Mixing up series and parallel configurations.
Not considering all layers or paths in the composite system.

rules.title: Use Correct Sign Conventions for Heat Flow
rules.description: Heat flow is typically considered positive when it flows into a system and negative when it flows out. The chosen sign convention must remain consistent throughout the problem.
rules.check_logic: Verify that the sign convention for heat flow is consistently applied across all calculations and matches the physical scenario.
common_errors: Inconsistently assigning heat flow as positive or negative.
Forgetting to account for the chosen sign convention in intermediate steps.
Reversing the sign of heat flow in composite systems.

rules.title: Check Validity Conditions for Heat Transfer Equations
rules.description: Heat transfer equations (conduction, convection, radiation) have specific conditions for validity. Fourier's Law requires steady-state conduction, Newton's Law of Cooling assumes convective heat transfer, and Stefan-Boltzmann Law applies to radiative heat transfer in the absence of significant convection or conduction.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the heat transfer equation used is valid for the given physical conditions (e.g., steady state, type of heat transfer mechanism, absence of dominating alternate mechanisms).
common_errors: Using Fourier's Law when the system is not in steady state.
Applying Newton's Law of Cooling in the absence of fluid convection.
Using the Stefan-Boltzmann Law when conduction or convection dominates the heat transfer.

rules.title: Apply Correct Boundary Conditions
rules.description: Heat transfer problems often involve specific boundary conditions, such as constant temperature, constant heat flux, or convection at the boundary. These must be correctly incorporated into the solution.
rules.check_logic: Ensure that the boundary conditions are correctly applied, match the physical scenario, and are consistently used in solving the heat transfer equations.
common_errors: Misinterpreting or omitting boundary conditions.
Incorrectly applying a constant heat flux boundary condition.
Failing to match boundary conditions with the physical scenario (e.g., mixing convection and insulation).

rules.title: Account for Transient Heat Transfer
rules.description: In non-steady-state heat transfer, the temperature changes with time and must be modeled using transient heat transfer equations, such as the heat diffusion equation or lumped capacitance method.
rules.check_logic: Verify that transient heat transfer equations are used when the system is not in steady state and that initial and boundary conditions are correctly applied.
common_errors: Using steady-state equations for transient problems.
Ignoring initial conditions or time-dependent boundary conditions.
Incorrectly applying the lumped capacitance method when Biot number is not small.

topics.name: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.title: Verify Ideal Gas Law Formulation
rules.description: The ideal gas law is expressed as PV = nRT, where P is pressure, V is volume, n is the number of moles, R is the universal gas constant, and T is temperature in kelvins. This relationship applies to ideal gases under standard conditions.

tags.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.check_logic: Ensure the equation is explicitly written as PV = nRT with all variables correctly assigned and units suitable for the context.
common_errors: Using incorrect units for R (e.g., J/mol·K with P in atm)
Failure to convert temperature to kelvins
Misplacing or misinterpreting variables within the equation

rules.title: Ensure Temperature is in Kelvins
rules.description: The ideal gas law requires the absolute temperature in kelvins. Celsius or Fahrenheit must be converted to kelvins using T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.

tags.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.check_logic: Verify that the temperature has been converted to kelvins before using it in the ideal gas equation and note any errors in conversion.
common_errors: Using Celsius or Fahrenheit directly in calculations
Forgetting to add 273.15 when converting from Celsius to kelvins

rules.title: Check Dimensional Consistency of Ideal Gas Law
rules.description: Each term in the ideal gas law must have consistent units. For example, P in Pascals, V in cubic meters, n in moles, T in kelvins, and R in J/(mol·K).

tags.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.check_logic: Ensure that units for each variable are coherent and consistent throughout calculations, especially when mixing English and SI units.
common_errors: Mixing units that are not compatible (e.g., atm for pressure and cubic meters for volume)
Using non-SI units without proper conversion

rules.title: Check Validity of Ideal Gas Law Assumptions
rules.description: The ideal gas law assumes negligible intermolecular forces and that gas particles occupy no volume. It is valid at low pressures and high temperatures where these assumptions are close.

tags.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.check_logic: Evaluate the pressure and temperature conditions of the problem and determine the appropriateness of applying the ideal gas law.
common_errors: Applying the ideal gas law to high-pressure or low-temperature scenarios
Ignoring intermolecular forces in dense gases

rules.title: Consider Real Gas Corrections (Van der Waals Equation)
rules.description: For real gases, the Van der Waals equation (P + a(n/V)^2)(V - nb) = nRT accounts for intermolecular forces and finite particle volume. Use this equation under non-ideal conditions.

tags.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.check_logic: Determine if the problem presents conditions that require accounting for real gas behavior, notably at high pressure or low temperature.
common_errors: Using the ideal gas law when real gas behavior is significant
Neglecting correction terms a and b

rules.title: Verify Work Sign Convention in Gas Expansion/Compression
rules.description: When a gas expands, work is done by the gas, and W is positive. When compressed, work is done on the gas, and W is negative.

tags.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.check_logic: Confirm the direction of work based on volume changes to apply correct sign convention, ensuring consistency with the first law of thermodynamics.
common_errors: Flipping the sign of work
Inconsistencies in work calculations within the context of ΔU = Q - W

rules.title: Verify Constraints for Isothermal, Isobaric, Isochoric, and Adiabatic Processes
rules.description: Verify fixed or zero values for properties specific to these processes: T constant for isothermal, P constant for isobaric, V constant for isochoric, and Q = 0 for adiabatic process.

tags.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.check_logic: Ensure the correct variable is being treated according to the type of process and verify constraints are appropriately applied.
common_errors: Not maintaining constant temperature in isothermal processes
Neglecting Q = 0 in adiabatic processes
Failing to maintain P or V constant in isobaric or isochoric processes

rules.title: Check Molar Mass and Mass-Volume Conversions
rules.description: Verify correct calculation of mole number using n = m/M, where m is mass and M is molar mass, important for correct use in gas law equations.

tags.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.check_logic: Confirm the mass and volume conversions, ensuring the molar mass is accurate and correctly used to convert mass to moles.
common_errors: Omitting division of mass by molar mass
Utilizing incorrect molar mass figures

rules.title: Check Entropy Change Calculations in Thermodynamic Processes
rules.description: Ensure correct assessment of entropy changes (ΔS) based on process type and whether the gas is ideal or real.

tags.topic: Ideal Gas Law and Real Gas Behavior

rules.check_logic: Evaluate entropy changes considering the process specifics, such as temperature changes and phase transitions, applicable to ideal and real gas scenarios.
common_errors: Ignoring factors impacting entropy change
Assuming no entropy change during irreversible processes without proper justification

rules.title: Verify Ideal Gas Law Application
rules.description: The Ideal Gas Law PV = nRT relates pressure (P), volume (V), number of moles (n), and temperature (T). It applies to ideal gases, which are assumed to have perfectly elastic collisions and negligible volume occupied by the gas particles.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the problem conditions specify an ideal gas, often monoatomic and low-pressure conditions. Check if all the variables in PV = nRT are accounted for, and verify units: P in pascal, V in cubic meters, n in moles, R = 8.314 J/mol·K, and T in Kelvin.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin for temperature
Incorrect unit conversion for pressure or volume
Omitting gas constant R
Confusion between atmospheric pressure and pressure in pascal

rules.title: Calculate Average Kinetic Energy per Molecule
rules.description: Average kinetic energy per molecule in an ideal gas is given by (3/2)kT, where k is Boltzmann's constant and T is absolute temperature.
rules.check_logic: Verify that temperature is expressed in Kelvin and k is correctly used as 1.38 x 10^-23 J/K. Check dimensional consistency for energy output in joules.
common_errors: Using Celsius instead of Kelvin
Misplacement of 3/2 factor in kinetic energy calculation
Incorrect value or units for Boltzmann's constant

rules.title: Verify Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution Assumptions
rules.description: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution describes the distribution of speeds of particles in a gas at a given temperature. It assumes non-interacting and identical particles.
rules.check_logic: Ensure the system being analyzed is monoatomic and exhibits classical behavior, no quantum effects. This distribution is valid for a large number of particles and at thermal equilibrium.
common_errors: Incorrectly applying Maxwell-Boltzmann to quantum or interacting systems
Calculations outside validity range

rules.title: Verify Mean Free Path Calculation
rules.description: Mean free path is the average distance traveled by a molecule between collisions. Use the formula λ = kT / (sqrt(2) * π * d^2 * P), where d is the molecular diameter.
rules.check_logic: Check units: λ in meters, diameter d in meters, pressure P in pascal, temperature T in Kelvin. Ensure conditions describe an ideal gas scenario.
common_errors: Incorrect diameter units
Failing to include sqrt(2) factor
Using non-ideal gas conditions
Incorrect conditions for low density or high temperature cases

rules.title: Relate Temperature to Internal Energy
rules.description: For a monoatomic ideal gas, internal energy U is proportional to temperature T as U = (3/2)nRT. This applies only to monoatomic gases.
rules.check_logic: Confirm the gas type is monoatomic and temperature is clearly defined in Kelvin. Ensure correct usage of mole quantity n and gas constant R.
common_errors: Applying relation to non-monoatomic gases
Misinterpretation of temperature scale
Neglecting mole count or incorrect R
Incorrect conditions for systems at very high or low temperatures

rules.title: Validate Degrees of Freedom in Energy Distribution
rules.description: Equipartition theorem states that each degree of freedom contributes (1/2)kT to the energy for ideal gases.
rules.check_logic: Ensure degrees of freedom are correctly determined based on molecular structure (e.g., 3 translational for monoatomic gases).
common_errors: Incorrect count of degrees of freedom
Misapplication of (1/2)kT per degree of freedom
Wrong assumption for polyatomic gases
Not accounting for rotational and vibrational degrees in complex molecules

rules.title: Verify Thermal Boundary Conditions
rules.description: Ensure that thermal boundary conditions are properly defined and adhered to, concerning ideal and real gas behaviors.
rules.check_logic: Identify whether boundary conditions for pressure, volume, and temperature are specified and align with thermodynamic assumptions for ideal gases.
common_errors: Ignoring effects of container materials affecting thermal boundaries
Assuming perfectly insulated systems without specification
Omitting consideration of external temperature fluctuations
